the structure of small-scale and large-scale spatial skills and their relations with mathematics performance abstract spatial skills are consistently associated with mathematics performance, yet the role of scale is rarely considered. there remains an open question about how small-scale versus large-scale spatial skills relate to distinct domains of mathematics. in the present study, the structure of spatial skills and their relation to mathematics performance was examined using structural equation modeling (sem). a total of 248 undergraduate students residing in a major urban center ( m = 20 years, 8 months, 63.7% female) completed an online battery of assessments measuring cognitive skills (perspective taking, mental rotation, navigation, and fluid reasoning) and mathematics abilities (geometry and number). factor analysis revealed a three-factor structure of cognitive skills: (1) small-scale spatial skills (combining perspective taking and mental rotation), (2) large-scale navigation skills, and (3) fluid reasoning. the sem results showed a significant path from small-scale spatial skills to mathematics performance, with this relation partially mediated by fluid reasoning. although navigation was correlated with small-scale spatial skills, it was not related to mathematics outcomes in the sem. further multivariate regression analyses indicated that fluid reasoning was significantly associated with both number and geometry performance, while perspective taking accounted for unique variance in number task performance. these findings underscore the crucial role of perspective taking within the domain of small-scale spatial skills and highlight the nuanced, domain-specific contributions of distinct spatial and cognitive skills to mathematical thinking. cognitive research-principles and implications

the effect of perceived similarity and accuracy in ideal partner preferences on relationship satisfaction abstract how partners perceive one another may be important for relationship satisfaction, particularly when those perceptions concern ideal partner preferences. the present study tested whether perceived similarity (alignment between one's own ideals and one's perceptions of a partner's ideals) and accuracy (alignment between one's perceptions of a partner's ideals and a partner's reported ideals) are associated with relationship satisfaction. a sample of 136 mixed‐gender couples ( n = 272), dating for an average of 16 months, reported their own ideals, their perceptions of their partner's ideals, and their relationship satisfaction. actor‐partner interdependence models (apims) revealed that individuals' perceived similarity predicted their own, and their partner's, relationship satisfaction. by contrast, accuracy did not predict relationship satisfaction, although exploratory analyses showed that other aspects of accuracy (e.g., the degree to which one perceives themselves as accurate about their partner) were associated with greater satisfaction. taken together, these findings suggest that subjective beliefs about similarity and accuracy might be more strongly linked to relationship satisfaction than objective correspondence. personal relationships

spontaneous uses of typicality in narratives of positive and negative inter‐ethnic contact in a scottish community abstract research on intergroup contact shows that positive encounters are more likely to improve attitudes when the outgroup member involved is viewed as typical of their group. however, existing studies have treated typicality as a researcher‐defined cognitive judgement, leaving unclear whether and how people spontaneously invoke typicality when making sense of everyday contact experiences. we addressed this question through 25 semi‐structured interviews with adults of migrant and non‐migrant backgrounds living in an ethnically diverse area of north‐east scotland. using a qualitative narrative analysis, we examined how participants interpreted contact events and situated them within a broader narrative of intergroup relations. participants deployed various strategies to frame contact events as typical or atypical of the group concerned. these included appeals to frequency, exceptionality, subgroup membership and emphasising personal characteristics. framing contact as atypical enabled some participants to acknowledge experiences that contradicted their overall stance towards an outgroup, while framing contact as typical supported generalisation. typicality therefore functioned as a narrative resource which may enable reconciliation of multiple and sometimes conflicting contact experiences within a coherent narrative of self and other. we argue that generalisation of contact events is shaped not only by cognitive categorisation processes but also by narrative processes of meaning‐making. journal of community & applied social psychology

transnational relational resilience: ‘ souvenir de syrie ’ as mnemonic artistic renderings in romania the paper zooms in on parallel memories of migration and displacement enacted in romanian art after 1989, with a focus on dan acostioaei’s body of artistic memory work. the focus is on drawing parallels between two phenomena: on the one hand, the migration mobility of the labour force from communist romania to the middle east (in the 1970s and 1980s) and, on the other hand, the massive work-related migration after 1989 to the west. the exploration moves beyond regional ‘mnemonic diplomacy’ and focuses on transnationally distant constellations of memory alliances. the research employed photo-elicitation and interviews as a point of departure for prompting memories of movement and uprootedness. by drawing parallels between multi-folded memories of migration/displacement, the paper aims to explore how ‘working through’ past emergencies act as a coping strategy in the wake of the syrian refugee crisis (2011–2024). the argument revolves around how art can foster transnational relational mnemonic resilience. memory studies

myth and memory: the lemko path from displacement to renewal how does remembering forced displacement become a means of protecting collective identity? drawing on ethnographic research and published testimonies concerning the lemkos in poland, this article develops the trauma-myth-mnemonic security model. it distinguishes historical rupture, the symbolisation of collective harm, mythic stabilisation and protective mobilisation as overlapping, contingent processes. building on mälksoo’s concept of mnemonical security, trauma-myth-mnemonic security explains how foundational narratives become resources for sustaining belonging and interpretive sovereignty under conditions of dispersion and unequal narrative power. the analysis traces this mechanism through displacement testimonies, representations of homeland, cultural gatherings, community collections and renewed access to religious sites. it argues that memory’s protective capacity depends on practices connecting durable meanings to opportunities for transmission and participation. preserving heritage does not necessarily preserve these relationships. mnemonic security emerges where actors mobilise remembered loss to sustain the social and interpretive conditions of collective continuity, through minority initiatives and cooperation beyond the group. memory studies

a new story for žižkov? making sense of street renaming in a prague neighborhood after russia’s invasion of ukraine this article examines the 2023 renaming of koněvova street in prague’s žižkov district as a case of late post-socialist mnemonic reconfiguration amid geopolitical tensions following russia’s invasion of ukraine. drawing on interviews with urban actors involved in the renaming and members of the local community, the study elucidates the interaction between authorised narratives and everyday meaning-making. the paper does so by revisiting wulf kansteiner’s (2002) understanding of collective memory production as a dynamic relationship between memory makers, memory consumers and discursive objects shaped by specific traditions of representation. the renaming has reconfigured the local symbolic landscape by combining the removal of a soviet-associated figure with the introduction of a locally significant historical actor, an intervention invested with reparative potential. the mnemonic revision has thereby introduced a learning process with potential implications for community resilience. the findings, however, reveal heterogeneous responses, showing how public memory re-evaluation, as envisioned from above, encounters locally rooted understandings, attachments and senses of belonging. the article demonstrates how the intervention is interpreted divergently within locally embedded mnemonic frameworks and against a changing geopolitical context that has renewed the salience of soviet commemorative legacies across the post-socialist region. memory studies

end or beginning? memory and the narrative negotiation of peripherality as a form of resilience in the czech–slovak borderland this study examines everyday experiences of life in the czech–slovak borderland following the dissolution of czechoslovakia in 1993 and analyses how local residents negotiate a sense of peripherality associated with the emergence of a newly delineated state border. by shifting the debates towards an anthropological understanding of peripheries as culturally and memory-produced experiences, the study demonstrates how memory-based resilience allows individuals to navigate, challenge and even reframe their position in the borderland. drawing on oral history research conducted between 2023 and 2024 in selected localities of the czech–slovak borderland, comprising 50 interviews, we identify border narratives where collective memory functions as a shared cultural resource – or borderland capital – enabling inhabitants to transcend national divides through historical imaginaries of a common past. in this context, memory not only functions as a key source of imaginaries of the border, borderland and processes of peripheralisation, but also as a resource for resisting, escaping or rejecting these processes. we therefore argue that the memory of borderland inhabitants represents an important form of resilience, grounded in specific local knowledge. memory studies

toward an integrative process-based framework of psychological experience. contemporary psychology and cognitive science have generated increasingly sophisticated accounts of cognition, emotion, behavior, embodiment, and neural functioning. at the same time, substantial fragmentation remains across explanatory traditions concerned with lived psychological experience, including constructivist, phenomenological, predictive processing, dynamic systems, affective neuroscience, and clinical process-based perspectives. the present article advances a process-oriented integrative framework intended to synthesize converging insights across these domains while clarifying how psychological experience may be continuously organized in real time across changing states and contexts. the framework proposes two dynamically interrelated generative processes-interpretive activity and experiential rendering-together with intrinsic regulatory potential, a hypothesized potential for reorganization. interpretive activity refers to the ongoing organization of meaning through which situations, memories, bodily sensations, and anticipations become psychologically significant. experiential rendering refers to the manner in which interpretations become experientially salient, emotionally compelling, and subjectively real. intrinsic regulatory potential refers to the conditional capacity for broader, more flexible, and context-responsive reorganization as restrictive organization loosens. related constructs include experiential authority, experiential constriction, experiential flexibility, state-dependent organization, and affect as directional signaling. psychological distress is conceptualized not primarily as fixed pathology or static dysfunction, but as varying patterns of experiential organization emerging across changing states and contexts. the article situates the framework in relation to contemporary constructivist, enactive, phenomenological, predictive processing, and dynamic systems perspectives while outlining implications for psychotherapy, resilience, emotional wellbeing, and future process-oriented psychological research. integrative psychological and behavioral science

a single-center retrospective analysis of artificial intelligence-based emotion recognition systems for attention-regulation training in children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder abstract introduction: children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (adhd) often experience attention instability and emotion dysregulation. existing interventions typically lack real-time responsiveness and ecological validity. this study retrospectively examined historical training records from an ai-assisted closed-loop system integrating emotion recognition and behavioral feedback for attention regulation in children with adhd. methods: this single-center retrospective analysis included historical training records from 60 children with adhd who had completed either ai-assisted attention training or conventional attention training between 2021 and 2024. the ai-assisted training-record group comprised children whose archived records included 12 sessions of integrated cognitive training involving go/no-go, cpt, and flanker tasks with real-time ai-generated feedback based on task performance and facial-emotion monitoring. the conventional training-record group completed the same attention tasks without ai-based feedback. assessments included task performance, conners continuous performance test, 3rd edition (cpt-3), teacher ratings, and emotion metrics, analyzed using linear mixed-effects models, linear growth modeling, and structural equation modeling (sem). results: compared with conventional training records, ai-assisted training records showed greater pre-post changes in reaction time (rt), rt variability, and task accuracy, together with fewer commission errors in cpt-3. post-feedback behavioral recovery was observed in 78.3% of feedback events. teacher ratings showed consistent pre-post improvements across attention maintenance, emotional regulation, and task execution. negative emotion labels decreased from 42.3% to 24.6% (p = 0.003). sem supported an associative pathway linking emotion recognition frequency, feedback frequency, and rt reduction (95% ci: 0.15-0.38). conclusions: the retrospective findings suggest that ai-assisted closed-loop training records were associated with favorable changes in attention and emotional-state indicators in children with adhd. these exploratory results support further prospective, externally validated studies before broader clinical or educational implementation. neuropsychobiology

narrative identity at work in digital cultures: a cultural–analytical psychological framework this article develops a cultural–psychological account of narrative identity at work in digital cultures. while narrative approaches have been central to understanding professional identity as a process of meaning-making, much existing research remains oriented toward language-centred and coherence-based models that offer limited resources for analysing work experience under conditions of digital mediation. drawing on cultural psychology, narrative research, and studies of digital work, the article argues that digital work cultures reshape the conditions of narrative identity by intensifying regimes of visibility, evaluation, and recognition, while fragmenting professional experience across platforms and organisational contexts. under such conditions, narrative identity cannot be understood solely through explicitly articulated self-stories. to address this limitation, the article advances a cultural–analytical framework that conceptualises narrative identity at work as a symbolically and affectively mediated process. while language remains central to narrative identity, the framework argues that explicit verbal self-narration does not exhaust it. accordingly, it foregrounds symbolic forms, evaluative infrastructures, and affective orientations embedded in digital work environments as constitutive — alongside discourse — of professional meaning-making. analytical psychology is mobilised as a cultural and symbolic resource, decoupled from its clinical origins. by reconceptualising narrative identity as a culturally mediated process embedded in digital work cultures, the article contributes to cultural–psychological debates on identity, work, and meaning-making. culture & psychology

after the covid ‐19 pandemic, cinema attendance in c hina was higher in provinces with tighter norms abstract in this paper, we showed that post‐covid cinema attendance was positively predicted by cultural tightness, across 31 mainland china provinces. this result suggests that cultural tightness accompanies a societal tendency of recovering from a disruption of social routines. psych journal

developing and validating the chinese version of the perceived trustworthiness of large language models scale (pt-llm-8) abstract the trustworthiness of technology constitutes a critical determinant of user adoption, particularly regarding artificial intelligence (ai) in daily life. currently, prominent ai products rely on large language models (llms), and such llms assist users in personal and professional contexts. to systematically investigate the perceived trustworthiness of llms, we provide a psychometrically sound measurement instrument for assessing perceived trustworthiness of llms. given the importance of the chinese market for current ai developments, the present study examined the psychometric properties of a chinese version of the perceived trustworthiness of large language models scale (pt-llm-8) [1] and its association with big five personality traits, self-efficacy, and self-esteem. based on the responses of 478 chinese adults, the chinese pt-llm-8 showed good psychometric properties, including strong internal consistency and a clear unidimensional factor structure. evidence of construct validity was provided by theoretically expected associations between pt-llm-8 score and self-efficacy, self-esteem, agreeableness, and conscientiousness. these findings provide psychometric support for the chinese version of the pt-llm-8 as a measure of perceived trustworthiness of llms, consistent with the cumulative cross-linguistic evidence for the instrument across its english [1], german [2] and chinese versions. discover psychology

building and maintaining rapport within a telehealth service delivery model abstract building and maintaining rapport throughout service delivery is vital to the therapeutic relationship between clinicians and staff/caregivers. during service delivery, effective communication and positive interactions may produce sustainable changes that benefit the staff/caregiver and the client as well as programmatic outcomes. a systematic review of 55 studies spanning the past decade of aba telehealth research was conducted and not a single article operationalized rapport‐building as a trainable clinician skill, leaving a gap between the field's reliance on rapport and its guidance for building it. this paper addresses that gap by outlining effective interpersonal therapeutic skills based on an active listening model. this model has been identified as an effective tool and may be particularly beneficial in aba‐based service delivery, given telehealth's decade‐long presence in aba service delivery. the target responses involved in the active listening model include both verbal and non‐verbal behavior, therefore, we analyzed target clinician responses in accordance with skinner's analysis of verbal behavior, including the use of echoics and intraverbals. a task analysis and fidelity checklist were created to ensure clinicians acquire and incorporate these skills during a therapeutic session. behavioral interventions

“a soul as vast as the world”: frantz fanon and humanistic psychology (editor’s introduction to the special issue) this special issue introduction by leswin laubscher and derek hook addresses the contemporary “fanonian turn” in academic and clinical discourse, positioning frantz fanon’s work as a vital response to a global climate of systemic racism, state violence, and political silencing. despite fanon’s historical exclusion from mainstream western psychology – a neglect the authors frame as a structural consequence of the very colonial dynamics fanon analyzed – his insights into the “poetics of care” and the sociogeny of mental health remain profoundly apposite. the authors provide a biographical overview, detailing fanon’s trajectory from colonial martinique to the battlefields of wwii and his subsequent psychiatric residency at saint-alban under françois tosquelles. central to the discussion is fanon’s development of “sociotherapy” and institutional psychotherapy, which emphasizes that “curing the patient” necessitates “curing the hospital” and dismantling oppressive social structures. the abstract highlights the resurgence of fanon in the wake of the black lives matter movement, where his concepts of “combat breathing” and “new humanism” provide a theoretical framework for understanding the psychological impact of atmospheric violence. ultimately, the issue seeks to integrate fanon’s decolonial praxis into humanistic and existential psychology, advocating for a universalism premised on reciprocal human recognition and the ethical imperative of action. journal of humanistic psychology

psychic tomb to triadic womb: toward a developmental ecology of relational sacred mindfulness this article presents the triadic good-enough womb, an integrative developmental ecology within relational sacred mindfulness (rsm), a winnicottian-informed humanistic and transpersonal psychotherapy for reactivating interrupted maturational processes and receiving dissociated somatosensory affect. using hermeneutic phenomenology, i trace an evolving quinean epistemological web shaped by monastic training, spiritual direction, dissertation research, a 10-year follow-up inquiry, published clinical theorizing, disconfirming phenomena, postdoctoral coursework, archetypal guidance, and reflexive therapist-researcher participation. the phenomenon that most disrupted my earlier web occurred when a client experienced jesus holding her infant self and then dropping her, revealing that the appearance of a loving sacred presence did not necessarily constitute a developmentally facilitating relationship. in dialogue with gadamer, winnicott, jung, kalsched, kohut, benjamin, woodman, tillich, may, and others, the intervention expanded from facilitating a sacred relationship that receives dissociated affect to tending a developmental ecology. relational somatic mindfulness forms the first layer of the triadic good-enough womb, therapeutic attunement, empathy and mirroring the second, and rsm the third. together, somatic holding, assessment of projection, and attachment to a transpersonal presence capable of receiving dissociated affect may create conditions in which a psychic tomb becomes less necessary and protected life resumes movement toward maturation. journal of humanistic psychology

a liberation psychology framework for supporting student activism in repressive times u.s. universities are increasingly becoming arenas where student activism for self-determination, justice, and liberation confronts escalating institutional and state repression. pro-palestinian student protests during the 2023 to 2025 academic years exemplify how university administrations and state actors can intensify measures to suppress dissent. this repression can exacerbate the inherent psychosocial risks of student activism, contributing to adverse mental health outcomes. however, activism can also foster student well-being by cultivating a sense of purpose and solidarity. this manuscript addresses a critical gap in psychological scholarship by proposing liberation psychology (lp) as an essential framework for psychology faculty to navigate and support their activist students amidst rising authoritarianism and the corporatization of higher education. i discuss key lp principles, including recovering historical memory, cultivating conscientization (problematization, denaturalization, deideologization, and praxis), prioritizing oppressed majorities, and practicing acompañamiento . building on these principles, i offer six actionable recommendations for psychology faculty to actively support student activism: engage in conscientization, decolonize curricula, nurture dialogical pedagogy, resist neutrality, practice acompañamiento , and establish the psychology department as a site of institutional praxis. to facilitate psychology faculty’s own conscientization process, a series of reflection questions are provided. journal of humanistic psychology

ai-assisted narrative mapping: a trauma-informed framework for narrative-based assessment this paper introduces a six-dimensional framework for ai-assisted narrative analysis in psychological assessment, grounded in humanistic and existential psychology. as ai systems become prevalent in daily life, they create new contexts for narrative identity formation and psychological risk, including documented cases of ai-induced dependency, delusional thinking, and social withdrawal. yet, no existing frameworks integrate narrative psychology, dimensional assessment, and trauma-informed design to address these phenomena. the proposed framework operationalizes assessment across six dimensions: self-awareness (rogers), emotional processing (greenberg, fosha), relational connection (bowlby, jordan), purpose and meaning (frankl, steger), integration of parts (schwartz, mcadams), and transcendent/existential alignment (yalom, maslow). each dimension is assessed on a continuum, enabling identification of specific patterns of strength and vulnerability within client narratives. framework application is demonstrated through a fictionalized composite case in which extended ai interaction preceded delusional beliefs and psychological crisis. the dimensional analysis reveals how narrative themes can illuminate therapeutic targets while honoring the meaning-making functions such narratives serve. a four-stage trauma-informed assessment protocol provides structured clinical methodology. the framework positions ai as an assessment tool augmenting clinical judgment rather than replacing human therapeutic relationships. journal of humanistic psychology

taking back the “permission to narrate”: examining a grassroots organization’s process of supporting bipoc youth in developing counternarratives and counterspaces as decolonial resistance decolonial scholars have conceptualized the continuation of colonial systems of oppression as “coloniality.” central to coloniality is the use of narrative to shape discourse, which makes colonialism possible. colonial master narratives, a force of coloniality, deny black, indigenous, and people of color (bipoc) the right to self-determination and restrict lived experiences as an aspect to be constructed “through the eyes of others”. in resistance against coloniality, a critical enactment of decoloniality involves bipoc communities taking back the “permission to narrate” through “counternarratives” and “counterspaces.” youth-focused grassroots organizations can play pivotal roles in supporting bipoc youth in cultivating “counternarratives” and “counterspaces” as critical to decolonial and antiracism processes. this study used community-based, decolonial qualitative methods in partnership with the city school (tcs), a grassroots youth-focused organization in boston, to explore how they support young bipocs’ resistance against coloniality and interrelated systems of oppression. findings suggest that tcs acts as a decolonial counterspace in which young bipoc can take back the power to tell their own stories, challenge colonial logics, construct identity, and resist alienation through community connection. journal of humanistic psychology

demography and social learning impact norm misperception and belief revision following intervention abstract misperception about prevailing norms, sometimes referred to as ‘pluralistic ignorance’, is a pervasive phenomenon, yet is largely unaddressed in cultural evolution scholarship. focusing on gender norms, we used a two-stage experiment (n = 903 americans) to test hypotheses about norm misperception and the role of social learning in correcting misperception. we hypothesized that reliance on outdated or limited social information would make older and less educated individuals most prone to perception errors. in contrast, norm misperception was greatest among younger and well-educated individuals, suggesting elevated exposure to misinformation. we then supplied participants with no feedback or identical estimates of others’ beliefs attributed to either an arbitrary source or to the majority opinion (priming conformity), adults over 40, or highly educated individuals (priming model-based social learning). consistent with our hypotheses, social information improved accuracy in all treatment conditions relative to the no-feedback control. however, age and conformity cues produced the strongest updating, whereas the education-based prestige cue was indistinguishable from the arbitrary-source condition. these results demonstrate underappreciated variability in misperception dynamics and that, in this context, social learning privileges information from the majority and older, but not well-educated others. implications for research on misinformation, cultural transmission, and intervention design are discussed. evolutionary human sciences

contemporary scientific racism in psychology: “cold winters” then and now abstract i discuss persistent problems of conceptualizing and recognizing scientific racism in psychology, that is, “the use of scientific concepts and data to create and justify ideas of an enduring, biologically based racial hierarchy” (winston, 2022). this formulation leaves a number of issues unexamined : first, the barriers in psychology to categorizing this academic work as a form of racism, especially due to the view of racism as a personal attribute; second, the difficulty of evaluating individual journal submissions when their relationship to a broader program and to political uses of scientific racism is unclear or obscured, and third, the recent trend to argue for or imply a racial hierarchy without using racial taxonomy or even mentioning “race.” i use the history of “cold winters theory” of group and regional differences in intelligence test scores to illustrate how the scientific racism community in psychology uses evolutionary discourse to revive and preserve long discredited and pernicious ideas. evolutionary human sciences

remote delivery of problem management plus by nonclinicians for adults with psychological distress in new york city: a pilot feasibility study. a single-arm trial was conducted to assess the feasibility, acceptability, and perceived utility of remotely delivered problem management plus (pm+) in new york city. two settings were used to evaluate these parameters: a graduate psychology training clinic and community-based organizations (cbos) with staff without clinical training. participants (= 45) received five sessions of pm+ delivered via zoom. primary clinical outcomes were distress related to client-generated problems (psychological outcomes profile), depression symptoms (patient health questionnaire-9), and anxiety symptoms (generalized anxiety disorder-7) administered at baseline and 1 week postintervention. semistructured interviews were conducted with a subsample of participants and providers. twenty-four helpers were trained in pm+: 15 students from the university training clinic and nine staff from two cbos. twenty-seven clients received pm+ from graduate students, and 18 clients received pm+ from cbo staff. most clients (92.6% university clinic, 88.9% cbos) completed all five pm+ sessions. change from baseline to end line showed a medium to large effect across primary outcome measures in both settings. qualitative interviews further supported the feasibility and acceptability of remote pm+. remotely delivered pm+ appears to be feasible, acceptable, and safe, which supports its potential to expand the mental health workforce. additional research is warranted to evaluate the effectiveness of remotely delivered pm+. concerns about multiple crises and covid-19-related stress symptoms in tyrolean children (austria) during and after the pandemic abstract the multiple systemic crises of recent years have the potential to impact child and adolescent mental health. there is extensive evidence on short-term mental health declines during the covid-19 crisis. however, research on post-pandemic consequences and the relevance of other crises is limited. here, we combined parent and child perspectives to analyse covid-19-related stress over time and its association with concerns about other crises. we used repeated cross-sectional surveys of parents in tyrol, austria, regarding their children’s (3–13 years) covid-19-related stress symptoms (cats-2) between 2020 and 2025 (n = 5,056 measurements). children (7–13 years) participated in cross-sectional surveys about their symptoms (cries-13, n = 575) and concerns about different crises (n = 259) in 2025. based on parent information, we identified a peak in children’s covid-19-related stress symptom prevalence during the pandemic winters of 2020/21 and 2021/22. in 2025, parents reported no symptoms for 99% (95% ci [95.3, 99.7]) of preschool children. however, approximately 10% (95% ci [7.3, 13.5]) of then school-aged children had covid-19-related stress symptoms according to parents. the post-pandemic survey of children corroborated prevalence rates identified in parent reports. additionally, children reported concerns about different crises. concerns about all crises were particularly prevalent in children with covid-19-related stress symptoms. the findings point to the long-term significance of temporary crises for children. children are concerned about themselves and others and may struggle to navigate the threat of multiple crises. discover mental health

measuring and reducing anxious thoughts and feelings of middle schoolers: an inner behavior intervention abstract the present study investigated the effects of a daily 1-min counting procedure of confident thoughts on self-counted anxious inner behaviors among four middle school students who, following referral by school psychologists, self-identified problematic levels of anxious thoughts and feelings at school. no participant was recruited on the basis of an anxiety diagnosis. using a multiple baseline design across participants, coupled with pre- and post-intervention interviews, the study systematically evaluated changes in the frequency, celeration, and variability of anxious thoughts and feelings before and during implementation of the intervention. the investigation extends previous inner behavior research by targeting a critical developmental period where anxiety often emerges and can significantly impact academic performance and social development. the pattern and magnitude of change varied across participants. three participants showed a reversal from accelerating to decelerating anxious thought frequency together with reduced day-to-day variability, and one of the three also showed a substantial reduction in level. the fourth entered the study with an already low and already decelerating frequency and showed no quantitative change that can be attributed to the intervention, though she reported fewer and less severe anxiety attacks. thematic analysis revealed increased self-awareness, enhanced ability to identify anxiety triggers, and improved emotional regulation strategies. the intervention proved to be feasible, time-efficient, and well-received. the findings support the use of the 1-min counting procedure for confident thoughts as a promising school-based approach for addressing anxiety in adolescents. behavior analysis in practice

psychometric evaluation of the korean camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire: evidence of measurement invariance and sex-related camouflaging patterns. social camouflaging involves complex strategies used to navigate social challenges, which are increasingly recognized across varying levels of autistic traits. despite its clinical importance in explaining diagnostic disparities, no validated measure exists in korea. this study evaluated the psychometric properties and factor structure of the korean version of the camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (cat-q) across levels of autistic traits. a total of 1,079 korean adults completed an online survey and were classified into high and low autistic trait groups. exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a refined 13-item, three-factor structure (compensation, masking, and assimilation) with strong model fit. the scale demonstrated good internal consistency and convergent validity, correlating significantly with social anxiety, depression, and interpersonal competence. full measurement invariance was established across autistic trait levels and sex. the high autistic trait group, particularly females, reported significantly greater camouflaging across all dimensions. the korean cat-q is a psychometrically sound tool for assessing camouflaging behaviors, with higher scores significantly associated with greater psychological distress. this instrument is essential for examining sex-related camouflaging patterns and fostering inclusive environments that reduce the burden of concealment in south korea.lay abstractmany individuals, particularly those with higher autistic traits, use social camouflaging to cope with or adapt to everyday social situations. they often hide or compensate for their autistic traits to fit in with others. the camouflaging autistic traits questionnaire (cat-q) was developed to measure social camouflaging, but there has been no tool in korea. we developed and tested a 13-item korean version of the cat-q with 1,079 adults from the general population. participants were grouped based on their levels of self-reported autistic traits. our study found that this tool is reliable and useful. it successfully measures three types of social camouflaging: compensation, masking, and assimilation, and it works well for both males and females. females and people with higher autistic traits use camouflaging more frequently. this suggests that camouflaging can be an exhausting task to meet social expectations, rather than a simple choice. this tool provides a useful basis for future research on social camouflaging. future studies using this tool can help us better understand the hidden struggles and find ways to lessen camouflaging. this research could help build a more inclusive society where everyone feels safe to be their true selves without fear of judgment. autism

cross-cultural adaptation and validation of the european portuguese version of the problem gambling severity index. the problem gambling severity index (pgsi) is widely used to assess the prevalence of problem gambling on a community level. no cultural adaptation or psychometric validation of the instrument has been conducted for european portuguese. the sample comprised 171 individuals, aged 18 to 75 years old. internal consistency, construct validity, and criterion validity were assessed using mcdonald's omega (ω), the south oaks gambling screen, and gambling disorder criteria based on the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders, respectively. the unidimensional structure of the pgsi was assessed through confirmatory factor analysis (cfa). cut-off point for problem gambling was established based on the receiver operating characteristic (roc) and precision recall (pr) curves. the portuguese version of the pgsi has excellent internal consistency (ω = 0.89). construct validity (ρ = 0.515, p < .001) and criterion validity (ρ = 0.482, p < .001) were established through significant positive correlations. cfa confirms the one-factor solution as the best fit for the pgsi (cfi = 0.995). roc and pr curves estimates point to different cut-off scores, with the cut-off of eight being the recommended threshold for problem gambling. our data suggest that the european portuguese version of the pgsi is a reliable tool for assessing gambling severity. journal of gambling studies

the hangover of oppression: an ecological momentary assessment study of oppression-based stressors and daily alcohol use and hazardous drinking outcomes among sexual and gender minoritized young adults. sexual and gender minoritized (sgm) young adults are at greater risk for hazardous drinking and alcohol use disorder (aud) than their heterosexual and cisgender counterparts. these inequities are often explained with oppression frameworks, which posit that oppression-based stressors (i.e., discrimination) contribute to hazardous drinking and the development of aud. however, research examining the daily and within-person associations between oppression-based stressors and alcohol use among sgm young adults is nascent and equivocal. we conducted a 30-day ecological momentary assessment of daily within- and between-person oppression-based stressors and same-day alcohol use outcomes (i.e., alcohol use, quantity of drinks, heavy drinking, alcohol-related consequences, hangover symptoms) among 98 sgm young adults who engaged in heavy drinking (71.4% met criteria for aud). we also examined multiple person-level moderators (e.g., sociodemographics, addiction severity, stress exposure and sensitivity) to identify for whom oppression-based stressors confer risk for hazardous drinking. results indicated that on days participants experienced more oppression-based stressors than their average, they reported greater odds of daily heavy drinking. participants who experienced greater oppression-based stressors overall reported more daily negative and positive alcohol-related consequences and hangovers. the within-person associations between oppression-based stressors and some of the hazardous drinking outcomes were moderated by aud symptoms, a family history of alcohol problems, greater lifetime exposure to cisheterosexism, and identification as plurisexual (e.g., bisexual). our findings provide support for oppression and addiction frameworks and further highlight risks that plurisexual young adults experience. the results underscore the need to target oppression to reduce hazardous drinking among sgm young adults. validity and reliability of the almli handedness assessment (aha) in children with autism spectrum disorder. handedness is a key behavioral marker of hemispheric specialization and is closely associated with motor, perceptual, and cognitive development. although standardized questionnaires such as the edinburgh handedness inventory-short form (ehi-short) provide indirect measures of manual lateralization, observational tools are needed to capture children's functional hand use in everyday activities. this study evaluated the reliability and validity of the turkish version of the almli handedness assessment (aha) in 188 children aged 5-12 years, including 81 children with asd and 107 typically developing (td) peers. inter-rater reliability was assessed using cohen's kappa, and convergent validity was evaluated through agreement analyses, classification accuracy, and correlations with the ehi-short. inter-rater agreement was almost perfect (κ = 0.885,< .001) and test-retest agreement over a 14-day interval demonstrated excellent stability in the asd group (κ = 0.870) and perfect agreement in an availability-based td subsample (= 50; κ = 1.000). aha and ehi-short handedness classifications showed strong categorical agreement (asd: κ = 0.914; td: κ = 0.868), and aha laterality indices were strongly correlated with ehi-short laterality coefficients (asd:= .939; td:= .982). children with asd showed a higher prevalence of atypical handedness than td peers, and asd status remained associated with atypical handedness after adjustment for age and gender. category-specific estimates for mixed-handedness in the td group should be interpreted cautiously because no td children were classified as mixed-handed by the aha. overall, the turkish aha demonstrated good reliability, with evidence of convergent validity, and agreement with the ehi-short. these findings should be regarded as preliminary psychometric evidence, and further validation in larger and more diverse samples is warranted. perceptual and motor skills

what are the relations between medical professionalism and burnout, empathy, personality traits, and socio-educational measures? a network perspective. medical professionalism (mp) is a multidimensional construct that underpins physicians' ethical conduct, responsibility, and relationships with patients and colleagues. no study to date has conceptualized mp and related psychosocial constructs as an interconnected relational system. this study applied network analysis to examine the complex interrelations operating simultaneously among mp, burnout, empathy, personality traits, and socio-educational variables in 325 spanish medical residents (mean age = 29.24 years; 70.8% female). partial correlation networks were estimated using regularization techniques that shrink small coefficients toward zero, with accuracy assessed through bootstrap resampling. mp-comprising professional responsibility, ethical commitment, and fellowship-emerged as the most central construct, with ethical commitment showing particularly strong connectivity. personal accomplishment and taking the patient's perspective were the most central non-mp nodes. professional responsibility was positively associated with personal accomplishment and conscientiousness; ethical commitment was positively linked to taking the patient's perspective and negatively to depersonalization; and fellowship was associated with extraversion. network structure was invariant across gender and specialty groups. these findings position mp as a structurally central component within a broader psychosocial system, with implications for both physician well-being and the quality of patient care. acta psychologica

how indigenous psychologies resemble mathematics: the epistemic role of conceptual innovation. this paper argues that indigenous psychologies and mathematics share an important methodological feature: both advance understanding by refining conceptual systems and terminology. throughout the history of mathematics, the reformulation of concepts has often enabled mathematicians to solve problems that had remained unresolved for centuries. similarly, indigenous psychologies emerged from the recognition that the concepts of mainstream psychology do not always adequately capture the psychological realities of indigenous populations. they therefore develop culturally grounded concepts and terminology that improve the understanding of psychological phenomena within specific cultural contexts. most indigenous psychology concepts belong to the field of social psychology. if the primary goal of social psychology is to understand human social behavior and experience, then indigenous psychologies pursue this goal through conceptual innovation in much the same way that mathematics advances through the refinement of its own conceptual framework. the paper also identifies important limits to this analogy: unlike mathematical concepts, the usefulness of indigenous psychological concepts may be difficult to appreciate without experience of the relevant cultural environment. the paper therefore discusses cultural experience and social success as possible ways of assessing the value of indigenous psychological concepts. integrative psychological and behavioral science

from temporal mindsets to the finish line: a prospective study of time perspectives and trail-running performance. recent research has highlighted the role of time perspectives in distance running performance, supporting the core predictions of the conceptual model of time perspective in athletic functioning. we examined whether time perspectives predict trail-running performance in 227 participants of the ultra roztocze in poland. the event featured five international trail running association-certified distances, spanning submarathons (11.5-35.6 km) and ultramarathons (65.2-124.5 km). performance was operationalized using rate my trail score, a time-based metric allowing cross-distance comparisons. we aimed to replicate prior findings, test their robustness while controlling for big five traits and body mass index, and examine race distance as a moderator. future-positive consistently predicted better outcomes, whereas present-fatalistic was negatively associated with performance, even after accounting for personality and body mass index. the effects of present-hedonistic varied by distance. these findings demonstrate the incremental validity of time perspectives, highlighting temporal orientation as a valuable target for endurance athletes' psychological preparation. journal of sport & exercise psychology

from context to contextualizing processes: new directions for the study of human development abstract this special issue advances a dynamic reconceptualization of context in developmental science. although contemporary developmental theories widely acknowledge that human development is contextualized, context has often been treated as an external and relatively stable set of conditions that influence development. in contrast, the contributions to this issue conceptualize contexts as an emergent, relational, and continuously evolving processes that both are shaped by and shape human action. across six target articles, authors examine how individuals actively participate in the co-construction of bio-socio-cultural contexts through interaction, meaning-making, interpretation, imagination, and the use of symbolic and material resources. the articles further explore how different levels of analysis, from interpersonal and institutional to cultural and historical, are theorized and studied within process-oriented accounts of development. this issue also explicitly considers the implications of a dynamic view of these processes for research, practice and policy making. in the concluding article, the guest editors offer a contextualizing processes framework around three themes: constitutive relationality, semiotic and material mediation, and the role of histories and futures in development and then state their hope that this contextualizing processes framework can help research, practice, and policy to meet some of the challenges faced in a rapidly changing world. human development

carrying grief into training: reproductive loss and counselor identity development abstract this preliminary study examined how counselors‐in‐training (cits) with lived experience of reproductive loss made sense of those experiences in relation to their developing counselor identity and how they described the role of shared grief vocabulary in that sense‐making. three cits enrolled in or recently graduated from a cacrep‐accredited program, all members of a voluntary grief exploration student group, completed semi‐structured interviews analyzed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. three themes were developed, addressing disenfranchised grief and identity disruption, misattuned support, and counselor identity development. participants described their reproductive grief as a source of clinical attunement and of specific countertransference pulls and described having language for the experience as both personally validating and professionally clarifying. implications for grief content in counselor preparation and for grief‐attuned supervision are considered within the study's preliminary scope. journal of humanistic counseling

parenting styles and intergenerational transmission of internet addiction risk: a cross-cultural latent class analysis problematic internet use in early and middle adolescence (ages 12–15) is increasingly recognized as a family-level concern, yet little is known about whether internet addiction (ia) risk shows a similar underlying structure across generations and cultures. using parent reports from 1,530 families across five countries, this study identified latent ia risk profiles based on ratings of both parents and their children and examined associations with parenting style and cultural context. low, moderate, and high ia risk classes emerged for both parents and children. profile structure was stable across countries, although prevalence varied. parents rated children as having higher ia than themselves, and parent-child association was evident: high-risk parents were more likely to have high- or moderate-risk children, whereas low-risk parents were mainly linked with low-risk children. authoritative parenting was associated with lower risk, and authoritarian parenting with higher risk. these findings support profile-based ia assessment and culturally sensitive family interventions. journal of early adolescence

conventionality in the perspective of the popular responses of the zulliger test and the personality trait openness to experience abstract: conventionality represents a key aspect of behavior in social contexts and can be assessed through the openness to experience trait or by popular (p) responses in performance-based methods such as the rorschach test. although the rorschach’s validity for assessing conventionality is well established, comparable evidence for the zulliger test is lacking. this study aimed to identify p responses on the zulliger test and examine their concurrent validity with socially adaptive conventionality, defined as the relationship between the frequency of popular responses and informant-rated openness to experience. two studies were conducted with samples of 100 and 73 participants. study 1 produced an updated list of p responses for the zulliger test; study 2 replicated and validated these findings. informant ratings of openness were related to p-response frequency, and the association followed an inverted u-shaped pattern. participants with a moderate p response frequency were described as more open to experience than those with low or very high frequencies. these findings support the conclusion that the zulliger test captures aspects of conventionality similar to those reflected in the rorschach, underscoring its potential for assessing socially adaptive and maladaptive forms of (un)conventional behavior. rorschachiana

associations of post-migration difficulties and religious coping with psychological distress among syrian refugee youth background: syrian refugee youth in jordan experience persistent post-migration difficulties that may affect psychological well-being. religious coping represents a culturally relevant response to adversity, although its relationship with psychological distress remains unclear. objective: to examine the associations of post-migration living difficulties (pmld) and positive and negative religious coping with psychological distress among syrian refugee youth in jordan. methods: a cross-sectional study was conducted among 460 syrian refugees aged 15–29 years residing in refugee camps and host communities in jordan. data were collected between august and september 2025 using the arabic pmld scale, brief religious coping scale, and brief symptom inventory-53. multivariable linear regression examined associations with psychological distress, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. separate interaction models examined the moderating roles of positive and negative religious coping. results: the mean pmld score was 35.20 ± 4.95, with financial hardship, difficulties obtaining financial assistance, family-related concerns, and employment challenges receiving the highest ratings. positive religious coping was more frequently reported than negative religious coping (19.01 ± 3.00 vs. 8.08 ± 3.29). the mean raw global severity index (gsi) was 1.47 ± 0.17. pmld was not significantly correlated with gsi (r = −0.022, p = .637). in the adjusted regression model, pmld (p = 0.351), positive religious coping (p = 0.345), and negative religious coping (p = 0.848) were not significantly associated with gsi. neither positive (p = 0.860) nor negative religious coping (p = 0.190) significantly moderated the pmld–gsi association. conclusion: post-migration adversity and religious coping were not independently associated with psychological distress in this sample. findings should be interpreted cautiously given limitations in measurement reliability. culturally responsive psychosocial services should consider both psychological needs and persistent socioeconomic challenges affecting refugee youth. health psychology research

sex differences in adult depression treatment outcome: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses major depressive disorder is common and burdensome, with a higher prevalence in women and documented sex differences in treatment response across medicine. however, whether sex differences in adult depression treatment outcomes are consistently reported and synthesized remains unclear. this study aims to synthesize evidence on sex differences in adult depression treatment outcomes and to assess the quality of reviews reporting these differences. it is a secondary analysis of a campbell collaboration evidence and gap map (egm). it is not prospectively registered. prior guidance for overviews of reviews was consulted. we screened 9,475 database records and 995 egm records; 1,397 full-text reports were assessed, and 48 systematic reviews met inclusion criteria (e.g., reported sex-disaggregated treatment outcomes). we extracted intervention, outcome, and analytical data, assessed methodological quality with amstar-2, and synthesized findings narratively. among included reviews, 13 (27.1%; 95% ci: 16.6–41.0) found significant sex differences, all with small effect sizes. pharmacological interventions (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, venlafaxine) tended to favor women, psychotherapy (cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness) tended to favor men, and complementary and alternative treatments showed variable effects. over half (52%, 25/48; 95% ci: 38.3–65.5) were critically low quality; 81% (39/48; 95% ci: 68.1–89.8) were low or critically low quality. sex differences in depression treatment response are underreported. preliminary trends of female benefit for pharmacotherapy and male benefit for psychotherapy rest on weak evidence. routine sex-disaggregated reporting and high-quality sex-stratified research are needed. limitations include restriction to english- and chinese-language publications, potential overlap of primary studies, and no formal grade assessment. health psychology research

a network analysis of teachers’ coping with preschoolers’ negative emotions teachers’ coping with children’s negative emotions (tccne) plays a key role in shaping preschoolers’ social skills and socio-emotional development during early childhood. this study used network analysis to examine the interrelationships among six coping reaction orientations: distress reactions (dr), punitive reactions (pr), minimization reactions (mr), expressive encouragement (ee), emotion-focused reactions (efr), and problem-focused reactions (pfr). participants included 241 preschool teachers (240 women; m age = 32.63 years, sd = 7.94). teachers completed the coping with children’s negative emotions scale, which comprises six dimensions. findings revealed that emotion-focused and problem-focused coping orientations were most central in the network, linked to each other and to ee. dr and pr were also closely connected. these patterns were broadly similar across the career stages examined. these findings deepen our understanding of how preschool teachers’ coping orientations are structured and interconnected. journal of emotional and behavioral disorders

becoming a cultural being: a dynamic systems view of human development this paper proposes a dynamical systems account of human cultural development grounded in a process-relational worldview. in contrast to mechanistic approaches that treat culture as an external influence on development, this framework conceptualizes culture and development as inseparable, co-constituting processes that unfold across situational, ontogenetic, and sociocultural levels. drawing on infant–caregiver interactions as a “slices of life” example, we illustrate how culturally patterned routines emerge, stabilize and transform through self-organization, and how historical, material and sociocultural conditions afford and constrain developmental trajectories. we apply key concepts from the dynamic systems approach, including emergence, self-organization, attractor stabilization, circular causality, and historical constraint, to explain human cultural development. we treat emergent processual structures as formal causes and adopt explanatory pluralism. inspired by the work of vygotsky, rogoff, and dynamic systems theorists, we propose a prototheoretical framework for reconceptualising, systematising, and advancing integrative, process-oriented explanations of human cultural development. culture & psychology

rejuvenating the ecological self: traditional indian theories as interpretative frameworks for environmental well-being conventional psychological models often frame well-being as a private, internal state, frequently neglecting the active role of cultural and material environments. this article proposes a philosophy-driven psycho-cultural account of well-being by analysing indian sculpture and architecture as indigenous psychological systems. drawing on rasa theory, ayurvedic ecology, and the bhāva–rasa framework, the study argues that well-being is an emergent property of embodied engagement with culturally meaningful spaces. by mapping these indigenous frameworks onto constructs such as the dialogical self and semiotic mediation, the paper demonstrates how traditional built environments function as active modulators of affective grammar. the analysis moves beyond “restoration” (the recovery from cognitive depletion) to “instoration” (the active cultivation of personal and ethical competencies), positioning the indian aesthetical tradition as a tool for psychological rejuvenation. through a synthesis of the rasa framework and contemporary environmental psychology, the article calls for a shift toward an “ecological mind.” it concludes by proposing a research agenda that integrates biometric tools, such as eye-tracking, to measure how traditional semiotic nodes foster cognitive recovery and emotional equilibrium in the modern built environment. culture & psychology

awe and wise reasoning: cultural differences in solomon's paradox abstract previous research has shown that individuals often reason less wisely about self‐conflicts than about other‐conflicts, a phenomenon known as solomon's paradox. however, less is known about whether this self–other asymmetry varies across cultural contexts and whether awe shapes this pattern. across three studies ( n = 1168), the present research examined cultural differences in solomon's paradox and the role of awe in wise reasoning. study 1 suggested that the other‐conflict advantage was descriptively more apparent among american participants than among chinese participants. study 2 suggested that trait awe was positively associated with wise reasoning and that its moderating role in the self–other difference appeared primarily among american participants high in trait awe. study 3 experimentally induced state awe among chinese participants and examined whether state awe shaped wise reasoning across self‐ and other‐conflict situations. overall, the findings suggest that solomon's paradox may vary across cultural contexts and that awe‐related experiences may contribute to wise reasoning in interpersonal conflicts. psych journal

training preschool teachers to implement and interpret data from a trial‐based functional analysis abstract this study partially replicated and extended standish et al. (2023) by evaluating a modified behavioral skills training (bst) package for training preschool special educators to implement trial‐based functional analysis (tbfa). tbfa implementation fidelity, data interpretation, and data management, including application of the trial‐based ongoing visual inspection (tb‐ovi) stop/go criteria, were evaluated across four participants. generalization to preschool settings and maintenance at 10‐week follow‐up were also evaluated. participants had varying levels of prior experience with applied behavior analysis. all participants demonstrated substantial improvement across the targeted competencies from pretest to posttest. high levels of implementation fidelity were observed at posttest and generally maintained during implementation with children in preschool settings and at follow‐up, although some variability was observed across participants and conditions. improvements were also observed in data interpretation and data management, including application of tb‐ovi stop/go criteria. overall, the findings extend previous research by providing descriptive evidence of substantial improvements in a broader set of competencies relevant to conducting and evaluating tbfa following structured bst, including implementation, data interpretation, data management, and ongoing data‐based decision‐making. implications for tbfa training and implementation in applied educational settings are discussed. behavioral interventions

developmental differences in risk patterns among children and adolescents: a latent profile analysis abstract guided by the bioecological model of human development, this study used a person-centered method to examine the underlying risk patterns between children and adolescents. using a nationally representative dataset ( n = 36,905), the latent profile analysis explored risk across five domains (individual, family, school, neighborhood, and sociocultural) and compared them between children and adolescents. children were exposed to low risk (83%), safety risk (6%), and school risk (10%) while adolescents were exposed to low risk (78%), individual risk (9%), and comprehensive risk (13%). as the developmental stages differ between children and adolescents, the risk across domains presented different patterns between the two age groups. findings suggest that a more nuanced approach should be considered for children and adolescents considering their developmental stages. adversity and resilience science

preliminary validation of a newly developed spanish-language patient-perceived scale of lgb clinical competence and sensitivity in psychotherapy abstract lesbian, gay, and bisexual (lgb) people face minority stress that can also shape their experience of psychotherapy. their perceptions of therapists’ attitudes and competence are associated with satisfaction and the therapeutic alliance, yet few instruments assess these perceptions from the patient’s perspective. this cross-sectional study aimed to develop and provide initial psychometric evidence for a spanish-language patient-perceived lgb clinical competence and sensitivity scale (eccs-lgb-p) to assess lgb patients’ perceptions of their therapists’ clinical competence and sensitivity. data were collected from 203 spanish-speaking lgb adults. exploratory factor analysis (efa) yielded a provisional two-factor structure (sensitivity and positive clinical competence; microaggressions and discriminatory practices) that largely coincided with positive versus negative item wording. the final 30-item scale showed high internal consistency ( $$\alpha = .96$$ ; mcdonald’s $$\omega = .96$$ ), which may partly reflect item redundancy. eccs-lgb-p scores were moderately associated with patients’ ratings of the therapeutic alliance ( $$\rho = .55$$ , $$p < .001$$ ). no statistically reliable associations were detected with symptom measures. these findings provide promising preliminary evidence concerning the internal structure, internal consistency, and relations with the therapeutic alliance of the eccs-lgb-p, mainly for research, training, and group-level quality improvement. confirmatory factor analysis, measurement invariance testing, and test–retest reliability in independent samples are needed before broad implementation. discover mental health

healthy people, healthy climate? understanding the connection of well-being (sdg 3) and climate action (sdg 13) through health psychology. growing recognition of the interdependence between human health, climate change and environmental sustainability has highlighted the importance of understanding how climate-friendly behaviours can simultaneously promote individual health, climate and environmental protection. concepts such as one health, planetary health and the sustainable development goals (sdgs) emphasize that human well-being depends on healthy ecosystems, a stable climate and supportive social systems. yet achieving these goals remains challenging because many climate-friendly behaviours involve trade-offs between short-term individual benefits and long-term collective outcomes. this special issue addresses these challenges at the intersection of sdg 3 (good health and well-being) and sdg 13 (climate action). the contributing papers span topics including mobility, nutrition, climate emotions, self-regulation, social norms and behaviour-change interventions. collectively, the papers demonstrate that health and climate outcomes are deeply interconnected but that co-benefits are conditional on psychological mechanisms, social contexts and structural opportunities. based on this evidence, we propose an integrative framework linking environmental conditions, psychological processes and behavioural responses, as well as health and climate outcomes for researchers, practitioners and policy-makers. to achieve sdg 3 and sdg 13 together, psychology must promote well-being not as an end point in itself but as a foundation and driver for responsible and sustainable behaviour, using evidence-based behaviour-change theories, techniques and interventions. applied psychology-health and well being

the development and evolution of tbr2-positive cells in the vertebrate pallium abstract the mammalian neocortex is a highly complex, six-layered structure composed of diverse neuronal and glial cell types that support sensory processing, motor integration, and higher cognitive functions. excitatory neurons originate from neural progenitors in the embryonic pallium, primarily within the ventricular and subventricular zones. radial glial cells function as key nscs, generating neurons directly or via intermediate progenitors, which act as transit-amplifying cells committed to neuronal differentiation. this review focuses on tbr2-positive cells, widely used as markers for ips, and summarize their characteristics, regulation, and evolutionary significance across species. because tbr2 expression is not necessarily restricted to intermediate progenitors across diverse species, the conventional assumption that tbr2-positive cells are synonymous with ips should be reconsidered in a comparative developmental context. understanding the diversity, regulation, and evolutionary origins of tbr2-positive cells will provide insights into the development and evolution of neocortical structure and neural progenitor diversity. brain behavior and evolution

outcome versus process focused future thinking: results from a randomised experiment. objectives: future thinking plays a central role in emotion and behaviour, yet different modes of simulation may have distinct effects. this pre-registered experiment compared outcome- and process-focused future thinking on affective and cognitive responses to imagined events. it was hypothesised that anticipated pleasure, anticipatory pleasure and positive affect would be higher in an outcome-focused task relative to a process-focused task. further, ratings of perceived control and likelihood of the future event will be higher after a process-focused task relative to the outcome-focused.
methods: participants ( = 134; m = 35.1 years (age), sd = 13.1) generated personally relevant future events online, were randomly assigned to focus on either outcomes or the steps required to achieve them, and completed pre-post questionnaires relating to these future events.
results: outcome-focused thinking increased anticipatory pleasure, motivation and personal significance. in contrast, process-focused thinking reduced perceived control and was associated with reductions in both anticipated and anticipatory pleasure. no effects were observed for perceived likelihood, and positive affect increased modestly across conditions.
conclusions: these findings indicate that outcome-focused future thinking enhances affective engagement, whereas process-focused thinking may introduce constraints that attenuate perceived control and reward-related responses. distinguishing between these modes of future thinking has implications for models of motivation and interventions targeting future-oriented cognition. australian journal of psychology
