electrophysiological correlates of emotion processing in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of p300 event-related potentials abstract introduction: schizophrenia is characterized by deficits in social cognition, including impaired facial emotion recognition (fer). the p300 event-related potential (erp) indexes attention and context updating and is reduced in schizophrenia. whether this reduction varies by facial-emotion valence is unclear. we quantified valence-specific p300 differences, comparing adults with schizophrenia and healthy controls across explicit fer and implicit facial emotion processing (ifep) tasks. methods: we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis following prisma guidelines. pubmed, web of science, and scopus were searched through may 2025. studies were included if they reported p300 responses to positive or negative facial expressions. results: ten studies met the inclusion criteria; six were eligible for meta-analysis. in response to positive facial expressions (k=5; n=237), p300 amplitude was significantly reduced in schizophrenia (hedges’ g=−0.40, 95%ci [−0.59,−0.21], p<0.001). for negative expressions (k=6; n=281), a smaller, marginally significant reduction was observed (hedges’ g=−0.31, 95%ci [−0.62,0.00], p=0.05). one ifep study found no differences. conclusions: results suggest valence-specific p300 attenuation during emotion processing in schizophrenia, particularly for positive expressions, potentially reflecting impaired salience attribution. p300 may represent a candidate electrophysiological, temporally resolved erp biomarker for impaired social-affective processing and a candidate endpoint for cognitive remediation studies. neuropsychobiology

emerging evidence on online preventive parenting interventions and children’s outcomes: a systematic review abstract background online preventive parenting interventions have been increasingly recognized as an important platform in recent years, broadening accessibility and eliminating barriers related to time and resources for attending intervention services. objective this study sought to explore the effects of online preventive parenting interventions on child psychological and behavioral outcomes while examining moderators and mediators underlying these interventions, as well as program engagement. method the review followed the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (prisma) guidelines. randomized controlled trial studies of preventive interventions directly targeting parents of children aged between 3 and 12 with measured child outcomes were included in the review. results the final sample included 14 studies focusing on 11 online interventions. primary outcomes for most studies included child behavior problems and mental health. most studies reported positive intervention effects at post-intervention, while several reported nonsignificant changes. few studies examined relevant moderating and mediating processes. of the 14 studies reviewed, 11 provided information about program engagement, typically through module completion and session attendance. conclusions longitudinal tests of mechanisms of change and of the subgroups that benefit most from online interventions would help clarify how and for whom these programs work. combining multiple informants, such as parent, child, teacher, and observer reports, would strengthen the evidence on child outcomes. research on optimal dosage, the role of human support, and effective, sustainable delivery formats may also be informative. child & youth care forum

assessing rumination about competition-related problems in athletes abstract: the present project aimed to validate the state sports competition rumination scale (s-scrs), a self-report measure designed to assess key characteristics of rumination – repetitiveness, intrusiveness, and uncontrollability – in athletes in relation to their current psychological state. the s-scrs is a 3-item measure based on the original scrs short form ( michel-kröhler, krys, & berti et al., 2025 ), with instructions adapted to capture current state rumination about competition-related problems. in two studies using data from 355 competitive athletes across various sports, construct validity was tested in terms of a multistate-single trait model and confirmed in a nomological network by negative correlations with self-compassion and positive correlations with depression, anxiety, stress, anger, and poor social support. in addition, reliability was examined in three stages with (1) nested alpha, (2) intraclass coefficients (iccs), and (3) spearman’s correlations for examining the score consistency over time. results showed that the s-scrs is fairly consistent but exhibits slight changes over time (icc = .61). additionally, a linear regression model confirmed that the s-scrs is sensitive to competition performance. overall, the s-scrs appears to be a brief, reliable, and valid measure of state rumination about competition-related problems, suitable for use in future research and applied sport psychology. european journal of psychological assessment

development and evaluation of the altruistic orientation towards strangers scale (aots) abstract: trait altruism reflects a tendency to engage in voluntary behavior that benefits others, with personal cost in terms of time, resources, and/or effort, and without expectation of direct reward. current measures of altruism focus on assessing the frequency of engaging in prosocial behaviors assumed to be altruistically motivated. to address this limitation, we developed the altruistic orientation towards strangers (aots) scale following a review of the literature and identification of key elements of altruism. in exploratory studies, the aots was developed using data from three convenience samples, including students at a large canadian university (sample 1: n = 1,295), prolific users in canada and the united states (sample 2: n = 302), and prolific users in the united kingdom (sample 3: n = 297). after addressing a volunteering factor and negative-wording nuisance factor, exploratory factor analysis suggested a one-factor structure. scores on the final aots were significantly correlated with related traits and demonstrated criterion-related validity with prosocial outcomes, including covid-19 behaviors (samples 1–2) and generosity (samples 1–3). these results provide preliminary evidence for the aots as a new measure of altruistic tendencies toward strangers; however, additional research is needed to evaluate discriminant validity and explore other prosocial outcomes. european journal of psychological assessment

zero‐sum beliefs and system justification: the roles of perceived involutionary climate and perceived legitimacy of involutionary behaviour abstract zero‐sum beliefs reflect a win‐lose worldview in which one party's gains are perceived as another party's losses. although these beliefs are known to undermine interpersonal and intergroup relations, their implications for evaluations of broader social systems remain underexplored. the present research examines how zero‐sum beliefs relate to system justification, focusing on the mediating role of perceived involutionary climate and the moderating role of perceived legitimacy of involutionary behaviour. in study 1, a cross‐sectional survey ( n = 546) examined associations among zero‐sum beliefs, system justification, perceived involutionary climate, and perceived legitimacy of involutionary behaviour. study 2 ( n = 260) experimentally manipulated zero‐sum beliefs to further test the proposed mediation and moderation processes. zero‐sum beliefs were negatively associated with system justification in study 1, and experimentally induced zero‐sum beliefs resulted in lower system justification in study 2. in both studies, perceived involutionary climate mediated this relationship, and the indirect effect was weaker when involutionary behaviour was perceived as more legitimate. these findings shed light on how zero‐sum beliefs may shape individuals' evaluations of the social system by influencing how they perceive their social context, thereby advancing understanding of the broader psychological consequences of such beliefs. asian journal of social psychology

relationships between dog caregiving, stress coping, and online peer support: a mixed-methods study of parent and adolescent perspectives abstract background: adolescence is a critical developmental period of seeking social connection as well as coping with stress related to those relationships. little is known about whether the peer relationships that become so crucial during adolescence might be associated with an adolescent’s ability and motivation to take care of their pets. in addition, few studies examine pet caregiving from both the parents’ and adolescents’ perspectives. methods: this mixed-methods study of us parents and adolescents (aged 13–17) employed survey and interview methods to analyze relationships between dog caregiving, coping with peer stress, and seeking online peer support. results: we found that adaptive coping with peer stress was significantly associated with dog caregiving, whereas maladaptive coping was not associated with dog caregiving. a unique finding of social media help-seeking was significantly associated with stress coping strategies and involvement with dog caregiving in the home. parent interviews emphasized observable behaviors such as self-isolation in bedrooms or scrolling on phones as maladaptive coping strategies; however, adolescent interviews also revealed the content of their online activities that included social support-seeking, sharing dog stories and photos/videos, and seeking positive content to regulate their emotions. conclusions: these findings have implications for parents, counselors, and social workers who want guidance in affirming that peer stress does not seem to deter adolescents from taking care of their pet dogs; in fact, the more they nurture their pets, the better they cope with peer stress as well as seek online social support. human-animal interactions

programming and reprogramming the nervous system via cut homeobox genes abstract background: a central question in neurobiology is how the transcriptional programs that define a neuron are established in development and held stable thereafter. the cut homeobox genes offer an unusually revealing window onto this problem. summary: we review the function of the cux and onecut families across phyla: dosage-dependent control of sensory fate and dendritic morphology in flies, redundant maintenance of pan-neuronal identity in the nematode, and combinatorial neuronal subtype specification in the vertebrate cortex, retina and spinal cord. we then examine how the same factors are deployed in neuronal reprogramming, acting as both exogenous drivers and endogenously recruited effectors, following a recurrent hierarchy from proneural initiation to cut-mediated specification. key messages. by tracing cut function from invertebrate sensory circuits to vertebrate reprogramming, this review positions invertebrate models as tractable entry points for dissecting how neuronal identity is built and restored. brain behavior and evolution

ethanol consumption during rich-to-lean transitions of food reinforcement: manipulation of ethanol delivery mode in the absence of a sucrose fade abstract previous research in our laboratory demonstrated that transitions from rich-to-lean food reinforcers engender oral ethanol (etoh) consumption in rats when etoh was freely available and previously presented in a sucrose solution. here, we determined whether shifts in food-reward context would establish etoh consumption in the absence of a sucrose fade and when access was contingent upon a lever press. six food-restricted male long-evans rats lever pressed on a two-component multiple fixed-ratio, fixed-ratio (fr fr) schedule with signaled rich (3 or 4 pellets; lower fr) and lean (1 pellet; higher fr) components. four transitions between food reinforcers were arranged: lean-to-lean, lean-to-rich, rich-to-rich, and rich-to-lean. after establishing a baseline, an etoh solution (20% v/v) was made freely available during the session in a bottle. licks were recorded and sorted by food transition type. after five sessions, the bottle was removed, and rats could produce 0.1-cc, 5-s etoh (20% v/v) deliveries via a dipper by pressing (fr 1) a concurrently available second lever. five subsequent extinction sessions were conducted under lever-press conditions using tap water. the schedule of food reinforcement occasioned moderate levels of etoh consumption, with increased consumption during lean components, and particularly during the rich-to-lean transition. most rats consumed more etoh when it was freely available in a bottle, but this difference was not statistically significant. lever press responding for fluid decreased during extinction but occurred at higher rates in the rich-to-lean transition. overall, the results demonstrate that rats acquired etoh consumption in the absence of a sucrose fade, including when a lever press was required to produce it, under transition-type control. psychological record

the ‘ebb-and-flow’ distance illusion two dots can appear to approach and recede from each other even when their physical separation is constant. in our stimulus, a central dot is surrounded by grey discs whose diameters expand and contract while the whole configuration translates back and forth, resembling the dynamic ebbinghaus display. during disc expansion (and one translation direction), the dots often look closer together, whereas during disc contraction (and the opposite translation direction), they look farther apart. a set of informal demonstrations suggests that translation of the entire configuration is necessary. the effect weakens when either disc-diameter change or dot–disc-centre spacing change is removed, and it largely disappears when translation and disc dynamics are shifted by half a cycle. with as few as two surrounding discs, the illusion remains robust. i-perception

the role of color expertise in color preference: evidence from color naming ability expertise can shape how aesthetic stimuli are perceived and interpreted, but its role in color preference remains unclear. the present study examined whether color expertise and color naming ability are associated with preferences for individual colors. an independent color-name generation stage was first conducted to select non-basic and specialized color terms for stimulus development. seventy-five participants with different artistic backgrounds then completed a color-preference rating task, a three-alternative forced-choice color-naming task, and a color expertise questionnaire. greater expertise was associated with more accurate selection of intended color labels, indicating that expertise improved identification of specialized color terms. however, neither expertise nor naming accuracy was significantly associated with color preference. instead, preference ratings were more closely summarized by the perceptual properties of the stimuli. these findings help distinguish perceptual, linguistic, and experiential influences on color preference by showing that expertise improved color identification but did not systematically alter color liking. i-perception

professional development, supervisor roles, and functions: role of the school counselling internship school counselling internships are widely regarded as a key component of counsellor training and professional development. however, research has focussed primarily on supervisees’ experiences, leaving supervisors’ roles and functions in school-based internship settings comparatively underexplored. this study employed a qualitative research design using reflexive thematic analysis to examine how school counselling internships contribute to supervisees’ professional development and to identify the roles and functions of both site-based school counsellor supervisors and academic supervisors. data were collected through semi-structured interviews with eight site-based school counsellor supervisors and four academic supervisors. data were analysed using inductive thematic analysis, through which codes were generated from the data and organised into themes. for site-based school counsellors, the impact of internship practices on supervisees’ professional development was structured around three themes: progression in emotional experiences, personal factors, and attainments. the site-based school counsellors frequently adopted coordinator, adviser, teacher, and mentor roles in supervision; they also performed functions such as monitoring-evaluating, modelling, giving suggestions, and supporting. academic supervisors perceived internship practices on supervisees’ professional development yielded two sub-themes: professional identity and self-awareness, and counselling skills. academic supervisors were found to adopt the roles of coordinator, adviser, and teacher, and to perform functions such as modelling, supporting, monitoring-evaluating, informing, and providing suggestions. journal of psychologists and counsellors in schools

everyday sensory experiences of autistic university students in australia: an experience sampling approach. sensory differences and discomfort are significant on-campus barriers for many autistic postsecondary students, but we know relatively little about what makes sensory environments accessible or inaccessible for autistic students. in this study, 19 autistic university students in australia answered experience sampling questions thrice daily for 2 weeks. quantitative sensory comfort ratings were significantly poorer when participants reported states of greater anxiety, irritability, emotional reactivity and exhaustion. participants also reported more quantitative sensory discomfort when open-ended answers described feeling tired/exhausted, anxious or stressed/overwhelmed, rather than feeling relaxed/good. our study cannot resolve the causality of these relationships. notably, however, between-person trait differences in anxiety, irritability and exhaustion were not statistically related to sensory comfort. qualitative-quantitative triangulation suggested that participants experienced less sensory comfort: in open-access spaces (notably, on campus, travelling and shopping) compared to closed-access spaces (notably, at home); to high-intensity (e.g., loud) than low-intensity (e.g., quiet) or non-notable stimulation; to most sounds over visual, feel and taste stimuli; to people-related sounds than touch sensations; and to crowds over environments with fewer people. these findings suggest sensory environments systematically shape many autistic people's everyday experiences and thus that we should modify these environments to be more accessible and inclusive. autism

validation and likelihood-ratio calibration of the italian ritvo autism asperger diagnostic scale-revised (raads-r). purpose: italian psychometric evidence on the raads-r has been limited. this case-control validation examined the reliability, structure, and measurement invariance of the italian raads-r, its discrimination between autistic and non-autistic adults with candidate cut-offs and likelihood-ratio (lr) bands, subscale contributions, gender differences, and aq convergence.
methods: sample 1 comprised 376 autistic adults referred to a specialized adult-autism service and diagnosed by blind multidisciplinary assessment, compared with 376 self-declared non-autistic community adults; sample 2 comprised 354 adults with self-reported previously established diagnoses and 354 comparison adults, matched on age within gender. analyses covered reliability, cfa/bifactor/esem structure, invariance, roc analysis with cross-sample threshold application, lr bands, a group × gender mancova, and aq convergence.
results: internal consistency was excellent (ω = 0.98); a strong general factor (ω = 0.96-0.97) indicated that the dsm-5 subscales describe content rather than distinct dimensions. in sample 1, auc was 0.91 and the candidate cut-off of 92 gave sensitivity 0.89 and specificity 0.81; sample 2 yielded 104 (sensitivity 0.94, specificity 0.77). across samples, 92 favored sensitivity and 104 specificity. four lr bands graded the score (≤ 70, 71-91, 92-136, ≥ 137). autistic women reported higher sensory scores than men, with item-level invariance supported. raads-r and aq totals correlated strongly (r = .86).
conclusion: the italian raads-r is a reliable screening aid within multidisciplinary assessment. because accuracy was estimated against community adults, the cut-offs and lr bands are preliminary, require validation in consecutive clinical samples, and should not be used to rule out autism when clinical suspicion exists. journal of autism and developmental disorders

major depressive disorder involves motivational conflicts in emotion regulation in daily life. 重性抑郁障碍涉及日常生活中情绪调节的动机冲突 what do individuals with major depressive disorder (mdd) want to achieve when regulating their emotions? the answer has not been clear, given that some evidence suggests they are more motivated and other evidence suggests they are less motivated to feel better, than healthy controls are. tracking emotion regulation in an ecological momentary assessment study in individuals with mdd (= 94) and in healthy individuals (= 90), and using multilevel modeling, we demonstrated that compared with healthy individuals, those with mdd were more likely to experience motivational conflicts (i.e., they endorsed competing goals) in emotion regulation in daily life. joint frequency analyses showed that compared with healthy individuals, individuals with mdd wanted to both decrease and increase unpleasant emotions more frequently. they were also more motivated to increase and decrease pleasant emotions. such motivational conflicts carried negative implications. the more individuals with mdd experienced motivational conflicts in emotion regulation, the more severe their clinical symptoms became over time. in follow-up semistructured interviews on experienced conflict and attraction to sadness, individuals with mdd explicitly reported experiencing conflict in emotion regulation more often than healthy individuals, and being more attracted to sadness. thematic analyses validated by a large language model revealed that, when individuals with mdd were attracted to sadness, they were more likely to describe it as self-consistent. healthy individuals were more likely to describe sadness as appropriate or useful in the situation. motivational conflicts in emotion regulation may exacerbate distress and impair success in emotion regulation in mdd. psychometric performance and implementation of the dutchclinician-administered ptsd scale for children and adolescents-dsm-5. objective: posttraumatic stress disorder (ptsd) in children and adolescents is often difficult to diagnose due to symptom overlap with other psychiatric conditions and avoidance behaviors from the child, caregiver, or therapist. to improve diagnostic accuracy, the clinician-administered ptsd scale for children and adolescents-, fifth edition (caps-ca-5) was developed. this study evaluated its diagnostic accuracy, psychometric properties, and feasibility in routine child and adolescent mental health care in the netherlands.
method: the caps-ca-5 was implemented in four dutch mental health institutions. data from 189 interviews with children and adolescents aged 7-23 years were analyzed, alongside measures of trauma, anxiety, and depression. psychometric evaluation included confirmatory factor analysis, internal consistency, interrater reliability, and convergent/divergent validity.
results: the caps-ca-5 demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = .91) and interrater reliability (κ = .81). confirmatory factor analysis supported thefifth edition, four-factor model. caps-ca-5 scores correlated strongly with trauma symptoms and moderately with anxiety and depression. compared with caps-ca-5, clinical judgment showed low sensitivity (44.4%) but high specificity (84.1%), indicating it often missed true ptsd cases. online training was found feasible and helped clinicians apply the tool effectively.
conclusions: the caps-ca-5 is a reliable, valid instrument for ptsd assessment in children and adolescents. the caps-ca-5 identified more detailed and a higher number of ptsd consistent cases than unstructured clinical judgment and supports individualized case conceptualization and treatment planning. with proper training, the assessment can be effectively integrated into clinical practice, allowing for earlier and more targeted interventions for traumatized children and adolescents. characterizing symptom prominence in persistent postconcussion symptoms using random ensembles of person-specific networks. objective: this article aimed to evaluate the feasibility of an idiographic, network-based symptom prominence classification approach using short-term ecological momentary assessment (ema) data in individuals with persistent postconcussion symptoms and to examine its associations with clinical and demographic characteristics.
method: forty adults with clinician-diagnosed concussion completed baseline neuropsychological assessment and 20 days of ema (21 symptoms, five assessments daily). random symptom ensembles of graphical vector autoregressive models were used to estimate individualized symptom networks.
results: thirty-eight participants (= 42.5; 23 female) provided sufficient ema data (mean adherence = 79.1%). person-specific symptom ensembles met classification criteria for classification in 31 of the 38 participants (81.6%). symptom prominence classifications (emotional, cognitive, somatic) were derived using centrality metrics, with moderate agreement across operationalizations (κ = 0.55; 71.0%). somatic and cognitive classifications were the most common. greater psychological distress was associated with higher odds of emotional relative to cognitive classification across both operationalizations, whereas higher overall symptom burden showed the opposite pattern. sex was not reliably estimable: all participants with an emotional-dominant classification under the highest mean operationalization were female, producing complete separation.
conclusions: idiographic network modeling from short-term ema data is feasible and may support characterization of symptom network organization in persistent postconcussion symptoms. findings are preliminary and exploratory given the modest sample size and lack of external validation. further research is needed to determine the validity, stability, and clinical utility of these classifications. beyond the time constant: output–persistence dissociation in human post-rotatory eye-movement responses classical velocity-storage models describe post-rotatory eye velocity as the observable output of direct and stored vestibular components, yet rotational testing is often summarized primarily by the decay time constant. we examined whether the magnitudes of directional output asymmetry and decay-persistence asymmetry covary. this single-center registry-based observational analysis used source-reconciled data from 40 fast-domain-eligible patients; 31 had complete bilateral post-rotatory slow-phase velocity (spv) and time-constant (tc) measurements. spv-ar and tc-ar were calculated as normalized absolute inter-directional differences, thus retaining asymmetry magnitude but not its sign. in the 31 complete datasets (16 women, 15 men; median age 56 years, iqr 40.5–61.5; range 19–78), the median spv-ar was 26.9% (iqr 12.5–37.0) and the median tc-ar was 34.8% (iqr 12.7–59.6). the magnitudes of spv-ar and tc-ar were not detectably associated (spearman ρ = 0.091, p = 0.626; pearson r = 0.031, p = 0.868). mean post-rotatory spv and mean tc also showed no statistically significant association. output magnitude and temporal persistence provide complementary, non-interchangeable descriptors of the measured ocular response; this analysis does not establish directional sign concordance, physiological independence, or diagnostic thresholds. journal of eye movement research

peer scale for the social acceptance of students with special needs: a validity and reliability study. this study aimed to develop the peer scale for the social acceptance of students with special needs (ps-sassn) and examine its psychometric properties for assessing social acceptance as perceived by typically developing peers in inclusive settings. to establish robust construct validity and prevent overfitting, the study utilized two independent samples of third- and fourth-grade students in türkiye: the first sample (n₁ = 300) for exploratory factor analysis (efa), and the second independent sample (n₂ = 300) for confirmatory factor analysis (cfa). data suitability for efa was confirmed (kmo = 0.922, bartlett's test p < .001). efa revealed a three-factor structure explaining 43.88% of the total variance, comprising "togetherness and closeness," "conflict and avoidance," and "help, protection, and trust." cfa fully supported this three-factor model, yielding acceptable fit indices (χ/df = 2.78, rmsea = 0.058, srmr = 0.065, cfi = 0.921, tli = 0.914). reliability analyses indicated high internal consistency, with an overall cronbach's alpha of 0.936 and subscale coefficients ranging from.823 to.962. the findings provide robust evidence that the ps-sassn is a valid and reliable multidimensional instrument for assessing peer acceptance in inclusive classrooms, serving as an evidence-based tool for monitoring social interactions and evaluating intervention programs. acta psychologica

trait emotional intelligence in italian primary school children: psychometric evaluation of the trait emotional intelligence questionnaire-child short form and a network analysis of socioemotional and school functioning trait emotional intelligence (trait ei) is relevant to children’s emotional and social functioning, yet its psychometric organization and its position within the broader school context remain incompletely understood during middle childhood. the present research addressed these issues across two complementary studies with italian primary school children. study 1 (n = 668) examined the psychometric properties of the trait emotional intelligence questionnaire child short form (teique-csf), including internal consistency, exploratory and confirmatory factor structure, measurement invariance, and percentile-based descriptive reference values. the general-plus-wording model improved fit relative to a one-factor model, but residual misfit and wording-related variance limit the interpretation of the total score. measurement invariance was supported across sex. exploratory analyses suggested partial metric invariance across grades; scalar invariance across grades was not established. study 2 (n = 203), a secondary analysis of cross-sectional data, used network analysis to examine trait ei in relation to social intelligence, internalizing symptoms, academic performance, and classroom behavior. trait ei showed high overall connectivity, with its strongest direct associations involving lower depressive symptoms and scholastic anxiety and higher social skills and social information processing. direct connections with academic performance were weak despite positive bivariate correlations. additional factor-saturation indices supported a meaningful, although not dominant, general trait ei factor, while confirming substantial wording-related variance. overall, the findings support use of the teique-csf total score as a broad summary index rather than as a strictly unidimensional measure, with additional caution required for comparisons across grades. in the cross-sectional network, trait ei was conditionally associated primarily with internalizing symptoms and self-reported social functioning. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

navigating infertility together: the influence of romantic attachment on couple outcomes—a systematic review and meta‐analysis abstract infertility is a significant public health concern, profoundly affecting both individuals and couples. this systematic review and meta‐analysis aims to explore whether romantic attachment serves as a protective or risk factor in how couples navigate infertility diagnoses, treatments, and outcomes, with a specific focus on relational correlates. a systematic search was conducted across six databases from january 1, 2011, to february 3, 2025. seventeen studies met the inclusion criteria, examining the link between romantic attachment and couple‐related psychological outcomes. five of these studies were included in a meta‐analysis assessing the associations between attachment anxiety and avoidance and dyadic adjustment. findings highlight significant associations between insecure attachment dimensions (both anxiety and avoidance) and reduced relationship and sexual satisfaction among individuals facing infertility. meta‐analytic results revealed moderate negative associations between attachment insecurities and dyadic adjustment. additionally, cross‐partner effects were observed, indicating that one partner's attachment style can impact the other's infertility experience. this study underscores the pivotal role of romantic attachment in managing infertility‐related challenges, distinguishing the distinct impacts of attachment anxiety and avoidance, and offering valuable clinical insights for supporting couples undergoing fertility treatments. personal relationships

rebuilding community through sport: a commentary on the role of pickup soccer and basketball in addressing loneliness and isolation abstract loneliness and social isolation represent a public health crisis with serious consequences for overall well‐being. with access to medical and mental health care in the united states hindered by stigma, cost and time constraints, alternative pathways to holistic wellness are urgently needed. sports, especially team sports like basketball and soccer, offer an effective way to promote health among youth due to their cultural resonance and accessibility. while the sport for development (sfd) and positive youth development (pyd) literature has well‐documented the individual‐level benefits of sport participation, scholars increasingly call for a shift towards community‐centred theory and practice that extends beyond personal gains. this conceptual paper contributes to that conversation by examining how basketball and soccer can address loneliness and isolation at both the individual and community level with an emphasis on informal play in the form of pickup games. we highlight how these sports foster social connection and buffer against the harmful effects of the current loneliness epidemic. we also offer practical recommendations for stakeholders seeking to integrate basketball and soccer into sfd programming and other recreational spaces. finally, we conclude with a call to action urging the adoption of a transformative sfd model, one that actively counters loneliness and cultivates meaningful community connections. journal of community & applied social psychology

sleep in school‐age children at elevated familial likelihood of autism abstract background clinically significant sleep problems are common in autism spectrum disorder (asd) and can have negative impacts on child cognition, behavior, and health. however, few studies have evaluated sleep in school‐aged children with elevated familial likelihood of autism using objective and subjective sleep measures in the home environment. methods we obtained objective measures of sleep using actigraphy and parent‐report of sleep problems using daily sleep diaries and the children's sleep habits questionnaire. direct assessment established asd diagnosis in 7‐14‐year‐old children at higher familial likelihood (hl‐asd n = 39; hl‐noasd n = 83) and lower familial likelihood of asd (ll n = 64). results child sleep problems reported by parents, controlling for age, differed across groups following an endophenotypic pattern (hl‐asd > hl‐noasd > ll) and hl‐asd females demonstrated increased sleep problems. actigraphy and daily sleep diaries did not demonstrate significant group differences. there were significant group differences in psychotropic medication and melatonin use. conclusion in one of the first studies to evaluate sleep in school‐age children at higher familial likelihood of asd, parent‐report of sleep problems was increased in hl‐asd versus hl‐noasd versus ll children. this suggests shared familial influences between asd and parent‐reported sleep problems which could include genetic factors or shared aspects of the home environment. however, sleep characteristics measured objectively by actigraphy and daily sleep diaries revealed a different pattern. multimodal sleep data can reveal less understood dimensions of sleep patterns in naturalistic home environments and may lead to improved sleep interventions for autistic youth and their siblings. jcpp advances

impact of technological demands and work–family conflict on emotional exhaustion in knowledge workers job demands associated with the use of information and communication technologies (ict) in knowledge‐intensive organizations expose their employees (kiow) to psychosocial risks. drawing on the job demands–resources (jd–r) and effort–reward imbalance (eri) models, this mixed‐method research (qualitative and quantitative) measured the impact of ict demands (extended work availability, telepressure, and communication overload) and work–family conflict (wfc) on emotional exhaustion. this study also examines the role of overcommitment as a mediating variable on this impact and the degree to which e‐working effectiveness functions as a resource. the sample comprised 20 kiow in the qualitative study and 137 kiow in the quantitative study. it was found that ict demands and wfc not only correlate positively with emotional exhaustion but also with e-working effectiveness and that overcommitment plays a mediating role between wfc and telepressure and emotional exhaustion. human behavior and emerging technologies

when the outcome is uncertain: how competition and expectation errors increase cheating abstract why do individuals cheat in some situations but refrain from doing so in others? existing research has primarily explained dishonest behavior in terms of achievement motivation, performance pressure, and expected payoffs, with less attention to how the predictability of behavioral outcomes shapes cheating decisions. across four experiments, the present research examined the effects of competition, performance proximity, and outcome expectation accuracy on cheating and proposed a unified framework centered on outcome ambiguity. study 1 showed that competition increased cheating magnitude relative to a noncompetitive context. study 2 further demonstrated that cheating increased when competitors' performance was closer and the final outcome was therefore more difficult to predict. studies 3 and 4 extended this pattern beyond competitive contexts, showing that inaccurate outcome expectations increased cheating magnitude, whereas accurate expectations reduced it. taken together, these findings suggest that competition, close competitive outcomes, and inaccurate outcome expectations, although distinct situational factors, may share a common feature: they reduce the predictability of final outcomes and make it less clear whether and how one's actions will influence those outcomes. such outcome ambiguity, in turn, may increase cheating magnitude. these findings suggest that cheating is driven not only by the pursuit of favorable outcomes but also by uncertainty regarding the relationship between one's actions and their consequences. drawing on compensatory control theory, we further propose that when individuals have difficulty predicting or controlling final outcomes, cheating may serve as a compensatory strategy for regaining a sense of control over those outcomes. the present research extends behavioral decision research on dishonesty by highlighting outcome predictability and perceived controllability as potentially important determinants of cheating decisions. journal of behavioral decision making

psychoanalysis and school psychology: toward a psychoanalytically informed framework for educational practice abstract although the relationship between psychoanalysis and education has long been marked by tension—not least because the two fields approach the human subject from different epistemological and institutional positions—both have much to offer to each other by deepening understanding of students, learning, and educational life. moreover, contemporary school psychology has developed into a prevention‐oriented, systems‐based profession with strong commitments to assessment, intervention, consultation, and evidence‐based practice. yet this development has also left comparatively less room for sustained attention to unconscious communication, defensive processes, emotional meaning, and the affective life of educational institutions. this paper argues that psychoanalytic thinking offers school psychology a distinctive reflective framework for understanding educational difficulties as unconscious, relational, and institutional phenomena. drawing on key psychoanalytic and group‐analytic traditions, the paper examines how concepts such as transference, countertransference, containment, holding, symbolization, and social defense can deepen understanding of classroom life, teacher–student relationships, school culture, and family–school work. it further proposes that a psychoanalytically informed school psychologist does not function as a clinician within the school, but as a reflective practitioner who can collaborate with school communities in thinking more deeply about behavior, anxiety, conflict, exclusion, and the emotional meanings attached to learning. the paper also considers the limits and risks of this perspective, including time pressures, accountability demands, institutional resistance, and the danger of overinterpretation. it concludes that psychoanalysis does not replace school psychology; rather, it expands its interpretive and ethical capacities by restoring attention to the emotional and unconscious dimensions of educational practice. international journal of applied psychoanalytic studies

mapping methodologies: exploring visual narratives of identities, families, and power with immigrant‐origin and marginalized youth abstract mapping methodologies offer a versatile and innovative approach to understanding the complexity of youth identities, families, and communities, while also attending to the systems of power, privilege, and marginality in which they are embedded. mapping involves participant‐generated drawings that are integrated into broader qualitative interview protocols, amplifying youth voices in the process. participants are given colored pencils, paper, and an open‐ended prompt inviting them to depict their identities, families, and/or communities. these “visual narratives” serve as entry points for deeper qualitative inquiries into topics that are often multifaceted, sensitive, and especially salient for individuals at the intersections of multiple marginalities. this methodological paper presents mapping as a qualitative research tool and offers a practical guide for planning, implementing, and analyzing maps with diverse adolescent and emerging adult populations. journal of research on adolescence

belonging in crisis: a mixed‐methods exploration of school disruption among marginalized girls in india abstract school closures can disrupt not only educational access but also the relational and institutional conditions through which adolescents experience school belonging. this sequential mixed‐methods study examined how covid‐19–related school closures reshaped school belonging among marginalized adolescent girls in rural india. guided by bioecological systems theory and intersectionality, we integrated surveys administered in 2021 ( n = 90) and 2022 ( n = 60) with two waves of focus group discussions. school belonging was conceptualized as a multidimensional, ecological, and relational experience reflected in peer and teacher connection, recognition, perceived fit, opportunities for agency, and aspirational attachment to school. findings showed that belonging was increasingly constrained as closures continued. girls reported growing household responsibilities, gendered restrictions on digital access, weakened contact with teachers, and heightened exposure to early marriage discussions; reported family conversations about marriage increased from 2% in 2021 to 20% in 2022. sibling relationships, particularly girls' accounts of brothers' authority over household labor and phone access, revealed how broader gender norms were enacted within everyday family interactions. at the same time, peer relationships, teacher recognition, memories of residential school life, and educational aspirations sustained girls' connection to school despite prolonged physical absence. girls consistently contrasted school as a space of relational connection, agency, and future possibility with home environments characterized by greater gendered constraints. the findings demonstrate that school belonging during crisis is dynamically produced across individual, relational, structural, and temporal contexts and underscore the importance of gender‐transformative approaches to educational continuity and post‐crisis recovery. journal of research on adolescence

facial emotion recognition in gifted children: an early phase advantage? the literature suggests that gifted children outperform peers in information-processing tasks. also, research shows that facial emotion recognition accuracy is affected by expression intensity, which can be depicted as different amounts of information available for the observer during the emotion recognition process. to test if an information-processing advantage for gifted children also exists in the emotional domain, in this study we compared gifted children’s and a control peer group’s performance on dynamic facial emotion recognition as expressed at different intensity levels (40–100%). participants (7–11 years old) completed an emotional recognition task involving six basic emotions (anger, disgust, fear, happiness, sadness and surprise) presented as morphed videoclips. a strong positive correlation between age and general accuracy was found within the whole sample, confirming that the ability develops progressively as children mature. results indicated that the gifted group shows significantly higher accuracy on disgust and surprise recognition. an interaction effect group by intensity level was found, with the gifted group reporting significantly better performance in accuracy at low intensity (40%) compared to controls, indicating that their advantage in information-processing may be more detectable in the early phase of emotion expression, despite the emotion’s type. future studies are needed to clarify the nature of these results. journal of intelligence

trait cross-cultural curiosity: its measurement and relation to inclusive values, inclusive behaviors, and intergroup contact abstract what motivates people to commit themselves to cultural inclusiveness? building on intergroup emotions theory and prior research on the dispositional correlates of inclusiveness, we propose that a stable tendency to be curious about other cultures could motivate inclusiveness. we conducted two studies to develop a measure of trait cross-cultural curiosity and test this prediction. this measure proved to be reliable. as hypothesized, it was related to universalist values, open-mindedness (especially its tolerance facet), positive cross-cultural contact, and collective action intentions. it predicted these forms of cross-cultural engagement above and beyond other aspects of trait curiosity. also consistent with predictions, it was related to appraising cross-cultural interactions as novel, complex, but also comprehensible. finally, it mediated the effect of these cross-cultural appraisals on positive contact and activist intentions. although causal conclusions cannot be made based on these initial studies, they nonetheless lay the groundwork for research on a potential catalyst for change. motivation and emotion

the perceived suitability of digitally delivered impulse‐focused techniques in binge eating: a qualitative intervention development study abstract objective impulsivity and inhibitory control difficulties are key mechanisms in binge eating behaviour in individuals with eating disorders. digital interventions targeting these mechanisms are primarily developed for weight loss rather than the specific psychological and clinical needs of the population with binge eating, creating a gap in treatment. this study explored lived experience perceptions of digitally delivered impulse‐focused techniques to inform future intervention development. method fourteen participants (2 males, 12 females) were recruited via social media for online semi‐structured interviews. participants viewed a short demonstration video of an existing impulse‐focused dietary change intervention (impulsepal) and discussed the perceived suitability of its techniques for binge eating contexts. data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. results three overarching themes were generated regarding the perceived suitability and potential risks of digitally delivered impulse‐focused techniques; designing for accessibility, personalisation, and supportive communication; and unmet needs extending beyond impulse management, including connection, reflection, and self‐awareness. initial guiding principles for future digital intervention development in binge eating contexts are presented. conclusions with careful adaptation, an impulse‐focused intervention like impulsepal could complement existing support pathways, but further development and feasibility testing are required before wider testing or use in people with binge eating. european eating disorders review

high school contexts and stem career pathways: math self-efficacy, teacher diversity, and student–teacher race matching guided by social cognitive career theory, this study examined how relational and structural school contexts were associated with postsecondary stem major choice. using nationally representative, time-lagged data from els:2002, we tested whether student–teacher racial matching in high school was linked to stem major selection 4 years later through math self-efficacy, math achievement, and perceptions of student–teacher relationships, while accounting for school-level teacher racial diversity. multilevel structural equation modeling showed that racial matching was not directly associated with stem major choice but was indirectly associated through math achievement, including a serial pathway through math self-efficacy and achievement. teacher racial diversity was positively associated with stem major selection and moderated the math self-efficacy–stem choice association. exploratory analyses indicated that the racial-matching association with stem major choice varied across racial/ethnic groups. findings highlight the importance of integrating interpersonal and institutional contexts in understanding stem pathway development. journal of career development

from past to present: the roles of attachment and social support in buffering lifetime adversity and intergenerational trauma abstract adverse childhood experiences (aces) predict greater adulthood adversity and offspring trauma exposure. nurturing relationships (for example, with friends, family members, and romantic partners) have been shown to protect against negative health outcomes of aces during adulthood, but less is known regarding their capacity to buffer continuity in adversity over the lifespan and across generations. the current study examined whether adult attachment security and social support moderated the associations between a parent’s history of aces, adulthood adversity, and children’s early adversity. data were drawn from a longitudinal study of early social-emotional development in a socioeconomically diverse community sample ( n = 205 parent-child dyads; parents 94.1% female, 69.3% white/non-hispanic; 14.2% at or below federal poverty line). at t1 (children aged 1–2 years), parents self-reported their ace history, completed a semi-structured interview on social support, and participated in a story stem task assessing attachment security. at t2 (children aged 3–4 years), parents reported on recent adversity and their child’s exposure to adversity. findings showed parental aces were positively associated with adulthood adversity and children’s early adversity. social support significantly moderated these associations, rendering them non-significant at above-average levels of support. planned follow-up analyses revealed similar patterns for emotional and instrumental support, although instrumental support did not significantly buffer the association between parental aces and children’s early adversity. attachment security did not moderate any of the examined associations. findings suggest that enhancing social support may be a promising strategy for preventionefforts designed to disrupt continuity of adversity and foster parent-child dyad well-being. adversity and resilience science

validación de la escala de temores económicos en contextos de incertidumbre en psicólogos y psicólogas de chile las sociedades actuales se encuentran en constante riesgo debido al aumento de amenazas producidas por las sociedades postmodernas. este aumento en el nivel de incertidumbre, y su relación con el aumento del miedo, tiene un efecto importante en los procesos de racionalidad al momento de determinar una acción económica. la presente investigación tuvo como objetivo validar la escala de temores económicos en contextos de incertidumbre en psicólogos y psicólogas chilenas. se recurrió a un diseño no experimental transversal de alcance instrumental bajo un enfoque cuantitativo. por medio de un muestreo no probabilístico por conveniencia, se utilizó una muestra de 994 participantes. los datos fueron sometidos a análisis factorial exploratorio y confirmatorio para identificar su estructura interna. los resultados dan cuenta de una estructura unifactorial con adecuados índices de bondad de ajuste. se hace necesario replicar estos hallazgos en poblaciones con diferentes características y en otros contextos. acta colombiana de psicologia

impact of mood and neurocognitive diagnosis on california verbal learning test intrusions, repetitions and recognition abstract mood symptoms, including both depression and anxiety, have been shown to have differential patterns on neuropsychological test results. specific patterns of mood impacting the outcomes of the california verbal learning test (cvlt) have not been fully explored, especially as they may interact with cognitive diagnoses. this study analysed data from 402 adult participants across two sites who underwent outpatient neuropsychological assessment. specific analyses included whether the interaction between depression symptomatology with cognitive diagnosis (no diagnosis, mild neurocognitive disorder, or major neurocognitive disorder) was associated with cvlt repetition, intrusions, recognition hits and recognition false positives covarying for age, gender, education and site. these analyses were then repeated for the interaction between anxiety symptomatology and cognitive diagnosis. results identified patterns of predictability, with significant interactions between depression and cognitive diagnosis predicting intrusion errors ( β = −11.770, p < .001) and false positive errors ( β = −3.942, p = .006), such that significant depression symptoms and a cognitive diagnosis were associated with fewer intrusion and false positive errors. there were also main effects for depression predicting recognition hits ( β = −.664, p = .005), cognitive diagnosis predicting recognition hits ( β = −1.273, p < .001; β = −.813, p = .002) and anxiety predicting repetition errors ( β = −.896, p = .044). these results show potential patterns for clinicians to analyse in their patient populations to help differentiate whether cognitive diagnosis, mood symptomatology and/or an interaction between the two may be present for their patients. journal of neuropsychology

a two-stage approach to detecting differential item functioning: combining regularization with the mantel–haenszel method (reg-mh) 检测项目功能差异的两阶段方法：正则化与mantel–haenszel法的结合（reg-mh） test bias is a critical concern in educational and psychological measurement. differential item functioning (dif) is widely used to identify potential test bias. although regularization methods have shown promise in dif detection, interpreting the resulting dif parameters remains challenging. this study proposes a two-stage approach, termed reg-mh, that combines regularization with the mantel–haenszel (mh) method. specifically, regularization is first used to select anchor items, followed by mh testing to identify dif items, combining the anchor selection advantages of regularization with the interpretability of mh. a pilot simulation study examined alternative regularization-based anchor selection strategies and the number of anchor items. a main simulation study evaluated the performance of reg-mh against traditional mh and regularized dif (reg-dif) methods across varying sample sizes, dif magnitudes, dif proportions, and ability distributions. an empirical illustration using pisa 2012 data further demonstrated its practical application. the simulation results showed that reg-mh generally achieved a more favorable balance between type i error control and statistical power than the competing methods. compared with traditional mh, reg-mh reduced type i error rates while maintaining higher statistical power than reg-dif. type i error rates generally increased with sample size, dif magnitude, and dif proportion, whereas statistical power increased with sample size and dif magnitude but decreased as dif proportion increased. overall, reg-mh provides a promising approach to dif detection by integrating regularization-based anchor selection with conventional statistical testing. applied psychological measurement

consider an alternative: mitigating anchoring effects in professional judges’ sentencing decisions abstract we investigate the impact of a cognitive intervention on the anchoring effect in the context of criminal justice, where public prosecutors’ sentencing recommendations influence judicial decisions. we predicted that prompting judges to engage in more deliberative thinking about the prosecutor’s demand would reduce its influence on sentencing decisions. we conducted an experiment on french professional judges ( n = 139) where they evaluated a criminal case in which the prosecutor’s sentencing demands served as anchors. as expected, we found judges exhibited an anchoring effect: they pronounced more severe sentences after high (vs. low) demands from the prosecutor. the cognitive intervention consisted in asking judges to consider an alternative, that is, to generate arguments supporting both the proposed sentence and an opposite (lower or higher) sentence. this intervention substantially reduced the anchoring effect. these findings suggest that judges may rely on the prosecutor’s demands when making sentencing decisions but can be prompted to engage in more deliberative processing. although these findings should be considered exploratory given the use of a single vignette and the incomplete randomization of experimental conditions across sessions, they suggest that prompting judges to consider alternative sentencing arguments may help reduce the influence of anchoring on judicial decisions. such simple, effective procedural safeguards may help courts promote fair sentencing. cognitive research-principles and implications

ethnicity‐ and gender‐based social stressors and parental socialization in korean chinese adolescent adjustment abstract although extensive research has documented the adverse effects of social stressors, such as ethnicity‐ and gender‐based discrimination, on adolescent development, much of this work has focused on western contexts. this survey study was conducted with 267 korean chinese adolescents (59% female; m age = 15.24 years, sd age = 1.66, age range: 12–18 years), examining how three forms of perceived discrimination linked to adolescents' psychosocial and academic adjustment, as well as the roles of parental socialization practices. perceived discrimination by south koreans, but not by han chinese, was linked to more depressive symptoms and delinquency. gender nonconformity teasing was associated with more depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation. parental cultural socialization was associated with lower suicidal ideation and delinquency and higher school attachment. parental gender norm socialization was positively associated with school attachment. these findings underscore the negative implications of ethnicity‐ and gender‐based discrimination, highlight the positive developmental correlates of parental cultural socialization, and suggest that parental gender norm socialization might serve a context‐specific adaptive function. british journal of developmental psychology

what is gratitude? a qualitative analysis of gratitude for a culturally sensitive understanding with brazilians research on gratitude, conducted mainly in the global north, may not adequately capture the nuances of the phenomenon in other cultures. this qualitative study investigated the manifestations and meanings of gratitude in a group of brazilian adults. through semi-structured interviews with 19 participants, content analysis revealed that gratitude is a multidimensional phenomenon, encompassing emotional, cognitive-reflective, behavioural, social-relational, and existential/transcendental facets. participants situated gratitude collectively and existentially, addressing it not only to benefactors and the divine but also to life, nature, and society, and experienced it in adversity as a way of reframing loss. in some accounts gratitude arose in the act of giving rather than in receiving a benefit. its opposite was described not as the mere absence of gratitude but as a distinct phenomenon, encompassing indifference, rejection, and failures of empathy with their own relational costs. these findings underscore the need for theoretical models that incorporate a culturally sensitive perspective, capable of capturing the complexity of gratitude in diverse social contexts. culture & psychology

development and validation of the visual stress scale (vss) in a parent sample abstract single-item measures offer a low-burden alternative to the lengthy questionnaires typically used to assess parental stress. for single-item measures, graphical formats using pictorial or metaphor-based illustrations have been recommended; however, no such graphic single-item instrument currently exists for assessing stress. we therefore developed the visual stress scale (vss). convergent, and concurrent validity, as well as test–retest reliability of the vss, were examined in a sample of 329 parents in germany using two online surveys with a two-week retest interval. the vss correlated positively with established stress measures (parenting stress index: r = .44–.55; perceived stress questionnaire1. by convention, correlation coefficients and other measures that take values between 0 and 1 are reported without a leading zero before the decimal point. i have therefore removed the leading zeros for now.2. a few extra spaces have inadvertently been introduced, but unfortunately, i am unable to remove them.: r = .66, dass-21 stress subscale: r = .68) and showed a strong loading alongside the psq items in the one-factor model (λ = .62, all p s < .001). higher vss scores were associated with higher depression ( r = .67) and anxiety ( r = .43), and with lower well-being ( r = –.63) and perceived social support ( r = –.37; all p s < .001). test–retest reliability was moderate among participants successfully matched across the two measurement time points ( icc (2,1) = .56, p < .001). the exploratory factor analysis provided preliminary insights into how the vss relates to different aspects of parental stress within abidin’s framework [1]. overall, the findings provide initial evidence for the convergence of the vss with established stress measures, its two-week temporal stability, and its expected associations with theoretically related constructs. the vss may be particularly useful in high-burden settings. further research is needed to examine its discriminant validity, particularly whether it assesses stress specifically or reflects broader psychological distress, and to evaluate its psychometric properties using different study designs and populations. discover psychology

increasing productive communications statements in esports players abstract esports is a rapidly expanding competitive domain in which effective team communication is frequently identified as a critical determinant of performance, especially within the video game, league of legends. although applied behavior analysis (aba) has extensively targeted communication in clinical populations, and organizational behavior management (obm) has addressed communication in workplace settings, communication in esports has yet to be experimentally evaluated as behavior for change. the present study evaluated the effects of an obm intervention package (task clarification, verbal and graphic feedback, and goal setting) on rates of productive in‐game communication among members of a collegiate league of legends team. a concurrent multiple baseline design across four participants was used. the results showed increases in rates of productive communication, relative to baseline, across all four participants. these findings extend obm applications to esports and demonstrate that team‐based communication in competitive gaming environments can be defined as specific behaviors, objectively measured, and improved using obm techniques. significance for behavioral interventions in esports and future research are discussed. behavioral interventions
