scam compliance and nonsexual grooming: a scoping review of qualitative and quantitative evidence in scam compliance research, grooming for financial exploitation is often unexplored or undefined. the purpose of this scoping review was to provide a comprehensive overview of the etiology of nonsexual grooming in relational scams, focusing on definitions and frameworks, perpetrator behaviors, victim warning signs, and study methods, design, and discipline. a scoping review was performed on literature published between 2012 and 2025 in the following academic databases: scopus, pubmed, google scholar, proquest, and sage. the search was conducted for all scam-related literature regarding financial grooming, with key terms including definitions, predictors, persuasion techniques, perpetrator and/or victim perspectives, susceptibility, theories and/or models, and warning signs. studies were included if they investigated financial grooming in online cases of romance fraud, investment fraud, or romance baiting. scams that did not involve grooming, that is, phishing scams or face-to-face schemes, were excluded. this review found no scam-specific definition of grooming that encompassed all relational scams. most studies reported on grooming behaviors and techniques typically observed in romance scams, with few studies investigating investment fraud and romance baiting. victim warning signs were mentioned minimally and often in the context of domestic violence. researchers in criminology using qualitative methods dominate the field of scam compliance, and although several studies drew upon cyberpsychological concepts, there was no explicit mention of cyberpsychology as a discipline. in conclusion, there is a need for an evidence-informed, clearer discourse on financial grooming, with cyberpsychology being in a unique position to address this gap in scam compliance research. cyberpsychology behavior and social networking

honesty: conceptualization, assessment, prediction, and processes the present virtual special issue (vsi) focuses on honesty, a construct of foundational importance for social life that remains conceptually and empirically challenging because it spans partially overlapping components (e.g., truthfulness and non-exploitation) and is inherently difficult to measure using self-reports. the seven contributions in this vsi advance three intertwined aims. first, they sharpen conceptualization and assessment by contrasting honesty-as-non-exploitation with honesty-as-truthfulness and by introducing complementary measurement approaches, including new truthfulness scales and a psycholexically grounded adjective checklist. second, they consolidate evidence on the prediction of (dis)honest behavior, showing robust associations with broad moral versus exploitative trait dispositions and clarifying limited incremental value of several adjacent trait measures in cheating paradigms. third, they move beyond prediction to processes by testing when and why trait–dishonesty links emerge, highlighting the roles of justifications, motive-relevant contexts, and sensitivity to sanctions. overall, this vsi advances our understanding of honesty by integrating conceptual and assessment precision, predictive research, and process-oriented inquiries into a cohesive research agenda that defines the next generation of honesty research from a personality perspective. european journal of personality

crowded minds, ordered designs: how social crowding shapes aesthetic preferences abstract social crowding is a common daily experience that shapes visual preferences. prior research has focused on isolated, low‐level processing visual features (e.g., shape and boundary), with less attention to integrated, high‐level processing visual aesthetics. this research examines how social crowding influences visual aesthetic preferences across three preregistered studies using real‐life dining scenarios, images, and videos, and employing stimuli including food plating, light bulbs, and promotional posters. a field study (study 1a) and an online study (study 1b) show that social crowding increases preferences for classical rather than expressive aesthetics. study 2 demonstrates that the need for order explains this effect. study 3 shows that group type further moderates this pattern: social crowding enhances classical aesthetic preferences when people are surrounded by out‐groups but increases expressive aesthetic preferences when they are surrounded by in‐groups. these findings provide meaningful implications for visual communication strategies. journal of applied social psychology

when team members perceive alike—or do not: the role of dispersion in social emergent states for team performance abstract research on teams most often presumes that team members converge on a common view of their social environment, so empirical work has largely relied on mean‐level approaches to examine how social variables predict team performance. the present study posits that within‐team disparity in social emergent states provides important information beyond team mean levels by not only directly influencing team performance but also moderating the relationships of mean‐level social team aspects with leader‐rated team performance. in addition, we examined whether teams cluster into qualitatively different dispersion profiles. data were collected from 838 employees nested within 156 teams. results showed that the relative variance of psychological safety climate and the skewness of team trust were associated with leader‐rated team performance beyond mean‐level effects. additionally, the relative variance of psychological safety climate and the skewness of distributive justice, as well as team trust, moderated the relationships with team performance. in particular, the positive relationships between these social emergent states and team performance were stronger when skewness was more negative. moreover, hierarchical cluster analysis indicated distinct dispersion patterns consistent with existing theoretical assumptions, highlighting the importance of within‐team distributions for informing organizational interventions. journal of applied social psychology

“saying ‘i love you’ with icons”: imagined communication and the relational production of digital offerings this paper explores the motivations, ritual practices, and cultural meanings of digital offerings on chinese virtual memorials. drawing on four years of online observation, auto-ethnography, and in-depth interviews, it finds digital offerings feature distinctive persistence, traceability, networked circulation and personalization. these affordances reshape mourning into an individualized, frequent, and flexible mediated practice, foregrounding mourner ’ s agency. their circulation transforms private grief into a networked relational practice that challenges the utilitarian logic of traditional rituals. in this process, digital offerings and virtual memorials function as collective coping mechanisms, enabling bereaved parents to form affective communities grounded in shared trauma. meanwhile, they are embedded in the digital economy of symbolic goods, producing intersections between emotional expression, affective labor, and commercial logics. overall, as a mediated relational practice, digital offerings facilitate self-healing and filial piety while fostering connective mourning and social support networks, offering new possibilities for emotional communication and relationship building in china. omega-journal of death and dying

parental stress and parent–child dyadic outcomes in preterm populations: a systematic review and meta-analysis abstract objective despite established theoretical links between parental stress and parent–child dyadic functioning, no systematic review has examined these associations in preterm samples. we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on associations between parental stress and dyadic outcomes across the first year of life with preterm parent–child dyads. methods four databases were searched through may 2026 (inplasy #2025110019). eligible studies assessed parental stress and parent–child dyadic outcomes in preterm samples within the first year of life. effects were synthesized based on the timing of stress and dyadic outcome measurement. parental stress was categorized into four types [parenting, neonatal intensive care unit (nicu)-specific, general, and perceived social support] and dyadic outcomes were categorized into three types (caregiving quality, dyadic coordination, and attachment). risk of bias/certainty of evidence was assessed. results thirty-four studies were included (n = 3,079 dyads). a significant small association between parental stress and dyadic outcomes was found during nicu hospitalization (r = −.20; low heterogeneity) and at 0–6 months corrected age (r = −.11) postdischarge. no reliable association was found at 7–12 months corrected age. conclusions parental stress is most reliably linked to dyadic functioning when measured concurrently during nicu hospitalization and did not reliably predict postdischarge dyadic outcomes. parenting stress and caregiving quality showed the most consistent associations descriptively, though differences across stress types were not statistically supported. findings suggest that the nicu stay may be an important period for supporting dyadic functioning, with attention to parenting stress and moment-to-moment caregiver responsiveness. journal of pediatric psychology

when risk lies in inaction: age differences in protective intervention during sequential health‐risk decisions abstract adolescent risk research often reports elevated risk‐taking in active, reward‐salient contexts, but age differences vary across tasks and domains. we examined age differences in protective sequential decisions in which delaying action can carry potential cost. a total of 277 consenting participants (224 adolescents and 53 adults; age recorded categorically), recruited through uk school, parent, and teacher networks, evaluated hypothetical health scenarios unfolding across up to five stages. at each reached stage, they chose whether to continue monitoring or seek help; the first help‐seeking response defined the intervention threshold. the primary analysis used a standardized presentation of symptoms, experimental urgency scores, and a visual bar. adolescents intervened in 98.9% of analyzable scenarios, compared with 94.7% for adults. among scenarios with an observed intervention, adolescents acted at lower experimental urgency scores ( m = 14.37 vs. 18.22) and earlier steps ( m = 2.66 vs. 3.32). a discrete‐time logistic model estimated with participant‐clustered generalized estimating equations (gee) showed higher adolescent intervention odds at the analytical reference urgency of 12 (or = 8.45, 95% ci [4.53, 15.76]). model‐predicted probabilities at a reached stage with this urgency were 74.0% and 26.6%, respectively. lower adolescent thresholds in this protective task highlight the value of testing developmental age patterns across decision contexts while specifying what the available actions represent. journal of research on adolescence

cognitive regulation in generative ai use: a network study of anxiety and dependence among foreign language majors anxiety accompanying students’ reliance on generative ai has been linked to appraisals of their own competence and to comparison with peers, two complementary routes usually modeled separately. this study asked which nodes retain conditional associations with ai-related anxiety and dependence when both routes are modeled together. survey responses from 283 foreign language majors formed a 17-node regularized partial correlation network, supplemented by written responses from 21 students. social-comparison anxiety was the only anxiety node connected with dependence (partial r = 0.177, 95% bootstrap interval [0.077, 0.280]); exploratory facet analyses located it mainly in fear of falling behind or missing out, less consistently in peer competence pressure, and not in upward comparison. the three measured self-appraisal nodes, which assessed broad confidence, were unrelated to anxiety conditionally and at the zero-order level. the dependence association was modest, had no resolved direction, and was retained only in the fourth-year network; no cohort difference was established, and study year was confounded with collection period. written responses did not corroborate this association but revealed integrity boundaries, guilt, and redefined language competence, which the survey omitted. the findings identify candidate correlates of reliance that require replication in independent samples, and content missing from ai anxiety instruments. journal of intelligence

problematic smartphone use and academic well-being in adolescents: emotion dysregulation and metacognitive self-regulation in a cross-sectional serial mediation model background: problematic smartphone use is associated with poorer student outcomes, but the regulatory processes involved remain unclear, and emotional and metacognitive regulation have rarely been modelled together. objective: to test whether emotion dysregulation and metacognitive self-regulation statistically account for the association between problematic smartphone use and academic well-being in adolescents, in parallel or in series. methods: in this cross-sectional study, 471 adolescents aged 12–18 (56.1% girls) from i̇stanbul, enrolled in state or private secondary schools, were recruited through convenience and snowball sampling and completed self-report measures. a latent serial mediation model (10,000 bootstrap resamples) controlled for age, gender, school type, and daily smartphone use, and was re-estimated with the mediator order reversed. results: scalar measurement invariance held across gender and school type. problematic smartphone use was associated with greater emotion dysregulation (β = 0.412), which was associated with lower metacognitive self-regulation (β = −0.281), the strongest correlate of academic well-being (β = 0.386). the total indirect effect (β = −0.200; 68% of the total association) was independent of order, but specific effects were not: the emotion dysregulation pathway was largest when entered first (β = −0.104) and the metacognitive pathway was largest when entered first (β = −0.096). the serial pathway was smallest in both orders. school burnout showed a similar pattern, with reversed signs. conclusions: the mediators statistically accounted for most of the association, but these cross-sectional data cannot establish their order or which pathway dominates; metacognitive instruction as an independent intervention target is a hypothesis for longitudinal research. journal of intelligence

development of cognitive processes in l2 reading comprehension: a longitudinal bayesian knowledge tracing study of chinese efl university students understanding how the cognitive processes underlying second language (l2) reading comprehension change over time is crucial for characterizing reading development among english as a foreign language (efl) learners. guided by kintsch’s construction–integration (c-i) model and complex dynamic systems theory (cdst), this study examines the development of four cognitive processes in reading comprehension in terms of longitudinal changes in their estimated mastery: extracting explicit information, interpreting and rephrasing information, making inferences, and synthesizing information across text. data from 303 undergraduate efl learners across three semesters were analyzed using bayesian knowledge tracing (bkt), with item difficulty incorporated to improve the estimation of process mastery. the results showed differentiated trajectories of estimated mastery across the four processes. extracting explicit information and making inferences showed increases in estimated mastery, whereas interpreting and rephrasing information and synthesizing information across text changed more slowly. cluster analysis further identified four learner profiles based on estimated mastery changes (early decliners, moderate maintainers, imbalanced performers, and advanced achievers), highlighting substantial variability in efl reading development. these findings advance understanding of l2 reading comprehension by showing that component cognitive processes follow differentiated and heterogeneous trajectories over time, and also demonstrating the utility of bkt for tracing process-level changes from longitudinal item-response data. journal of intelligence

experiencing the queer collective through time: exploring perceptions of cultural and historical continuity among lgbtq + emerging adults abstract objective using a pre‐registered explanatory sequential mixed method design, we examined collective continuity , which until now has been studied in populations where its transmission is assumed to occur naturally via familial and cultural engagement. we examined collective continuity among lgbtq+ emerging adults for whom access to the culture and history of the collective is not always available. method study 1 in study 1, we examined associations across three measures of collective continuity and their associations with lgbtq+ identity and well‐being in college and community samples of emerging adults ( n = 246). results study 1 we found little association between the measures of collective continuity, modest associations between collective continuity and lgbtq+ identity, and no relations between collective continuity and well‐being. method study 2 given the lack of empirical overlap in measures of collective continuity, in study 2 we employed a qualitative interview approach ( n = 8) to provide greater descriptive data on the phenomenon. results study 2 these analyses revealed a lack of collective continuity and highlighted unique factors that facilitate or forestall the development of collective continuity among lgbtq+ people, distinguishing this process from other groups (e.g., ethnic and national) in important ways. conclusion together, these findings provide the opportunity for theoretical refinement and expansion of collective continuity. journal of personality

the development and initial validation of the mentoring engagement scale abstract professional mentoring is a potential protective factor against burnout and stress in school counselors. however, existing mentoring measures are limited by weak development procedures, inconsistent psychometric support, and limited practical use. we sought to develop and evaluate the mentoring engagement scale (mes), a self‐report instrument designed to measure a person's level of engagement in receiving professional mentoring, among a sample of us school counselors. the research was conducted in two studies. in the first study, content validity was assessed using lawshe's quantitative approach to capture expert evaluation of item essentialness. the refined scale was then administered to a sample of 324 practicing us school counselors. exploratory factor analyses revealed a two‐factor structure— investment and impact —accounting for 64.2% of variance. mes scores demonstrated strong internal consistency and evidence of response validity. these findings provide initial support for the mes as a measure of school counselors’ mentoring engagement. journal of counseling and development

psychometric properties of the international trauma questionnaire–child and adolescent version (itq-ca) among portuguese adolescents from the community. objective: the international trauma questionnaire (itq) was developed to assessposttraumatic stress disorder (ptsd) and complex ptsd. although extensively validated in adults across diverse contexts, evidence for the child and adolescent version (itq-ca) is still limited. few studies have examined its latent structure or validity in youth, and none have validated it in portuguese adolescents. moreover, measurement invariance across sex has not yet been established in this age group, despite documented sex differences in trauma exposure and symptom expression. this study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the itq-ca in portuguese adolescents by testing factorial structure, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, and measurement invariance across sex.
method: a school-based sample of 530 adolescents (11-16 years) completed the itq-ca and measures of trauma exposure, ptsd symptoms, emotion dysregulation, and resilience. confirmatory factor analyses compared four latent structures and tested measurement invariance across sex (configural, metric, scalar). convergent and discriminant validity were assessed using average variance extracted and composite reliability and pearson correlations.
results: the correlated six-factor model showed the best fit. full configural, metric, and scalar invariance supported cross-sex comparability. convergent validity was adequate, and discriminant validity was supported by the fornell-larcker criterion and external patterns, with disturbances in self-organization factors showing stronger associations with dysregulation and resilience than ptsd factors. internal consistency was acceptable to good.
conclusions: the itq-ca is a reliable, valid, and sex-invariant measure ofptsd and disturbances in self-organization in portuguese adolescents, with practical utility for research and rapid screening in schools and community services. the polish version of the survey of autobiographical memory (sam): factor structure and psychometric evaluation the present study evaluated the psychometric properties of the polish version of the(sam) as a self-report measure of perceived recollective capacity. we examined its reliability, tested several competing structural models, and assessed convergent validity with the(art). confirmatory factor analyses indicated that neither a one-factor nor an orthogonal four-factor model provided an adequate fit to the data. in contrast, the correlated four-factor solution - comprising episodic, semantic, spatial, and future components - offered the best representation of the data, replicating the original structure reported in prior validations. correlations among subscales showed that the episodic, future, and semantic dimensions shared substantial variance, whereas spatial memory was relatively distinct. convergent validity analyses revealed that the episodic and future subscales were most strongly associated with art indices of vividness, coherence, imagery, and scene construction, consistent with theoretical models emphasising shared constructive processes in remembering and imagining. overall, the polish sam demonstrated robust psychometric properties and strong theoretical coherence with contemporary accounts of autobiographical memory, providing a valid and reliable tool for assessing individual differences in the perceived richness and organisation of personal memories. memory

expert aspects of studying parental attitudes and parenting styles in legal disputes between parents regarding child upbringing context and relevance. the steady increase in the number of complex forensic psychological and psychiatric examinations (cfpe) in parental disputes over child custody places high demands on the methodological unity and categorical consistency of expert opinions. despite the commonality of the terminology used, the content of many key psychological concepts is vague and allows for various interpretations, which is unacceptable for legal psychology and highlights the need for a review of their content and expert significance. goal. identification of the components of the psychological concepts "parental attitudes", "parental position", and "educational style" that are significant for expert analysis. theoretical approaches. the principles of forensic clinical and psychological expertise are used. results. the article considers scientific approaches to the study of parental attitudes, positions, and styles, and substantiates the ineffectiveness of using various models of parental position for expert practice due to the danger of replacing individual specifics with template constructs with evaluative nominations. the article analyzes and summarizes the components of the above-mentioned psychological categories that are significant for the expert qualification of the features of parental position and parenting approaches of adult subjects in this specific type of ksppe. conclusion. the study made it possible to identify and organize psychological indicators that reveal the content of integral psychological formations, which can be used to analyze and evaluate the parental position, attitudes, and parenting styles in an informative, individualized, and evidence-based manner. psychology and law

joint trajectories of positive affect and negative affect during the college transition: a parallel-process latent class growth analysis positive affect (pa) and negative affect (na) are related but distinct dimensions of affective experience during the transition to college. examining their joint trajectories and the factors associated with these patterns may clarify heterogeneity in affective change during the college transition. this three-wave longitudinal study followed first-year students from two universities in northwestern china over six months (baseline n = 583, initial m age = 18.04, sd = 0.76; 69.6% female). pa and na were assessed at each wave, whereas internet addiction (ia) and self-concept clarity (scc) were assessed only at baseline. parallel-process latent class growth analysis with full-information maximum likelihood identified four joint trajectory classes: moderate pa–decreasing na (47.86%), high pa–low na (25.04%), increasing pa–decreasing na (10.63%), and moderate pa–increasing na (16.47%). relative to the high pa–low na class, higher ia was associated with greater odds of membership in each of the other three classes, whereas higher scc was associated with lower odds of membership in those classes. contrary to expectation, the association between ia and membership in the moderate pa–decreasing na and increasing pa–decreasing na classes was stronger at higher levels of scc. these findings reveal heterogeneous affective trajectories during the college transition and underscore the value of considering pa and na jointly in understanding affective change. emerging adulthood

religion, spirituality, and mental health: comparative insights from western and chinese contexts for spiritual care in china cultural context shapes how religion and spirituality are understood in relation to mental health and incorporated into clinical care. this review critically compares the interplay between religion, spirituality, and mental health in western (primarily north american and european) and chinese contexts. synthesizing english-language literature with a chronological analysis of chinese-language studies, it examines how cultural, philosophical, and sociopolitical factors shape understandings of belief and mental illness, particularly psychosis, where spiritual experiences may overlap with symptoms. western paradigms emphasize duality, viewing faith as either a coping resource or a risk, and have developed professionalized spiritual care through hospital chaplaincy and biopsychosocial-spiritual models. in contrast, chinese research has evolved from portraying “superstition” as a barrier to psychiatric treatment in the 1990s to recognizing spirituality amid modernization. influenced by diffuse forms of religious life and traditions such as confucianism, daoism, and buddhism, and holistic concepts such as shen in traditional chinese medicine, early chinese research emphasized family- and community-oriented help-seeking and external behavioral factors. comparative analysis reveals shared quests for meaning, hope, and connection, alongside differences in institutional versus diffuse religion, individual versus collective orientations, internal processes versus external barriers, and culturally shaped experiences. the review advocates culturally syntonic spiritual care in china through thoughtful localization of western models. recommendations include clinician training in cultural humility, integration of indigenous approaches such as chinese traditional culture therapy and buddhist/daoist mindfulness, family-inclusive interventions, and policy, institutional, and clinical integration. future research should empirically evaluate culturally adapted interventions for chinese populations. health psychology research

maternal meaning-making under uncertainty in xiaohongshu autism-related narratives background: parenting an autistic child can involve uncertainty about educational pathways, family responsibilities, and personal continuity. objective: this study examines how self-identified chinese mothers of autistic children negotiate these concerns through serial xiaohongshu narratives and associated comments. methods: this interpretive qualitative analysis combined meaning-making theory with narrative and positioning perspectives. the corpus comprised 416 posts from seven maternal accounts and 6,826 first-level comments collected manually from xiaohongshu. the posts and comments were published between march 2024 and december 2025. reflexive thematic interpretation considered narrative episodes, within-account sequences, and responses attached to posts. results: seven connected themes concerned recurrent disruption of developmental futures; love moralized as debt and intensive action; oscillation between collapse, hope, and provisional acceptance; redefinition of progress through relational micro-events; peer recognition and experiential expertise; a contested comment ecology that validated, disciplined, stigmatized, or commercialized mothers; and reclamation of a self beyond caregiving. conclusion: meaning-making emerged as a continuing negotiation of anticipated futures, maternal responsibility, and personal identity, shaped by relationships within and beyond the family. these findings may inform further research into caregiver support, the moral expectations associated with care, and the quality of guidance circulating in online communities. health psychology research

early childhood development in rural china: caregiver‐child relationships and parenting behaviours among parents and grandparents abstract in impoverished rural china, grandparents often serve as primary caregivers for children separated from their parents, but how their parenting quality compares to that of non‐migrant parents remains unclear. this study compared caregiver‐child relationships and parenting behaviours between parents and grandparents, examining their impacts on child development. participants included 546 han chinese children aged 0–3 years (m age = 20.38 months, sd = 9.27; 50.2% girls) and their primary caregivers from rural china. among them, 237 children without parent–child separation were raised by parents, while 309 children experiencing parent–child separation were raised by grandparents. the results indicated no significant differences between parent–child and grandparent–child relationships ( t = −1.06, p = 0.290), but there were significant differences in some parenting behaviours between parents and grandparents. the path analysis model indicated that in the parent‐cared group, parent–child relationship predicted children's personal‐social skills, and parental acceptance predicted personal‐social and problem‐solving skills; in the grandparent‐cared group, grandparents' acceptance predicted all five developmental domains, and punitive behaviour also positively predicted personal‐social skills. multiple‐group analysis indicated significant between‐group differences in these predictive effects (δs‐bχ 2 = 62.31, δdf = 35, p = 0.003). these findings highlight the importance of assessing different caregiving contexts and provide crucial evidence for targeted early interventions. infant and child development

towards decolonising mental health in india: perspectives, challenges and the way forward the existing theories and models of mental health have been criticised for being somewhat ambiguous, imposing eurocentric values, and thus perpetuating coloniality. this calls for the need to decolonise mental health and well-being to appreciate the ‘other (indigenous) ways’ of knowing and doing. our particular concern here is with how decolonising mental health and well-being is understood (or misunderstood) and its implications for an indian approach to healing. building on previous literature, we make three related arguments. first, the ambiguity surrounding the concept of mental health demands critical inquiry of the very concept, and the decolonial framework enables us to challenge eurocentric or western perspectives on psychological healthcare. second, there is a greater need now to think in terms of decolonising mental health. here, we develop our argument along the lines of the foucauldian idea of governmentality and the marxist-derived concept of necessary false consciousness . third, there is a unique indian way of looking at health and well-being that has been invalidated as pseudo- or non-science under colonial rule. here, we elaborate on an indian approach to health and well-being, contesting some of the problematic assumptions of western constructions. this is followed by how the decolonial project of mental health and well-being, especially in the indian context, looks like and the possible challenges the psychology fraternity might face. we conclude by outlining the implications of decolonising mental health for research, practice and policy in the country. psychology and developing societies

viewpoint on multisensory perception for action abstract in this viewpoint, laurence harris and marc ernst reflect on their careers studying how the brain combines information from multiple sensory systems — vision, hearing, touch, and the vestibular sense — to perceive the world and guide action. they trace the field’s evolution from early psychophysical and neurophysiological work to the introduction of bayesian models, which reframed multisensory integration as a problem of statistical inference under uncertainty and provided a principled link between behavioural findings and normative theory. both authors highlight open challenges: bridging computational, algorithmic, and neural levels of explanation; understanding how the brain represents and approximates complex, context-dependent probabilistic information; and characterising the naturalistic sensory signals generated during active behaviours such as walking, grasping, and navigating. they discuss the growing role of virtual reality in enabling more ecologically valid experiments while preserving experimental control and note that progress has been uneven across modalities — most advanced in vision, less so in audition and haptics. the authors also address open-science practices, the value and limits of replication, and the anticipated role of artificial intelligence as a tool that accelerates research workflows rather than replaces scientific reasoning. they close with reflections on mentorship and curiosity as drivers of scientific careers, and a shared conviction that no sense operates in isolation — multisensory integration is fundamental to perception and action and remains one of the most promising frontiers in cognitive science. multisensory research

an innovative indirect measure of socioeconomic status (ses)‐related intergroup differentiation among adolescents abstract introduction adolescence is a critical period for understanding social class, forming class‐related attitudes, and shaping future social engagement. however, the global educational segregation trend may hinder this learning by separating adolescents into socioeconomic status (ses)‐based school settings, thereby fostering intergroup misunderstandings, prejudice, and weakening social cohesion. before implementing interventions to reduce these divides, a reliable, valid, and age‐appropriate measure of ses‐related attitudes is needed. to address socially desirable responding in explicit measures, this study developed and evaluated the intergroup indirect attitude‐relevant differentiation measure (iiam) for assessing adolescents' ses‐related attitude‐relevant differentiation. methods a total of 328 year 7–9 students from relatively advantaged secondary school contexts (higher‐ses) ( m age = 13.06, including both female and male students) in mainland china and hong kong participated. the iiam was developed using the error‐choice technique, with items informed by a literature review and expert panel input. face and content validity were examined through cognitive interviews, construct validity was assessed through exploratory factor analysis (efa) and confirmatory factor analysis (cfa), and internal consistency was assessed using cronbach's alpha. results findings indicated that the iiam showed good face validity and strong internal consistency, with cronbach's alpha values in the 0.80s. both efa and cfa supported a unidimensional, seven‐item structure with satisfactory model fit. conclusion the iiam appears to be a feasible indirect measure of ses‐related attitude‐relevant intergroup differentiation, with preliminary evidence supporting its internal consistency and dimensional structure among higher‐ses adolescents. further research is encouraged to confirm the internal consistency, construct validity of the measure in socioeconomically heterogeneous samples, including adolescents from lower‐ses backgrounds. journal of adolescence

need for fighting: a psychoanalytic exploration of drivers who engaged in physical aggression in traffic abstract physical aggression in traffic settings is one of the concerning manifestations of aggressive driving that is a threat to public safety and health. despite the rich literature on aggression in traffic settings, studies investigating physical aggression in this context are limited. the current study aimed to investigate the reasons for engaging in physical aggression while driving, based on the accounts of participants who had been involved in such incidents. since traffic settings involve clear rules that all participants must follow, along with an inherent element of rivalry among them, the study's findings were discussed from a lacanian perspective to provide a theoretical explanation for the behavior. a qualitative methodology was used in this study. semi‐structured interviews were conducted with five male participants, aged between 48 and 55, using convenience sampling. the interview transcripts were analyzed using the interpretative phenomenological analysis approach. based on the results, three superordinate themes were detected: “irregularities as a cause for conflict”, “need to secure justice”, and “power struggle”. experiences of physical aggression in traffic appear to be closely tied to power struggles, often accompanied by an intolerance for rule‐breaking. the participants' discourse also reveals underlying themes related to masculinity and gendered expectations. international journal of applied psychoanalytic studies

the importance of embedding diversity science frameworks in affective science: illustrations from research on identity-based stigma. both affective experience and affect regulation can be influenced by various social, historical, political, and economic systems and structures. these contingent and particularized influences arise in part through the shaping of how people and communities construct, navigate, and are affected by personal and collective identities, intergroup relations, and social hierarchies. in this commentary, we argue that greater integration of affective science and diversity science-"the study of the interpretation and construction of human differences"-would enhance the field's understanding of a wide variety of consequential affective phenomena. throughout, we illustrate this premise by drawing primarily on examples of research on affective consequences of, and affect regulation in the context of, identity-based stigma. we highlight several implications for methods, measurement, and inference. systemic neglect of individual-structure interplay: interlevel cycles of invisibility, ignorance, and denial perpetuate racism racism is deeply embedded in american society, yet many americans fail to recognize its pervasiveness or how interactions between individuals and structures (e.g., policies and institutions) create and sustain it. among laypeople and perhaps social psychologists, this failure stems from a phenomenon we term “systemic neglect of individual-structure interplay”—a psychological and structural process through which people overlook the dynamic interplay between individual and structural forces that produce and sustain systemic racism. we identify three interconnected mechanisms that perpetuate this neglect: invisibility (failure to perceive systemic racism), ignorance (lack of knowledge and experience), and denial (motivated rejection of racism’s systemic nature). these mechanisms create a self-reinforcing cycle that obscures how structures shape individuals and how individuals reproduce those structures. we propose a framework highlighting these reciprocal influences and the consequences of neglecting them, including widespread misunderstanding of racism, misplaced blame, and ineffective interventions. we outline implications for social psychology, arguing that the field would benefit from greater attention to this interplay, as several researchers and theorists have previously recommended. by illuminating the process of systemic neglect, our framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of racism to laypeople and social-psychological researchers alike and identifies key leverage points for social change. perspectives on psychological science

discovering semantic structures in psychological scales: a response-free front-end to efficient simplification. 发现心理量表语义结构：通向高效简化的无作答前端 psychological scale refinement traditionally relies on response-based methods such as factor analysis, item response theory, and network psychometrics to uncover latent constructs and optimize item composition. although methodologically rigorous, these approaches require large respondent samples and may be limited by data availability, cross-cultural comparability, and replication constraints. recent advances in natural language processing suggest that the wording of questionnaire items contains construct-relevant semantic organization, offering a complementary response-free perspective. we introduce a topic-modeling framework that operationalizes item-level semantic structure to systematically simplify scales. we encode items using contextual sentence embeddings and group them through density-based clustering to identify semantic topics without predefining their number. within each cluster, class-based term weighting identifies representative keywords that summarize each topic and support an interpretable semantic pre-structure of the item pool. the framework then hierarchically merges semantically related clusters and selects representative items using structure-aware membership criteria within an integrated reduction pipeline. we evaluated the framework on three widely used instruments: dass, ipip, and epoch, covering negative affect, personality traits, and well-being. results showed that the identified semantic topics often formed factor-like groupings aligned with established constructs. representative items selected through semantic membership probabilities reduced item counts by 60.5% on average while maintaining acceptable psychometric properties and preserving factor correlation patterns. these findings support semantic topic-structure modeling as an interpretable front-end for theory-consistent scale construction and simplification, guiding rather than replacing subsequent psychometric validation. an integrated visualization-supported tool further enables one-click semantic analysis and structured item selection. behavior research methods

the good, the bad, and the cringy: introducing the empatom-pos and empatom-embarrass as tools for assessing empathy and theory of mind in diverse emotional contexts. 好、坏与尴尬：引入empatom-pos和empatom-embarrass作为评估多元情绪情境中共情与心理理论的工具 empathizing and mentalizing are crucial to social understanding, yet few instruments capture these processes across a broad emotional spectrum. the empatom is a video-based paradigm that independently measures empathy and theory of mind (tom) and can additionally incorporate a prosociality measure. as its current form is limited to negatively valenced emotional contexts, we introduce two expanded german versions: empatom-pos, featuring positively valenced narrations, and empatom-embarrass, featuring embarrassing narrations, alongside the original neutral and negative conditions. in two pilot studies (ns = 28/27), we tested novel video stimuli and corresponding questions, revised them based on the data, and subsequently evaluated them in two higher-powered studies (ns = 60/55). results confirmed successful empathy induction in all emotional conditions: participants reported feeling worse after negative, more joyful after positive, and more embarrassed after embarrassing narrations (compared to all other valence conditions, respectively). emotional valence also influenced prosociality: negative narrations prompted the highest willingness to invest, but positive and embarrassing narrations also elicited greater prosociality than the neutral condition. both expanded versions supported reliable tom assessment without ceiling effects and with similar performance levels in the tom and control conditions. analyses further revealed that, on an interindividual level, empathic resonance in both negative and positive contexts was positively correlated with the degree of prosociality, highlighting the interrelation between empathizing and social decision-making. by incorporating positive and embarrassing emotional contexts, the empatom-pos and empatom-embarrass broaden the range of assessable social-emotional experiences, offering new opportunities to investigate empathy, tom, and prosociality in more ecologically valid and diverse settings. behavior research methods

investigating associations between personality and problematic social media use by considering trait and state fomo as mediators. high neuroticism and low conscientiousness robustly correlate with both problematic social media use (psmu) and fear of missing out (fomo). however studies investigating these concepts simultaneously are relatively rare, and few have examined the associations between the personality traits and psmu by investigating both trait and state fomo as potential mediators. in a sample of 576 german-speaking participants (of whom n = 94 were aged 13-17), we observed that higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were associated with higher psmu. mediation results indicated that neuroticism was indirectly associated with psmu via both state fomo (β = 0.10, b = 0.63, proportion mediated [pm] = 27.3%, 95% ci [0.36, 0.91]) and trait fomo (β = 0.05, b = 0.33, pm = 14.3%, 95% ci [0.13, 0.53], p < .001). conversely, for conscientiousness, only state fomo emerged as a significant mediator (β = -0.06, b = -0.48, pm = 33.8%, 95% ci [-0.81, -0.16], p = .002); the indirect pathway via trait fomo was non-significant (β = -0.02, b = -0.12, 95% ci [-0.28, 0.02], p = .09). these findings suggest that state fomo, which reflects online-specific anxiety, is a more consistent factor linking personality traits to psmu than general trait fomo. this distinction suggests that state fomo could be considered a potential target for practical interventions, as it is more situational and might be easier to change than personality traits. bmc psychology

presence, social capital, social isolation in virtual environments: the role of extraversion in shaping relational outcomes virtual environment communication has been increasingly discussed as a potential means of addressing social isolation, yet little is known about how different forms of presence become relational resources. this study examines how physical presence and social presence in virtual environments are associated with social isolation through virtual-environment bonding and bridging social capital, and whether these relationships differ by users’ level of extraversion. data were collected from 500 korean adults with experience using zepeto and analyzed using cb-sem and multi-group analysis. the results show that physical presence is positively associated with both bonding and bridging social capital, suggesting that perceived realism is associated with both forms of relational resources. social presence is negatively associated with bonding social capital but positively associated with bridging social capital, indicating that the sense of being with others may be more closely associated with weak-tie expansion rather than close relational cohesion. bonding social capital is positively associated with social isolation, whereas bridging social capital is not significantly associated with social isolation in the overall model. multi-group analysis revealed that the positive association between bonding social capital and social isolation was significantly stronger among extraverted users. bridging social capital was negatively associated with social isolation only in the extraversion group, although the between-group difference was not statistically significant at the 0.05 level. these findings suggest that the socio-psychological outcomes associated with ve-comm vary not simply on the overall level of presence, but on the type of presence, the form of social capital reported, and users’ personality traits. cyberpsychology behavior and social networking

beyond ownership: how direct experience shapes employee perceptions of pet-friendly workplaces abstract background : pet-friendly workplaces (pfws) are increasingly promoted as a strategy to support employee well-being and workplace culture, yet most research has focused on pet owners or employees evaluating hypothetical workplace scenarios. far less is known about how perceptions differ between employees who have and have not directly experienced a pfw. methods : using a vetted sample of 195 full-time employees recruited through amazon’s mechanical turk, this exploratory study examined perceptions of the benefits (e.g., mental well-being, physical activity, interpersonal functioning, and personal work performance), issues, and governance of pfws, with pet ownership and prior pfw experience as focal variables. group differences were examined with two-way factorial models crossing prior pfw experience and pet ownership, with ordinal-logistic and false-discovery-rate sensitivity analyses. results : employees generally viewed pfws positively, with mental health and interpersonal benefits receiving the strongest support. pet owners reported greater perceived mental, physical, and personal-work benefits than non-owners and viewed several workplace issues as less frequent. the study’s primary finding, however, concerned experience. employees with prior pfw experience reported smaller perceived benefits, rated issues such as distraction and allergies as more frequent, and expressed stronger support for ongoing governance than employees without such experience. no significant experience × ownership interactions were detected. across all groups, clear office rules emerged as the most important policy safeguard. conclusions : perceptions of pfws are shaped not only by pet ownership but also by direct experience. employees with prior pfw experience consistently reported more tempered views than those without it, raising the possibility that the literature’s generally favorable picture reflects anticipation as much as lived experience. understanding pfws, therefore, requires knowing who is being asked and whether they have actually experienced one. longitudinal study on the relationship between club participation tendency and subjective social capital and psychological distress among university students abstract this study investigated the longitudinal associations among club participation tendency, changes in subjective social capital, and psychological distress in university students. panel data were collected from students at a private university in japan, spanning their first to fourth academic years. latent growth curve modeling yielded four principal findings. first, participation tendency in sports clubs was negatively associated with the slope of psychological distress. second, increases in subjective social capital were likewise negatively associated with the slope of psychological distress. third, participation in volunteer clubs, sports clubs, and multiple club types was positively related to the slope of subjective social capital. fourth, although club participation tendency was significantly associated with changes in subjective social capital, and changes in subjective social capital were significantly associated with changes in psychological distress, the indirect effect via changes in subjective social capital was not statistically significant. this may be partly due to the fact that subjective social capital was not assessed across different relational domains, potentially obscuring domain‐specific pathways linking club participation tendency to psychological distress. these findings suggest that club participation tendency and subjective social capital may be important factors contributing to improvements in psychological adjustment among university students. japanese psychological research

the relationship between workplace loneliness, person–organization fit, employee silence, and deviant behavior abstract the workplace has become a social context where individuals can feel loneliness. even though loneliness has been studied for many decades, loneliness at the workplace has yet to be comprehensively examined and understood. further, research has called for more studies on the boundary conditions that can help mitigate the negative impact of loneliness on organizational outcomes. hence, the study empirically tested the moderating effect of person–organization (p–o) fit for the relationship between workplace loneliness and employee silence and the mediating effect of employee silence for the relationship between workplace loneliness and deviant behavior. data were collected from 214 police officers in south korea using a multi‐wave time‐lagged procedure. hierarchical regression analyses were conducted, and the results showed that p–o fit significantly moderated the relationship between workplace loneliness and employee silence, and employee silence mediated the relationship between workplace loneliness and deviant behavior. furthermore, additional analysis found moderated mediation for the hypothesized research model. the study contributes to the existing body of research by discovering the proximal and distal outcomes of workplace loneliness and how p–o fit can influence the relationship. japanese psychological research

from career fit to ecosystem regulation: practitioner constructions of career health in singapore career health has emerged within singapore’s workforce policy as a way of encouraging individuals to develop meaningful and resilient careers, yet little is known about how career practitioners understand and apply this idea in practice. using constructivist grounded theory, this study examined how eight experienced career development practitioners in singapore made sense of career health through their work with clients. analysis generated five interrelated categories: multidimensional career functioning, reflective agency, meaning and values alignment, proactive resilience, and relational and structural embeddedness. practitioners understood career health as extending beyond employment status or skills relevance to encompass changing interactions among personal, material, relational, and contextual conditions. the findings provide an empirically grounded practitioner perspective on career health and suggest that career development practice may support clients not only through occupational choice and skills development, but also through reflection, preparedness, meaning-making, and navigation of structural constraints. journal of career development

stem career interest and perceived gendered barriers: support patterns in bolivia, brazil, and peru this cross-sectional secondary analysis examines science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (stem) career interest among 9,732 stem and non-stem students and professionals in bolivia, brazil, and peru. among 1,139 respondents whose policy-related adversity and gender-discrimination scores both exceeded the response midpoint, 72.3% reported interest scores averaging at least 5 ( somewhat agree ) on a seven-point scale. within this subset, the mean interest was 4.56 when family support and perceived policy presence were both below 5 and 5.82 when both were at least 5. adjusted analyses showed positive conditional associations for both supports; evidence for their interaction and an association with mentor presence remained inconclusive. the support contrast persisted across alternative thresholds and a restricted policy-adversity measure. findings identify assessment priorities for career counseling and institutional support; this nonprobability study does not establish adaptation, intervention effects, or population prevalence. journal of career development

career-related parental support and career indecision in health science students: a serial mediating analysis graduating health science students confront career indecision, which is significantly influenced by parental support. however, little is known about the underlying mechanisms between the two variables among health science students. this study explored the multiple mediating roles of career decision-making self-efficacy (cdmse) and future work self in the relationship between career-related parental support (crps) and career indecision among health science students. data were collected using online questionnaires from 1257 chinese health science students. we found that 49.32% students experienced moderate-to-high career indecision. crps affected career indecision directly and indirectly through three pathways: (1) cdmse; (2) future work self; and (3) cdmse and future work self in serial, with a total mediation effect of 60.80%. our findings emphasize focusing on health science students’ career indecision and valuing the supportive role of crps. in addition, targeted interventions to improve cdmse and future work self may be conducive to alleviating students’ career indecision. journal of career development

the psychology of genius: creative eminence in the making this paper reviews psychology’s long history of writings about human genius. a definition of genius is offered and explicated: “the capacity to imagine and implement a generally unforeseen domain change that, when eventually recognized, is widely accepted as an advance in that domain.” the review synthesizes informative findings from existing studies of genius, regarding: (1) the mental and personal dispositions of geniuses; (2) the roles of heredity and native talent; (3) the consequences of early giftedness; (4) the ways that individuals of genius interact with their social environments; (5) the workings of highly creative thinking; (6) the cognitive and social relations between geniuses and the domains they transform; (7) the roles of life conditions such as family composition, birth order, schooling, and mental health; (8) the importance of motivational factors such as purpose; and (9) the developmental trajectory of creative eminence. the review confirms the validity of the concept of individual genius, despite recent critical arguments to the contrary; and it asserts the usefulness of the concept for providing an understanding of the workings and potentials of peak human creativity. review of general psychology

racial trauma, loneliness, and disordered eating among racially/ethnically minoritized college students although research has examined associations between experiences of discrimination and disordered eating, less is known about what may explain this link. thus, the present study examined links between racial trauma, loneliness, and disordered eating among a large sample of racially/ethnically minoritized college students. participants included 30,377 college students self-identifying as people of color (poc) from the 2022-2023 healthy minds study. results indicated that racial trauma and loneliness were significant predictors of disordered eating, after controlling for age, gender, and financial stress. in addition, loneliness explained the link between racial trauma and disordered eating. findings suggest the need for culturally responsive therapeutic services when psychologists are working with racially/ethnically minoritized college students with disordered eating. counseling psychologist

psychological flexibility and anxiety—a systematic review and meta‐analysis abstract objectives the association of psychological flexibility (pf) with anxiety has been widely studied. however, concerns about the measurement of pf raise questions regarding the validity and comparability of existing findings. this meta‐analysis examined the association between pf and anxiety using a stringent set of validated pf measures and explored potential moderators of this relationship. design this study employed a systematic review and meta‐analysis design. methods a literature search was conducted across five databases: cinahl, embase, medline, psycinfo and web of science. results a total of 29 studies, yielding 31 effect sizes, were included. random‐effects meta‐analysis revealed a significant, moderate negative association between pf and anxiety ( r = −.466, 95% ci [−0.52, −0.41]). subgroup and meta‐regression analyses showed that the pf instrument, anxiety construct and sample size significantly moderated the relationship between pf and anxiety. conclusions overall, findings suggest that greater pf is associated with lower anxiety symptoms, although the magnitude of this relationship varies depending on how pf is operationalized. these results highlight the importance of measurement choice in pf research and support pf as a clinically relevant transdiagnostic target in interventions for anxiety. british journal of clinical psychology

the consciousness-first commitment of integrated information theory abstract integrated information theory (iit) accounts for consciousness through its explanatory identity: an experience (the explanandum) is identical to a causal structure (or φ-structure, the explanans). in other identities in science (e.g. ‘water is h2o’), the power of the explanans (h2o) comes from the presumption that it somehow exists more fundamentally. yet when our explanandum is experience itself, as in iit, we must recalibrate the norms of explanation to the fact that experience exists immediately and irrefutably, while whatever we may posit about the world beyond experience is always an inference within experience. neuroscience of consciousness

overcoming essentialism: evaluation of theories of consciousness by the lawful regularities they predict abstract a common objection to consciousness research is that researchers cannot agree on what consciousness is. but how should a consensus on the nature of consciousness be reached? does consciousness have essential features that one can be right or wrong about? should we select theories of consciousness based on their descriptions of the essential features of experience alone? in this article, we will argue with the help of popper that determining unquestionable essential features of consciousness is neither possible nor desirable. instead, any account of what consciousness is, should be understood as a subjective selection of features and should not count as an insight. according to popper, insights in science are achieved when novel regularities between observations are discovered that generalize to scientific laws. furthermore, all results of research can be stated independently of the definitions that were used in their making. therefore, no consensus on the nature of consciousness or on a theory of consciousness is needed for consciousness research to progress—in fact, a multitude of definitions and theories may be beneficial. based on this, we argue that theories of consciousness be evaluated by their ability to propose concrete, testable laws rather than by their description of what consciousness is. highlights how to define consciousness and how to determine its essential features are often considered to be major obstacles in consciousness research, but we argue in this article that this view is a misconception of scientific progress. according to karl popper, there is no way to determine indisputable essential features of a concept (such as consciousness), and it is also not the task of science to find essential features of concepts. theories of consciousness often regard their definition of consciousness (what they consider its essential features) as an insight in itself, but we argue that definitions constitute untestable elements of a theory and should therefore not serve as a basis for evaluation of a theory. according to popper, science progresses not by revealing essential features of concepts but when scientific laws that state regularities between observations are corroborated. in the process of proposing and testing scientific laws, concepts such as consciousness play only a temporary and subordinate role. we conclude that theories of consciousness should be solely evaluated by the scientific laws that they propose, which includes rejecting theories of consciousness that propose no laws at all and focusing on the predictive value of theories of consciousness in experimental settings. neuroscience of consciousness

the role of negative affect regulation in the maintenance of restriction in anorexia nervosa spectrum disorders. restriction is a core behavioral symptom of anorexia nervosa spectrum disorders (ansd), including anorexia nervosa (an) and atypical an (aan). emotion regulation theories of eating pathology posit that restriction and restraint are maintained via their influence on affective processes, but prior research has not firmly established the affect regulatory role of restriction and restraint. using 30 days of ecological momentary assessment data collected from 83 adults with ansd (an = 47, aan = 36), we specified a series of dynamic structural equation models to clarify the temporal interplay between restriction/restraint and negative affect. we also tested whether the relationship between restriction/restraint and negative affect was moderated by diagnosis (i.e., an vs. aan). group-level analyses suggested inconsistent effects of restriction and restraint on affect, whereas increases in negative affect reliably predicted restriction and restraint. however, there was considerable idiographic heterogeneity in cross-lagged effects across models. temporal dynamics between restriction/restraint and affect did not systematically differ as a function of diagnosis. although restriction and restraint may provide relief from negative affect for many individuals, the present findings suggest that they may not serve a universal or lasting affect regulatory function in ansd. these results underscore the importance of idiographic approaches to eating disorder research and treatment. gender segregation in european muslim youths’ social interaction: differences between friends, out-of-school interaction partners, and homework peers recent research shows that muslim youth have fewer cross-gender friends than their non-muslim peers, a pattern attributed to norms that discourage close cross-gender interaction. this study examines whether differences in cross-gender interaction between muslim and non-muslim youth are also present in other relationships, including with out-of-school interaction partners and homework peers. in a sample of 15,066 adolescents ( m age = 15.0 years, 49 percent female, 18 percent muslim) from england, germany, the netherlands, and sweden, gender segregation proves stronger among muslim than non-muslim youth for friendships and out-of-school interactions but not for homework peers. however, it is less likely among muslim than non-muslim youth that cross-gender homework peers are also friends. these findings indicate that constraints to cross-gender interaction vary by relationship type, suggesting that the stronger gender segregation in muslim youths’ friendship networks reported in previous research does not extend to all types of cross-gender interaction. at the same time, cross-gender friends, out-of-school interaction partners, and homework peers are all related to more egalitarian gender role attitudes among adolescents. accordingly, considering different types of cross-gender ties and the different regulations they come with has implications for our understanding of both adolescents’ gender segregation and their gender-related developmental outcomes. social psychology quarterly

where do we look? visual attention competition between hyper-salient objects and ai-generated virtual endorsers in generative artificial intelligence advertising 我们看向何处？生成式人工智能广告中高凸显物体与ai生成虚拟代言人的视觉注意竞争 generative artificial intelligence (ai) advertising, defined as advertising content created or substantially assisted by generative ai systems (aigc), has introduced new visual features that combine algorithmically generated objects with human-like representations. hyper-salient objects, defined by exaggerated perceptual prominence and semantic incongruity, and ai-generated virtual endorsers, represented by human-like ai-created figures, have become increasingly common in such advertisements. however, little is known about how these distinct visual cues compete for consumers’ limited attentional resources when presented together. drawing on visual attention and scene perception perspectives, this study investigated how hyper-salient objects and ai-generated virtual endorsers influence visual attention allocation in ai-generated advertising. a 2 (hyper-salient object: present vs. absent) × 2 (ai endorser: present vs. absent) between-subjects eye-tracking experiment was conducted with 160 participants in a controlled laboratory setting using static ai-generated advertisements. eye movements were recorded, and memory was the visible and invisible scars of childhood cancer: a qualitative study of body image and identity in survivorship 童年癌症可见与不可见的伤痕：癌症生存者身体意象与身份认同的质性研究 abstract objectives this study explored the lived experiences of young adult childhood cancer survivors regarding the impact of visible physical differences on body image and identity. although clinical survival rates have increased, the long‐term psychological implications of treatment‐related physical alterations remain under‐researched. design a qualitative study adopting a constructivist‐interpretivist approach. methods we conducted semi‐structured interviews with 41 survivors (aged 19–28) recruited from a spanish paediatric oncology unit. data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. results this analysis revealed a complex trajectory of embodiment across four central themes: permanent body changes and physical consequences ; damage to body image, self‐perception and identity ; insecurity and isolation in the social/sexual sphere ; and coping strategies—from hiding to acceptance . this trajectory spans from the initial trauma of permanent physical consequences and functional limitations to a sense of “spoiled identity” characterized by body shame and social avoidance. the findings highlight how visible scars and developmental delays often disrupt socio‐sexual integration, creating a significant “disclosure burden” in romantic contexts. however, the analysis also identifies a dynamic shift towards resilience, where survivors increasingly re‐signify physical marks as symbols of strength and survival. conclusion these results underscore the need for developmentally sensitive, lifelong psychosocial support that moves beyond biomedical metrics to address the nuanced, experiential reality of life after childhood cancer. 分析归纳出四个核心主题：永久性身体改变与身体后果；身体意象、自我感知与身份认同受损；社会/性领域中的不安全感与孤立；从隐藏到接纳的应对策略。 参与者经历从永久身体后果与功能限制的初始创伤，到以身体羞耻和社会回避为特征的“受损身份”感。 可见疤痕与发育延迟常干扰社会-性整合，并在恋爱情境中形成显著的“披露负担”。 分析也识别出向韧性发展的动态转变，生存者逐渐将身体印记重新赋义为力量与生存的象征。 british journal of health psychology

fidelity of intervention delivery in the trace programme randomised controlled trial, a complex behavioural intervention for food addiction the 3-arm targeted research on addictive and compulsive eating (trace) randomised controlled trial, aimed to decrease addictive eating symptoms in adults with the active intervention (dietitian-led telehealth sessions) compared to the passive intervention (self-guided workbook) and control group. the current study evaluated fidelity of the trace active intervention delivery to determine if telehealth sessions were delivered according to the intended service parameters: session durations (min), frequency and content. differences between actual and intended schedules, for participants in the telehealth intervention arm ( n = 39) were analysed. a subgroup of participants’ ( n = 5) sessions were audio recorded ( n = 25 sessions) with n = 24 analysed to determine fidelity of session content against an observer implementation record. fidelity of telehealth session duration and frequency was classified as ‘good’ and ‘very good’, respectively, with the median duration and days between each session within ±5 min or days, respectively. the dietitian’s fidelity in delivering key components was rated as ‘very good’ by both independent reviewers (82% and 87.2%) respectively. the ‘session summary’ was the least covered topic, followed by ‘determining the client’s main food intake concerns’ . the trace programme was delivered as intended based on the session duration and frequency, however observations made during the content analysis identified key content, including the ‘session summary’ , was not always covered. future trials should monitor fidelity in diverse settings and a range of professionals with variations in training and experience. australian new zealand clinical trials registry (actrn12621001079831) behavior modification

the puzzle of language without syntax: a review of steven mithen's the language puzzle in the language puzzle , steven mithen assumes that universal grammar has been altogether debunked, and argues that the question of the origin of natural‐language syntax and compositionality has largely been answered by the work of computational evolutionary linguists simon kirby and collaborators, thus: “syntax spontaneously emerges from the generation‐to‐generation language‐learning process itself”. i show that kirby and collaborators' work in fact presupposes the entirety of syntax in an innate language of thought, and that it subscribes to a notion of universal grammar no weaker than the mainstream one from generative linguistics in the 21st century. mind & language

language without syntax? what a crazy idea! a reply to salvador mascarenhas salvador mascarenhas's review of my 2024 book the language puzzle focusses on one specific issue: the existence or otherwise of universal grammar. while this has been a valuable notion within the history of linguistics, it is an idea that lacks evolutionary credibility and needs to be discarded. when defending universal grammar, mascarenhas inadvertently misrepresents how i draw on that idea and my reasons for rejecting its validity. if mascarenhas and other linguists wish to maintain the idea of universal grammar and persuade others of its veracity, they need to explain when, how, and why it could have evolved. mind & language

the effect of parenting interventions to support language and literacy development in 3-7-year-old children in low- and middle-income countries: systematic review and meta-analysis. children in low- and middle-income countries (lmics) often have limited access to the structured home learning experiences that support language and literacy development during the critical years around school entry. we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of parenting interventions targeting children's language or literacy in these settings. twenty-six experimental and quasi-experimental studies from 15 countries involving 6,264 children aged 3-7 were included. dependent effect sizes were synthesized using random-effects models with robust variance estimation. parenting interventions were found to be associated with positive pooled effects on language (k = 21, g = 1.35, 95% ci [0.62, 2.09]) and literacy (k = 19, g = 0.94, 95% ci [0.56, 1.33]). estimates were similar when restricted to the subset of 23 randomized controlled trials. heterogeneity was substantial for both child outcomes. exploratory moderator analyses suggested larger effects for both language and literacy in contexts with morphosyllabic script and, for literacy, in interventions that included shared book reading. risk of bias was judged to be moderate, principally because most studies lacked prespecified analysis plans. we conclude that parenting interventions can support early language and literacy development in lmics, although some uncertainty remains concerning the magnitude of effects, especially for language. child development

what works, what doesn’t, and why we can’t tell the difference: contextualizing evidence-based practice in public education and school psychology. public schools are charged with educating every child who enters them under a legal and ethical mandate that practice be grounded in evidence, yet the gap between that mandate and routine practice remains substantial across public education. using school psychology as a case study, we argue that evidence-based practice's persistent failure to close this gap reflects a mismatch between the inherited framework and the structural and institutional conditions of public education rather than practitioner values alone. six interrelated failures are documented: conflation of evidence-based practice as a decision-making model with specific intervention adoption; inconsistent evidentiary standards; demographic mismatch between research samples and served populations; commercial capture of the evidence infrastructure; failures of contextual fit and transportability; and the absence of mechanisms for discontinuing ineffective practices. these failures persist through professional ossification and school psychology's location within education bureaucracies. in response, we propose an epistemological architecture adapted from evidence-based public health, operationalized here as the evidence-based school psychology model, with a three-level evidentiary sequence that provides the de-implementation mechanism the current framework structurally lacks. we offer recommendations for practitioners, trainers, and researchers to operationalize this model in practice.
