existential–humanistic self-development theory: a three-pillar framework this article consolidates two decades of work on existential–humanistic self-development theory (ehsdt) and advances a new conceptual architecture to enhance its accessibility for scholars and emerging humanistic psychologists. a three-pillar framework is presented. this framework addresses what develops, how development occurs, and the direction of development. the first pillar articulates ehsdt’s ontological grounding in existential–humanistic thought, conceptualizing development as the unfolding lived meaning of a person’s nexus of world-relations (their being-and-becoming-in-the-world). the second pillar situates ehsdt among field-theoretical, systems-oriented perspectives, framing development as a differential–integrative process propelled by existential tensions and the imaginative reorganization of the multicultural self-system. the third pillar clarifies ehsdt’s distinctive character as a relational developmental perspective, conceptualizing optimal development as a lifelong process of self-cultivation oriented toward cooperative culture creation through a confluence of learning and creating. ehsdt is presented as an inclusive, value-conscious human science perspective with evolving priorities for developmental inquiry. self-cultivation is proposed as a 21st-century alternative to the concept of self-actualization. journal of humanistic psychology

pyequate: a python package for test equating pyequate：用于测验等值的python包 test equating adjusts scores across alternate forms of a test so that they may be used interchangeably, and is a routine requirement of any testing program that administers more than one form. software for equating is well established in r and in standalone programs. there is no current native option in python, despite its role as the working environment for a growing share of assessment data and downstream modeling. analysts working in python must therefore leave their pipeline or reimplement methods themselves. the package pyequate closes this gap. it provides observed-score equating under random groups and common-item nonequivalent groups designs, including the mean, linear, equipercentile, tucker, levine, frequency estimation, and braun-holland methods, together with presmoothing and analytical standard errors of equating. it also provides item response theory parameter linking and true-score and observed-score equating. applied psychological measurement

parents' diagnostic resolution and activation: examining a mediation model on emotional and behavioral outcomes in autistic children and adolescents. a diagnosis of autism spectrum disorder poses significant emotional and practical challenges for parents. although diagnostic resolution and parent activation have been examined separately, little is known about whether parents' psychological adjustment relates to active caregiving and, in turn, to child outcomes. this study tested: (1) a mediation model linking diagnostic resolution to child emotional-behavioral difficulties through parent activation; (2) psychometric properties of the italian parent activation measure for developmental disabilities (pam-dd). we hypothesized that diagnostic resolution would be indirectly associated with lower levels of children's emotional-behavioral difficulties through higher parent activation. participants were 179 parents (87.7% mothers;= 43.91; = 5.63) of autistic children aged 6-13 years (81.6% boys;= 9.50; = 2.32). diagnostic resolution was operationalized as a reliable reduction in negative emotional responses, and child difficulties were assessed using the strengths and difficulties questionnaire (sdq). confirmatory factor analysis (cfa) examined pam-dd structure, and path analysis tested the mediation model, controlling for child age and time since diagnosis. cfa supported a two-factor model (activated and passive dimensions) with acceptable fit (cfi = .92, tli = .90, rmsea = .06, 90% ci [.05, .08], srmr = .07). resolution was associated only with the activated dimension (= .19,< .05), which was negatively related to children's emotional-behavioral difficulties (= -.25,< .01). findings suggest that psychological integration of the diagnosis may foster action-oriented parental engagement, which is linked to fewer child emotional-behavioral difficulties, highlighting parent activation as a potential intervention target. journal of genetic psychology

academic resilience and students’ well-being: the role of mindfulness and academic engagement as mediators considering limited research on high school students’ well-being within the indonesian context, the present study aims to advance research in this educational context by investigating the roles of mindfulness and academic engagement as mediators in the relationship between academic resilience and student well-being. a cross-sectional survey was conducted with 235 high school students aged 14–18 years ( m age = 16.38, sd = 0.84; 57.87% male and 42.13% female; 25.10% 10 th grade, 38.30% 11 th grade, and 36.60% 12 th grade), recruited through convenience sampling. participants completed four validated instruments: the academic risk and resilience scale (arrs), the student subjective well-being questionnaire (sswq), the five facet mindfulness questionnaire short form (ffmq-sf), and the utrecht work engagement scale for students (uwes-9s). findings revealed that academic resilience significantly predicted student well-being, with mindfulness and academic engagement serving as significant serial mediating variables. these findings highlight the importance of fostering resilience, mindfulness, and engagement to support well-being in educational settings. school psychology international

coaching versus mentoring for entrepreneurial self-efficacy: a scoping review and decision framework entrepreneurial self-efficacy frequently predicts business venture success, yet practitioners in resource-constrained markets lack evidence-based guidance on whether coaching or mentoring better develops distinct entrepreneurial self-efficacy dimensions. following prisma-scr guidelines, this scoping review maps 14 empirical studies across five self-efficacy dimensions and heron's six intervention categories. findings show facilitative coaching supports self-regulatory processes and overall confidence, while authoritative mentoring is likely to develop opportunity recognition and business management competencies. the resulting dual-lens decision framework offers programme designers’ and practitioners’ selection criteria for choosing coaching, mentoring, or hybrid approaches based on the specific entrepreneurial self-efficacy dimension targeted. international journal of evidence based coaching & mentoring

enacted love: capitalization responses signal love, including toward strangers. 被践行的爱：积极建设性回应传递爱意，包括对陌生人 what behavior is seen as "love" and why does it matter? we theorize active-constructive responding to another's disclosure of good news is prototypical "enacted love" and test hypotheses about implications for a loving person's relationship development. we use three distinct methods-dyadic interactions between romantic couples (study 1, n = 160), real spontaneous responses to a stranger's good news (study 2, n = 204), and observation of others' real capitalization responses to a stranger's good news (studies 3-5, n = 97, 105, and 402, respectively)-to assess convergent and discriminant evidence for the construct. study 2 uses experience sampling to track the development of capitalization respondents' social lives over time. studies 4 and 5 use within-subjects experiments to test hypotheses that loving behavior could influence others' interactions with loving people. results have theoretical implications for close relationships and the concept of "loving one's neighbor," plus practical implications for building bridges in a divided society. toward equitable fidelity measurement of evidence-based psychosocial interventions. accurately measuring clinician fidelity to psychosocial evidence-based interventions (ebis) is essential to advance equitable ebi implementation. observational measures of live or recorded therapy sessions are widely considered the most reliable and valid metrics for indexing fidelity. however, they are costly, time and resource intensive, and rarely used in underresourced clinical settings; this makes it challenging to assess the quality of care delivered to underserved populations. further, many fidelity coding schemes originated from clinical trials testing relatively structured clinical protocols with primarily white, middle-class individuals. this raises equity considerations for their use and interpretation in settings serving individuals with diverse identities and adverse social determinants of health, where flexible ebi application is often required to meet needs. for example, fidelity coding schemes do not always consider patient cultural and contextual factors that may lead clinicians to "stray" from fidelity standards. guided by the health equity implementation framework, we outline key equity considerations related to observational fidelity measurement and interpretation in mental health. we describe several ongoing efforts to equitably assess fidelity to psychosocial ebis in underresourced community settings using a variety of strategies including standardized patient paradigms codeveloped with community partners, snapshot coding of session recordings, artificial intelligence models that automate fidelity score generations, and leveraging expert consultation encounters to generate actionable fidelity data. we conclude by discussing implications for future research. teenage childbirth and risk of inpatient hospitalization for mental illness, substance use disorders and offending during young adulthood abstract teenage childbirth is considered a contributing factor to lifelong health and social disparities for mothers; however, evidence is mostly derived from cross-sectional studies utilizing self-report surveys and is often limited to one or a few psychosocial outcomes. we compared the risk of adverse psychosocial outcomes during young adulthood, including inpatient hospitalization for mental illness (mi) or substance use disorder (sud), and offending, among teenage mothers (< 20 years), adult mothers (≥ 20 years) and non-mothers. data included females born in queensland, australia, in 1983 and 1984, followed to age 29–31 years who were registered as mothers via birth records ( n = 18,188). mi and sud were identified from inpatient hospital records, while offending data were obtained from police and court records. risks of adverse psychosocial outcomes in young adulthood were compared between teenage mothers, adult mothers and non-mothers using regression analyses. the lifetime prevalence of adverse psychosocial outcomes was significantly higher among teenage mothers (55.0%) than adult mothers (22.9%) and non-mothers (13.6%). offending was the most common adverse outcome across all groups. both adjusted analyses and propensity-scored matched analyses revealed that teenage childbirth was a significant risk factor for adverse psychosocial outcomes in young adulthood. teenage mothers were at increased risk of inpatient hospitalizations with mi or sud and involvement in offending compared with adult or nonmothers, even after controlling for known covariates. these findings highlight the need for holistic, continual, and integrated support for teenage mothers to improve their long-term health and social outcomes. journal of child and family studies

personality, marital quality, and psychological distress in fathers’ positive and negative parenting abstract parenting behaviors play a critical role in child development, yet factors associated with fathers’ parenting behaviors remain underexplored. this study examined the associations and interactions between paternal personality traits, marital quality, psychological distress, and both positive and negative parenting behaviors. a cross-sectional web-based survey was conducted with 497 japanese fathers of children aged 18 months to 3 years. parenting behaviors, personality traits, marital quality, and psychological distress were assessed using the positive and negative parenting scale, ten-item personality inventory, marital satisfaction scale, and kessler psychological distress scale, respectively. multiple regression analyses revealed that agreeableness was negatively associated with inconsistent parenting and harsh discipline. marital quality was positively associated with positive responsivity and respect for will. psychological distress was negatively related to positive responsivity and positively to negative parenting. furthermore, marital quality and psychological distress moderated some associations; notably, neuroticism was positively associated with inconsistency and harsh discipline only under low psychological distress. overall, paternal personality traits, marital quality, and psychological distress were directly and interactively related to fathers’ parenting behaviors. these findings suggest that integrating paternal personality traits, marital quality, and psychological well-being into parenting support services may contribute to fostering positive fathering and enhancing child development outcomes. journal of child and family studies

computation or weight adaptation? rethinking the role of plasticity in learning abstract the human brain is an adaptive learning system that can generalize to new tasks and unfamiliar environments. the traditional view is that such adaptive behavior requires a structural change of the learning system (e.g., via neural plasticity). in this work, we use artificial neural networks, specifically large language models (llms), to challenge this traditional view and suggest that such adaptive behavior can be also achieved solely through computation if the learning system is sufficiently trained. we focus on statistical learning paradigms. these require identifying underlying regularities in seemingly arbitrary word sequences and are primarily considered to require neural plasticity. llms can capture arbitrary structures without requiring weight adaptation, even though these structures carry no semantic content and lie far from the natural language distribution on which the models were trained. our work provides novel insights into the role of plasticity in learning, demonstrating that sufficiently trained learning systems are highly flexible, adapting to new tasks and environments solely through computation, much more than previously acknowledged. furthermore, our work opens the door for future research to use deep learning models to conjure hypotheses about the brain. cognitive science

visual perception in children who play chess: a cross‐sectional study based on chess practice, interest, performance and sports participation abstract this study examined visual perception skills in children who play chess using a quantitative, cross‐sectional comparative design. the sample included 70 children aged 60–72 months. data were collected via the frostig visual perception test, a personal information form, structured interviews, and a chess interest questionnaire. based on teacher and parent reports, children were grouped as more versus less interested and successful in chess. results showed no significant group differences in visual–motor coordination, form constancy, position‐in‐space perception, or total visual perception. however, significant differences were found in figure–ground perception and spatial relations. additionally, children who regularly participated in extracurricular sports activities demonstrated higher total visual perception scores and better figure–ground perception than non‐participants. these findings suggest that the relationship between chess education and visual perception may be limited to specific subcomponents, and that physical activity may play a complementary role, warranting further research using more controlled designs. applied cognitive psychology

distress, emotional well‐being, and sleep quality in daily life: a dual‐continuum perspective abstract we examined whether daily distress and emotional well‐being form related but distinguishable dimensions, as suggested by a dual‐continuum perspective, and how they relate to perceived sleep quality. evening diaries assessed these variables in 831 university students over 14 days. emotional well‐being comprised positive affect and life satisfaction, whereas distress comprised emotional exhaustion, depressed affect, anxiety, and negative affect. multilevel confirmatory factor analysis supported two correlated within‐person higher order factors over a single higher order factor, with a factor correlation of −.501. a bayesian multilevel vector autoregressive model of order 1 (var(1)) estimated adjacent‐day associations. higher‐than‐usual distress predicted lower subsequent emotional well‐being ( β = −.032, 95% credible interval [cri] [−.053, −.012]). distress predicted poorer perceived quality of the subsequent sleep episode ( β = −.057, 95% cri [−.078, −.037]), and sleep quality reported at the preceding diary occasion predicted lower current distress ( β = −.024, 95% cri [−.043, −.004]) and higher emotional well‐being ( β = .021, 95% cri [.001, .040]). the paths from emotional well‐being to subsequent distress and sleep quality had 95% cris that included zero. the within‐person measurement structure is consistent with a dual‐continuum perspective on daily distress and emotional well‐being. applied psychology-health and well being

capturing the hostile attribution bias through conditional reasoning tasks: the hostile reasoning test as an indirect measure of aggressiveness abstract the hostile attribution bias is considered a central component of aggressiveness. it is thought to be a rather impulsive mechanism which justifies (reactive) aggressive behaviour as logical and reasonable. therefore, reasoning tasks may provide an unobtrusive means to make the hostile attribution bias accessible to measurement. in this manuscript, we developed such a task, the hostile reasoning test (hrt), and assessed its psychometric properties. in three studies, we found that the hrt is reliable, shows convergent and discriminant validity for a male (study 1, n = 206) and female (study 3, n = 207) sample, and demonstrates incremental validity beyond self‐reported aggressiveness in predicting reactive aggressive behaviour (study 2, n = 78). the present results indicate that reasoning tasks such as the hrt are a promising complement to self‐report measures, in particular if the more reactive and impulsive aspects of aggressiveness are of interest. european journal of social psychology

misguided convictions? from maladaptive beliefs about emotions to conspiracy theories endorsement abstract negative emotions can catalyse perceptions of a hostile world, promoting conspiracy theories that involve beliefs in malevolent forces behind events. in our research, we propose that maladaptive emotion beliefs (i.e., beliefs about the uselessness and uncontrollability of emotions) are likely to underpin conspiracy beliefs. this hypothesis was tested across five studies conducted among british and polish participants. in three cross‐sectional studies ( n 1 = 403, n 2 = 1143 and n 4 = 432), we demonstrated a significant relationship between maladaptive emotion beliefs and higher conspiracy beliefs, with higher psychological distress potentially accounting for the observed link. experimental studies ( n 3 = 814 and n 5 = 1140) suggested that the link between maladaptive emotion beliefs and conspiracy beliefs might be causal, as they demonstrated that inducing maladaptive emotion beliefs increased conspiracy beliefs. we highlight the importance of exploring emotion‐related phenomena in research on conspiracy theories endorsement. european journal of social psychology

improving descriptive diagnostics of autism in people with moderate or severe intellectual disabilities: a qualitative participatory study. purpose: this study aimed to improve descriptive autism assessment for people with moderate to severe intellectual disabilities (id) in the netherlands. the goal was to co-design a framework including an overview of assessment instruments, and recommendations for evaluating broader functioning, for translating findings into daily care and for involving representatives and staff.
methods: we used a participatory design, involving parents/representatives, clinicians, care staff, and management from id and mental health services. the process included a literature study of autism-related instruments, a delphi study to reach consensus on suitable instruments, and four focus group discussions (fgds) exploring stakeholder involvement and the role of assessment instruments in the diagnostic process.
results: the literature study identified 20 relevant instruments, of which 13 were selected through the delphi study (n=37, three rounds). key selection criteria included low burden for individuals, use of multiple information sources, and strong psychometric quality. while quick assessments were preferred, concerns arose about oversimplifying the autism assessment. fgds (n=5-12) highlighted eight themes on stakeholder involvement, focusing on timing, roles, and goals. although no consensus emerged on an optimal combination of tools, clarity about an instrument's purpose and implications proved important. the final fgd identified five potentially overlapping phases in the diagnostic process.
conclusion: the co-designed framework provides an overview of instruments for the assessment of autism and emphasises early and continuous involvement of parents and caregivers. their participation is essential for defining concerns, guiding assessment goals, sharing information, and applying diagnostic outcomes to improve daily care and support. journal of autism and developmental disorders

exploring community nurses' perspectives on adolescent suicide prevention in indonesia: a descriptive qualitative study. background: adolescent suicide prevention is not only a clinical or service-delivery problem; it is also socially organized through stigma, family and community norms, trust, help-seeking expectations, and the relationships that connect adolescents with potential helpers. in indonesia, community nurses work at the interface of adolescents, families, schools, primary health care, and community institutions, yet little is known about how they interpret and negotiate this role.
purpose: to explore community nurses' perspectives on adolescent suicide prevention in indonesia, focusing on how suicide risk becomes visible or remains hidden, how nurses understand their preventive roles, the barriers that constrain action, and the support and system conditions needed to strengthen practice.
method: a descriptive qualitative study was conducted in bandung, west java, indonesia with 14 purposively selected community nurses. individual semi-structured interviews were analyzed using a codebook-oriented thematic analysis. reporting was guided by the consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (coreq).
results: four interpretative themes were developed: suicide risk is socially hidden before it becomes clinically visible; community nurses function as relational gatekeepers whose effectiveness depends on trust; normative stigma and professional uncertainty constrain preventive action; and nurses are expected to coordinate across sectors without sufficient structural enablement. participants described shame, fear of judgment, family responses, and religious or moral sensitivities as shaping disclosure and help-seeking. they also described roles in mental health education, early recognition, supportive communication, family engagement, and referral, while emphasizing limited suicide-specific training, unclear pathways, and fragmented school-family-health service coordination.
conclusions: community nurses occupy a potentially important social-psychological and service-system position in adolescent suicide prevention in indonesia. their effectiveness depends not only on individual knowledge but also on the social conditions that make disclosure safe and help-seeking legitimate, together with clear protocols, referral pathways, cross-sector collaboration, and institutional support within existing indonesian adolescent and primary-care platforms. acta psychologica

adaptation and psychometric evaluation of selected scales from the resilience portfolio questionnaire in school-going adolescents from northern chile the resilience portfolio model distinguishes regulatory, meaning-making and interpersonal strengths that help adolescents adapt to adversity, but no measure aligned with this model has been examined in chile. this study adapted 13 scales (63 items) of the resilience portfolio questionnaire and evaluated the internal structure, reliability and criterion relations of their scores in 889 adolescents aged 14–18 from northern chile, 43.1% of whom reported a non-chilean nationality. items were purified in a calibration subsample (n = 445), and the retained specifications were tested without modification in a validation subsample (n = 444) and then re-estimated in the full sample. the theoretical structure was not reproduced, and three subdimensions were excluded. a bifactor exploratory structural equation model with one general and ten specific factors (41 items) was reproduced as the best-fitting specification in the validation subsample, although its fit was approximate and some misspecification remained (cfi = 0.934, tli = 0.872, rmsea = 0.063). it also fitted best in the full sample, which includes the calibration data (cfi = 0.969, tli = 0.939, rmsea = 0.041). in the full sample, the general factor was well defined (ωh = 0.78, h = 0.92), the specific reliability of the subscales ranged from 0.38 to 0.81, and the general factor had a correlation of −0.22 with psychological distress and 0.47 with life satisfaction. the results provide preliminary support for a short measure of ten resilient strengths that does not cover the full structure of the model and requires invariance testing across national groups. adolescents

a health literacy-based intervention to promote safer weight-control dietary supplement use among female vocational students: a quasi-experimental study weight-control dietary supplement use among female vocational students may be influenced by sociocultural pressures related to body image and may pose potential health risks when products are used inappropriately. health literacy may strengthen their ability to access, understand, evaluate, and apply health information when making decisions about dietary supplement use. this study evaluated the effectiveness of a health literacy-based intervention (3 × 3 × 3 program) in promoting health literacy and safer weight-control dietary supplement use among female vocational students in bangkok, thailand. a quasi-experimental study was conducted among 76 female vocational students aged 18–21 years assigned to an intervention group (n = 38) or a control group (n = 38). the intervention group participated in the 3 × 3 × 3 program, comprising three structured learning sessions, each incorporating three learning steps over three hours, based on a health literacy framework, while the control group received the standard curriculum. health literacy and weight-control dietary supplement use behaviors were assessed at baseline, immediately post-intervention, and at one-month follow-up using self-administered questionnaires. intervention effects were analyzed using two-way mixed-design repeated-measures anova. the intervention group showed significantly greater improvements in health literacy and safer weight-control dietary supplement use behaviors than the control group at both post-intervention and one-month follow-up (p < 0.001). large effect sizes were observed for health literacy (partial η2 = 0.864) and supplement-use behavior (partial η2 = 0.928). these findings suggest that health literacy-based interventions may be an effective approach to strengthening female vocational students’ capacity to make safer decisions regarding weight-control dietary supplements and may inform health promotion initiatives for this population. adolescents

correlates of prosocial behaviour in children and adolescents accessing outpatient psychiatry background: adolescent psychiatric illness is a serious health problem, though the prosocial behaviours of patients presenting with internalizing concerns has gained little attention. the purpose of this study was to explore prosocial behaviours and their correlates in adolescents accessing outpatient psychiatry in a cross-sectional exploratory study. methods: a survey was administered to patients on their first appointment to outpatient psychiatry. results: participants’ (n = 51) reported prosocial behaviours were positively associated with self-care in the final model; bivariate negative associations were evident between prosocial behaviours and attachment problems and peer problems. conclusions: adolescent patients might benefit from a clinical focus on self-care, in particular, maintaining positive connections with others. adolescents

the words of our inner worlds: emotional language use in mind-wandering and dream reports reflects mental ill-being abstract do the words we use reveal how we feel? while much research has explored language use in social media, little is known about how the content of spontaneous thoughts and experiences, such as daytime mind-wandering and nighttime dreaming, reflects well-being, and ill-being. we analyzed 1 496 mind-wandering reports (n = 152) and 1781 dream reports (n = 172) using the linguistic inquiry and word count. participants also self-reported their well-being and ill-being. linear mixed-effects models showed that ill-being (negative affect, anxiety, and depression symptoms) was associated with the use of negative tone and negative emotion words (including anxiety, anger, sadness words) in mind-wandering reports. ill-being (specifically, negative affect) was also associated with greater use of anxiety words in dream reports. well-being (eudaimonic well-being and peace of mind) was associated with the use of positive tone words in mind-wandering reports, but this association was not robust in sensitivity analyses. these findings indicate that the way people describe their feelings in reports of different conscious states reflects aspects of their mental health and may contribute to future diagnostic tools in psychology and psychiatry. neuroscience of consciousness

predictive biases in emotional perception: differential influence of mood and affective primes in individuals with and without mood disorders abstract predictive processing models perception as an interplay between top-down predictions and bottom-up sensory inputs. when signals are ambiguous, perception increasingly relies on prior expectations. in emotional contexts, mood and affective primes may act as endogenous and exogenous predictions, biasing emotional perception, particularly in mood disorders, where predictions may become overly strong or unstable. eighty-four participants (53 healthy controls, hc; 31 with self-reported mood disorders) completed an online affective priming task on unambiguous and ambiguous (morphs) facial expressions, preceded by masked or unmasked faces. participants rated target emotions and completed mood questionnaires. principal component analysis extracted latent mood dimensions. drift diffusion modeling (ddm) estimated cognitive processes underlying ambiguous face perception. in hc and bipolar disorder (bd), happy primes increased positive morph categorization, while in depression (dep), masked sad primes increased negative categorizations more than in hc and bd. masked primes accelerated responses to morphs in hc, while bd showed faster responses regardless of priming type, with stronger facilitation than hc and dep. no reaction time priming effects were observed in dep. ddm revealed pre-decisional biases induced by primes, while mood only subtly influenced evidence accumulation. findings suggest group-specific predictive biases: hc used masked primes to resolve emotional ambiguity, bd showed stronger reliance on external cues regardless of priming type, and dep showed reduced sensitivity to primes alongside a selective negativity categorization bias. these biases may underlie core clinical features of mood disorders and may point to new targets for interventions aiming to restore adaptive emotional inference. neuroscience of consciousness

norms for a german version of the phenomenological control scalemeasuring the capacity for creating and controlling experience. the ability to create experiences which misrepresent reality and thereby meet strategic goals is a stable trait that varies substantially in the general population. the capacity for such phenomenological control can be measured by response to imaginative suggestions for a variety of experiences, e.g. hallucination in various modalities, amnesia, paralysis, or motor actions, which are experienced as involuntary. here, we present norms for a german translation of the phenomenological control scale [lush(the phenomenological control scale: measuring the capacity for creating illusory nonvolition, hallucination, and delusion.2021;7:29542)]. data were collected from a representative sample of native-german speakers ( = 299) using a single-session online screening procedure. we show that the translated scale is psychometrically sound, and in line with the results of the original scale in terms of mean scores, distribution, and internal consistency. all analyses, code, data, materials, and the full questionnaire script are made freely available. other researchers in the field of psychology are welcome to access and encouraged to use the german norms for the phenomenological control scale, e.g. to assess the degree to which trait phenomenological control may be involved in other psychological effects. neuroscience of consciousness

habitus, reflexivity, and micro‐hysteresis: an experimental dialogue between bourdieu's praxeology and pragmatist theories of action abstract the article explores an analytical strategy through which bourdieu's theory of practice and (neo)pragmatist theories of action, especially dewey's, may be synthesised into an integrated model of the subjective motors of social conduct, one capable of granting due explanatory weight to both habitual dispositions and reflexive processes. on the one hand, pragmatists show that disjunctions between habitual dispositions and the social circumstances of action, which demand a greater role for reflexive deliberation in relation to habitual propensities as subjective motors of conduct, do not occur only in the scenarios of radical structural crisis that bourdieu termed the ‘hysteresis effect.’ situated along a continuum of greater or lesser intensities, including what we may call ‘micro‐hystereses,’ such disjunctions are part of agents' everyday relationship to their collective contexts of experience. on the other hand, as a theory of the ‘regulated improvisations’ of ‘practical sense,’ bourdieu's praxeology not only captures the creative component of habitual dispositions themselves, but may also combine the non‐mechanistic notion of ‘habit’ proposed by dewey's pragmatism with a concept of habitus as a system of habits or dispositions. finally, the article explores different modes of reflexivity and the circuits of reciprocal influence they establish with habitual dispositions, including both the role of reflexivity in dispositional self‐transformation and the possibility that reflexive processes may themselves have dysfunctional effects. journal for the theory of social behaviour

cognitive functioning in very preterm children and links with socio‐family risk and parenting abstract children born very preterm are at elevated risk of developing cognitive difficulties, yet the contribution of family and social factors to their neurodevelopment remains unclear. this cross‐sectional study examines their cognitive performance relative to normative standards and uses an exploratory framework linking socio‐family risk and intellectual functioning through potential indirect pathways via parenting styles. a sample of 135 children born before 32 weeks of gestation and/or very low birth weight (< 1500 g) (mean age = 8.67 years) was assessed using the wechsler intelligence scale for children–fifth edition (wisc‐v). socio‐family risk was measured through a cumulative index, and parenting was evaluated using the parenting styles and dimensions questionnaire. very preterm children showed significantly lower average scores across full‐scale iq ( t (134) = −6.68, p < 0.001, d = −0.58) and all indices compared to the normative population. fluid reasoning, working memory, and processing speed showed the greatest vulnerabilities. mediation analyses suggested that an authoritative parenting style partially accounts for the association between socio‐family risk and intellectual outcomes. these findings suggest that positive parenting was associated with better intellectual outcomes and support the potential value of family‐centered interventions for very preterm children. scandinavian journal of psychology

training and knowledge of women’s health topics: a survey of neuropsychologists and trainees training in women's health topics is limited, impacting clinicians' preparedness to address sex-specific concerns. little is known about the extent neuropsychologists receive structured education in these areas or their comfort with addressing women-specific neurocognitive concerns in practice. this study examined neuropsychologists' self-reported training exposure, clinical comfort, and objective knowledge regarding women's health.a cross-sectional online survey was completed by neuropsychology trainees (29%) and professionals (34% early-, 20% mid-, 17% senior-career) recruited through listservs and social media. demographics, self-reported training exposure and clinical comfort, and an objective 5-item knowledge quiz were collected. descriptive statistics examined differences in comfort and knowledge by training, work setting, and career stage.participants ( = 122) were predominantly white/non-hispanic (84%) women (91%) in the united states (89%), with diverse professional roles and work settings. results showed 59% reported no formal training and 41% reported "slight to no comfort" addressing women's health concerns. although item-level accuracy on the knowledge quiz was high (68.03-95.08%), 48% of participants answered all items correctly; performance did not differ by training, setting, or career stage.findings indicate limited formal training, low comfort addressing women-specific neurocognitive issues in clinical care but intact knowledge on common women's health questions. this gap may perpetuate sex-related disparities in patient care and research in this area. formalized training initiatives are warranted to improve confidence and competence for neuropsychologists. clinical neuropsychologist

the differential role of executive functions in reading fluency in children with reading difficulties, children with autism and typically developing children. purpose: reading fluency depends in part on executive functions (ef). dysfluent reading and reduced ef occur in both autism spectrum disorder (asd) and reading disability (rd), but whether the ef-reading fluency associations established in rd also characterize asd is unclear. we tested whether diagnostic group moderates these associations.
methods: two hundred twenty-three english-speaking children aged 8-12 years with asd (n = 35), rd (n = 99), and typical development (td; n = 89) completed measures of single-word, pseudoword, and contextual reading fluency, working memory (digit span), and processing speed (coding, symbol search). welch's anovas compared groups; linear models with group×ef interactions and simple slopes tested moderation, with age covaried in sensitivity models.
results: both clinical groups showed lower reading fluency and ef than td. coding predicted word and pseudoword fluency most strongly in asd (β = 0.40 and 0.43) and less strongly in td, but not in rd. digit span predicted word fluency in asd, and pseudoword fluency in asd and rd. for contextual fluency, a significant group × symbol search interaction (p = .003) indicated that symbol search predicted performance in asd (β = 0.52) and td (β = 0.29) but not rd. results were unchanged with age covaried.
conclusion: ef-reading fluency associations were strongest and most widespread in asd, whereas in rd executive measures predicted decoding-level but not contextual fluency. comparable dysfluency thus rests on distinct executive profiles, supporting the inclusion of ef measures in reading assessment for children with autism and cautioning against transferring rd-derived interventions without adaptation. journal of autism and developmental disorders

exploring the heterogeneity of the externalizing spectrum in youth abstract child and adolescent externalizing problems have often been conceptualized broadly with imprecise language (e.g., “disruptive behavior”) or inconsistently across varying taxonomies (e.g., oppositional defiant and conduct disorder symptoms, aggressive and rule-breaking behaviors). establishing clarity around dimensions of externalizing problems is an essential step toward more accurate measurement and construct validity across the externalizing domain. to that end, the current study investigated fine-grained dimensions in the structure of youth externalizing psychopathology. caregiver-report survey data were collected for a national community sample of 576 youth (ages 6–14; 45% female, 25% hispanic), including measures of irritability, oppositionality, reactive and proactive aggression, conduct problems, hyperactivity/impulsivity, and inattention. we used exploratory factor analysis (efa) to examine relations among externalizing dimensions at the item-level followed by confirmatory factor analysis (cfa) to examine relations at the construct-level. efa results suggested that a 3-factor model best fit the data, including factors characterized by externalizing affect (e.g., “felt mad”), externalizing behavior (e.g., “bullies, threatens, or intimidates others”), and adhd symptoms (e.g., “talks excessively”), with a few cross-loadings. similarly, confirmatory models indicated that a 3-factor, non-hierarchical structure fit the data best when compared to three other models. results provide support for distinct facets of the externalizing spectrum in child psychopathology, suggesting a preliminary direction for a unifying framework. these findings highlight the potential for future measurement research to further disentangle the distinct and overlapping facets of externalizing constructs, particularly using multiple methods and informants and with replication across samples. journal of psychopathology and behavioral assessment

an incentivized belief elicitation experiment on gender stereotypes in peer ability attribution abstract beliefs about ability shape hiring, promotion, and pay even when objective performance does not differ by gender. drawing on status characteristics theory, statistical discrimination, and the representativeness account of stereotypes, this study asks whether peer evaluators differentiate their ability estimates by target gender when accuracy is financially rewarded and the task is fully visible. in a two-stage design, 18 undergraduates first completed mathematical, verbal, and effort-based tasks, producing benchmark scores for six gender-by-major cells. a separate sample of 344 undergraduate raters then inspected the tasks and estimated the score of each target cell, identified by gender, academic major, and year of study, with payment tied to estimation accuracy. raters did not differentiate by target gender overall ( $$d = -0.001$$ ) or within any task domain ( $$|d| \le 0.05$$ ). however, gender differentiation was conditional on the target’s field. in mathematics the major-by-gender interaction was significant. female economics targets received higher estimates than male economics targets ( $$d = -0.41$$ ), a difference that survived correction for multiple comparisons, whereas the differences among engineering and education targets did not. female raters also assigned higher estimates than male raters in the mathematical and effort domains, independently of target gender. the findings indicate that when evaluators hold both a diffuse status cue (gender) and a task-relevant cue (field of study), the field dominates, and that gender expectations in this population are field-conditional rather than uniformly stereotyped. implications for the design of evaluative environments are discussed. discover psychology

the impact of acute sleep restriction on executive functions: a quasi-experimental within-subjects examination of inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility acute sleep restriction can affect several aspects of higher-order cognition, including executive functioning. the present study examined how one night of acute sleep restriction affected three core components of executive functioning-inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility-using a within-subjects experimental design. thirty-three healthy adults aged 18-35 years completed a standardized neurocognitive battery consisting of the stroop color-word task, go/no-go task, n-back task, task-switching paradigm, and wisconsin card sorting test under two counterbalanced conditions: normal sleep (7-9 hours) and acute sleep restriction (≤4 hours). sleep duration was monitored objectively using wrist actigraphy and supplemented with standardized sleep diaries. performance declined across all three executive-function components following sleep restriction. the largest effects were observed in measures of cognitive flexibility, including increased switch costs and perseverative errors. overall, the findings suggest that even a single night of substantial sleep restriction can adversely affect executive functioning, with cognitive flexibility appearing particularly sensitive to reduced sleep. applied neuropsychology-adult

should we expect expected value? abstract expected value (ev) is commonly treated as the central determinant of risky choice, either directly or as a reference point for higher‐order representations of risk. however, people's valuations of gambles often deviate from ev, and it is unclear whether this reflects biases in representing and integrating numerical information or preferences for other properties of the outcome distribution. we compared explicit ev estimation with certainty equivalent–based attractiveness evaluation across four instructional conditions in a sample of 137 participants. participants evaluated two‐outcome gambles varying in ev, standard deviation, and skewness. analyses showed that participants estimated ev accurately when instructed to do so, and these estimates were largely unaffected by variance or skewness. in contrast, subjective valuation was strongly influenced by skewness but not by standard deviation. positively skewed gambles were valued above their ev, whereas negatively skewed gambles were valued below it. the findings indicate a dissociation between ev computation and subjective valuation: people can estimate ev directly, yet broader evaluations of risky options rely on additional psychologically salient features, particularly skewness. thus, biases in processing the displayed numbers explain only a minor part of the deviations of valuations from ev; most of the deviation arises when gambles are valued. journal of behavioral decision making

comprehenders' error correction mechanisms are finely calibrated to language production statistics abstract an essential feature of human communication is robustness to errors: even when speakers and writers make mistakes, listeners and readers can usually determine the intended meaning. a leading hypothesis is that comprehenders achieve robust error correction by internally deploying a “noisy‐channel” model of the language production process. crucially, to best achieve error robustness, a comprehender's noisy‐channel model should be finely calibrated to the environmental statistics of language production, incorporating not only prior expectations about communicative intents but also structure‐sensitive likelihoods of different types of speaker error. this environmentally calibrated noisy‐channel hypothesis has been difficult to test, because the rates of most types of language production errors are hard to estimate. here, we test this hypothesis by experimentally investigating comprehenders' interpretations of subject–verb agreement errors, for which context‐contingent language production error rates are feasible to estimate. in a novel free‐form error correction task, participants edited sentences with subject–verb agreement mismatches to indicate what they think was intended. bayesian analysis of the resulting data shows that comprehenders' interpretations reflect both item‐specific prior expectations and structure‐sensitive error likelihoods that closely correspond to error rates in language production. these results provide quantitative evidence that humans closely track prior statistics over linguistic forms and deploy a noisy‐channel model finely calibrated to statistics of the linguistic environment to achieve robust language understanding. cognitive science

capturing thought dynamics: modeling the structure of spontaneous associations abstract human thought unfolds in patterns that vary across individuals; some move fluidly across ideas, whereas others return to narrower or more repetitive paths. here, we asked whether structural aspects of associative thinking—its breadth, trajectory, and temporal pace—can account for individual differences in repetitive thought styles such as rumination. participants completed brief free‐association tasks, and their responses were quantified using a model trained on large‐scale free association data to derive individual structural profiles of associative flow. across two independent samples, these profiles predicted self‐reported measures of rumination and repetitive thinking, with nonlinear models accounting for meaningful inter‐individual variation and showing generalization across tasks and datasets. these findings suggest that individual differences in repetitive thought are reflected not only in what people think about but also in how associations are organized and unfold over time. structural modeling therefore provides a viable approach to characterizing spontaneous cognition through patterns of associative organization. cognitive science

timing matters: cross‐codal integration of bridging event information happens while viewing picture stories abstract despite the prevalence of multi‐codal narratives—such as comics consisting of pictures and text—in everyday life, little is understood about how individuals integrate information across different codalities to form cohesive mental representations. in the present study, we explored when processing costs emerged during cross‐codal integration of bridging event information in multi‐codal narratives. participants were presented with uni‐codal (i.e., consisting only of pictures or of text) and multi‐codal stories in which the bridging event information was presented in the other codality. we measured viewing times for the bridging event and end‐state panels to reflect the cognitive costs associated with integration. the results showed a significant interaction between codality switch and panel position. while the presence of a codality switch increased viewing times for both panel positions, there was a much larger increase for the bridging event panel than the end‐state panel. this result supports a hypothesis suggesting that during narrative understanding, information of a different codality is integrated into the mental representation of the narrative upon encountering it. our results underscore the influence of codality on narrative integration, indicating that understanding may be affected by the format in which information is presented. future models of event cognition should incorporate codality as a factor in narrative comprehension. cognitive science

viewers actively extract and maintain spontaneous theory of mind representations in dramatic irony scenes abstract understanding others’ mental states is a cornerstone of human cognition, yet how spontaneous belief attribution operates in complex, naturalistic perception remains underexplored. dramatic irony (di)—a narrative device through which viewers are aware of information unknown to characters—provides a controlled but naturalistic context to examine these processes. using a curated di film corpus, we combined eye‐tracking with (a) self‐paced and (b) video viewing to investigate how spontaneous theory of mind shapes real‐time processing. across two experiments, participants viewed edited harold lloyd silent film excerpts that either provided privileged information (installation condition) or aligned viewer and character knowledge (control condition), reflecting false‐ and true‐belief scenarios. clips were either presented as a self‐paced static series of frames (experiment 1) or dynamic film clips (experiment 2). we analyzed narrative comprehension, reaction times, and eye‐tracking measures indexing cognitive effort. results showed that, relative to the control condition, the installation condition yielded longer viewing times at moments of representational conflict, indicating increased cognitive demands associated with maintaining and applying false‐belief representations. in experiment 1, these effects emerged at discrete moments and were accompanied by longer fixation durations in the installation condition. in experiment 2, longer fixation durations in the installation condition were again observed, alongside reduced fixation rates and saccade amplitudes, consistent with more sustained local processing. these findings indicate that viewers spontaneously construct and maintain false‐belief representations during di, which modulate real‐time processing during scene comprehension, providing a tractable framework for investigating social reasoning in dynamic visual contexts. cognitive science

the longitudinal association between students’ extrinsic–dynamic spatial ability and achievement in science education in elementary school: a random‐intercept cross‐lagged panel model abstract research has shown that extrinsic–dynamic spatial ability is relevant to achievement in science education. however, the direction of the relationship between extrinsic–dynamic spatial ability and achievement remains unclear; this issue was thus addressed in a longitudinal study. fourth graders ( n = 335) from hong kong were assessed on these two constructs three times, at 4‐month intervals; control variables were also included during the first assessment. data were analyzed using a random‐intercept cross‐lagged panel model (ri‐clpm). after accounting for between‐person variation, within‐person variation in science achievement at time 1 significantly predicted within‐person variation in extrinsic–dynamic spatial ability at time 2, which in turn predicted within‐person variation in achievement at time 3. the findings confirmed the dynamic reciprocal relationship between these two constructs. overall, they suggest that spatial and scientific skills co‐develop over time. furthermore, they indicate that tasks involving extrinsic–dynamic spatial ability can be incorporated into elementary science curricula to foster students’ cognitive development, thereby enhancing learning outcomes in science education. developmental science

profiling phubbing practitioners using machine learning. phubbing is a heterogeneous digital behavior that may occur within different configurations of personality and problematic social media use. this study identified multivariate profiles of brazilian adults on the basis of big five personality traits, problematic instagram use, and the communication disturbance and phone obsession dimensions of phubbing. the initial sample included 1,551 adults; the primary analysis included 1,470 current instagram users. eight standardized indicators were analyzed using gaussian mixture models with one to six components and alternative covariance structures. model selection prioritized the bayesian information criterion (bic), with the akaike information criterion (aic) used as complementary evidence. the five-component diagonal model had the lowest bic, whereas the aic favored a six-component diagonal solution. the bic-preferred model identified five partially overlapping profiles: regulated low-digital (16.9%), introverted low-digital (15.6%), moderate digital (21.1%), socially engaged digital (20.8%), and digitally vulnerable (25.6%). the average maximum posterior membership probability was 0.803, indicating meaningful classification uncertainty. the profiles differed most strongly in problematic instagram use, phone obsession, communication disturbance, conscientiousness, and extraversion. the findings indicate that phubbing-related behaviors occur within heterogeneous personality-digital configurations rather than a single psychological pattern. the profiles should be interpreted as probabilistic and descriptive, not as fixed psychological types or diagnostic categories. longitudinal and independent replication studies are needed to examine their stability and practical relevance. frontiers in psychology

is there a social cure for climate change distress and impairment? initial evidence that group‐based control might shield general well‐being abstract climate change undermines well‐being through helplessness and loss of control. the social identity approach to health (“social cure”) and group‐based control theory suggest that identification with ingroups may maintain resilience to climate threats by sustaining a sense of control. drawing on these accounts, the present study examines whether national identification moderates the negative associations of climate change distress and climate change impairment with well‐being. pooling data from a german adult population sample ( n = 1136) across three waves, we find that the negative associations of climate change distress and climate change impairment with well‐being are weaker among individuals with stronger national identification, even after controlling for sociodemographic and political‐ideological characteristics. importantly, moderated mediation analyses indicate that these patterns are statistically associated with a preserved sense of personal control, consistent with social cure and group‐based control perspectives. extending prior findings on group‐based control in health contexts, our results highlight the potential relevance of social identification and collective control for mitigating the negative psychological impacts of climate change on well‐being. journal of applied social psychology

negative affectivity moderates the association between job demands and hair cortisol in healthcare workers: a cross-sectional multi-method study. aims: healthcare workers (hcws) are frequently exposed to psychosocial job demands (jds) that may lead to work-related stress. this study investigates the association between jds-specifically time pressure, problem solving, overload, and emotional demands-and hair cortisol concentration (hcc), as biomarker of long-term hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, in a sample of hcws. it further examines the moderating role of negative affectivity (na), an individual characteristic linked to heightened stress reactivity. drawing on the job demands-resources theory and the allostatic load model, we hypothesized that (1) jds would be positively associated with hcc and (2) this relationship would be stronger for individuals high in na.
design: participants were 67 healthcare professionals working in a healthcare facility located in northern italy. participants completed a self-report questionnaire designed to assess jds and na. next, participants provided a hair sample for the assessment of hcc.
results: although data from a sample of hcws revealed some positive but non-significant trends for problem solving and overload, generally jds were not associated with hcc at average levels of na. interestingly, na moderated the relationship between problem solving/time pressure and hcc, with stronger positive associations among individuals with high na.
conclusion: findings from this exploratory cross-sectional study suggest that na may act as a vulnerability factor, implying that hcws high in na may have a heightened strain response to certain jds. by integrating psychological and biological measures, this study offers novel insights into the interplay between workplace stressors, personality traits, and physiological responses to stress. these findings highlight the potential relevance of individual differences in occupational stress research, and point to hcc as a promising indicator of chronic stress among hcws.
implications for the profession: the findings suggest the need for occupational health interventions tailored to individual traits, such as na, to reduce stress reactivity, foster well-being, and enhance the quality of care provided. frontiers in psychology

societal and personal social mobility beliefs and prosocial behavior in chinese adolescents: the mediating role of belief in a just world and urban‐rural differences abstract introduction china's urban‐rural dual structure creates distinct social contexts that may be associated with differences in adolescents’ societal and personal social mobility beliefs. however, it remains unclear how societal and personal social mobility beliefs relate to prosocial behavior across urban‐rural contexts. this longitudinal study examined whether belief in a just world mediates the associations between societal and personal social mobility beliefs and prosocial behavior, and whether these pathways differ between urban and rural adolescents. method a total of 895 chinese adolescents ( m age = 12.70 ± 2.15 years; 57% girls; 56% rural) were surveyed at time 1, with 811 participants (attrition = 9.4%) completing a follow‐up 6 months later. results a cross‐lagged panel model within a half‐longitudinal design indicated that societal social mobility belief was negatively associated with subsequent prosocial behavior, whereas personal social mobility belief was positively associated with subsequent prosocial behavior. belief in a just world mediated the associations of both societal and personal social mobility beliefs with prosocial behavior. multigroup analyses further revealed urban–rural differences. among urban adolescents, belief in a just world mediated the associations of both societal and personal social mobility beliefs with prosocial behavior. among rural adolescents, however, belief in a just world mediated only the association between personal social mobility belief and prosocial behavior. conclusion these findings suggest that social mobility beliefs are indirectly associated with prosocial behavior through belief in a just world, and that these indirect associations differ across urban and rural contexts. journal of adolescence
the effects of drawing and writing encoding methods on item and associative recognition in younger and older adults memory

parental psychological control and symptoms of depression and anxiety in predominantly hispanic middle school students: investigating the mediating role of emotional regulation difficulties abstract youth mental health is crucial for overall well‐being, and its absence can have detrimental consequences. parenting behaviors play a significant role in promoting or hindering youths' psychosocial development. in particular, parental psychological control has been linked to increased levels of internalizing and externalizing problems in adolescents. guided by theories and previous research, the current study investigated the associations between parental psychological control and symptoms of depression and anxiety and explored emotional regulation difficulties as a mediator in a sample of 144 predominantly hispanic middle school students. the study found that parental psychological control was positively and significantly associated with middle school students' depression and anxiety symptoms, and emotional regulation difficulties mediated these associations. the findings offer important implications for school psychology practice by informing the development of culturally responsive and school‐based interventions aimed at strengthening emotional regulation skills among predominantly hispanic adolescents exposed to parental psychological control and at risk for depression and anxiety. psychology in the schools

prevalence and predictors of death-related distress among cancer patients in a multi-ethnic asian setting: a cross-sectional study this study examined the prevalence, pattern, and predictors of death-related distress among 156 cancer patients in a multi-ethnic malaysian setting. the main concerns related to the dying process and its consequences, particularly prolonged dying, becoming a burden to others, the impact of death on loved ones, and unfinished life goals. moderate-or-greater distress affected 39% of patients for prolonged dying and approximately one-third for the other major concerns. multivariable analysis showed that greater death-related distress was independently associated with younger age, mild functional decline reflected by ecog performance status 1, higher anxiety, and greater suffering. these factors collectively explained a substantial proportion of variation in distress scores. the findings indicate that death-related distress is common among cancer patients and may not be limited to those with advanced physical impairment. routine screening should therefore focus particularly on younger patients, those showing early functional deterioration, and individuals experiencing significant anxiety or global suffering. omega-journal of death and dying

mental health of university students in valència following the 2024 cutoff low (dana): a cross-sectional study natural disasters are stress factors that can affect university students’ mental health. during the floods caused by the 2024 cutoff low (dana in spanish) in valencia, the media recognized the remarkable volunteer work carried out by students during the recovery effort. this study assessed the consequences of the dana event on stress, well-being, and distress symptomatology (depression and anxiety) among 793 spanish university students, 593 of whom were enrolled in affected universities. the results revealed that, compared with those who were not exposed, students who were exposed to dana had higher levels of positive affect and life satisfaction alongside fewer depressive symptoms. however, participants who experienced direct losses evidenced lower levels of well-being and greater distress, as did women and individuals combining studies with work. structural equation modeling enabled the testing of a theoretically specified structural model between perceived stress and mental health. in both groups, stress affected anxiety and depression directly. nevertheless, among those affected by dana, stress was associated with life satisfaction solely indirectly via affect. these findings underscore the coexistence of adaptation and vulnerability processes in the aftermath of the disaster and highlight the need to focus the actions of higher education institutions on prevention and psychosocial support. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

decent education in china: context, conceptualization, and assessment decent education has been theorized as a foundation for career development, yet its measurement has not been validated outside western contexts. across two complementary but non-equivalent studies, we adapted the decent education scale (des) for 457 chinese senior high-school students and the retrospective decent education scale (rdes) for 661 university students recalling high school. confirmatory factor analyses and nomological-network tests provided initial structural and construct-validity evidence. brief open-ended responses, analyzed as an exploratory content-validity component, broadly supported the six-domain framework and highlighted extracurricular enrichment, study-life balance, physical infrastructure, and personal development as contextual expressions or candidate areas for future item development. by illuminating how these two scales operate in china, this study extends the assessment of decent education beyond its original swiss and u.s. validation contexts, and establishes a foundation for future cross-cultural, longitudinal, and equity-oriented research in career assessment. journal of career assessment

mental health implications of (mal-)adaptive approaches to leisure music engagement: the role of motivation and self-criticism the relationship between music engagement and health has attracted growing academic interest over the past decades, pointing to mostly beneficial associations, especially with music listening and music interventions. however, recent research indicates a more complex relationship emphasizing the relevance of exploring how and why people engage with music. since playing music and singing are common leisure-time activities for many people, this study aimed to investigate potential (mal-)adaptive approaches to music engagement, that is, self-determined motivation, and its association with mental health in amateur musicians. one hundred and ninety-eight participants completed an online survey on their motivation to make music, as well as depression, anxiety, stress, and self-criticism. structural equation models showed that controlled motivation (more external reasons) positively predicted depression, stress, and self-criticism, but not anxiety. further, results provided evidence for a full mediation of the association between controlled motivation and depression, anxiety, and stress via self-criticism. our findings highlight the importance of individual motivations and dispositions in music engagement, pointing to potentially harmful effects on mental health. practical implications for effective health promotion include considering individual motivations and dispositions and enhancing autonomy and self-compassion in leisure interventions and recreational therapy. future research should investigate further individual and situational determinants. psychology of music

high school music participation: the role of identity, value, expectancy, and cost while secondary music programs enjoy participation from many students, school music enrollment often does not reflect the demographics of the broader student population. this study examined how high-school students’ musical identities and sociocognitive beliefs influenced their intentions to enroll in high-school music classes. drawing on situated expectancy-value theory, we developed a model of how musical identity and expectancy-value constructs influence students’ enrollment decisions in three music classes: large ensembles, music technology/production, and piano/guitar. we surveyed 486 students at a large u.s. public high school, measuring musical identity, expectancy-value constructs, and intentions to enroll in each of the three class contexts. structural equation models showed musical identity positively predicted expectancy and value; expectancy negatively predicted cost; and both value and cost predicted enrollment intentions (positively and negatively, respectively). notably, expectancy influenced intentions only indirectly via cost. although both value and cost predicted intentions across all class types, cost was more strongly associated with intentions for large ensembles, whereas value was more strongly associated with intentions for music technology/production and piano/guitar. these findings suggest motivational beliefs are context-dependent and deeply interrelated. music teachers may benefit from considering the context-specific roles of cost, value, and expectancy when recruiting students for classes. psychology of music

trusting the ai rather than the expert? evidence from sports-related assessments in relation to the olympic games 2024 abstract we investigated how predictions regarding the outcome of sports competitions are affected by concurrent predictions which were believed to originate from either a human sports expert or an ai system. participants were asked to estimate the probability of a certain team to win a group match against the respective opponent in various matches of the 2024 olympic games and to report their confidence in that estimate. moreover, they received numerical estimates for that probability which were either high or low, and which were believed to originate from a human expert or an ai system. participants’ estimates were biased towards these supplementary estimates, thus reflecting an anchoring effect. yet, this effect’s size was independent of the believed source of the anchor and even non-significantly higher for ai support. confidence in provided judgments was even significantly higher when the believed origin of supplementary estimates was ai rather than human. altogether, the results suggest no bias against ai-generated sports outcome predictions, highlighting the task-dependency of reliance on ai. psychological research-psychologische forschung

risky alcohol use in individuals with anxiety disorders: relationships and predictors based on early maladaptive schemas and attachment styles abstract background and aim this study aims to evaluate the differences between the groups with and without risky alcohol use (rau) in terms of sociodemographic characteristics, anxiety level, adult attachment styles (aass) and early maladaptive schemas (emss) in individuals diagnosed with anxiety disorders (ads). furthermore, we aim to investigate whether rau in individuals with ads can be predicted by ems or aas. methods in this prospective study, a total of 128 individuals diagnosed with ads were divided into two groups based on the michigan alcoholism screening test (mast) cut‐off score (≥ 5). scores from the adult attachment style scale, young schema questionnaire and beck anxiety inventory (bai), as well as demographic and clinical variables, were analysed. results the rau group showed higher rates of suicide history and higher scores on the abandonment and unrelenting standards (us) schemas. higher scores on abandonment and us schemas were associated with a greater likelihood of rau. mast scores positively correlated with emotional deprivation, failure to achieve, pessimism, social isolation, as, dependence, abandonment, vulnerability schema scores and bai scores in individuals with rau. hierarchical regression showed that attachment and schema subscales accounted for 42% of the variance in mast scores. the higher scores on emotional inhibition, defectiveness, vulnerability schemas and anxious attachment style significantly predicted mast scores. conclusion these findings support the theoretical basis for attachment‐based and schema therapy‐based interventions, highlighting the importance of assessing especially abandonment, us, defectiveness, vulnerability schemas and anxious attachment style. clinical psychology & psychotherapy

treatment of eating disorder—posttraumatic stress disorder patients in residential care with and without cognitive processing therapy abstract objective posttraumatic stress disorder (ptsd) is a common co‐occurring diagnosis for individuals with eating disorders (eds) admitted to residential treatment (rt). while cognitive processing therapy (cpt) has shown promise for ed‐ptsd populations, few large‐scale naturalistic studies have evaluated cpt in residential ed treatment settings. this study examined outcomes for ed‐ptsd patients who elected to receive cpt compared to those who did not. methods participants ( n = 348) (including 247 who received cpt [cpt+] and 101 who did not [cpt–]) completed standardized self‐report measures at admission and discharge: ptsd checklist for dsm‐5 (pcl‐5), eating disorder examination questionnaire (ede‐q), eating disorders inventory (edi‐2), and patient health questionnaire (phq‐9). outcomes included changes in pcl‐5, ede‐q, and phq‐9 scores, and edi‐2 ineffectiveness and interoceptive awareness subscale scores. results significant time × group interactions indicated that symptom change differed by cpt participation for some outcomes. cpt + participants had greater reductions in ede‐q global, pcl‐5 total, and phq‐9 total scores than cpt− participants. changes in ineffectiveness and interoceptive awareness scores did not differ significantly between groups. discussion: cpt participation during rt was associated with greater reductions in ptsd, depressive, and ed symptoms through discharge—the nonrandomised design and variation in cpt exposure limit causal interpretation. european eating disorders review
