facing far forward: mental health in large-scale combat operations. large-scale combat operations (lsco) present unprecedented challenges to the provision of medical and mental health care on the battlefield. characterized by restricted mobility, contested logistics, disrupted communication, drone attacks, subterranean environments and the necessity for prolonged field care, the lsco environment will severely disrupt traditional models of combat and operational stress control (cosc) that rely on far-forward specialty providers and fixed facilities. this article introduces a special issue ofdedicated to reviewing mental health in lsco. by outlining the anticipated psychological demands of future near-peer conflicts, the goal of this special issue is to facilitate a shared and comprehensive understanding of possible threats and lay the groundwork for a way ahead to manage mental health in lsco. specifically, to maintain warfighter readiness and operational effectiveness, foundational cosc principles - proximity, immediacy, expectancy, and simplicity - must be reimagined. we highlight possible shifts in conceptualizing mental health care, including relying on leader-led interventions, peer-to-peer support and the training of non-specialty medical personnel (e.g. medics and corpsmen) to manage acute combat stress reactions using evidence-informed, rapid-intervention protocols. ultimately, the goal is to synthesize current research, lessons learned from global operations, and conceptual frameworks to establish priorities for mental health training, intervention development, and policy in preparation for managing mental health in lsco environments. military psychology

brace for impact: a roadmap for the future of mental health in large-scale combat operations. large-scale combat operations (lsco) are expected to present critical challenges to military units in terms of austere conditions, the potential for misinformation, specific lsco-related threats, and the limitations of access to traditional medical care. as part of a special issue ofdedicated to the topic of mental health in lsco, 25 articles address these challenges. articles cover key threats such as mass casualty events, drone warfare, and threats to the community. articles also identify how traditional military mental health support may need to be adapted to take prolonged field care into account, with a focus on mental health support becoming the responsibility of individuals, informal peers, trained peers, and leaders. furthermore, the articles address special topics such as the impact of lsco on medical personnel burnout, attitudes toward novel solutions such as mindfulness, and training models for integrating mental skills into simulations and field-based exercises. collectively, these articles inform the development of a schematic model of lsco mental health. in addition, future research topics provide direction for assessing, preventing, and intervening with mental health health and cognitive strain in the lsco context. by bringing this array of articles together, the field can prepare more effectively to meet the psychological demands of the lsco battlespace. military psychology

does adding nocebo avoidance strategies increase the strength of nocebo education? abstract: background: medication side effects are common and sometimes result from the nocebo effect – when expectations or anxiety exacerbate side effect experience. nocebo education is a health communication intervention for minimizing nocebo effects in which individuals learn about the nocebo effect. aims: we suggest that nocebo education interventions can be improved by also describing cognitive and behavioral strategies by which patients can actively minimize their own nocebo effects. method: in an online preregistered cross-sectional study, participants ( n = 436) were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: conventional nocebo education (cne), nocebo education supplemented with avoidance tactics (neat), or a control condition (health behavior education). following the manipulation, participants read about a statin medication and completed a broad palette of nocebo-relevant psychological outcomes. results: cne elevated perceived side effect control, tolerance, and intentions to avoid side effect information and decreased side effect information seeking intentions as compared to controls. the neat intervention surpassed the cne intervention, further increasing control and information avoidance intentions, while decreasing global side effect expectations, side effect worry, information seeking intentions, and discontinuation intentions. limitations: this study assessed only immediate psychological changes, so future work is needed with side effect reports and longitudinal designs to understand the applicability of the intervention. conclusion: we conclude that supplementing nocebo education with specific actionable reduction strategies increases its psychological impact, providing a valuable future direction for nocebo reduction research. european journal of health psychology

translating post‐training knowledge into psychotherapy practice: a reflexive thematic analysis of therapists' accounts following istdp and se training abstract background although therapists value formal continuing education, little is known about how it translates into clinical practice. aim this study addresses this gap by examining how therapists translate knowledge from intensive postgraduate training in intensive short‐term dynamic psychotherapy and somatic experiencing into practice. method we conducted semi‐structured interviews ( n = 15) within a critical realist qualitative design. we analysed participants' accounts using reflexive thematic analysis, guided theoretically by sensitising concepts from the revised version of eraut's performance model, to examine how therapists described applying acquired knowledge in sessions. results findings identified six themes describing a cyclical translation process, including readiness to apply new principles, reframing the therapeutic encounter, contextualised use of interventions and monitoring of client responses. therapists described new ways of interpreting clinical situations, alongside introducing interventions and techniques. discussion participants associated continued application with metacognitive monitoring and evaluation of client responsiveness. application involved clinical judgement about when and with whom to use new approaches, informed by model‐related interpretations and experience‐based assessments. conclusion within these accounts, knowledge translation emerged as a complex, individualised process involving metacognitive awareness and continuous adaptation. the model also offers a structured framework for describing self‐reported performance changes. findings are discussed in relation to training and context‐sensitive application. counselling & psychotherapy research

remainder, estrangement, and the pressure toward coherence in analytic process this paper examines moments in analytic process in which self-experience loses vitality when drawn too quickly into coherence through explanation or interpretation. remainder names what psychic life leaves beyond every act of formulation—not only experience that has not yet found symbolic form, but the excess formulation itself generates—and whose vitality depends on not being prematurely assimilated into settled meaning. consensus defense names the pressure within the analytic field to stabilize uncertainty through a prematurely shared understanding that protects analyst and patient from the anxiety of partially symbolized experience. the argument is developed as an elaboration of how unformulated experience works across the arc of formulation, rather than as a rival vocabulary: where d. b. stern’s account centers the defensive refusal of formulation, this paper describes the complementary defensive operation, in which formulation itself is recruited, jointly and prematurely, against what remains. a clinical account shows how pressures toward explanation and reassurance can make experience feel less real—both by foreclosing meanings it might still have become and by installing formulations that do not tally with what is real in the patient—and how greater tolerance for incompletion may deepen the patient’s relation to self-experience. journal of the american psychoanalytic association

cognitive reflection predicts utilitarian behavior in the monetary moral dilemma after 17 months abstract the dual-process model of moral judgment proposes that utilitarian choices arise from reflective processes that can override intuitive, rule-based responses. yet most supporting evidence relies on sacrificial dilemmas with limited ecological validity and problematic associations with antisocial traits. this preregistered study investigated whether individual differences in reflection predict utilitarian behavior in an incentivized setting. at time 1, 1,200 u.s. participants completed performance-based measures of reflection, reasoning ability, dispositional thinking styles, and the oxford utilitarianism scale (ous). seventeen months later, 321 participants completed a monetary moral dilemma with real economic consequences and reported their moral justifications. initial measures of reflection, including the cognitive performance test, raven’s matrices, and open-minded thinking, predicted utilitarian behavior. neither impartial beneficence nor instrumental harm subscales of the ous predicted utilitarian behavior. exploratory analyses showed that religiosity moderated the reflection–utilitarian behavior association: reflection predicted utilitarian behavior more strongly among non-believers than believers. these findings highlight reflection as a predictor of utilitarian behavior across time, question the validity of self-report utilitarianism scales such as the ous, and underscore the importance of religious belief in cognitive reflection when examining individual differences in moral behavior. judgment and decision making

multisensory research in transition: viewpoints on the past, present, and future of the field abstract the field of multisensory integration is entering a transitional phase. methodological, technological, and computational advances now allow long-held assumptions to be tested under more realistic conditions and with far greater analytical power. those assumptions, and the methods that produced them, deserve renewed scrutiny. this special issue brings together fifteen viewpoint articles, in which 38 renowned researchers share and discuss their perspectives on the past, present, and future of the field. a shared interview format draws out opinions and behind-the-scenes knowledge that rarely surface in empirical papers. the viewpoints cover multisensory mechanisms, including single-neuron dynamics, neural oscillations, crossmodal plasticity, and the hierarchical organization of integration and segregation, as well as perceptual phenomena such as illusions and the perception of time, body, and speech. further viewpoints address computational modelling, decision-making, and multisensory perception for action, as well as lifespan development, psychiatric disorders, multisensory technologies, and real-world applications. beyond their specific topics, the authors reflect on the relevance of open-science practices, the growing influence of artificial intelligence, anticipated breakthroughs, and the challenges and opportunities facing the field. they also offer practical advice on how to build a career in multisensory research. across the viewpoints, the authors urge openness to new methods, theories, and emerging phenomena such as humanoid multisensory robots. the viewpoints were written with early-career researchers in mind, but we hope they will inform and inspire scientists at all career stages, and stimulate the open, passionate, and controversial debate that has long defined this field. multisensory research

heterogeneity of contraceptive attitudes and usage patterns among youth in poland: a cross-sectional study reproductive behaviors and contraceptive attitudes among adolescents represent a pivotal public health challenge. despite high subjective confidence, young individuals face increased risks of contraceptive failure and unintended pregnancy. within the specific socio-legal framework in poland, characterized by restricted contraceptive access, recognizing population heterogeneity is essential. this study aimed to identify latent patterns regarding information sources, expectations toward sex education curricula, and decision-making motives using a person-centered approach. a cross-sectional observational study was conducted among n = 310 participants aged 16–21 years (m = 18.09, sd = 1.51; 86.5% female). a self-developed, standardized survey assessing sexual knowledge, information acquisition, method evaluation, and contraceptive motives was administered. latent class analysis (lca) and latent profile analysis (lpa) were applied using maximum likelihood estimation. optimal subgroup extraction was validated using bayesian information criterion (bic) minimization, entropy indices, and bootstrapped likelihood ratio tests (blrt). although 98.4% of respondents declared familiarity with contraceptive methods, 50.65% reported unmet informational needs. lpa on information sources revealed 4 profiles: mainstream digital and peer (74.8%), integrated multi-source (10.7%), informal sources exclusive (10.7%), and internet exclusive (3.9%). lca on educational expectations distinguished 3 latent paradigms: comprehensive content (60.0%), biomedical-focused content (22.6%), and topical/selective topics (17.4%). among sexually active participants (n = 123), decision-making lpa identified: priority 1: efficacy and comfort (43.1%), priority 2: multidimensional criteria (39.8%), and priority 3: unspecified or undecided (17.1%). short-acting user-dependent methods predominated, while long-acting reversible contraception (larc) usage was virtually absent. crucially, cross-tabulation revealed no significant associations among the different classification schemes (e.g., information profiles vs. decision-making motives), highlighting a disconnect between informational preparedness and actual decision-making in youth reproductive health behaviors. the identified multidimensional diversity, which primarily reflects the perspectives of young women due to sample composition, indicates that “one-size-fits-all” public health strategies are insufficient. crucially, due to the marked sex imbalance and limited statistical power to detect gender-specific differences, these findings cannot be robustly generalized to the broader adolescent and young-adult population and require highly cautious interpretation. implementing evidence-based comprehensive sexuality education (cse) and designing targeted, profile-adapted public health interventions are urgently required to meet the specific informational and contraceptive needs of youth. adolescents

ai as an apparatus of fantasy: a lacanian perspective on the limits of contemporary artificial intelligence abstract contemporary debate on artificial intelligence is organized around two seductive questions: whether ai is, or is becoming, a subject, and whether it can occupy the place of the analyst. this article argues that both questions are themselves symptomatic, and that the lacanian contribution is not to answer them but to displace them. rather than asking what kind of subject ai is and cataloging what it lacks , i treat ai as an apparatus—a technoscientific inference engine—and ask how it mobilizes the human subject's fantasy, transference, and alienation within contemporary capitalism. across lacan's three registers, i argue that large language models compute a statistical syntax detached from lalangue , the equivocal, jouissance ‐bearing substrate of the speaking body (the symbolic); function as a digital mirror and a lathouse , a gadget that plugs the division of the subject (the imaginary); and generate not an irruption of the real but a sampling variance that the user nonetheless receives as an address (the real). i locate automated diagnostic systems within the university discourse serving the master, and argue that the decisive risk of ai is not that the machine feels nothing but that, as an other that never falls silent, it insulates the subject from the castrating friction of alterity. writing avowedly from the position of the hysteric, i close by rotating that discourse, outlining where a lacanian orientation could inform, rather than only criticize, the design and clinical deployment of these systems. international journal of applied psychoanalytic studies

closeness and distance conflicts on the social media platform whatsapp abstract this paper proposes that, beyond the familiar reasons for whatsapp's widespread use—such as its cost‐free nature, user‐friendly interface, and immense popularity—the app possesses features that evoke common, often unconscious, psychodynamics linked to universal conflicts between unity and separation, or the negotiation of closeness and distance in relationships, making it particularly compelling. drawing on two vignettes, the paper examines how conflicts around closeness and distance are expressed through whatsapp interactions, inviting broader reflection on whatsapp use. it contributes to a growing body of psychoanalytic work on increasingly nuanced facets of social media use, and of whatsapp in particular. the material was drawn from psychoanalytically informed, unstructured interviews with emerging adults about their mobile phone use. across seven of the eight interviews, whatsapp emerged spontaneously as a distinct theme. two especially compelling vignettes were selected for analysis, which focused on the interpersonal and intrapsychic dynamics evident in the narratives. international journal of applied psychoanalytic studies

psychometric validation of the difficulties in emotion regulation scales among adult psychiatric outpatients with high rates of borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders 情绪调节困难量表在边缘型人格障碍与物质使用障碍高发成人精神科门诊患者中的心理测量学验证 challenges with regulating emotions are common across a number of psychiatric conditions and particularly relevant among adults with borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders. the current study evaluated the structural validity of the difficulties in emotion regulation scale, both full form (ders-36) and short form (ders-16) in a sample ( = 414) of adult psychiatric outpatients with high rates of borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders. both versions of the ders demonstrated good internal consistency but confirmatory factor analysis (cfa) did not support the previously supported 5- and 6-factor structures for the ders-36. conversely, cfa supported the previously validated 5-factor structure for the ders-16. furthermore, the ders-16 subscales exhibited robust associations with measures of psychiatric severity and disability, and convergent validity with multiple indices of impulsivity. taken together, these findings provide limited support for the ders-36 and adequate support for the ders-16 for measuring emotion regulation difficulties among psychiatric outpatients with high rates of borderline personality disorder and substance use disorders. future research examining other psychometric properties of the ders-16 in clinical samples, such as predictive validity in relation to treatment outcome, are warranted. journal of personality assessment

an intelligible mathematical framework for quantifying neuro-behavioural fatigue and adaptive risk evaluation in educational settings. university students often experience multiple sources of stress, including academic, digital, and lifestyle-related factors. traditional fatigue assessment tools are largely based on psychometric questionnaires capturing subjective evaluations of fatigue. however, such tools rarely account for multiple interrelated factors in a cohesive framework. this paper introduces the interpretable computational framework known as the neuro-behavioural fatigue assessment model (nfam) for identifying neuro-behavioural fatigue based on commonly reported questionnaire data. the framework employs a composite fatigue index characterized by three underlying components. the first component is the cognitive fatigue index (cfi), which represents fatigue-related factors associated with attention and recovery. the second component is the digital overload multiplier (dom), which accounts for interaction effects between digital activity and academic engagement. the third component is the sleep efficiency model (sem), which estimates the sleep-related contribution to overall fatigue using lifestyle factors. the components were combined to form the composite score (i.e., the nfam composite). the framework was evaluated using the data from 1000 university students. preliminary assessment of the questionnaire variables suggested that the nfam is better conceptualised as a formative computational framework rather than a reflective psychometric instrument. the sensitivity analysis of the weightings indicated that the framework remained stable under alternative weighting configurations. the statistical analysis indicated significant differences between the defined fatigue-risk categories, consistent framework performance across the evaluated participants, and the ability to explain individual responses using the composite index. overall, the current study provides an interpretable framework for assessing neuro-behavioural fatigue in a university student population. future research will include external validation of the nfam using independent datasets and established psychometric fatigue measures. acta psychologica

understanding children's "tinkering" in innovative problem-solving: the roles of knowledge integration, relational reasoning, and design stance. a key feature of human societies is the presence of technological traditions. different cultural groups develop and impart a vast array of problem-solving methods to future generations that are suited for their living environment and cultural lifestyle. central to this process is our capacity for innovative problem-solving to generate adaptive solutions. the extant developmental psychology literature has focused on invention and novel idea generation, typically assessed empirically using tool making, tool use, and divergent thinking tasks, and focusing on the end product of innovation (creative invention) and goal attainment. yet, we still know little about the iterative process of 'tinkering' that involves purposeful exploration and experimentation of possible combinations of sub-components leading up to an innovative end product. in light of recent evidence, we propose that 'tinkering' plays a pivotal role in children's capacity for tool innovation and that further exploration of the development of this process is warranted. in this article, we suggest additional cognitive mechanisms that underpin tinkering behaviors: the ability to evaluate and integrate knowledge, along with relational and abstraction reasoning, and the design stance. we hope this proposal spurs additional work for exploring the cognitive foundations for developing innovative problem-solving. acta psychologica

eye gaze is not inversion-proof: a robust gaze inversion effect in a large, sex-balanced sample turning a face upside down markedly impairs face recognition. yet gaze judgements can be supported substantially by local eye-region information, so a strict account in which inversion preserves feature-based processing predicts little or no gaze inversion cost. previous whole-face studies, generally based on small samples, have yielded mixed results. we estimated the magnitude of the inversion cost in a large, sex-balanced sample of 190 participants. they judged whether briefly presented upright or inverted faces, each followed by a mask, were looking directly at them. inversion widened the cone of direct gaze: the mean 50% threshold rose from 7.29° for upright faces to 9.74° for inverted faces, an increase of 2.45° (95% ci [1.99°, 2.91°]; cohen's d = 0.76). inversion also produced modestly but consistently shallower psychometric functions, indicating that direct and averted gaze were distinguished less sharply. females showed a narrower cone of direct gaze than males in both orientations, with no consistent evidence for a sex difference in slope. the inversion-related threshold increase was 0.67° larger in male participants than in female participants (95% ci [−0.25°, 1.59°]; cohen's d = 0.21), but the between-sex difference was not statistically significant and the confidence interval was too wide to establish equivalence. under brief, masked viewing, eye gaze is therefore not inversion-proof. these findings constrain strict feature-preservation accounts and provide a more precise estimate of the gaze inversion effect than was available from previous small-sample studies. perception

reducing self-injurious behavior in an adolescent with williams syndrome: a case study of an adaptive behavioral intervention this case study evaluated an adaptive behavioral intervention designed to reduce self-injurious behavior (sib) in a 13-year-old adolescent diagnosed with williams syndrome (ws), autism spectrum disorder, and severe intellectual disability. the intervention was implemented in the home setting and progressed through three sequential phases: response blocking, verbal reprimand, and a combined response interruption and redirection (rird) package with differential reinforcement of alternative behavior (dra). parents were trained to implement all procedures. visual analysis of parent-collected data demonstrated a marked and sustained reduction in sib observed concurrently with the final phase, which incorporated the combined rird and dra package. the case highlights the clinical utility of systematically adapting intervention components based on functional behavior assessment (fba) findings and ongoing adaptation, underscoring the importance of individualized and flexible treatment approaches for youth with complex needs. clinical case studies

fear of falling in a younger adult: integrated cbt and physiotherapy in a 4-year follow-up case study fear of falling (fof) is well documented among older adults but has received little attention in younger populations. this case report describes the assessment and treatment of angela, a 37-year-old woman with obesity who developed a phobic fof. her fear resulted in panic symptoms and extensive avoidance, which led to impaired mobility including dependency on mobility aids and compromised her engagement in physiotherapy. body size appeared to contribute to the content of the patient’s catastrophic fears, particularly concerns regarding her ability to recover independently following a fall. treatment involved values-guided graded cue exposure with response prevention alongside physiotherapy targeting balance and mobility. functional impairment and phobic avoidance decreased substantially, with gains maintained at 1-month follow-up and remaining evident 4 years later. unlike many interventions for older adults with fof, which often require cautious progression because of frailty and fall risk, treatment for angela progressed relatively quickly through exposure and rehabilitation tasks. her younger age and the absence of age-related physical decline may have allowed a more rapid approach to rehabilitation. this case describes the application of integrated cbt-based exposure and physiotherapy in a younger adult whose fof appeared to be maintained primarily by fear-related avoidance and addresses a gap in a literature focused predominantly on older adults. clinical case studies

effects of skippable ads on viewers' reactance and brand attitudes abstract skippable advertisements have become common on video‐sharing platforms, yet their effects on brand attitudes remain underexplored. drawing on psychological reactance theory and the theory of interactive media effects (time), this study examines whether the skippable ad reduces viewers' reactance and improves brand attitudes, and whether these effects differ by advertisement placement. a 2 (ad format: non‐skippable vs. skippable) × 2 (ad position: pre‐roll vs. mid‐roll) between‐subject online experiment was conducted in japan. participants watched a 2‐min video containing a 10‐ or 15‐s advertisement. results showed that viewers exposed to the skippable‐ad format reported a greater sense of control, lower psychological reactance, and more favorable brand attitudes than those exposed to the non‐skippable format. exploratory analyses suggested different patterns among skipping and non‐skipping participants, with cue‐consistent patterns emerging mainly in the pre‐roll condition and use‐consistent patterns appearing across ad positions. although these exploratory findings should be interpreted cautiously because skipping behavior was self‐selected, they highlight perceived control as a key mechanism in interactive online advertising. japanese psychological research

birth weight, cognitive reserve and outcomes after first-episode psychosis nature mental health, published online: 28 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00751-0 forte et al. investigated whether birth weight influences functional outcomes 1 year after first-episode psychosis, and whether this association is mediated by cognitive reserve and cognitive performance, using a longitudinal cohort and serial mediation analyses. nature mental health

development, validation and ai chatbot evaluation of the adolescent mental health ai response tool nature mental health, published online: 28 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00753-y the authors developed and tested the adolescent mental health ai response tool (amhart), a clinician-informed tool to evaluate ai chatbot responses to adolescents disclosing anxiety or depression. applying amhart to four widely used ai chatbots revealed that these models have greater coverage for anxiety than depression and for moderate than severe presentations, also identifying gaps for coping guidance. nature mental health
