associations between icd-11 trauma-related disorders, treatment engagement and outcomes of substance-use treatment purpose the co-occurrence of post-traumatic stress disorder (ptsd) and substance use disorder (sud) presents significant challenges for substance-use treatment services. there is mixed evidence, however, regarding how this presentation impacts on treatment engagement and outcome, and no existing research has examined this in the context of icd-11 ptsd and complex ptsd (cptsd). this study aims to then examine associations between trauma-related disorders, treatment engagement and substance use outcomes – in the context of the icd-11 diagnostic system. design/methodology/approach in all, 72 individuals entering substance use treatment were recruited into this prospective cohort study. data on treatment engagement were obtained from medical records and was available for all participants. data on trauma-related symptoms and substance use outcomes were obtained via interviews undertaken at baseline and three-month follow-up (n = 40, follow-up rate = 55.6%). findings both ptsd- and cptsd-related functional impairment were associated with higher levels of treatment engagement; however, no trauma-related symptoms demonstrated associations to premature disengagement from treatment. there was little evidence of reliable changes in trauma-related symptoms or substance use outcomes. changes in cptsd- but not ptsd-related symptoms were associated with changes in psychological dependence. neither ptsd- nor cptsd-related symptom changes were associated with changes in recent substance use. individuals presenting with comorbid trauma-related symptoms are no more likely to disengage from treatment; however, those with greater functional impairment related to their symptoms will likely require higher levels of service. further research is required to determine the added benefit of trauma-focussed treatment in addition to substance-use treatment alone. originality/value this study provides the first examination of how symptoms of icd-11 ptsd and complex ptsd change during substance use treatment. the results of this study can inform the expansion of trauma-informed and trauma-focussed treatment approaches embedded in substance use treatment. advances in dual diagnosis

the positive transformation of therapy dog handlers throughout the animal-assisted services: an exploratory qualitative study in hong kong abstract background: animal-assisted services (aas) provide promising positive effects on the improvement of the psychosocial well-being of diverse populations who received these services. however, the aas delivery process is less reported in the literature. the perspectives of therapy dog handlers and the impact of their presence in service on aas process and outcomes remain underexplored. in hong kong, due to socio-geographical constraints and a relatively low rate of dog ownership, deliveries of aas rely heavily on volunteer therapy dog-handler dyads. hence, understanding the handlers’ experiences is essential for the sustainable development of aas in urbanized cities such as hong kong. methods: this exploratory qualitative study explored the roles, motivations, and experiences of therapy dog handlers involved in aas. semi-structured interviews were conducted with ten registered volunteer therapy dog handlers, and the data were analyzed using reflective thematic analysis. results: this study revealed five core themes: (1) volunteer training in aas aligned with animal welfare; (2) insight on self-reflection and strength; (3) transformational service experience; (4) aligned virtues in animal welfare in the organization; and (5) lessened mental health stigma. the themes are summarized as the acronym “vital” which captured the ethical standards, shared visions, and support provided by the animal-related organization. these factors contribute to the well-being and development of handlers and may have ripple effects that spread to the larger community under the one welfare model. conclusions: this study highlights the transformative potential of aas for volunteers and proposes the integrative vital model to pave the future development of ethical and sustainable handler-dog teams under the diamond model. human-animal interactions

career orientations, career management, and adaptability under career constraints individuals manage their careers under uncertainty and constrained opportunities. drawing on career orientation theory, the social cognitive model of career self-management, and career construction theory, this study examines how boundaryless and protean career orientations relate to career management behaviors (career planning and career learning) and career adaptability. survey data were collected from 310 athletes competing within south korea’s elite and semi-professional sport system and analyzed using structural equation modeling. results indicated that protean career orientation was positively associated with career planning and career learning, whereas boundaryless career orientation was associated only with career planning. both career management behaviors were positively related to career adaptability. the findings suggest that self-directed, values-based career orientations are more consistently associated with sustained engagement than openness to opportunities alone in regulated career environments. the study contributes to career development research by clarifying how career orientations relate to career management behaviors and adaptability under structural constraint. journal of career development

meaning after the multimodal revolution: seven things signs and gestures teach us about meaning abstract following a “multimodal revolution” in the language sciences, meaning is now studied not just in speech but also in sign languages (“sign”) and in gestures. seven lessons can be drawn from recent semantic research. (1) sometimes sign makes visible key logical elements that are covert in speech. (2) sign combines the same meaning operations as speech with a richer depictive component. (3) sign combines the same kind of syntax as speech with a dedicated syntax for its depictive elements. (4) even the purely depictive component of sign is linguistically structured. (5) gestures that replace words share some non‐trivial properties with signs—but unlike signs, they are not words. (6) gestures that accompany predicates usually make backgrounded (non‐assertive) contributions. (7) several of these properties apply beyond signs and gestures, suggesting that they have a deeper cognitive source, not a narrowly linguistic one. these lessons show that human meaning results from both discrete, logical‐like and gradient, iconic components, integrated through powerful cognitive mechanisms across sign, speech, and gestures. wiley interdisciplinary reviews-cognitive science
intrusive memories review of philosophy and psychology

the effects of status and performance output visibility on participation in groups i develop and test an argument that explains how status organizing processes and visibility of performance outputs affect participation rates in collective problem-solving groups. drawing on status characteristics theory and reward expectations theory, i argue that actors expect rewards that are commensurate with the performance outputs that they make toward the group task. when group members’ performance outputs are anonymous, this disconnects performance output from reward by removing a basis on which rewards are allocated. accordingly, failure to receive expected rewards reduces performance outputs. findings from a laboratory experiment show that higher status actors participate more when their performance outputs are known to others. when performance outputs are invisible, higher status actors’ performance outputs are not statistically different from lower status actors in either condition. status-based participation inequality suggests differences in motives for higher and lower status actors in task groups and supports prior findings that task success is but one motivation for which actors engage in status organizing processes. social psychology quarterly

advice inequality in personal networks: do gender dynamics matter? who is granted the privilege of knowing things? drawing from status characteristics theory and homophily, this article examines how gender structures epistemic authority in personal advice networks. using three waves of the uc berkeley social networks study panel, we analyze longitudinal changes in who is named, who is retained, and who transitions into or out of advice-giving roles. although women and men are more likely to name same-gender alters as advisors, homophily alone is insufficient for explaining advice-giving as network dynamics are asymmetric and operate differently across genders. men are more likely to retain male advisors and drop female advisors over time, while women more commonly transition female advisors into other network roles and recruit advice-givers from the women already present in their networks. we propose next steps for understanding how advice-giving sustains gender inequality by structuring not only what we know but also whose knowledge counts. social psychology quarterly

bridging divides: the dynamic effects of contact on minority-majority relations this study advances intergroup contact theory by demonstrating that the effects of contact valence and its psychological mediators vary systematically by group status and context. using multigroup regression analysis, we examined how positive and negative contact influence intergroup anxiety, perceived threat, and prejudice among black african minorities (n = 215) and hong kong chinese majorities (n = 476). the findings reveal asymmetries in both the frequency and impact of contact: minorities reported a broader range of contact experiences, while majorities expressed stronger prejudice. positive contact reduced prejudice and anxiety among majority participants but had limited effects among minorities. negative contact increased anxiety in both groups but heightened prejudice only among the majority. mediation analyses further showed that anxiety, not threat, is a more pivotal mediator of contact effects on prejudice among high-status majority group members, whereas its role is weaker among low-status minorities. these findings underscore an important theoretical nuance, clarifying how the valence of contact can have asymmetric effects depending on group status and offering insights into the boundary conditions of intergroup contact theory. social psychology quarterly
communicative strategy selection in language anxiety: eye-tracking evidence of efl learners’ multimodal pragmatic regulation npj science of learning

parental influence on adolescent career decision‐making self‐efficacy: a longitudinal latent transition analysis of career expectations and parent–adolescent congruence abstract this study investigates the dynamic development of adolescents’ career decision‐making self‐efficacy (cdmse) over time, focusing on the roles of parental career expectations (pce) and adolescent–parent career congruence (apcc). using a longitudinal, person‐centered approach, we identified distinct profiles of cdmse in adolescents and tracked their transitions over two time points. findings reveal that cdmse varies significantly across individuals, with some adolescents experiencing increases in self‐efficacy, while others show stability or decline. crucially, apcc was found to predict both the stability and growth of cdmse, highlighting the importance of relational alignment between adolescents and their parents. in contrast, pce had minimal direct impact on transitions. these results underscore the significance of parent–child communication and support in fostering adolescents’ confidence in making career decisions. the study provides insights into how parental involvement can enhance adolescents’ self‐efficacy, with practical implications for career counseling and family‐based interventions. career development quarterly
the effectiveness of dialogic reading for children with disabilities: a meta-analysis of single-case experimental studies review journal of autism and developmental disorders

does tonal l2 learning influence early-stage l3/ln tone perception by altering cue weighting? abstract learning a second language (l2) influences speech perception in a third or additional language (l3/ln) at an early stage. however, the mechanism underlying this influence remains unclear. our study aimed to address this gap in the context of tone. specifically, l1-urdu/hindi speakers with varying degrees of l2 cantonese proficiency completed a novel tone identification task, two abx novel tone discrimination tasks and the cantonese elicited imitation task. the results showed that (i) l2 cantonese proficiency positively correlated with novel tone perception across the three tone perception tasks; (ii) no evidence indicated that l2 proficiency influenced the weighting of pitch cues in either abx task. however, the weighting of pitch cues differed between the two tasks. we suggest that tonal l2 learning influences early-stage l3/ln tone perception, but no evidence suggests this effect stems from shifts in cue weighting. furthermore, cognitive load does not modulate the effect of tonal l2 learning on early-stage l3/ln tone perception; however, it directly alters the weighting of pitch cues. language and cognition

the semantics‐pragmatics divide in cartographic representation philosophers who take maps to have a semantics (i.e., rules that assign contents to cartographic marks) also typically hold that semantics fully determines the truth‐conditional meaning of maps. in this paper, i tackle this form of literalism, which assigns no truth‐conditional role to pragmatics, by investigating the semantics‐pragmatics divide in cartographic representation. i rely on examples from google maps, whose widespread use makes it possible to draw general conclusions about the communicative behavior of maps. this behavior, i argue, supports a form of contextualism, on which pragmatics pervasively influences the truth conditions of maps by altering semantic elements. mind & language

dyadic influences of affect and depth of cognitive processing on how empathic expressions are perceived in supportive interactions abstract communicating empathy in supportive interactions can be an effective way for providers to help regulate receivers' emotions. partners' perceptions of empathic expressions can be influenced by various factors, including the affect they bring into an interaction and the extent to which they engage in cognitive processing. drawing on the affect infusion model (aim) and the emotion as social information (easi) model, this study examined the influence of incidental affect on perceptions of empathic expressions and how this influence is moderated by the depth of partners' cognitive processing regarding a conversation. partners in established relationships reported their affect before an interaction, were randomly assigned to be either support providers or receivers, engaged in a supportive interaction, and then reported their level of cognitive processing and perceptions of the providers' empathic expressions. individuals' positive affect positively influenced their own, but not their partner's perceptions of empathic expressions. how deeply participants engaged in cognitive processing moderated the influence of their affect on their perceptions of providers' empathic expressions. personal relationships

planting the future: fostering collective engagement with the energy transition by coordinated action abstract collective pro‐environmental engagement of communities is vital for addressing climate change challenges. to promote such engagement, individuals must go beyond their immediate personal interests, requiring the activation of a collective mindset. in the present research, we tested whether working on a simple task in high vs. low coordination would increase collective agency for the task and beyond. in a series of three studies (total n = 245), including one preregistered field experiment, we tested whether collaboration on a plant potting task in high vs. low coordination would boost collective agency (comprising efficacy, motivation, and responsibility) with the task and pro‐environmental behaviour more generally. across all three studies, we find that plant potting in high coordination promotes collective agency (but not individual agency) for the plant potting task. in the field study with community residents from existing groups we also find higher collective agency for contributing to a sustainable neighbourhood more generally as a result of coordinated plant potting. we do not find other spillover effects of coordinated plant potting in terms of intentions for participating in future sustainable activities. all in all, we conclude that working together in coordination may provide a powerful route for encouraging engagement with collective pro‐environmental action in real world settings. journal of community & applied social psychology
response inhibition in children and adolescents with fragile x syndrome child neuropsychology
threat appraisal mediates the link between self-uncertainty and group identification self and identity

statistical inference regularized with neural networks and its application in psychometrics 神经网络正则化的统计推断及其在心理测量学中的应用 abstract likelihood‐based methods such as marginal maximum likelihood and bayesian estimation via markov chain monte carlo (mcmc) are widely used for estimating item response theory (irt) models and perform well in large samples. in small samples, however, these approaches may yield unstable estimates due to insufficient information in the likelihood, unless strong prior distributions are imposed. we address this problem by turning to the fundamentals of estimation via decision theory, showing that small‐sample estimation can be viewed as an ill‐posed decision problem in the sense that the decision function is sensitive to small changes in the data and, therefore, may not be continuous. we discuss how such ill‐posed decision problems—both in irt estimation and more broadly—can be regularized using neural network (nn)‐based approaches that build a continuous map from observations into parameters. we formalize this approach within a general framework termed regularized decision theory and apply it to irt models. focusing on the 3pl, we study its properties via simulations. british journal of mathematical & statistical psychology

early socioeconomic deprivation, the preschool home learning environment, and language and literacy skills in ethnically diverse school children abstract children with more exposure to socioeconomic deprivation have lower language and literacy. minority ethnic children often experience more deprivation but are under‐represented in the research literature. we examined socioeconomic deprivation (during pregnancy), home learning environment (2 years), and language and literacy at school entry (4–5 years) and primary school (6–7 years) in a diverse uk cohort ( n = 7064). using latent structural equation modelling, we identified a persistent negative effect of deprivation on school language and literacy. despite higher deprivation, being read to less often and fewer learning resources during preschool, children of pakistani ethnicity had school language and literacy largely on par with white british children and children of other ethnicities. deprivation effects were not mediated by home learning environment; literacy in primary school was partially mediated by school‐entry language and literacy. there may be additional factors within minority ethnic families that help mitigate impacts of socioeconomic deprivation, and standard home learning environment measures may not fully capture experiences of pakistani ethnicity children. british journal of developmental psychology

the chomskyan unconscious: a psychoanalytic critique of illiberalism this paper traces the genealogy of contemporary illiberalism, arguing that it stems from a historical sedimentation that systematically narrows the space for the cause of liberation. grounding this trajectory in a marxist–lacanian framework, i demonstrate how elite-illiberalism operates through a dual structural mechanism of negation: ontic disavowal ( verleugnung ) and epistemic foreclosure ( verwerfung ). drawing on domenico losurdo’s counter-history of liberalism, the affective turn literature, and chris knight’s bifurcation thesis, i map how procedural (il)liberalism serves the power elite. these strands converge in a critical re-examination of noam chomsky, showing how his computational formulation of universal grammar executes an epistemic foreclosure that ejects the historical materiality of lalangue from language, while his institutional self-positioning at mit relies on an ontic disavowal that converts his theoretical radicalism into an instrumental legitimation of the ruling class. by demonstrating how therapeutic left-illiberalism and right-illiberalism function as complementary modalities of a single elite-illiberal system, i propose a program of radical liberalism premised on the truth of the split subject ( spaltung ), capable of sustaining difference without demanding consensus. theory & psychology

beyond the identity paradigm: self-addiction, anti-self psychology, and psychedelic ego-dissolution contemporary psychology treats the construction, maintenance, and enhancement of a coherent self-concept as the implicit telos of therapeutic intervention, an assumption so thoroughly embedded in clinical training, diagnostic frameworks, and outcome measurement that it functions less as a theoretical commitment than as a perceptual habit. this article argues that compulsive identity maintenance operates, across diverse clinical presentations and neurobiological substrates, as an addictive process: self-addiction , characterized by salience, tolerance, withdrawal, and persistence despite harm, with substantial selfhood itself as the object of dependence. drawing on post-kantian critical philosophy, predictive processing neuroscience, psychedelic ego-dissolution research, and deleuzian critiques of therapeutic capture, the article traces how independent intellectual and empirical traditions converge on a common finding: that rigid self-referential processing tracks suffering while its systematic loosening tracks improvement. the self-addiction framework is applied to five standing debates the identity paradigm has rendered intractable: the dodo bird verdict, process-based therapy’s unexamined stopping point, jungian outcome data, the narcissism epidemic paradox, and the ethics of ego-syntonic pathology. in each case, it both explains the debate and reveals the identity paradigm as the constraint that kept the explanation invisible. it proposes metacognitive agency, the bidirectional capacity to modulate both flexibility and rigidity in context, as an alternative therapeutic telos, while addressing the structural preconditions of flexible selfhood for marginalized communities and the recursive risk that dissolution becomes its own object of attachment. theory & psychology

deeds and words: the role of behavior-advocacy consistency of climate scientists in communicating the scientific consensus on climate change climate change mitigation requires effective ways to foster pro-environmental solutions and policies. this study examined whether messages highlighting scientific consensus on human-caused climate change — when delivered by climate scientists exhibiting varying levels of pro-environmental behaviour — will enhance public support for climate policies and willingness to adopt eco-friendly lifestyles. in an online experiment (n = 1,659), participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions: (1) control condition with no message; (2) simple consensus condition, featuring a message on the consensus regarding climate change; (3) consensus + inconsistent behaviour condition, where the consensus message was delivered by a scientist displaying anti-environmental behavior; or (4) consensus + consistent behaviour condition, where the message was delivered by a climate scientist demonstrating pro-environmental behaviour. results showed that scientists’ perceived credibility was highest when their behaviour was consistent with their advocacy and lowest when it was inconsistent. consistency also increased support for pro-environmental policies compared to the control condition, although no difference emerged between consistent and inconsistent conditions, providing only partial support for this hypothesis. no significant effects were observed for willingness to change one’s lifestyle. overall, while pro-environmental scientists may enhance their credibility, their impact on public attitudes and behavioural intentions appears limited. collabra-psychology

relationship management profiles in romantic relationships: integrating attachment orientations and conflict management tendencies attachment orientations and conflict-management tendencies shape romantic relationship functioning, but individuals may combine these characteristics in ways obscured by variable-centered analyses. the present study used a person-centered approach to identify relationship-management profiles based on attachment and conflict-management patterns and examine their associations with relationship outcomes and demographic characteristics. participants were 978 adults currently involved in a romantic relationship, assessed via self-report measures of attachment, conflict resolution, relationship functioning, jealousy, and sexual satisfaction. latent profile analysis identified five profiles: secure–harmonious (50.2%), fearful–avoidant (reactively destructive; 20.0%), secure–dominant (18.0%), anxious–volatile (7.5%), and dismissing–avoidant (4.3%). bch analyses revealed significant differences across profiles in relationship satisfaction, quality of alternatives, investment, commitment, trust, multidimensional jealousy, and sexual satisfaction. secure profiles demonstrated the most adaptive functioning, whereas dismissing–avoidant individuals reported the lowest investment, commitment, trust, emotional jealousy, and sexual satisfaction. the anxious–volatile profile was distinguished by elevated behavioral and cognitive jealousy alongside relatively high investment. r3step analyses indicated that gender was selectively associated with profile membership, whereas relationship duration showed only limited associations. these findings underscore meaningful heterogeneity in romantic relationship functioning and the value of integrating attachment and conflict-management processes within a person-centered framework. collabra-psychology

how to scream into the wind without losing your voice: a behavioral analysis of llm use and environmental impact abstract large language models (llms) are a type of ai (artificial intelligence). they are large-scale, sophisticated neural networks trained on vast amounts of text data to mimic human language. the increased adoption of llms warrants an analysis of their substantial, rapidly growing environmental footprint. this paper is structured in three broad sections. first, we offer a behavior-analytic lens into the rapidly increasing adoption of this technology. the analysis is provided at the individual, organizational, and cultural levels, with a discussion of efficiency gains being absorbed into productivity contingencies. second, we provide a cradle-to-grave overview of the environmental impact of this technology: cradle (building the infrastructure), life (training and running the model), grave (disposal of electronic waste), and the potential infrastructure lock-in costs. the analysis includes a discussion of embedded carbon, an area often overlooked in discussions of environmental impacts. to close, we provide suggestions for behavior analysts at the individual level to the cultural level, with an emphasis on where leverage is most possible. behavior analysis in practice

audiovisual temporal asynchrony differentially influences material property and action quality judgements: evidence for stable individual differences in material perception in everyday life, audiovisual temporal correspondence, action quality and material properties are perceived simultaneously during natural interactions. however, these aspects of perception have largely been investigated separately. examining how audiovisual temporal asynchrony affects material property and action quality judgements therefore provides a useful approach to identifying the information underlying multisensory perception. whether such effects are mediated primarily by temporal information or require additional event-related information beyond temporal correspondence remains unclear. the present study investigated how audiovisual temporal asynchrony affects material property and action quality judgements in relation to simultaneity judgement (sj) and temporal order judgement (toj). using naturalistic video stimuli depicting egg cracking (experiment 1) and grissini breaking (experiment 2), participants performed sj, toj and perceptual evaluation tasks to examine whether the observed effects generalised across different everyday material interactions. action quality judgement (skilfulness) was robustly and consistently modulated by temporal asynchrony, exhibiting patterns closely aligned with sj, indicating a primary reliance on temporal information. in contrast, material property judgement (hardness) exhibited marked inter-individual variability and no consistent group-level pattern. instead, observers exhibited distinct response profiles that remained highly stable across stimulus types and over extended time intervals. these results demonstrate a dissociation between action quality and material property judgements: whereas action quality judgement primarily depends on temporal correspondence, material property judgement reflects stable and reproducible individual response profiles in the use of event-related information beyond temporal correspondence rather than random variability. the findings highlight that audiovisual temporal asynchrony contributes differently to action quality and material property judgements. i-perception

when short is enough: comparing adaptive and fixed-item numerosity tests in early childhood understanding children's numerosity perception is essential for identifying the cognitive foundations of early mathematical learning, yet traditional assessment methods remain lengthy and inefficient. adaptive testing has emerged as a promising alternative, offering precise ability estimates while reducing task length and participant burden. in adaptive tests, item difficulty is dynamically adjusted to match each participant's estimated ability, so items are neither too difficult nor too easy. despite these advantages, few studies have applied adaptive testing to numerosity perception so far, and none have considered the multidimensional nature of the task, involving both numerical acuity and inhibitory control. this study compares an adaptive version of a numerosity comparison task with a long (128 items) and a short (48 items) fixed-item version in a sample of 146 children aged four to eight years ( m = 6.45). task performance in the three versions was compared across several dimensions. results showed that accuracy was correlated across the three versions, and all of them showed the expected congruency and ratio effects. number was the strongest predictor compared to the non-numerical cues, and it affected performance similarly in all three versions. all versions also revealed three different cognitive profiles that classified children with high consistency. finally, the measurement precision was comparable across versions. importantly, the adaptive and the short versions also elicited lower state math anxiety, particularly among participants with higher math anxiety. these findings suggest that an adaptive numerosity comparison task could offer the same type of information while reducing test length and improving participant experience. i-perception

teacher thinking: an activity-based approach to study and formation the article is the third publication in a series devoted to the examination of various aspects of teachers' thinking and the history of its study within different scientific paradigms. the first two articles were published in cultural-historical psychology (no. 1, 2026) and psychological science and education (no. 4, 2026). they addressed issues related to pedagogical decision-making and the structure of teachers’ professional knowledge. in the present article, the author considers teacher thinking as a form of practical thinking, drawing on the works of kornilov, teplov and kulyutkin, and analyses the role and place of such thinking in pedagogical activity. particular attention is paid to its distinction from scientific thinking and to its orientation not so much towards the study of objects as towards their transformation in accordance with the goals of professional activity. it is argued that the basic unit of pedagogical thinking is not a scientific concept but a practical generalisation. such a generalisation is image-based and comprises an invariant core of essential characteristics shared by recurring situations, together with variable, non-essential features. the relationship between these images of situations and the corresponding schemes of action aimed at transforming them is also analysed. the author further examines the role of professional knowledge as a component of practical generalisations and its transformation from a set of fragmented elements into instruments for solving pedagogical problems through the processes of operationalisation, contextualisation and integration. in conclusion, the author formulates a number of proposals aimed at modernising the traditional approach to the design of teacher education programmes. in the author’s view, the principal outcome of such programmes should be the development of graduates’ pedagogical thinking. the role of professional cases as the primary units of the activity-based content of teacher education is also emphasised. psikhologicheskaya nauka i obrazovanie-psychological science and education

inclusive local histories as an open pedagogy practice introduction the systemic absence of women and people of color in commercially-produced texts is well documented. statement of the problem open educational resources (oers) are frequently touted for filling representation gaps and promoting social justice. yet, oers are not inherently more inclusive. literature review emerging work on open pedagogy practices indicates potential to support recognitive justice by positioning students as knowledge creators rather than passive consumers. we argue that inclusive local histories, in which faculty and students co-create narratives and materials focusing on their home institution's historical context, can be used as a form of open pedagogy and support curricular diversification efforts. teaching implications we outline practical strategies, guiding questions, and ethical considerations for implementing open pedagogy through inclusive local histories in psychology courses. these approaches deepen students’ understanding of systemic barriers in psychology's past, and produce non-disposable educational resources benefitting future learners. conclusion open pedagogy offers a student-centered means of enriching course materials and promoting equity within psychology education. teaching of psychology

odour preferences of children and adults across four diverse cultures in africa, asia, europe, and oceania abstract odour perception plays a crucial role in various processes, yet the extent to which odour preferences are universal or shaped by cultural and ecological contexts remains debated. while some studies report substantial cross-cultural agreement in odour pleasantness, others highlight considerable variability. to address this question from a novel perspective, we collected data from 394 children and adults (aged 3–81) across four distinct cultures (hadza, pakistani, dani, and scottish). participants rated the pleasantness and familiarity of 11 odours (fish, garlic, butter, ginger, thyme, cinnamon, banana, peach, strawberry, jasmine, butanol). we observed both variability and agreement in odour pleasantness ratings across cultures, but overall, there was a similar level of agreement across age groups within each culture. furthermore, the most pleasant odours (jasmine, strawberry, peach) were rated more consistently across cultures than the most unpleasant ones (fish, garlic, butter). finally, familiarity was strongly and positively associated with pleasantness. these findings suggest that while some universal consensus in odour evaluation exists, ecological and cultural influences, as well as individual differences, may all play a substantial role in shaping olfactory perception. psychonomic bulletin & review

is the proust phenomenon fact or fiction? a systematic review and meta-analysis of odor-evoked autobiographical memory abstract odors are widely believed to be the most powerful trigger for autobiographical memory (am). this meta-analysis provides the first comprehensive meta-analytic test of this claim, known as the proust phenomenon. eighteen experimental/quasi-experimental studies were included in this meta-analysis. olfactory cueing was compared with a variety of cueing modalities, and seven key characteristics of evoked ams (specificity, vividness, emotional intensity, pleasantness, rarity, evocativeness, and age of ams) were assessed. olfactory cues showed a greater effect (advantage) over other cue types for emotional intensity, pleasantness, evocativeness, and age of ams. sample size was negatively associated with effect sizes for emotional intensity, pleasantness, and rarity, although the overall effect for rarity was not significant. higher proportions of females and more recent publication years were each associated with smaller effects for evocativeness and pleasantness, respectively. subgroup analyses showed that the advantage of olfactory cues for emotional intensity was stronger in within-subject than between-subject designs. moreover, their advantage in terms of pleasantness was greatest relative to label cues, followed by visual and auditory cues. although olfactory cues showed an advantage for four characteristics of ams, these results do not fully confirm the proust phenomenon. overall, these findings suggest that the olfactory advantage is selective rather than universal, and future studies should clarify the conditions under which it emerges. psychonomic bulletin & review
stronger mnemonic prediction errors can disproportionately impair memory updating in older adults. journal of experimental psychology-general

helpful and in danger: attributes and correlates of perceived occupational heroism some occupations such as firefighters are described as heroic, while others, such as healthcare workers, are applauded as “heroes” in crises. in two preregistered correlational studies conducted on representative u.k. samples, we evaluated theory-based attributes of occupational heroism, and its relationship to specific policy-relevant attitudes toward occupations. in study 1 ( n = 430), we confirmed that occupational heroism relates to the perceived helpfulness and risk exposure of workers. in study 2 ( n = 840), we further showed that occupational heroism is associated with a moral shield: workers’ hero status correlates with decreased acceptability of criticism toward them, and increased support for deregulating them and protecting them from punishment for rule-breaking. unlike previous findings suggesting a willingness to exploit heroized workers, heroism correlated with increased gratitude toward workers, support for their demands, and perception that they are vulnerable. societal consequences and relevance for policy-making are discussed. personality and social psychology bulletin

inferring struggle, judging strength: how inferred adversity and sympathy shape competence evaluations of black frontline employees how do racial inferences shape third-party evaluations of employee competence? across four experiments, white u.s. observers judged black frontline employees as more competent than otherwise comparable white employees in service-failure encounters involving a black customer. this pattern was consistent with a serial process in which employee race cued greater inferred adversity, which elicited sympathy, thereby elevating competence judgments. study 1 established the competence difference and its association with lower negative word of mouth. study 2 showed that behavioral awkwardness attenuated the difference. study 3 supported the serial indirect pathway, and the supplementary pilot reproduced it without a service failure. study 4 showed that structural-opportunity information increased inferred adversity for both employees and especially increased sympathy and competence judgments for the white employee, narrowing black–white differences. the findings identify a context-dependent, normatively complex route through which presumed adversity can produce comparatively favorable yet racialized competence judgments. personality and social psychology bulletin

joining the gender war online: entitativity, negative emotion, and engagement with gender-polarized posts. introduction: gender-polarized discourse has become increasingly visible on social media, where interpersonal conflicts are often generalized to broader gender groups. this study examined the associations of perceived group entitativity and negative intergroup emotion with individuals' responses to gender-polarized framing in online discourse.
methods: a total of 800 chinese adults were exposed to gender-conflict posts presented in rednote-like or zhihu-like social-media contexts. the posts described interpersonal conflicts and explicitly generalized these incidents to the target gender group. participants subsequently reported their perceived group entitativity, negative intergroup emotion, and responses to gender-polarized framing.
results: perceived group entitativity was strongly and positively associated with responses to gender-polarized framing, indicating greater alignment with negative group-based narratives among participants who perceived the target gender as a coherent social entity. negative intergroup emotion was also positively associated with these responses, although the hypothesized indirect effect of entitativity through negative emotion was not supported. responses differed modestly between the two gender-pairing conditions, whereas neither the main effect of platform context nor the gender-pairing × platform interaction was significant.
discussion: these findings suggest that perceived group coherence and negative intergroup emotion are associated with individuals' alignment with gender-polarized narratives on social media. the results highlight the importance of distinguishing the initial emergence of group generalization from psychological responses to generalizations already embedded in online discourse. frontiers in psychology

baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and ai avatars. people routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. the present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. across three experiments with chinese university students (total = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (ai) avatar designs (experiment 3). participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. the results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. these findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of ai systems. frontiers in psychology

young adults’ conspiracy beliefs, fear, and preventive behaviors during the covid-19 pandemic this study investigated how covid-19 conspiracy beliefs are linked with adoption of preventive behaviors over time, and whether fear of covid-19 is a potential moderator for this relation. a sample of 424 young adults (89.2% females, m age = 20.89) completed measures assessing covid-19-related conspiracy beliefs and preventive behaviors during the second wave of the pandemic, at time 1, and 352 returned six months later, at time 2, and completed measures assessing their covid-19 fear and preventive behaviors. our findings indicated that higher levels of conspiracy beliefs predicted lower adoption of preventive behaviors over time. participants who reported higher fear of covid-19 adopted more preventive behaviors at time 2. the link between conspiracy beliefs and adoption of preventive behaviors was moderated by covid-19 fear. participants who reported higher levels of conspiracy beliefs at time 1 adopted fewer preventive behaviors at time 2 only if they experienced lower or medium levels of covid-19 fear, but not if they experienced high levels of fear. by contrast, participants who reported lower levels of conspiracy beliefs at time 1 adopted more preventive behaviors at time 2 regardless of their level of covid-19 fear. our findings highlight the importance of countering misinformation and relatively high levels of fear in supporting young adults’ positive public attitudes towards protective measures during the pandemic. psychological reports

boredom proneness and attention-related experiences during the covid-19 pandemic during the sars-cov-2 (covid-19) pandemic, measures intended to prevent the spread of the virus (e.g., social distancing) constrained individuals’ range of available activities, potentially promoting increased engagement in certain attention-related behaviours. we explored this possibility by assessing whether, one year into the pandemic, participants perceived changes in their mind-wandering, dreaming and media use when comparing their experiences at the time of testing to their memory of these experiences before covid-19 prevention measures were implemented. given that boredom prone individuals often struggle to effectively engage their attention, we also investigated trait boredom proneness as a possible contributing factor to these perceived changes. participants perceived increases in many aspects of their mind-wandering and dreaming (e.g., frequency, pandemic-related content) as well as several forms of media use (e.g., smartphone use, media multitasking during work-related tasks). moreover, those higher in boredom proneness reported greater increases across many of these experiences. our findings suggest that individuals’ attention-related behaviours changed following the onset of the global crisis. they further suggest that adopting adaptive strategies for coping with boredom might have been effective in attenuating these perceived changes, and may be beneficial in the face of other major crises. psychological reports

potential for life skills growth in adults with profound autism abstract purpose research on autistic adults has expanded rapidly in recent years. however, few studies focus on adults with profound autism, despite this subgroup having substantial support needs across the life course. daily living skills (dls)—including personal care, household chores, and community tasks—are closely tied to independence and service needs in adulthood. the current study applied an item-level coding framework to informant-report dls data to identify intervention targets for this population. method parents and staff members of 36 autistic adults (m age = 35.23 [5.31], 19.4% female, 77% white) who met profound criteria (m verbal iq = 19.56 [13.17] m nonverbal iq = 25.0 [19.14]) completed the vineland adaptive behavior scales, third edition (vabs-3) caregiver interview. a coding scheme developed by teh and colleagues (2023) was applied to dls items scored as “never or seldom” completed independently to characterize why skills were not achieved. results patterns of reasons why skills were not achieved differed significantly across dls domains (i.e., personal, domestic, community; χ 2 (10) = 137.99, p < .001). domestic skills were significantly more likely to be rated “able—reminded,” while community skills were significantly more likely to be rated “unable—cognitive.” many unachieved skills reflected modifiable barriers (e.g., limited opportunities for learning, reliance on prompts) rather than inability, highlighting concrete targets for improving life skills in adults with profound autism. conclusion autistic adults with profound autism retain meaningful potential for continued growth in dls in adulthood. item-level analysis of adaptive behavior may pinpoint intervention targets that are not apparent from summary scores alone. journal of autism and developmental disorders

counting the uncounted dead: a population-anchored bayesian reconciliation of suicide mortality across five indian surveillance systems how a society counts its self-inflicted deaths shapes how it grieves, governs, and intervenes. india, which accounts for roughly one in four of the world’s suicide deaths, runs five surveillance systems that disagree sharply about how many of its people die by suicide. using the only nationally representative, population-based source—the sample registration system cause of death series (2014–2016 to 2022–2024)—as an anchor, this study reconciles police (2018–2024), modelled (2016–2023), who (2010–2021), and medical-certification (2016–2023) counts in a bayesian measurement-error framework, with a state-level decomposition for 2023. the population-anchored 2023 burden is approximately 265,000 deaths, 55% above the police count and 33% above the leading modelled estimate. among women aged 15–29, suicide was the largest single cause of death in every reporting window, at about one in five deaths. many of india’s suicide dead remain administratively invisible. omega-journal of death and dying

algorithmic grief invisibility & fragmented narratives: a theory-building framework for algorithmically mediated grief grief increasingly unfolds within digitally mediated environments in which automated systems shape visibility, continuity, and social acknowledgment. this article advances a theoretical contribution to thanatology by introducing algorithmic grief invisibility (agi), a framework for understanding how algorithmically mediated environments can function as contemporary sites of disenfranchised grief without attributing agency or intent to technology. drawing on doka’s disenfranchised grief, neimeyer’s meaning reconstruction, and continuing bonds scholarship, it theorizes that disruptions in visibility, moderation, sequencing, and social feedback may fragment three narrative threads central to bereavement adaptation: the event story of the loss, the relational back story through which continuing bonds are sustained, and identity reconstruction. as a pre-empirical contribution, agi is offered to support scholarly dialogue, clinical reflection, and future research questions, rather than to test hypotheses or document prevalence. clinical and educational implications are discussed as reflective extensions of established grief theory. omega-journal of death and dying

stability and change in life narratives by elderly adults with alzheimer's dementia, depression, and healthy controls abstract autobiographical memory is affected by alzheimer's dementia and depression in old age. we suggest that cognitive decline in alzheimer's dementia affects both the life narrative construction of personal stability and change, whereas the decline of vitality in depression affects only the construction of change, but not stability of personal identity. elderly adults with alzheimer's dementia ( n = 21), major depression ( n = 20), and healthy controls ( n = 20) did not differ in age ( m age = 76.9 years, range 65–94), gender (33 women), or education (mean years = 12.0) narrated their entire lives and provided turning point and self‐defining memory narratives. individuals with alzheimer's dementia were indeed affected both in indicators of stability and change. individuals with depression produced more negative life narratives but unexpectedly did not differ from healthy controls in narrative indicators of personal change. possibly, the expected reduction of personal change in life stories is limited to very severe depression in younger adults. applied cognitive psychology

longitudinal bidirectional associations between executive functioning and peer victimization in the early school years: a parallel growth model approach. peer victimization during early schooling has been linked to executive functioning (ef), yet little is known about their longitudinal associations. this study examined bidirectional associations between peer victimization and ef using four waves (2013-2016) from the early childhood longitudinal study-kindergarten cohort (nbaseline ≈ 13,840; 49% female; mage(baseline) ≈ 8 years; us sample). applying bivariate latent growth modeling, results indicated that peer victimization followed a nonlinear trajectory with an initial decline followed by stabilization. lower intercept-level ef predicted less steep declines in peer victimization (βs = [-.11, -.12]; ps = [.002, <.001]). importantly, higher intercept-level peer victimization was associated with greater increases in cognitive flexibility over time (β = .17, p < .001). these findings inform understanding of cognitive adaptation to early social stressors. child development

which morphological skills predict development in vocabulary? contrasting morphological awareness with morphological analysis. morphemes are the smallest units of meaning in language. this study examined which of two related morphological skills support vocabulary growth: morphological awareness (recognizing and manipulating morphemes) and morphological analysis (using morphemes to infer meanings). we studied 336 english-speaking children (f = 154, m = 182; mage = 6 years and 8 months; 55% european, with <10% each acadian, asian, african, aboriginal, and middle eastern). in grade 1, children completed morphological awareness and analysis tasks, and controls of reading comprehension, word identification, phonological awareness, nonverbal ability, and working memory. vocabulary was measured at grades 1 and 4. structural equation modeling revealed that only morphological analysis uniquely predicted gains in vocabulary. child development

the influence of zhong-yong thinking on the relationship between psychological capital and sense of power in adolescents: a latent profile and moderated network analysis journal of youth and adolescence

identifying problem-talk and co-rumination in adolescents’ social networks abstract co-rumination (excessive problem-talk) is linked to adolescents’ psychosocial well-being. traditional measures of co-rumination assess co-rumination tendencies with one (unspecified) friend. however, this approach overlooks both the number and characteristics of co-rumination partner(s). the current study identifies problem-talk partners and the degree to which individuals co-ruminate with each partner. the sample includes 579 finnish adolescents (grades 4–9; m age = 14.05, sd = 1.59; 52.3% self-identified as girl). more than half of adolescents (56%) nominated two or more problem-talk partners. number of problem-talk partners and co-rumination among problem-talk partners were both associated with friendship closeness/satisfaction, but only co-rumination among problem-talk partners was positively linked to internalizing symptoms. some evidence was found for a negative association between number of problem-talk partners and internalizing symptoms, underlining the importance of considering the specific ways in which problem-talk partners discuss problems. journal of youth and adolescence
advancing a model of mindful sexual communication: testing sexual communication as a mediator of the association between sexual mindfulness and sexual satisfaction journal of sex research

children’s resource distribution: when beauty bias meets fairness norms favorable biases toward attractive individuals significantly influence social interactions from early childhood. however, little is known about how such biases affect children’s resource allocation, particularly when they conflict with fairness norms. across three studies, we examined how 6-year-olds allocate resources between a high- and a low-attractive, same-gender, unfamiliar peer. in study 1 ( n = 42), children allocated more to high-attractive targets than to low-attractive ones. in study 2 ( n = 72) and 3 ( n = 128), both targets were also assigned merit information. when both targets had equal merit, children continued to favor the high-attractive target. however, when the high-attractive target was less productive, children prioritized merit over attractiveness, paralleling their behavior when only merit information was available. in both studies 1 and 3, children’s liking for the attractive target (rather than prosocial expectations) was positively associated with their allocation preferences, regardless of whether merit information was available. these findings identify conditions under which attractiveness influences young children’s allocation decisions and when equity concerns override this bias. they offer novel insights into the boundary conditions of the “beauty premium” in early childhood and how children balance fairness when navigating competing factors, such as merit and appearance. international journal of behavioral development

reciprocal dynamics of career adaptability and smartphone addiction among chinese adolescents: the mediating role of academic cynicism abstract this study examined the dynamic relationships among career adaptability, academic cynicism, and smartphone addiction in chinese adolescents. drawing on career construction theory, we proposed that career adaptability would be negatively associated with subsequent smartphone addiction and that smartphone addiction would, in turn, be negatively associated with subsequent career adaptability, with academic cynicism mediating both associations. data were collected across three waves at 6‐month intervals: t1 ( n = 1923), t2 ( n = 1550), and t3 ( n = 1177). using latent‐variable cross‐lagged panel models, we found support for the reciprocal longitudinal associations between career adaptability and smartphone addiction from t1 to t3. moreover, academic cynicism at t2 mediated both longitudinal associations. these findings offer valuable insights for interventions aimed at strengthening career adaptability, sustaining students' sense of meaning in learning, and reducing problematic smartphone use among adolescents. applied psychology-an international review-psychologie appliquee-revue internationale
more than just a happy ending? the role of orgasm consistency for sexual satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, and emotional intimacy in mixed-gender romantic relationships journal of sex research

selective social conformity in adolescents with non‐suicidal self‐injury: differential patterns across social influence sources and judgment contexts abstract introduction social conformity among adolescents with non‐suicidal self‐injury (nssi) may vary depending on the characteristics of social information and the context in which social judgments are made. this study examined social conformity patterns in adolescents with nssi across different social influence sources and judgment contexts. methods two independent behavioral experiments were conducted. study 1 included 39 adolescents with nssi and 50 healthy controls (hcs) and employed a risk perception task to examine conformity responses following social feedback from adolescents versus adults. study 2 included an independent sample of 53 adolescents with nssi and 40 hcs and used a facial attractiveness social evaluation task to examine conformity responses under the same two social influence source conditions. a cross‐study joint analysis was conducted to compare source‐related conformity patterns between the studies. results in study 1, adolescents with nssi showed greater conformity effects following adolescent feedback than adult feedback, whereas hcs did not show a significant difference between feedback sources. in study 2, adolescents with nssi exhibited significantly lower conformity effects than hcs under both adolescent and adult feedback conditions. hcs showed stronger conformity effects following adolescent feedback than adult feedback, whereas adolescents with nssi did not show a significant source‐related difference. the cross‐study joint analysis revealed a significant rating discrepancy × participant group × social influence source × study interaction, indicating that source‐related conformity patterns differed significantly between the two studies. conclusions social conformity among adolescents with nssi was not uniformly enhanced across the two judgment contexts. instead, conformity patterns differed in relation to social influence sources and between the two judgment paradigms. these findings extend research on peer‐related influences in nssi and provide experimental behavioral evidence for understanding how adolescents with nssi adjust their social judgments following feedback from others. journal of adolescence

distinct cross‐lagged relations of cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression with perceived social support among chinese adolescents abstract introduction converging evidence suggests a close relationship between emotion regulation (er) and perceived social support (pss) among adolescents. yet, little is currently known about their longitudinal cross‐lagged associations within the chinese cultural context, as well as the differential effects of different er strategies. to address these gaps, the present study aimed to examine the cross‐lagged associations between pss and two specific er strategies—cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression—in chinese adolescents. methods a total of 316 adolescents from zhoukou, china (45.9% female; m age = 16.42, sd = 0.61, aged 14–18 years) participated in a three‐wave longitudinal study, with data collected at 6‐month intervals during senior high school. to examine hypothesized cross‐lagged associations, we employed cross‐lagged panel models, a well‐established method for analyzing temporal associations (kenny 1975). results cross‐lagged panel model revealed that pss at time 1 was positively associated with cognitive reappraisal at time 2, which in turn was positively related to pss at time 3. pss at time 2 also showed a positive correlation with cognitive reappraisal at time 3. in contrast, no significant cross‐lagged effects were observed between pss and expressive suppression over time. conclusions these findings contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the longitudinal cross‐lagged associations between pss and er in adolescence, highlighting the association between supportive social environments and adolescents’ er strategies. journal of adolescence

social cohesion and place attachment in wildfire and flood mitigation in southern california as climate change intensifies wildfire and flood risks in the wildland urban interface, understanding the social factors that shape mitigation behavior is critical for resilience planning. this study examines how social cohesion and place attachment influence household and collective mitigation efforts using a survey of over 500 residents in southern california communities. structural equation modeling is used to assess relationships between socio-demographic and environmental factors, social cohesion, place attachment, and self-reported mitigation behaviors. mitigation outcomes include structural home improvements, defensible space creation, and participation in community preparedness initiatives. results show that place attachment is positively associated with wildfire mitigation, flood mitigation, and collective mitigation. social cohesion is positively associated only with collective mitigation. homeownership is associated with wildfire mitigation but not flood mitigation. these findings highlight the importance of fostering place attachment and leveraging neighborhood networks to promote collective action and context-specific strategies to reduce risk in multi-hazard wui settings. environment and behavior

time to jump: exploring the distribution of noise in evidence accumulation as a function of time pressure. the diffusion model conceptualizes binary decisions as emerging from continuous evidence accumulation with gaussian noise. the lévy-flight model (lfm) extends this by allowing accumulation noise to follow a heavier-tailed distribution, enabling sudden, large jumps in evidence accumulation. the heavy-tailedness is governed by the stability parameter α, with smaller α-values indicating more frequent and larger jumps. we demonstrate through simulation that the lfm can generate near-symmetrical response time (rt) distributions typical under strict deadlines. in study 1, we explored the influence of intense time pressure on α in a letter-number discrimination task, expecting higher time pressure to entail smaller α-values. participants (n = 341) were assigned to an accuracy (unlimited rt), implicit deadline (feedback discouraging rts over 500 ms), or explicit deadline condition (timeout at 500 ms). given the lfm's intractable likelihood, we used bayesflow, a framework for simulation-based inference with deep learning. model comparisons consistently favored the lfm over diffusion model variants-even in the accuracy condition. importantly, α-values decreased with increasing time pressure and were especially low in the explicit deadline condition, where rt distributions also approached symmetry. estimating both the lfm and a structurally matched diffusion model, with and without timeout modeling, further showed that accounting for timeout-related rt truncation led to substantially lower diffusion model drift rates, whereas lfm drift rates changed only modestly. study 2 (n = 160) replicated α's sensitivity to time pressure in a brightness discrimination task. overall, α responded systematically to temporal constraints across both tasks and timeout modeling specifications. cognitive psychology

muscular = fake? testing a picture‐word pairing procedure to increase muscle appearance satisfaction in young men abstract objective when men compare their bodies to those of muscular fitness models, this may result in dissatisfaction with their own muscularity. we tested whether pairing pictures of male muscular‐ideal models with synonyms of ‘fake’ results in an increase in muscle satisfaction and a decrease in self‐objectification among young men. method male participants ( n = 66, m age = 22.86, sd = 2.14) were randomly assigned to an experimental ( n = 32) or control ( n = 34) condition of a picture‐word pairing procedure. both conditions showed the same pictures of muscular‐ideal models. in the experimental condition these pictures were systemically paired with synonyms of ‘fake’; in the control condition these pictures were randomly paired with words related to sports and colours. results participants in the experimental condition showed a modest increase in muscle appearance satisfaction from pre‐ to posttest whereas control participants did not change. change in muscle appearance satisfaction was not moderated by internalisation of the appearance ideal. the predicted decrease in self‐objectification was not found. conclusions the present research provides initial evidence that pairing pictures of male muscular‐ideal models with ‘fake’ can enhance muscle appearance satisfaction in young men. trial registration the study was pre‐registered at https://aspredicted.org/uy9zp5.pdf european eating disorders review

identifying online racism: longitudinal pathways to depression symptomology among black adolescents abstract online racism is increasingly becoming a public health concern, with the short‐term psychological consequences of online racism on black adolescents well documented. although previous investigations have focused on the unidimensional and cross‐sectional effects of online racism related to depressive symptoms, our understanding of the multidimensional aspects and longitudinal effects of online racism on depressive symptoms among black adolescents remains limited. thus, the current investigation contributes to the growing body of literature on online racism exposure among black adolescents by exploring the longitudinal changes in the identification of online racism exposure and how it is related to later depressive symptoms. using a sample of 135 self‐identified black adolescents ranging from 11 to 19 years old (m age = 14 years; sd = 2.44), the results indicated that an increased positive change in individual ord exposure and vicarious ord, but not traumatic events online (teo), was associated with an increase in depression symptoms at wave 2. overall, these findings highlight the need to consider how changes in black adolescents' exposure to online racism over time may shape their psychological well‐being and underscore the importance of addressing both direct and indirect forms of online racism as salient developmental stressors for black adolescents. journal of research on adolescence

ai-enabled algorithmic management and frontline employee job crafting: the roles of control, support, and managerial orientation algorithmic management combines functions that regulate work with those that provide information and guidance, yet their distinct psychological and behavioral associations require further examination. drawing on the job demands–resources framework and a sociotechnical perspective, this study examines algorithmic control and support in relation to frontline employees’ job crafting, distinguishing system functions from perceived managerial enactment. three-wave time-lagged survey data from 547 employees in fast-food chain outlets were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. algorithmic support was positively associated with work engagement and negatively associated with exhaustion, whereas algorithmic control showed the opposite pattern. indirect-effect estimates were consistent with support being associated with greater promotion-focused crafting through engagement and lower prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion. control was associated with greater prevention-focused crafting through exhaustion and lower promotion-focused crafting through engagement. the support–engagement relationship was stronger at higher perceived managerial decision-support orientation, while the control–exhaustion relationship was stronger at higher perceived enforcement orientation. these findings highlight the value of examining algorithmic functions across both motivational and strain-related pathways and considering how managers enact system outputs. the observational design supports associations consistent with the proposed mechanisms rather than causal conclusions. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

the association between cognitive flexibility and eating behaviors in autistic women with eating disorders abstract objective reduced cognitive flexibility is a trait associated with autism and has also been implicated in eating disorders (eds). however, most studies have not distinguished between autistic and non‐autistic individuals in ed samples, potentially obscuring group‐specific patterns. this study investigated self‐reported cognitive flexibility and its association with eating behaviors (traditional ed pathology and arfid symptomatology) across four groups: autistic women with eds (asd + ed), non‐autistic women with eds (ed), autistic women without eds (asd), and non‐autistic controls. method participants included 30 asd + ed, 30 ed, 29 asd, and 60 control women ( n = 149). all completed the detail and flexibility questionnaire (dflex), the eating disorder examination questionnaire (ede‐q), and the nine item arfid screen (nias). group comparisons were conducted on self‐reported cognitive flexibility (cognitive rigidity, attention to detail), ed pathology, and arfid symptoms. associations between cognitive flexibility and eating behaviors were examined across and within groups. results asd + ed and asd groups showed significantly greater difficulties in self‐reported cognitive flexibility than ed and control groups, which did not differ from each other. associations between self‐reported cognitive flexibility and eating behaviors varied across groups, with attention to detail showing the clearest pattern. attention to detail was associated with ed pathology in the asd + ed group and with arfid symptomatology in the asd + ed, asd, and control groups, but not in the ed group. conclusion these exploratory findings suggest that self‐reported cognitive inflexibility may be more strongly associated with autism than with eds alone and highlight the importance of considering co‐occurring autism when examining cognitive characteristics in ed populations. public significance statement this study explored how cognitive traits ‐ like attention to detail ‐ relate to eating behaviors in autistic and non‐autistic women with and without eating disorders. findings suggest that certain thinking patterns may be more closely linked to autism than to eating disorders alone, underscoring the need for greater clinical awareness of autism‐specific features when assessing and supporting individuals with disordered eating. journal of clinical psychology
