implicit self-death associations and symptoms of depression and anxiety: a single-case experimental design death anxiety may operate as a transdiagnostic process underlying anxiety and depressive symptoms. this study used the death-implicit association task (d-iat) to index implicit self-death associations (isda) and evaluated a brief mindfulness intervention using a concurrent multiple-baseline design with maintenance across four students with prior anxiety/depressive diagnoses. across 20 daily sessions, d-iat d-scores and mini-dass depression and anxiety scores were collected. visual analysis suggested reductions in depression and anxiety for several participants, with lower scores often persisting into maintenance. casewise tau-b patterns were heterogeneous. exact randomisation tests showed a significant reduction in anxiety from baseline to intervention ( p = .04), while the reduction in depression was nonsignificant ( p = .08). neither outcome showed a significant baseline-to-maintenance effect, and d-scores showed no significant reduction. findings provide partial support for mindfulness-related symptom change but no evidence of corresponding change in isda. psychological reports

the complex relation between fiction, morality, truth, and ideology research on the effects of reading fiction typically treats fiction as a monolithic entity and interprets its effects as evidence that reading improves social cognition and makes people better. this article questions both the practice and the interpretation. fiction may exercise and reshape social-cognitive processes, but this does not imply greater accuracy, notably because, with few exceptions, social cognition has no external criterion of correctness. findings linking reading fiction to empathy, moral reasoning, psychological essentialism, or attributional complexity do not by themselves show that fiction makes us better people. many of these outcomes are self-reported styles and beliefs associated with ideological orientations, and whether people who score higher or lower on them are better people is a separate, normative question. moreover, fiction is not monolithic: literary and popular fiction differ systematically in formal and representational properties, including ambiguity, predictability, complexity, and reliance on conventional narrative structures, and may encourage, respectively, more schema-disruptive or more schema-reinforcing modes of social cognition. situating these effects within the psychology of art highlights a broader point: cognitive change, moral value, truth, political orientation, and aesthetic worth are related, but they should not be treated as equivalent. current opinion in psychology

organizational silence cultures. a conceptual framework and integrative review on how they develop, manifest, and persist organizational silence (a state in which certain issues are not addressed in an organization) prevents open discussion among employees, hampers error detection and innovation, and contributes to the endurance of inefficacy and toxic work places. applying a cultural lens, we develop a framework for understanding the environment in which organizational silence occurs. we propose that organizational silence cultures develop if silence deems adequate to solve adaptation problems, that they manifest at three layers in the form of artifacts, shared values and norms, and implicit basic assumptions, and that they persist through the combined operation of withholding, deafness, and censorship. using an integrative review, we examine the propositions of our framework and show its usefulness to synthesize and advance knowledge. we identified adaptive functions organizational silence fulfils and derived four organizational silence culture types, explain how they manifest at three cultural layers, and how withholding, deafness, and censorship make them persist. organizational psychology review

how memories feel real: the sense of reality in episodic remembering abstract episodic memories, like perceptions, possess a distinctive justificatory force: subjects naturally take their contents to be or to have been the case. this epistemic affinity between memory and perception, and their shared contrast with imagination, has received insufficient attention in the philosophy of memory. existing accounts emphasize phenomenological components such as pastness, self, familiarity, and singularity, but none of these fully explains the justificatory force characteristic of memory. drawing on the phenomenological conception of experiential justification, according to which justificatory force is grounded in phenomenal character, i argue in this paper that the missing explanatory component is the sense of reality, understood as the experience of the represented object or event as independent of one’s representation of it. building on work on perceptual objectivity, i propose that the sense of reality consists in two constitutive experiences, constancy and coming-into-view, and that episodic memory exhibits both. i further argue that the sense of reality involves two distinguishable dimensions: an existence aspect and an identity aspect, covering both whether and, if so, how objects and events are experienced as mind-independent. this distinction also sheds light on imagination. while imagination can involve partial degrees of the sense of reality, it is fundamentally characterized by a contrasting sense of creativity: the subject’s freedom to determine and modify the imagined content. the sense of reality thus explains both the justificatory force shared by memory and perception and their contrast with imagination. review of philosophy and psychology

peer-led examination simulation reshapes psychophysiological and emotional state profiles during problem-based medical learning abstract repeated problem-based learning (pbl) sessions are intended to sustain active, collaborative, and self-directed learning, yet evidence is mixed as to whether familiar pbl routines consistently maintain an appropriate level of learner activation over time. this repeated-measures study examined whether embedding a peer-led examination simulation into regular pbl reshapes psychophysiological and achievement-emotional state profiles. forty-two medical students were assessed during resting reference, regular pbl, and pbl with peer-led examination simulation. heart rate variability (hrv) was quantified using rmssd, sdnn, pnn50, and lf/hf, alongside anxiety, perceived stress, achievement emotions, motivation, self-rated performance, and post-session appraisal. both pbl formats reduced hrv relative to rest, indicating autonomic activation during regular pbl itself. compared with regular pbl, examination simulation produced additional hrv withdrawal, higher anxiety and perceived stress, and lower boredom. baseline-adjusted mixed models supported effects for rmssd and sdnn; pnn50 did not survive false-discovery-rate correction, and lf/hf showed no robust effect. enjoyment, motivation, and self-rated performance did not differ significantly. students reported greater perceived benefit from and stronger preference for the simulation format. peer-led examination simulation thus shifted pbl toward a more salient, assessment-like psychophysiological and emotional state profile. npj science of learning

social anxiety disorder counseling outcomes: meta‐analysis of studies from 2000 to 2024 abstract this meta‐analysis of 147 articles examined the effectiveness of counseling in reducing symptoms of social anxiety disorders (sads) and the durability of these treatments upon follow‐up assessments. depending upon the type of comparison group used, counselors can expect average posttreatment effect size gains of (cohen's d ) 0.466 (95% ci [0.294, 0.638]) to 1.047 (95% ci [0.946, 1.149]) (primarily moderate to large effects of treatment) and follow‐up effect size gains of 0.680 (95% ci [0.212, 1.149]) to 1.285 (95% ci [1.072, 1.498]) (primarily moderate to large effects of treatment) for placebo to single‐group comparisons, respectively. the hypothesized moderators used within the study revealed only one moderator analysis. homogeneity of effect size averages ( χ 2 , i 2 ) was evident across all comparison groups, so no moderation study follow‐ups were required. these results are consistent with and expand previous meta‐analyses of the treatment of sad using counseling interventions. counseling treatment of sad was effective regardless of approach, meaning that traditional counseling, internet‐based, and low‐contact interventions are all viable. earlier interventions, wider availability of treatment options, and cost‐effectiveness studies are needed. the prevalence, functional impairment, and treatment avoidance associated with sad reinforce the critical role of counseling in promoting recovery and enhancing quality of life. journal of counseling and development

psychosocial resources mediate stress and dual continua of mental health outcomes in college students: a structural equation model abstract mental health concerns among college students remain a pressing issue, yet most research examines psychopathology in isolation from positive mental health. this study integrated the stress process model (spm) and the dual‐continua model to test whether belongingness, resilience, and perfectionism‐standards mediate the associations between three stressors (sleep problems, perfectionism‐discrepancy, and loneliness) and both anxio‐depressive symptoms and flourishing. using structural equation modeling with 4744 students at a northeastern us university, we found that stressors were broadly associated with lower psychosocial resources, though perfectionism‐discrepancy was positively associated with perfectionism‐standards. mediation pathways diverged across the two continua: resilience was the primary mediator for anxio‐depressive symptoms, whereas belongingness was the dominant mediator for flourishing. in the structural model, perfectionism‐standards simultaneously predicted higher flourishing and slightly higher anxio‐depressive symptoms, a dual function invisible in single‐continuum frameworks. these findings provide evidence that psychopathology and well‐being are associated with distinct psychosocial mechanisms. practical implications are discussed. journal of counseling and development

a systematic review of observational and report-based measures of caregiver sensitivity: a latin american perspective. sensitivity is a cornerstone of early childhood mental health; however, its measurement relies heavily on tools developed in english-speaking, high-resource contexts. this systematic review identified observational and report-based instruments used to assess sensitivity in caregivers of children aged 0-6 years. it evaluated the methodological robustness and usability of these instruments within latin american contexts. following a systematic search in web of science, scopus, psycinfo, and redalyc, 732 eligible studies were identified. based on a frequency-of-use threshold, 16 instruments (14 observational and 2 report-based) represented across 616 papers were selected for in-depth evaluation. measures were coded for theoretical alignment with ainsworth's sensitivity definition, psychometric evidence, and usability-specifically training accessibility, administration complexity, and evidence of use with diverse latin american populations (e.g., caregivers in rural settings or with lower educational levels). results revealed that only a minority of measures adhered explicitly to ainsworth's original definition. most instruments prioritized warmth and positive affect, potentially leading to cross-cultural underdetection in contexts where responsiveness is expressed through proximity and routine-based care. while observational tools predominated, report-based measures showed limited validation and minimal regional use. these findings highlight the urgent need for culturally grounded validation and the development of accessible training programs for the region. infant mental health journal-infancy and early childhood

sleep disturbance scale for children subdomains and depressive severity in youth with major depressive disorder background most studies linking sleep disturbances to depressive symptoms in youth have relied on aggregate sleep scores rather than subdomain‐specific measures, leaving the role of specific sleep disturbance subdomains in clinical populations poorly understood. objective to examine whether specific subdomains of the sleep disturbance scale for children (sdsc) are differentially associated with depressive symptom severity in a clinical sample. methods cross‐sectional study of 52 children and adolescents (mean [sd] age, 15.05 [1.27] years; 86.5% female) diagnosed with major depressive disorder (mdd) at a public, referral‐based outpatient mental health clinic in brazil. associations between sdsc subdomains and cdi scores were examined using age‐ and sex‐adjusted logistic (cdi ≥ 17) and continuous cdi regression. discrimination was explored using roc analysis. results disorders of initiating and maintaining sleep (dims) showed the largest standardized difference between participants above and below the cdi threshold (cohen ′ s d = 1.09, 95% ci 0.45–1.72). in a multivariable model including dims and sleep hyperhidrosis, only dims remained associated with cdi ≥ 17 (or = 1.21, 95% ci 1.05–1.40). this pattern was consistent with cdi as a continuous outcome and after excluding the cdi sleep item. dims had the highest apparent auc among individual sleep measures (0.828). conclusions in this predominantly female sample of children and adolescents with mdd treated in a tertiary service, dims was the sdsc subdomain most consistently associated with depressive symptom severity. mental illness

knotted minds: knot theory as a framework for modelling psychological dynamics this article develops a conceptual framework connecting knot theory with the study of recurrent psychological dynamics. building on the relational and dynamic foundations of kurt lewin’s topological psychology, we examine whether knots, links, braids, and their invariants can provide a structural language for describing persistent patterns of thought, affect, and behaviour. we distinguish three levels of the proposal: knot language as metaphor, longitudinal psychological processes as trajectories in a theoretically specified state space, and recurrent trajectories as formal knot-theoretic objects. to demonstrate this progression, we develop a worked case grounded in cognitive and metacognitive accounts of generalized anxiety disorder. primary worry, meta-worry, and control or safety responses define the coordinates of a psychological state space in which intensive longitudinal observations may generate recurrent trajectories. a controlled synthetic comparison shows that trajectories with the same coordinate-wise means and standard deviations can nevertheless differ in their global topological organization. we specify the recurrence, closure, and stability conditions required for knot-theoretic classification and derive testable implications concerning symptom persistence, relapse, and treatment-related structural change. knot theory is not proposed as a replacement for psychological explanation, but as a complementary method for examining whether recurrent psychological trajectories differ only in intensity and timing or instantiate structurally different patterns of organization. theory & psychology

what exactly is the problem? in response to the article “the retreat to positionality statements: a critique of the assumptions (and how to avoid making them),” i argue that the authors’ critique is borne out of their own assumptions about the nature and function of positionality statements, the meaning of science, and the (alleged) tarnishing of objectivity owing to researchers’ personal, political, and ideological commitments. moreover, for all that the authors present themselves as the torchbearers of scientific inquiry, there are no examples of positionality statements, no explicit evidence of their putatively deleterious effects, and no compelling argument for why they ought to be abandoned. this suggests that other motives may inform their critique. what these motives are, however, remains unclear. theory & psychology

the gap is the point: drive, free energy, and the problem with the queen bee dall’aglio’s article asks a seductive question: what if lacanian drive theory could finally be translated into the language of neuroscience, predictive processing, and the free energy principle? this commentary argues that the proposed synthesis works less through conceptual rigor than through a series of increasingly unstable analogies. terms such as “constancy,” “fields,” “repression,” and “trajectory” slide between psychoanalysis, biology, and mathematics as if similarity of form guaranteed theoretical equivalence. the result is a strange conceptual universe in which lacanian drive appears simultaneously as structural impossibility, affective intensity, computational optimization, and solenoidal flow. focusing on the article’s treatment of constant pressure, predictive processing, nondeclarative memory, and dual-aspect monism, i argue that the article repeatedly mistakes metaphorical resonance for commensurability between explanatory domains. the problem is not simply reductionism. more fundamentally, the article stages a contemporary fantasy: that the constitutive gap between psychoanalysis and neuroscience can finally be overcome through theoretical synthesis. what emerges, however, is not a bridge between discourses, but a symptomatic attempt to make psychoanalysis legible within the dominant scientific imaginary of prediction, regulation, and self-organization. theory & psychology

relationship impasses in modern times: a lacanian perspective this article seeks to elucidate the impasses experienced in contemporary romantic relationships through the lens of lacanian psychoanalysis. within this scope, the transformation of modern relationships is examined through three fundamental concepts: the evaporation of the father, the capitalist discourse, and the imaginary order. the article initially examines how the decline of paternal authority undermines the subject’s capacity to enter and sustain a position within the symbolic order. it argues that this erosion of the paternal function generates a structural impasse in the constitution of desire. the discussion then turns to capitalist discourse, contending that it disavows constitutive lack and reorients subjects toward an endless cycle of consumption. in this context, online dating applications are conceptualized as spaces where the subject treats others through a logic of consumption. drawing on lacan’s theory of sexuation, the article contends that the failure of dating applications to provide a symbolic framework poses unique structural risks -particularly for subjects in the feminine position regarding their relation to other jouissance. finally, digital spaces trap the subject in identifications with flawless images by reproducing the mirror stage through the practice of the selfie. social media platforms, acting like a big other, set the standards for recognition and demand constant visibility. subjects seeking to avoid the lack and fragility inherent in the symbolic order are becoming unable to tolerate the imperfections that real encounters bring. consequently, the article demonstrates how contemporary socio-digital transformations damage the subject’s capacity to navigate lack, structure desire, and cultivate relational continuity. theory & psychology

conversational ai and the temporal ecology of self-reflection abstract self-reflection has historically depended on temporal transformations that no one had to arrange: memory faded and reworked what it returned, the standpoint from which the past was met shifted, and other people changed alongside the person reflecting. conversational ai separates these transformations from the person’s own. transcripts and selective system memory may change technically, yet they persist across the interval without undergoing it as lived time, and a responsive interlocutor answers without the relational time of a history shared with the person. drawing on cultural psychology’s premise that psychological processes unfold in irreversible time and on the phenomenology of time-consciousness, the paper describes the conditions of self-reflection as a temporal ecology of memory, standpoint, other people, and artefacts, related through their differing movement across time. externalising part of one’s past into conversational systems converts regulation that once proceeded tacitly into time work: deciding whether, when, in what order, and how often to return to earlier formulations. such work draws on attention and judgement; where it is left to defaults, it is performed by those who design and govern the systems. a system that remembers and answers may also lend earlier formulations a witness’s authority. the freedom to change, once protected by the coupling of fading and inaccessibility, thus comes to depend on regulatory work distributed between persons and infrastructures, and agency over one’s own past, as experienced and as exercised, becomes partly a matter of governance. the paper derives empirical questions and implications for society, wellbeing, education, and personal development. integrative psychological and behavioral science

bridging the language gap in maternal mental health: psychometric evaluation of the siswati edinburgh postnatal depression scale during pregnancy the integration of antenatal depression screening into routine antenatal care necessitates the validation of existing screening tools. this study investigated the validity and reliability of the siswati version of the edinburgh postnatal depression scale (epds) among antenatal women. this cross-sectional study included 505 antenatal women, half of whom ( n = 252) were included in exploratory factor analysis (efa) and the other half ( n = 253) in confirmatory factor analysis (cfa). cronbach’s alpha and intraclass correlation coefficients were determined to evaluate the scales’ reliability. the depression anxiety stress scales (dass) were used to examine concurrent validity. approximately 26% of the women had depressive symptoms. with acceptable model fit indices, the cfa confirmed the following two factors, which were identified during the efa: anhedonia (items 1 and 2) and anxiety/depression (items 3–10). the cronbach’s alpha and intraclass correlation coefficient values were .83 and .86, respectively. the epds had satisfactory concurrent validity. the siswati version of the epds is a valid and reliable tool for screening for antenatal depressive symptoms in primary care settings. future studies should explore the diagnostic accuracy of the scale. the tool will ensure early detection of perinatal depressive symptoms, enable timely interventions and improve maternal and child outcomes. south african journal of psychology

the longitudinal mediation pathways between positive mental health and prolonged grief disorder among refugees abstract the grief experience includes positive and negative factors that collectively contribute to its persistence, protective factors can buffer against the development of prolonged grief disorder (pgd). to investigate the longitudinal associations between positive mental health (pmh), anxiety, depression, and pgd among refugees who have experienced a loss related to a death event. in the present study, longitudinal data were assessed through an online self-report survey at the baseline (t1), at the 3-month follow-up (t2), and at the 6-month follow-up (t3). the total sample at baseline included 196 adult arabic-speaking refugees who reported prolonged grief symptoms at least six months after a death event of a close person, (78.6% women, mage 36.1, sd = 11.03, myears of refugee status 8.25 years, sd = 3.8). serial-parallel mediation models were used to investigate the longitudinal associations among pmht1, depressiont1,t2, anxietyt1,t2, and pgdt1,t2,t3. the results showed that pmht1 is associated with pgdt3 through the mediation of pgd, depression, and anxiety at t1 and t2, with total indirect effects b = − 0.139, se = 0.069. furthermore, the serial mediation model indicated that pmht1 was negatively associated with pgdt3 through the sequential mediation of depressiont2 and anxietyt2, with total indirect effects b = − 0.097, se = 0.050. the present findings corroborate the interactive association between pmh as a positive factor and grief-related disorders as a negative factor in maintaining pgd symptoms over time. pmh can indirectly foster integrated grief through its negative association with anxiety and depression. current psychology
