viewpoint on multisensory illusions abstract david alais and jean vroomen reflect on the field of multisensory perception and give their views on a range of topics, including how they were first attracted to the field and which researchers were prominent early influences. they also consider important findings such as bayesian cue combination and foundational neurophysiological work showing multisensory integration in the superior colliculus which shaped the field as a whole and influenced their own work on multisensory perception and illusions. the importance of separating response bias from perceptual sensitivity is noted as a critical point in understanding behavioural experiments and neural oscillations are put forward as a key element in understanding the mechanisms of multisensory perception. looking to the future, both agree that technological advances such as wearable sensors and virtual/augmented reality offer an opportunity to take multisensory research out of the lab and into the real-world environments for which our senses evolved and optimised. multisensory research

modulation of social preference and avoidance of zebrafish conspecifics treated with selected neuroactive compounds social interaction and preference are essential parts of human and animal behavior. zebrafish are rapidly emerging as a major model organism in neurobehavioral research and, as highly social animals, enable probing of their social preference and its pharmacological modulation. neuroactive drug effects, however, can also be socially transmittable, thereby indirectly affecting drug-free animal behavior as well. here, we examine this possibility in adult zebrafish by assessing their social preference for conspecifics treated using a wide range of neuroactive drugs with well established effects in zebrafish. zebrafish were treated with acute or chronic neuroactive drugs (gbr-12909, fluoxetine, reserpine, caffeine, arecoline, nicotine, cuprizone, ethanol, and atropine), and exposed to target fish in the three-chamber social preference test, scoring time the latter spent in each zone. overall, we found their overt social preference for conspecifics treated with acute nicotine and gbr-12909, and social avoidance of fish exposed to all other drugs used, except cuprizone and ethanol. these findings confirm altered social preference for central nervous system (cns) drug-treated zebrafish, but suggest that this preference is nonlinear and does not correlate with anxiolytic or anxiogenic drug profiles. further research is needed to explore why some cns drug-evoked behavioral effects render conspecifics socially attractive or aversive to observer zebrafish, and to determine potential practical and translational implications of these findings for neuropharmacology and biological psychiatry. behavioural pharmacology

towards valid translational models of parkinson’s disease in zebrafish parkinson’s disease is a common, highly prevalent and severely debilitating progressive neurodegenerative disorder. however, despite extensive clinical and preclinical research, the pathobiological complexity, underlying mechanisms and treatment strategies of this disorder remain poorly understood. animal models are a valuable tool to study human brain disorders, including parkinson’s disease. here, we discuss the pathobiology of parkinson’s disease, with a particular focus on zebrafish ( danio rerio ) based genetic, pharmacological, and behavioral models that provide important insights into genetic and environmental causes of this disorder. critically evaluating the advantages and limitations of modern zebrafish models relevant to parkinson’s disease, we emphasize the importance of addressing both motor and nonmotor symptoms of this disorder, and also outline how these fish can facilitate further anti-parkinson’s disease drug discovery. behavioural pharmacology

the role of long-term memory, flexible templates and learning in attentional guidance nature reviews psychology, published online: 23 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44159-026-00626-2 theories of visual search suggest that humans hold a veridical representation of the desired target in working memory to guide attention. in this review, carlisle and woodman synthesize evidence that attentional guidance is flexible, adaptive on the basis of experience, and driven by multiple coordinated mechanisms. nature reviews psychology

adaptación y validación de la escala de autenticidad en adultos argentinos la autenticidad se entiende como la capacidad de actuar en coherencia con los propios valores, pensamientos y emociones, y se vincula con el bienestar psicológico y subjetivo. pese a su relevancia, argentina carece de instrumentos adaptados y validados que permitan evaluar la autenticidad en la población adulta general. el objetivo del presente estudio fue adaptar lingüística y culturalmente la escala de autenticidad de wood et al. (2008) y analizar sus propiedades psicométricas en adultos argentinos. se empleó un diseño instrumental. los ítems fueron traducidos y evaluados por once jueces expertos, quienes analizaron su claridad, pertinencia y equivalencia semántica. la escala se administró a 457 adultos de entre 18 y 65 años (m = 38.50; de = 12.17), mayoritariamente mujeres (86.4%). se aplicaron la escala de flourishing (mesurado et al., 2021) y la escala de autocompasión breve (raes et al., 2011; klos et al., 2019) para obtener evidencias de validez concurrente. los resultados mostraron adecuada validez de contenido (v de aiken > .90). el análisis factorial confirmatorio respaldó la estructura de tres factores, con adecuada consistencia interna, y el modelo reducido de 11 ítems presentó mayor parsimonia y mejor validez convergente que la versión original (χ²/gl = 3.30; cfi = .96; gfi = .95; rmsea = .071). el factor vida auténtica correlacionó positivamente con flourishing y autocompasión, mientras que autoalienación y aceptación de influencias externas se asociaron negativamente con flourishing y autocompasión. en conclusión, la versión argentina de 11 ítems de la escala de autenticidad presenta evidencias favorables de validez y confiabilidad para su aplicación. revista ces psicologia

how system justification sustains sexual inequality: the case of the orgasm gap abstract the “orgasm gap”—the consistent disparity in orgasm rates in sexual encounters between women and men—represents a striking form of gender inequality. though orgasms strongly predict women's sexual satisfaction, many women downplay their importance. to explain this paradox, we drew on system justification theory (sjt) to investigate whether and how legitimizing the orgasm gap sustains sexual inequality between women and men across four studies with u.s. participants ( n = 1967). study 1 introduced a novel measure of orgasm gap‐system justification (ogsj), showing that stronger justification was associated with lower orgasm centrality and entitlement among women, and higher orgasm entitlement among men. studies 1 and 2 provided evidence for sjt's palliative function: irregularly‐orgasmic women who endorsed ogsj beliefs reported greater sexual satisfaction despite low orgasm frequency. studies 2 and 3 (the latter experimental) demonstrated the motivated nature of ogsj, as irregularly‐orgasmic women selectively endorsed system‐affirming explanations and judged system‐threatening information as less credible than system‐affirming information. in study 4, stronger ogsj was associated with reduced support for social change initiatives promoting orgasm equality among women and men. these findings highlight how system justification sustains sexual inequality, offering psychological comfort at the cost of structural change. british journal of social psychology

cancer-related awareness and health-seeking behavior among adolescents and young adults – a systematic review abstract evidence on cancer awareness among adolescents and young adults remains fragmented focusing on adult populations or the effectiveness of educational interventions. despite well-established benefits of early detection in improving cancer outcomes, delayed help seeking remains an ongoing challenge. the aim of this review was to explore the current literature on cancer awareness and health seeking behavior among adolescents and young adults. a comprehensive search of five databases was conducted between 2015 and 2025. findings from 58 studies, representing a wide range of cancer types, revealed that participants demonstrated higher awareness of common cancers but underestimated their personal vulnerability, consistent with the heightened perceived invulnerability characteristic of this developmental period. common barriers to timely health-seeking included cultural sensitivities, embarrassment, and perceived vulnerability, alongside gaps in specific symptom knowledge. cancer awareness amongst adolescents and young adults did not consistently translate into understanding their own personal risk or seeking help in a timely manner. the findings of this review suggest that the key challenge is not simply increasing cancer awareness in this group, but subsequently recognising their own vulnerability to cancer, identifying when health-seeking action is required, and overcoming barriers to accessing care. adolescent research review

a longitudinal study of lung cancer stigma across 6 months in a trial of supportive care interventions people with lung cancer commonly experience stigma, however, the temporal impacts are poorly understood. this study investigated changes (using linear mixed modelling) and trajectories (using latent growth modelling) of stigma over a 6-month period in people newly diagnosed with lung cancer, who were participants of a larger trial of supportive care interventions (actrn12615000932561). participants ( n = 192) completed surveys which included the cataldo lung cancer stigma scale. lung cancer stigma did not vary significantly over time, with mean scores of 53.2 ± 15.6 and 54.0 ± 16.7 reported at recruitment and 6 months respectively (range 31–124, higher scores indicate greater stigma). two main trajectory patterns were identified: (1) ‘relatively lower stigma trajectory’; and (2) ‘relatively higher stigma trajectory’. relatively higher stigma trajectories were associated with younger age and a history of smoking. further research is warranted to identify strategies to reduce lung cancer stigma and explore differences across sub-groups and stages of the lung cancer continuum. journal of health psychology

lonely, but not the same: exploring associations of emotional and social loneliness with psychological distress in older adults – a gendered perspective emotional and social loneliness contribute to psychological distress in older adults. gender differences may moderate these associations. this study investigates how emotional/social loneliness and gender relate to psychological distress. a postal survey was conducted with 3108 older adults (>60 years) in erlangen, germany, using kessler psychological distress scale, de jong gierveld loneliness scale, and additional psychosocial/health measures. multiple regressions examined associations between psychological distress and loneliness, gender and psychosocial/health factors. the regression model explained 45% of psychological distress variance (adjusted r 2 = 0.449). emotional and social loneliness, satisfaction with life, changes in psychological and physical health, and access to routine medical care were significant predictors for psychological distress. a gender interaction showed a stronger association between emotional loneliness and psychological distress for women; no such interaction was found for social loneliness. these findings underscore the importance of gender-sensitive interventions targeting emotional loneliness to reduce psychological distress. journal of health psychology

the self- and parent-report versions of the spence children’s anxiety scale: internal structure and multi-informant construct validity in portuguese adolescents and their parents the spence children’s anxiety scale (scas) and its parent version (scas-p) are widely used and psychometrically supported measures that contribute meaningfully to multi-informant assessment of adolescent anxiety. however, their internal structure and convergent validity within a multitrait–multimethod framework have not been examined. this study addressed this gap by evaluating the internal structure of the scas and scas-p in adolescent (n = 302; 12–19 years; 60.3% female) and parent samples (n = 314; 30–70 years; 83.8% female). the original six-factor model showed acceptable fit and was retained for both the scas and the scas-p measuring separation anxiety, social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, panic/agoraphobia, generalized anxiety, and fear of injury. a nested dyad sample (n = 198) was then used to test the multitrait–multimethod construct validity of this model. results generally supported multi-informant construct validity of the scas and the scas-p, though the specific perspective of each informant introduced substantial unique variance into the scores. furthermore, the validity of specific dimensions was qualified: multi-informant convergence was limited for obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and generalized anxiety was insufficiently distinct from the remaining measures. still, findings support the scas and scas-p as useful and flexible tools for assessing adolescent anxiety as reported by the adolescent and/or their parents, supporting the assessment of anxiety-related difficulties and providing a multi-informant understanding of adolescents’ anxiety symptoms in both research and clinical contexts. behavioral sciences

linking growth mindset with student creativity: a chain mediation model as a core competency of the 21st century, creativity is of great significance to students’ academic success and lifelong development. however, there remains a lack of systematic exploration regarding the underlying psychological mechanisms through which a growth mindset influences student creativity. based on amabile’s theory of the components of creativity, this study constructs a chained mediation model to examine the mediating roles of achievement motivation and resilience in the relationship between a growth mindset and student creativity. using data from suzhou, china, in the social and emotional skills survey (sses) conducted by the organisation for economic co-operation and development (oecd), this study employed structural equation modeling to test the mediating effects. the results indicate that (1) a growth mindset is significantly positively correlated with student creativity; (2) achievement motivation mediates the relationship between a growth mindset and creativity; (3) resilience mediates the relationship between a growth mindset and creativity; and (4) achievement motivation and resilience exert a chained mediating effect between growth mindset and creativity. this study reveals the multiple psychological pathways through which a growth mindset influences student creativity, providing theoretical grounds and empirical support for enhancing student creativity in educational practice by fostering a growth mindset, stimulating achievement motivation, and strengthening resilience. behavioral sciences

three-character training of social interaction (tct-s) for children with high-functioning autism spectrum disorder: a pilot randomized controlled trial children with high-functioning autism spectrum disorder (hfasd) often experience difficulties in social interaction, which affect both their daily functioning and well-being. this study introduced a novel cbt-based intervention called the three-character training of social interaction (tct-s), which aimed to teach children with hfasd how to appropriately initiate, maintain, and end social interactions as well as understand social cues and adjust their behavior accordingly. the effectiveness of tct-s was tested through a pilot randomized controlled trial. thirty-eight children (92% boys) aged six to ten years completed the study, including 18 children in the tct-s group and 20 children in the treatment-as-usual (tau) group. the trial demonstrated preliminary feasibility, with a low overall dropout rate (2.6%). among tct-s participants, intervention completion was 100%, with high implementation fidelity (95%) and positive parental acceptability ratings. outcome variables, including social interaction skills and parenting stress, were measured before training (t1), after training (t2), and eight weeks after training (t3). the results showed that children in the tct-s group demonstrated significant improvements in social interaction skills (ηp2 = 0.093, p = 0.030) compared to the tau group. in addition, parenting stress decreased significantly in the tct-s group compared to the tau group (ηp2 = 0.166, p = 0.041). these findings provide preliminary evidence that tct-s may be a promising intervention for enhancing social interaction skills among children with hfasd. behavioral sciences

associations between psychological buffers and death anxiety in younger and older adults: the moderating role of future time perspective this study aims to examine the associations of three death anxiety buffers, close relationships, cultural worldview, and self-esteem, with death anxiety in younger and older adults and to test whether future time perspective (ftp) moderated these associations within each age group. the current study recruited 208 older adults and 506 younger adults. the results showed that among older adults, cultural worldview had greater relative predictive importance for death anxiety than attachment orientations and self-esteem. however, none of the interactions involving ftp remained statistically significant after bonferroni correction. among younger adults, attachment orientations appeared to have relatively greater predictive importance for death anxiety, and ftp moderated the relationships between attachment anxiety, self-esteem, and death anxiety. these findings are consistent with the fluid compensation model, as the relative associations between different buffers and death anxiety showed distinct patterns across age groups. behavioral sciences

digital workplace monitoring, employee autonomy, and work-related stress, depression, or anxiety in post-pandemic europe: evidence from the 2022 osh pulse survey digital technologies are increasingly used to supervise, direct, and evaluate work, yet european evidence on their psychosocial implications remains limited. this study examined how work-related stress, depression, or anxiety (wrsda) varies with the number of digital monitoring practices, how much of this association is statistically attributable to lack of autonomy, and whether it differs across countries. using 2022 osh pulse data (22,856 employed respondents, eu-27), we estimated weighted logistic regression models with country-clustered standard errors, conducted a khb decomposition, and pooled country-specific estimates using random-effects meta-analysis. the predicted probability of wrsda was 22.7% with no monitoring practices and 35.9% with all three. the association remained after adjustment for personal and work-related characteristics and was the strongest for digital supervision and third-party evaluation; interaction analyses provided no evidence that the practices reinforced one another. in the statistical decomposition, 29.0% of the association was attributable to lack of autonomy. the association was positive in 24 countries, varied moderately, and was weaker where more employees reported increasing workplace surveillance. by examining distinct monitoring practices across all eu member states, this study adds to existing evidence; however, the findings are cross-sectional, exploratory, and based on single-item measures. behavioral sciences

self-reported investment performance and loneliness among individual investors in japan this study examines the association between self-reported recent investment performance and loneliness among 158,080 individual investors in japan using the 2025 survey on life and money. loneliness was measured using three ucla loneliness items, and investment performance was classified into five self-reported categories. we estimated probit models with break-even performance as the reference category, adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, financial, and other observed characteristics, and conducted robustness and wald tests. in the fully adjusted model, slight and considerable profits were associated with 2.23- and 7.34-percentage-point lower probabilities of loneliness, respectively, relative to break-even performance. these negative associations remained statistically significant under alternative definitions of loneliness. in contrast, results for reported losses were less consistent, with considerable losses positively associated with loneliness under some alternative measures. wald tests rejected coefficient symmetry between considerable profits and considerable losses, but not between slight profits and slight losses. joint tests did not find statistically significant evidence of differences in investment-performance coefficients by gender or age group. these findings highlight an association between perceived investment outcomes and loneliness, but the cross-sectional design and self-reported measures preclude causal conclusions. behavioral sciences

psychological distress among oncology nurses and their attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help oncology nursing is emotionally demanding and may place nurses at risk of psychological distress. however, distress does not necessarily translate into willingness to seek professional psychological support. this study aimed to assess psychological distress among oncology and non-oncology nurses and examine their attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help. a cross-sectional study was conducted among 155 registered nurses at a single government hospital in riyadh. psychological distress was assessed using the 10-item kessler psychological distress scale (k10), while attitudes toward professional psychological help were measured using the attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help scale–short form (atspph-sf). descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed to compare oncology and non-oncology nurses and examine the association between psychological distress and help-seeking attitudes. overall, nurses reported moderate psychological distress, with severe distress reported by a substantial proportion of participants. the distribution of psychological distress categories did not differ between oncology and non-oncology nurses (χ2(3) = 2.01, p = 0.571). attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help were generally close to the scale midpoint. these attitudes did not differ significantly between oncology and non-oncology nurses (u = 2771.5, p = 0.434) or across psychological distress categories (χ2(3) = 4.538, p = 0.209). psychological distress is a substantial concern among nurses, across both oncology and non-oncology departments. however, no statistically significant association was identified between the level of psychological distress and attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help. healthcare organizations should implement proactive, confidential, and accessible mental health support strategies and promote a workplace culture that normalizes professional psychological help-seeking among nurses. behavioral sciences

the construction and validation of the rula wellbeing scale. inroduction: psychotherapy outcome research has traditionally emphasized symptom reduction, yet psychotherapy may also enhance eudaimonic wellbeing, including meaning, purpose, connectedness, and adaptive functioning. despite growing interest in wellbeing as a treatment outcome, few ultra-brief measures are available for routine use in psychotherapy. the present series of studies developed and evaluated the rula wellbeing scale (rws), a four-item measure designed to assess core domains of eudaimonic wellbeing relevant to clinical practice.
methods: in study 1, exploratory factor analysis was used to refine an initial 12-item pool, resulting in a unidimensional four-item solution assessing social connectedness, daily functioning, purpose, and emotion regulation. in study 2, confirmatory factor analysis in an independent non-clinical sample supported a single-factor structure, whereas a bifactor model was not supported. in both study 1 & 2, the rws demonstrated good internal consistency and expected associations with related constructs, including positive correlations with life satisfaction, flourishing, and global wellbeing, and a negative correlation with loneliness. in study 3, the single-factor structure was replicated in a clinical sample of psychotherapy clients, and the scale demonstrated acceptable internal consistency.
results: as hypothesized, the rws scores were negatively associated with depression and anxiety. mean scores were also lower in the clinical sample than in the non-clinical sample, supporting sensitivity to differences in wellbeing across populations.
discussion: collectively, findings provide initial support for the rws as a psychometrically sound, ultra-brief measure of eudaimonic wellbeing. the scale may have particular utility in psychotherapy and measurement-based care contexts where brief, practical, and conceptually meaningful assessment tools are needed. frontiers in psychology

development of a shyness scale for chinese high school students. objective: grounded in chinese indigenous culture and the psychosocial developmental characteristics of high school adolescents, this study developed and validated a culturally adapted shyness scale for chinese high school students-the high school student shyness scale (hsss). the instrument aims to provide a valid and localized psychometric tool for objective shyness assessment and empirical research on adolescent shyness.
methods: the preliminary dimensional framework and items were established through literature review, open-ended questionnaire investigation, and expert review. participants were recruited from district and county-level high schools in chongqing, china, covering both urban and rural household registration backgrounds, using a combination of cluster sampling and convenience sampling. the study was conducted in stages: an open-ended questionnaire survey was first conducted with 138 high school students to generate indigenous items; 487 valid samples were used for item analysis and exploratory factor analysis (efa) to screen items and construct the initial factor structure; an independent cohort of 427 students was administered for confirmatory factor analysis (cfa), alternative model comparisons, measurement invariance tests, multivariate generalizability theory (mgt) analysis, and systematic reliability and validity assessment; an additional 176 students completed a four-week retest to evaluate test-retest reliability; and 200 participants completed the classic cheek and buss shyness scale to examine the criterion-related validity of the newly developed scale.
results: the final 18-item hsss comprises three dimensions: withdrawal from avoidant speech and behavior, negative self-consciousness, and negative emotional experience. efa using principal axis factoring with promax rotation and parallel analysis supported a three-factor structure (kmo = 0.947; cumulative variance explained = 50.084%). cfa confirmed that the three-factor model fit well ( = 2.798, rmsea = 0.065, cfi = 0.946, tli = 0.937, gfi = 0.906, nfi = 0.919), and its fit was superior to that of the one-factor and two-factor models. the higher-order model was mathematically equivalent to the first-order three-factor model, and the bifactor model did not yield clearly interpretable specific factors. the first-order three-factor model was therefore retained as the most parsimonious and interpretable solution. full measurement invariance across gender was supported (configural, metric, scalar, and strict invariance), whereas strict invariance across grade level was partially supported. mgt analysis yielded an overall scale generalizability coefficient of 0.948 and a reliability coefficient of 0.947, indicating high measurement precision across the three dimensions. the scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency (cronbach's = 0.935) and test-retest reliability ( = 0.894). validity analyses revealed acceptable convergent validity (ave = 0.510-0.610), content validity (i-cvi ≥ 0.78; s-cvi/ave = 0.91), and criterion-related validity ( = 0.771, < 0.001).
conclusion: the hsss demonstrates acceptable psychometric properties, including evidence of structural validity, high measurement precision, and measurement invariance across gender and grade level. the core three-factor structure was broadly replicated in an independent sample, although the fit was somewhat less optimal than in the primary sample. as a standardized and reliable psychometric instrument, it is suitable for quantitative shyness assessment and related empirical research among chinese high school populations. frontiers in psychology

patterns of attentional and recognition-memory processing of emotional information among chinese middle school students with different exercise volumes. background: physical exercise is closely associated with adolescent mental health, yet emotional information processing among adolescents with different exercise volumes remains insufficiently understood. this study examined attentional and recognition-memory processing of positive and negative emotional information among middle school students with different exercise volumes.
methods: using convenience sampling, 300 copies of a modified 3-month-recall version of the physical activity rating scale-3 (pars-3) were distributed at a middle school, yielding 291 valid questionnaires. in a cross-sectional extreme-group design, 60 students (30 per group) were recruited from the extreme ends of the high- and low-exercise-volume categories to complete the behavioral experiment. task 1 used a dot-probe task to examine reaction time, probe congruency, and vigilance and disengagement/avoidance indices in response to positive and negative emotional pictures. task 2 used a learning-recognition task to examine recognition accuracy, recognition sensitivity (d'), and response criterion (c) for positive and negative faces.
results: in the dot-probe task, the group × valence interaction was significant, and the low-exercise-volume group responded faster to negative than to positive pictures. the group × valence interaction for the attentional disengagement/avoidance index was also significant, with the low-exercise-volume group showing a larger positive-picture disengagement/avoidance index, a pattern consistent with greater difficulty disengaging attention from positive pictures. in the learning-recognition task, group × valence interactions were significant for both d' and recognition accuracy, whereas the corresponding interaction for c was not significant. the low-exercise-volume group showed lower d' for positive than for negative faces, and its d' for positive faces was lower than that of the high-exercise-volume group; the accuracy analysis showed a corresponding within-group valence difference.
conclusions: middle school students with different exercise volumes showed different valence-related patterns of emotional information processing, primarily in overall reaction time, the derived disengagement/avoidance index, and recognition sensitivity. overall, exercise volume was associated with emotional information processing in adolescents. because the behavioral sample was recruited from the extreme ends of the screening distribution, the observed group differences and effect sizes characterize selected extreme-group contrasts; they are not population-level estimates for typical high- versus low-exercise-volume adolescents. longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to examine causal relationships. bmc psychology

gender minority stress and resilience factors associated with persistent depressive symptoms among transgender and gender diverse adolescents and young adults accessing gender-affirming medical care. while many transgender and gender diverse (tgd) youth experience improved mental health after initiating gender-affirming hormone therapy (gaht), some continue to experience persistent depressive (pd) symptoms. we examined associations of risk factors (e.g., negative expectations for the future, internalized transphobia) and protective factors (e.g. self-efficacy) for pd among tgd youth accessing gaht. we used data from the trans youth care u.s. study, a national longitudinal prospective cohort study of tgd youth ages 12-20 years (n=315 at baseline). experiencing pd, gender minority stress, resilience, and other factors were assessed at four timepoints (baseline, 6, 12, 18, and 24-months). after identifying two groups based on reported pd, we estimated differences at baseline and change over time of risk and protective factors using linear mixed-effects models. we also examined the association between these rates and experiencing pd using logistic regression. two groups of pd youth (n=62) and non-pd youth (non-pd; n=253) were identified. greater negative expectation at baseline was associated with increased odds of pd, while the opposite was observed for greater self-efficacy. increased rate of change in body esteem was associated with decreased odds of pd. there was an interaction effect between negative expectation and self-efficacy. while self-efficacy was a protective factor, this effect lost its strength as perceived negative expectation increased. these findings identify important areas of assessment and intervention for tgd youth who experience pd despite accessing gaht. addressing these factors in treatment appears vital to ensuring adequate treatment for pd. psychology of sexual orientation and gender diversity

the effects of choice over external-focus instructional cues on countermovement jump performance: an exploratory study this exploratory study investigated whether providing autonomy support through choice over externally focused attentional cues would influence countermovement jump (cmj) performance, as predicted by the optimal theory. sixty young adults performed four cmjs under either a choice condition, in which participants selected one of four external focus instructions before each jump, or a yoked condition without choice. although participants in the choice group reported significantly greater perceived autonomy over instruction choice, autonomy support did not improve jump height. differences in jump height were observed between external focus instructions, suggesting that the semantic and linguistic properties of instructional cues may influence performance. however, manipulation check data indicated that participants did not consistently reproduce the specific linguistic features of the cues, instead frequently omitting or substituting elements such as action words and spatial references. these findings suggest that performance differences are unlikely to reflect the isolated effects of specific linguistic components, but rather how cues are interpreted and integrated by performers. no interaction between autonomy support and external focus was observed. overall, autonomy support enhanced perceived autonomy but did not improve immediate performance, and the effectiveness of instructional cues may depend on how performers represent task goals. these findings should be interpreted as exploratory and hypothesis-generating. perceptual and motor skills

longitudinal associations between adverse childhood experiences and moderate-risk to problem gambling in young adulthood: a prospective uk cohort study. previous research links adverse childhood experiences (aces) with problem gambling, but most studies rely on retrospective reporting and focus narrowly on maltreatment, overlooking adversities such as parental mental health issues. using data on 3794 young adults in the avon longitudinal study of parents and children, we examined longitudinal associations between 10 prospectively measured aces (individually and cumulatively), and being at least at moderate-risk of problem gambling (problem gambling severity index ≥ 3) at ages 17, 20 and 24, adjusted for socioeconomic and other background factors. population attributable fractions (pafs) estimated proportions of cases potentially attributable to aces. most aces were associated with higher odds of moderate-risk/problem gambling across ages (25/30 estimates) after adjustment, though effect sizes were generally small (median adjusted odds ratio [aor] 1.37, interquartile range 1.19-1.45), and confidence intervals (cis) wide. sexual abuse showed the strongest association (aors 1.8-2.8, cis 0.6-6.0), while bullying and parental conviction were associated at ages 17 and 20 only, parental separation age 24 only. evidence for a dose-response relationship was weak. pafs suggested aces accounted for up to 11% of moderate-risk/problem gambling cases. these findings highlight potential impacts of aces on later gambling behaviour, but imprecise estimates suggest findings should be interpreted cautiously and strengthened through larger sample sizes and meta-analyses. addictive behaviors reports

the development of creative imagination and symbolic thinking through thematic social role-play activity. grounded in vygotsky's cultural-historical paradigm, this article presents a theoretical analysis of the role of thematic social role-play in preschool psychological development, positioning it not merely as a recreational activity but as the leading activity driving psychological maturation. within this framework, we examine how high-level play serves as the critical foundation for the genesis of creative imagination and symbolic thought-all essential components of the developing child's psychological neoformations. specifically, we analyze the trajectory of adult-guided orientation, illustrating its necessity in transforming initial, fragmented play behaviors into advanced, mature role-play characterized by reflective initiative, internal rules, and symbolic verbal actions. furthermore, we delineate the transition from object-substituted actions to deep psychological internalization. based on this theoretical synthesis, we hypothesize that a child's readiness for formal school learning is a direct function of the semiotic and structural complexity of their thematic social role-play. we propose that the more intentional, collaborative, and creative the play behavior, the stronger the cognitive, volitional, and social foundations for subsequent academic success. finally, we argue for an educational shift that prioritizes structured, high-level thematic social role-play not as a leisure choice, but as a core, non-negotiable developmental necessity in early childhood education. frontiers in psychology

inclusive leadership and voice behavior among early-career nurses: the conditional roles of work meaningfulness and proactive personality. introduction: safety-focused explanations of nurse voice leave open whether the perceived value of work is associated with speaking up differently across proactive personality. drawing on social information processing theory and an interactionist perspective informed by trait activation theory, we examined this conditional association among early-career nurses.
methods: a cross-sectional survey of 464 nurses in five tertiary hospitals in harbin, china, assessed inclusive leadership, work meaningfulness, constructive voice, and proactive personality. item-level confirmatory factor analysis and composite-score conditional process analysis were conducted.
results: inclusive leadership was positively associated with meaningfulness and voice. the conditional indirect association through meaningfulness was positive at mean proactive personality (0.2502, 95% bootstrap ci [0.1857, 0.3197]) and increased with personality (index = 0.0744, 95% ci [0.0269, 0.1229]). the interaction added 1.29 percentage points of explained voice variance, indicating modest amplification; the personality-voice zero-order correlation was near zero.
discussion: the findings provide context-specific evidence for a conditional value-of-work account alongside safety-based explanations, without establishing causality or superiority over alternative pathways. inviting suggestions and communicating the value of nursing contributions are practices worth evaluating. the data concern constructive voice, not demonstrated improvements in patient safety, and require longitudinal, multisource replication. frontiers in psychology

temporal dynamics of moral semantic processing in chinese: an erp study of word categorization morality serves as a universal code of behavior and a foundation for social value systems. to investigate the cognitive architecture of moral information processing, the present study adopted event-related potentials (erps). we used chinese moral words as stimuli to characterize the temporal neural dynamics of moral processing. fifty-four participants completed a one-way repeated-measures lexical categorization task with four conditions (moral, immoral, neutral, and pseudowords), including response mapping as a between-subjects factor. behavioral responses and electroencephalography (eeg) activity were recorded simultaneously. behavioral analyses yielded robust response latency disparities: participants categorized moral words most rapidly, followed by neutral words and immoral words; pseudowords elicited the slowest responses. erp analyses revealed graded neural signatures across stimulus categories. during the p2 window (150–250 ms), immoral words elicited the largest amplitudes. at the n3 component (250–350 ms), real words showed attenuated negativity compared with pseudowords, and moral words also differed from neutral words, suggesting that n3 reflects lexical-semantic categorization with additional moral-relevance effects. at the lpp (400–800 ms), immoral words evoked the largest responses, significantly larger than those for neutral and pseudowords, whereas the moral–immoral contrast was not significant. collectively, these results are consistent with an affective-moral salience account: moral words show a behavioral recognition advantage, and immoral words elicit heightened early and late neurocognitive sensitivity. the findings highlight the utility of erp analysis for mapping moral semantic processing within the logographic chinese writing system, and may inform future cross-cultural neurocognitive research and semantic decoding in brain–computer interface paradigms. behavioral sciences

digital mindfulness and digital well-being among university students: the mediating role of fear of missing out background. digital mindfulness and fear of missing out (fomo) may help explain how university students experience their digital lives. this study examined whether fomo statistically accounted for the association between digital mindfulness and perceived digital well-being (pdw). methods. a cross-sectional online survey included 477 undergraduate students from three universities in riyadh, saudi arabia. structural equation modeling examined direct and indirect associations with a latent pdw factor indicated by emotional, social, and cognitive domain scores. results. greater digital mindfulness was associated with lower fomo, which was associated with more favorable pdw. the positive indirect association through fomo was substantial (β = 0.371, 95% bias-corrected bootstrap ci [0.310, 0.437]) and remained significant after correction for measurement error. the direct association was small and was not robust to this correction. the model accounted for 52.7% of the variance in latent pdw. conclusions. lower fomo was the main statistical pathway linking mindful digital engagement with better pdw. these findings suggest that student-support initiatives could examine awareness of checking urges and more intentional digital engagement as potential intervention targets. longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to establish temporal ordering and evaluate whether such approaches improve digital well-being. behavioral sciences

physical activity, physical fitness, and grade point average in tertiary students: a meta‐analysis abstract we conducted a meta‐analysis of correlations between physical activity, physical fitness, and academic performance among tertiary students. results with 96 samples showed a great degree of heterogeneity, with credibility intervals being consistent with both a strong negative and strong positive association for many predictor and outcome measures. thus, there was a great degree of uncertainty in our effect size estimates, and we conclude that much further research is needed on this topic. nevertheless, we found a small positive association ( ρ = 0.03, k = 69, n = 91,003) between physical activity frequency and grade point average (gpa). the association was slightly stronger when the predictor was physical fitness rather than physical activity frequency ( ρ = 0.16, k = 13, n = 15,358), when gpa was obtained from institutional records ( ρ = 0.11, k = 15, n = 5414), and when physical activity frequency was captured objectively ( ρ = 0.20, k = 4, n = 6888), although such moderator analyses were based on a limited number of studies. only the physical fitness–gpa correlation showed credibility intervals suggesting the correlation was positive in most cases. we could not confirm the presence of publication bias. applied psychology-health and well being

objectified appearance consciousness scale: preliminary psychometrics and racial/ethnic and sexual identity group invariance this study provided preliminary support for the objectified appearance consciousness scale (oacs) as an extension of the objectified body consciousness scale to assess body surveillance and body shame. new oacs items were generated to improve psychometrics and include additional physical features reflecting white heteronormative beauty standards (e.g., hair, skin, and facial features). survey data were analyzed from 918 women residing in the united states, recruited from prolific, and diverse in racial/ethnic and sexual identity. exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor structure comprising body surveillance related to overall appearance, body shape and size, and other physical features (6 items); body shape shame focused on body shape, size, and weight (3 items); and body features shame focused on hair, skin, and facial features (3 items). scalar invariance was supported across four racial/ethnic identity groups (african/african american/black, asian/asian american, caucasian/european american/white, and latina/o/x/hispanic american) and two sexual identity groups (heterosexual and sexual minority). cronbach's alphas were strong. all three subscales correlated positively with and accounted for unique variance in internalized sociocultural beauty standards, eating disorder symptoms, and psychological distress. results support using oacs subscale scores to model an overall objectified appearance consciousness latent variable or its three separate constructs. psychology of women quarterly

“what am i really doing with my own brain?”: college students on learning, ownership, and ai generative artificial intelligence gives college students new ways to support their learning, while also raising questions about what they still want to learn and do for themselves. this qualitative study draws on semi-structured interviews with 14 undergraduates at a northeastern liberal arts college to examine how students distinguish between ai use that supports their own thinking and ai use that substitutes for it, what they believe is worth doing on their own, and whether and how purpose enters their reasoning about learning and ai use. using the framework method with a cross-case matrix to compare patterns across participants and topics, we found that students repeatedly drew a line between using ai as a supportive tool and letting it take the place of their own thinking or authorship. students most often talked about wanting to keep developing their own skills, thinking independently, and knowing what they could actually do without ai. they also wanted the work to still feel “like theirs,” citing ownership, pride, authenticity, and ethical concerns. students also described pressures that made ai appealing, including heavy workloads, deadlines, grades, convenience, and concerns about falling behind their peers. although few participants explicitly connected their ai choices to a stated purpose, many described concerns that may be relevant to purpose development, including developing valued skills and strengths, acting on personal values, and becoming the kind of person they hoped to be. we consider these concerns through a purpose-mindset framework while distinguishing our interpretation from participants’ own explanations of their ai choices. the findings suggest that understanding students’ ai use requires attention to what they believe they need to learn and do for themselves. journal of intelligence

effects of brief breathwork under a state of cognitive fatigue on subjective well‐being and diaphragm function: a randomized crossover design abstract previous investigations have identified the effectiveness of breathwork on both psychological and physical health for individuals under a resting state. however, there was no study investigating the effects of breathwork under a mentally‐fatigued state. the purpose of this study was to examine the acute effects of breathwork administered after the induction of mental fatigue by a cognitive tasks on primary self‐reported outcomes including positive and negative affect and self‐reported stress indices, as well as on secondary physiological outcomes including diaphragm function and stress‐related physiological responses. this study was employed with a randomized cross‐over study design. twenty healthy university students voluntarily participated in this study. each of them performed a 20‐min breathwork and control (quiet bed rest) condition following the colour‐word stroop task (cwst) in a randomized sequence over two days separated at least by a week. participants completed self‐reported questionnaires for positive and negative affect and stress indices and underwent ultrasonographic assessments of the diaphragm function, saliva collection for cortisol and iga, and heart rate variability assessments at baseline, pre‐cwst, post‐cwst, and post‐intervention. the breathwork condition demonstrated significantly higher positive affect at post‐intervention compared to the control condition ( p = 0.021). right hemidiaphragm excursion and left hemidiaphragm thickness at end‐inspiration significantly increased from post‐cwst to post‐intervention in the breathwork condition. the breathwork condition appeared to improve positive affect and diaphragm function even under a mentally‐fatigued state, compared to the control condition. these findings indicate that breathwork may serve as a simple, accessible, and practical strategy to enhance subjective well‐being in a stressful environment and diaphragm function regardless of mental fatigue. stress and health

intentions to help friends across cultural groups: the role of emotional connectedness across five studies ( n = 1,859), we examined cross-cultural variation in emotional connectedness and intentions to help a family member, a friend, and a stranger. samples included a nationally representative dutch panel (study 1), turkish and dutch students (study 2), turkish and german working adults (study 3), culturally primed turkish-german biculturals (study 4), and bilingual turkish students (study 5). contrary to the traditional view that collectivists prioritize in-group ties more strongly than individualists, we hypothesized greater intentions to help friends among participants from relatively individualistic contexts or primed with an individualistic cultural frame. results consistently supported the hypothesized differences for intentions to help friends, while differences in intentions to help a family member and a stranger were less consistent and generally not reliable. study 1 further suggested that emotional connectedness statistically accounted for group differences in intentions to help friends, and study 5 provided tentative converging evidence that an english-language prime was associated with greater connectedness with friends than a turkish-language prime. together, these findings suggest that considering the role of particular relational targets within their cultural context may provide a more differentiated account of cross-cultural variation in helping than broad individualism–collectivism or in-group–out-group classifications alone. journal of cross-cultural psychology

parents have smaller support networks but more close-knit relationships than childfree and other non-parent adults declining fertility rates and growing numbers of adults forgoing parenthood highlight the need to understand how social integration differs across reproductive status groups. yet most research treats non-parents as a homogeneous group, overlooking differences among the childfree, childless, undecided, ambivalent and not-yet-parents. using an egocentric network approach, we examined structural and quality-related characteristics of support networks across six reproductive status groups ( n = 797; aged 18–86 years; 62% based in the united kingdom/united states). parents had smaller support networks but more close-knit relationships, suggesting a quality-quantity trade-off. childfree adults showed relatively stable network sizes across age, while not-yet-parents and undecided participants’ networks more closely resembled parents. age-related patterns hint at midlife as a dynamic period of network change. our findings highlight the importance of distinguishing between non-parent groups, with implications for social ageing, wellbeing and support interventions, while discrepancies with prior studies raise questions about possible methodological artefacts in network elicitation. social psychological and personality science

depoliticizing language improves attitudes toward diversity training political debates about diversity, equity, and inclusion (dei) and internal workplace communication about dei tend to use a common language. we examine whether decoupling workplace dei terminology from that used in the political sphere might improve attitudes toward diversity training. across three experiments and two supplemental studies (total n = 3,209) sampling employed democrats and republicans, replacing common dei terminology (e.g., “diversity”) with carefully matched alternative terminology (e.g., “differences”) in initial framings of diversity training increased republicans’ pre- and post-training enthusiasm. we identify a mechanism underlying this effect: alternative framing reduced republicans’ perceptions of the training’s political bias. critically, republicans’ expectations about whether the training would facilitate typical diversity-training goals did not differ by framing, and effects persisted when training content was held constant and only framing varied. these findings suggest that separating training content from politically coded dei language can improve attitudes toward diversity training. social psychological and personality science

head nodding and hand coordination across dyads in different conversational contexts abstract this paper aims to explore what different patterns of head nodding and hand movement coordination mean in conversation by recording and analysing interpersonal coordination as it naturally occurs in social interactions. understanding the timing and at which frequencies such movement behaviours occur can help us answer how and why we use these signals. here we use high-resolution motion capture to examine three different types of two-person conversation involving different types of information-sharing, in order to explore the potential meaning and coordination of head nodding and hand motion signals. we also test if the tendency to engage in fast or slow nodding behaviour is a fixed personality trait that differs between individuals. our results show coordinated slow nodding only in a picture-description task, which implies that this behaviour is not a universal signal of affiliation but is context driven. we also find robust fast nodding behaviour in the two contexts where novel information is exchanged. for hand movement, we found a non-significant trend toward low-frequency coordination during two-way information sharing in the meal planning task, but no effects survived correction for multiple comparisons. finally, nodding varied across contexts, and our exploratory analyses did not provide evidence that it indexes stable individual differences in social traits. we interpret these results in terms of theories of nonverbal communication and consider how these methods will help advance automated analyses of human conversation behaviours. journal of nonverbal behavior

the school psychologist shortage: a qualitative examination of doctoral‐level school psychologists' perspectives on employment in public schools abstract nationally, there is a shortage of school psychologists in public schools, and few practicing school psychologists hold doctoral degrees. this shortage puts an undue burden on practitioners and has implications for the quality of care provided to students. the current study explores the career choices of doctoral‐level school psychologists to better understand the national shortage as well as understand the benefits of pursuing a doctorate in school psychology. sixty‐two doctoral‐level school psychologists completed an online survey in which they described their career paths and the factors influencing them. thematic analysis of the qualitative data identified eight key themes shaping these trajectories: pay/compensation; lack of support/respect; politics; workload; stress and burnout; underutilization of skills; lack of autonomy; and external factors. additionally, a binomial logistic regression indicated that participants’ year of certification and years of experience predicted whether participants left a career as a school psychologist working in a school system. the current study provides a detailed understanding of what leads doctoral‐level practitioners to remain in or leave school employment and can be used to help recruit and retain doctoral‐level school psychologists, potentially shrinking the shortage. psychology in the schools

the efficacy of virtual reality for social skills in children with autism spectrum disorder: an umbrella systematic review introduction autism spectrum disorder (asd) is characterized by persistent difficulties in social communication and interaction. virtual reality (vr) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting social skill development in children with asd. this umbrella review synthesizes evidence from existing systematic reviews to evaluate the effectiveness of vr‐based interventions in improving social functioning among children aged 3–15 years. methods this review followed the joanna briggs institute (jbi) methodology for umbrella reviews and adhered to prisma 2020 guidelines. a comprehensive search was conducted in pubmed, scopus, and web of science. the methodological quality of the included reviews was assessed using the jbi critical appraisal checklist. six systematic reviews met the eligibility criteria. results vr‐based interventions were associated with improvements across three key social skill domains in children and adolescents with asd: social interaction (e.g., turn‐taking and joint attention), communication skills (e.g., verbal and nonverbal expression), and social understanding (e.g., emotion recognition and perspective‐taking). overall, the strength of the evidence was moderate, largely due to heterogeneity in study quality, intervention characteristics, and outcome measures across the included reviews. although findings were generally positive, variability in methodologies and reporting limits the ability to draw firm conclusions. therefore, vr may be considered a potentially supportive approach for social skills training; however, further standardization of outcome measures is required before clinical recommendations can be made. conclusion vr‐based interventions show promise for improving social skills in children with asd; however, the current evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, primarily based on systematic reviews of varying methodological quality. future research should prioritize long‐term follow‐up, real‐world generalization, and the development of standardized intervention protocols and outcome measures to strengthen the evidence base and support clinical translation. human behavior and emerging technologies

attrition in autism research for challenging behavior: a preliminary investigation into parental stress and other predictors related to project completion the increasing prevalence of autism spectrum disorder (asd) in the united states has elevated the need for inclusive and representative intervention research. however, attrition within research initiatives that include autistic individuals who engage in challenging behavior remains understudied. this study examined predictors of study completion across three levels of engagement: consent only (full attrition), treatment only (partial attrition), and full study completion (no attrition). participants included 182 caregiver-child dyads enrolled in a multi-component study involving a behavior-analytic treatment and a severity tool research portion. using retrospective data and ordinal logistic regression, we explored whether participant challenging behavior topographies, demographics, and parental stress predicted study completion type. results indicated that child elopement and higher parental stress scores marginally predicted full study completion after a bonferroni adjustment, while demographic variables were not significant predictors. these findings may suggest that caregiver urgency regarding specific challenging behaviors and higher perceived stress may increase research engagement. routine examination of attrition patterns within multi-component intervention studies may support more equitable and representative participation in autism treatment research. behavior modification

making the body fit the machine: women's embodied and relational experiences of mammography mammography is central to early breast cancer detection, yet its embodied and affective dimensions remain underexamined. this study explored how women experience mammography as a sociomaterial encounter between body, machine, and clinical practice. seventeen women in israel who had undergone a mammography examination within the previous year participated in open-ended, experience-focused qualitative interviews guided by eight broad questions. the data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. three interrelated themes were developed. making the body fit the machine captured uneven discomfort arising from whole-body positioning, compression, bodily variability, and technologist-mediated adjustments. making the breast visible, making the woman recede described how diagnostic isolation could produce fragmentation, exposure, and relational vulnerability, although not all participants experienced objectification. endurance without endorsement showed that participants strongly affirmed mammography while simultaneously questioning its current embodied form and proposing improvements grounded in experiential knowledge. the findings conceptualize mammography discomfort not as a uniform response or merely a barrier to attendance, but as an outcome of a technologically and relationally structured interface. continued participation should not be interpreted as satisfaction with existing design. attending to women's embodied design knowledge may help improve comfort, dignity, and accessibility without diminishing the clinical importance of mammography in breast cancer detection. feminism & psychology

association between stigma and positive mental well-being among patients with diabetes: the mediating role of psychological distress background: diabetes can significantly impact patients’ positive mental well-being (pmwb). objective: this study aims to investigate the stigma, psychological distress, and pmwb of patients with diabetes, and explore the mediating role of psychological distress in the relationship between stigma and pmwb. methods: a multi-stage stratified random sampling method was used to randomly select 660 patients with diabetes from the central and western regions of shandong province, china. path analysis was used to examine the mediating role of psychological distress in the relationship between stigma and pmwb in patients with diabetes. results: the mean value of pmwb was 71.72 ± 18.70. the direct effect value of stigma on pmwb was −0.173, accounting for 55.42% of the total effect. the indirect effect value of stigma on pmwb through psychological distress was −0.139, accounting for 44.58%. conclusion: stigma not only directly impacts pmwb but also indirectly through its detrimental effect on psychological distress. therefore, it is necessary to address stigma and reduce psychological distress to enhance the pmwb of patients with diabetes. health psychology research

parkinson’s and alzheimer’s disease impairs temporal precision abstract several studies have reported temporal processing deficits in neurodegenerative diseases such as parkinson’s and alzheimer’s disease. these deficits can be quantified by interval timing paradigms that require participants to estimate or produce an interval of several seconds and require working memory for temporal rules as well as attention to time. timing performance can be quantified by a variety of measures; however, two relatively universal metrics include: (1) temporal accuracy, defined as the mean temporal estimate and (2) temporal precision, reflected by the variability of temporal estimates. we examined temporal accuracy and precision in a meta-analysis of 14 studies in patients with parkinson’s disease and 10 studies in patients with alzheimer’s disease. it is striking that, in both diseases, temporal precision was reliably impaired across studies, whereas temporal accuracy was affected in alzheimer’s but not parkinson’s disease. our meta-analysis suggests that despite the diversity of interval timing paradigms and the complexity of parkinson’s and alzheimer’s disease, temporal precision is consistently impaired in these diseases. these results advance interval timing as a reliable assay to study cognitive dysfunction in parkinson’s and alzheimer’s disease and may extend to other neurological and psychiatric disorders. perspectives on behavior science

shape of snarc: how task-dependent are spatial-numerical associations? a highly powered online experiment spatial-numerical associations are fundamental to numerical cognition. the spatial-numerical association of response codes (snarc) effect denotes faster responses to small/large numbers with the left/right, respectively (dehaene et al., 1993). it is typically measured in magnitude classification (mc: smaller vs. larger than 5) or parity judgment (pj: odd vs. even) with numbers 1–9 (excluding 5). these tasks differ in magnitude and parity processing, compatibility effects, and other aspects. in this highly powered online experiment, data from 611 participants in a within-subjects design demonstrated a rather categorical mc-snarc (i.e., similar left-hand advantage for 1–4, and similar right-hand advantage for 6–9) and a continuous pj-snarc (i.e., right-hand advantage increasing with magnitude). accordingly, the pj-snarc can be modeled using linear regression, while the mc-snarc requires a categorical or mixed analysis. explained variance and split-half reliability were higher for the mc-snarc than for the pj-snarc. we replicated the numerical size effect (slower responses for larger numbers; brysbaert, 1995) in mc and pj, the numerical distance effect (faster responses for larger numerical distance between stimulus and reference; moyer & landauer, 1967) in mc, and the odd effect in pj (faster responses to even numbers; hines, 1990; potentially masked by the numerical distance effect in mc), but not the marc effect (faster responses to odd/even with the left/right, respectively; nuerk et al., 2004). the mc-snarc and pj-snarc correlated slightly positively (r = 0.17), suggesting partly common underlying magnitude representations. altogether, the snarc effect appears highly task-dependent and should be modeled differently depending on the task. collabra-psychology

maternal mental health remains a missing priority nature mental health, published online: 22 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00752-z maternal mental health remains largely underfunded and understudied. drawing on evidence across species, this comment calls for greater investment in perinatal stress research, equitable funding, expanded data collection and cross-species approaches to better understand how stress during this critical period affects women’s lifelong health. nature mental health

voices of resilience: an interpretative phenomenological analysis of female african and caribbean adult survivors of child sexual abuse ( csa ) in england and wales abstract background child sexual abuse (csa) remains a significant public health and social justice concern, yet the experiences of survivors from racially minoritised communities in the united kingdom remain underrepresented in research. african and caribbean women may face additional barriers to disclosure and support due to cultural stigma, honour‐based expectations, racialised stereotypes and systemic inequities within statutory services. aims this study explored the lived experiences of african and caribbean female adult survivors of csa in england and wales, with particular attention to their interactions with statutory services and the sociocultural factors influencing disclosure, help‐seeking and meaning‐making. the research sought to understand how survivors interpret and navigate cultural, racial and institutional barriers throughout their recovery journeys. materials and methods a qualitative research design using interpretative phenomenological analysis (ipa) was employed. four african and caribbean female adult survivors of csa participated in semi‐structured interviews lasting approximately 60–75 min. interviews generated rich, idiographic accounts of trauma, resilience and identity. asian survivors were also sought during recruitment; however, none came forward, which emerged as a noteworthy finding in itself. data were analysed following ipa principles to identify shared and divergent aspects of participants' experiences. results analysis identified five superordinate themes: (1) cultural silence, honour and early meaning‐making; (2) intersectionality and the burden of stereotypes; (3) systemic barriers and retraumatisation within statutory services; (4) between silence and sanctuary: gaps in support services; and (5) “i rise”: resilience, agency and post‐traumatic growth. participants described prolonged delays, inadequate communication and repeated recounting of abuse within statutory systems, experiences that often mirrored earlier feelings of powerlessness and retraumatisation. despite these challenges, survivors demonstrated considerable resilience and highlighted the value of culturally attuned therapeutic support and community understanding. discussion the findings illustrate how cultural narratives, intersectional identities and systemic inequities shape survivors' experiences of disclosure, engagement with services and recovery. the absence of asian participants may also reflect particular cultural barriers to participation and disclosure that warrant further investigation. the study highlights the ongoing impact of institutional responses on survivor well‐being and underscores the importance of culturally responsive and trauma‐informed approaches across support services. conclusion this study contributes to the limited literature on csa among racially minoritised communities in the united kingdom. findings emphasise the need for trauma‐informed, culturally responsive practice within counselling, social care and justice settings. by centring survivors' voices, the research recognises their resilience while offering important insights for improving professional practice, reducing systemic barriers and promoting meaningful change for future survivors. counselling & psychotherapy research

‘it's not something you are meant to have’: exploring young men's anxiety. a small‐scale pilot reflexive thematic analysis of one uk focus group abstract young men's experiences of anxiety remain underexplored within mental health research, despite evidence that a substantial proportion report elevated distress. recent national data indicate that around 30% of men experience heightened anxiety, yet studies focusing exclusively on young men are scarce. this pilot study addresses this by exploring how young men describe anxiety in everyday life and how distress becomes identifiable and expressible in their social contexts. methods an online focus group was conducted with five young men aged 19–24, recruited through a uk young advisor network. a semi‐structured interview schedule guided the discussion, and reflexive thematic analysis (rta) interpreted shared meanings in the data. the study took place during a period of heightened population anxiety following the covid‐19 pandemic, which formed part of the wider context for participants' accounts. findings three interconnected themes were developed. silencing men's anxiety describes how stigma, gendered expectations and anticipated judgement discouraged acknowledgement and disclosure. literacy gaps for anxiety describe limited shared vocabulary and uncertainty about recognising or explaining distress. stigma and barriers to help‐seeking describe experiences of dismissal, misrecognition and unclear support routes that made anxiety less visible and harder to communicate. conclusion participants reported internalised shame, misrecognition and insufficient support from families and professionals. the findings suggest that counsellors, psychotherapists and youth mental health practitioners may need to attend to indirect anxiety, gendered shame and young men's everyday distress language. improved emotional literacy within families, educational settings and services may support earlier recognition. as a small pilot study, this work offers initial insight into young men's accounts of anxiety and highlights the value of further research with more diverse samples. counselling & psychotherapy viewpoint on multisensory decision-making abstract this viewpoint interview features adele diederich, thomas otto and cesare parise discussing multisensory decision-making from the perspectives of mathematical psychology, psychophysics, and computational modelling. they reflect on both current theories and their personal paths into the field, including key influences and scientific traditions that shaped their thinking. the conversation revisits major developments in multisensory research, from early work on intersensory facilitation and redundant-signals paradigms to later advances in race models, diffusion models, bayesian approaches, and more recent stimulus-computable mechanistic accounts. the authors highlight how these frameworks have shaped the field, ongoing controversies, and emerging trends. a shared theme is the need for conceptual clarity, rigorous methods, and integration across behavioural, neural and computational levels, alongside support for open-science practices. at the same time, differences remain in the emphasis placed on various modelling approaches, for example, in the relative weight given to race models, dynamic decision models, optimal frameworks, and mechanistic accounts of multisensory processing. overall, the interview presents multisensory decision-making as a dynamic and evolving field, whose future will depend on both new tools and continued critical evaluation of its theories and methods. multisensory research

exploring the supply–demand perception gap in team coaching: a multistakeholder qualitative study this study explores the supply–demand perception dynamics in team coaching, contrasting client expectations with practitioner delivery. through qualitative analysis of 25 semistructured interviews using a dual manual and large language model approach, the research uncovers significant perception gaps. key findings include a divergence in defining team coaching success—transactional resolution versus developmental transformation, and a conflict between “pedigree” and “presence” as markers of coach impact. results further identify cultural agility and “continuous contracting” as critical success factors. the research concludes with practical implications and questions for further research. international journal of evidence based coaching & mentoring
