connectome-wide dysconnectivity signature tracks clinical status in major depressive disorder nature mental health, published online: 21 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00747-w using polyconnectomic scores in japanese and german cohorts, the authors demonstrate that a whole-brain functional connectivity pattern in depression generalizes across diverse populations, distinguishing individuals with depression from healthy controls and correlates with symptom severity, particularly anhedonia. nature mental health

refining a new movement by practicing it upside down nature human behaviour, published online: 21 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s41562-026-02614-1 in this study, participants improved at copying an unfamiliar alphabet character even though they only practiced writing rotated versions of it. the experiments reveal that the motor system can refine movements by creating an abstraction of their structure, and not only by repeating the same mechanical muscle commands. nature human behaviour

psychosocial bouldering with refugee and host‐community adolescents in lebanon: a qualitative study abstract background adolescents in lebanon, particularly those affected by displacement, live under challenging conditions shaped by conflict, poverty, uncertainty and disruptions to everyday life. against this backdrop, climbaid developed youclimb, a psychosocial bouldering intervention for adolescents from refugee and host communities. an earlier quantitative study demonstrated significant improvements in well‐being and reductions in psychological distress among participants. building on these findings, the present qualitative study explored participants' life circumstances as context for their engagement with the intervention, perceived mechanisms of psychosocial change and the transfer of programme‐related learning to everyday life. methods youclimb is a group‐based, 8‐week programme integrating principles of bouldering therapy and experiential education. thirty‐eight semi‐structured interviews were conducted with adolescents from syria, palestine and lebanon residing in central bekaa. data were analysed with qualitative content analysis. results the availability of social support emerged as a key theme of participants' life circumstances, acting as either a resource or a vulnerability. three mechanisms of change were identified: bouldering as a source of well‐being, social connection in a safe space and the development of problem‐solving and coping strategies. participants reported multiple transfer effects, indicating that learning experiences at youclimb generalised to enhance their abilities to navigate everyday challenges. discussion youclimb offered a safe and engaging psychosocial space for fostering both individual and relational growth. as a low‐threshold intervention, structured bouldering programmes may reach adolescents with limited access to mental health and psychosocial support (mhpss), highlighting a promising pathway for sports‐based mental health interventions in settings affected by displacement and protracted crisis. trial registration all procedures were approved by the antonine university baabda ethics committee (approval number: 279‐2022) in february 2022, and the study was registered prospectively in april 2022 (isrctn13005983) counselling & psychotherapy research

‘i realised i have to do it myself’: experiences of clients with personality disorders in a compassion‐based positive psychology group intervention abstract objective effective treatment of personality disorders (pds) should target not only symptom reduction but also the enhancement of mental well‐being. compassion‐based positive psychology group intervention (cb‐ppgi) has shown promising effects in other clinical populations, yet little is known about how individuals with pds experience this intervention. this qualitative study explored participants' motivations for engaging in cb‐ppgi, experienced benefits, perceived mechanisms of change and facilitators and barriers to intervention success. methods semi‐structured interviews were conducted with 16 participants (12 completers, 4 non‐completers) who received cb‐ppgi while awaiting specialised treatment for pds. data were analysed using reflexive content analysis. results participants were motivated by a desire to restore daily functioning, balance and self‐control. experienced benefits included a more positive outlook, greater emotional awareness, increased self‐kindness, stronger personal agency, a greater sense of shared humanity, improved balance between activity and rest and reduced stress. perceived mechanisms of change included group connection, a strengths‐based focus, experiential learning, acceptance and self‐compassion, emotional depth without pressure and a sense of safety fostered by therapist presence. facilitators and barriers to intervention success included readiness for change, timing, motivation, group composition, trust, resilience and cognitive resources. conclusion participants experienced cb‐ppgi as supportive in strengthening agency, emotional awareness, self‐kindness and mental well‐being. these findings suggest that cb‐ppgi may complement established pd treatments by fostering recovery‐oriented and well‐being‐related processes alongside symptom‐focused therapeutic goals. counselling & psychotherapy research
beyond rhyme: a content analysis of phonological awareness affordances in traditional nursery rhymes reading psychology

superior classification of visuospatial neglect in the subacute phase through free‐viewing and considering overcompensation abstract visuospatial neglect is a common disorder of spatial attention after stroke. traditional paper‐and‐pencil tasks are widely used for diagnosis but show limited sensitivity in the subacute phase, partly due to compensatory and (over)compensatory strategies. state‐of‐the‐art measures, including gaze bias assessed with eye‐tracking during free viewing and refined line bisection scoring, may offer greater diagnostic accuracy but have rarely been tested in clinical samples. we compared traditional measures (centre of cancellation, directional bisection error) and state‐of‐the‐art measures (endpoint weightings bias, mean horizontal gaze position during free viewing) in stroke patients admitted to rehabilitation ( n = 34) and age‐matched healthy controls ( n = 32), examining which measures best discriminated neglect from non‐neglect in the subacute phase. we also tested whether direction‐independent (absolute) deviations better capture neglect than directional deviations, given that overcompensation can mask deficits in standard scoring. direction‐independent scores showed superior discrimination. furthermore, a logistic regression model based on state‐of‐the‐art measures outperformed one based on traditional measures. the strongest neglect detection was achieved by combining directional bisection error with mean horizontal gaze position. these findings support the complementary value of eye‐tracking‐based assessment alongside traditional neglect tasks, and highlight the importance of accounting for (over)compensatory behaviour. journal of neuropsychology

introducing a positive self-coaching framework: a flexible process-based approach to self-directed psychological change with demand for professional mental health services exceeding capacity, more ambitious and measurable approaches are called for to support and strengthen the psychological well-being of both adults and young people. this article introduces a novel positive self-coaching (psc) framework, integrating self-determination theory, positive psychology and process-based approaches, which is tested using a mixed-methods study design with parents raising children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. findings indicate that structured self-coaching, particularly when combined with peer support, was associated with reduced perceived stress and increased well-being alongside improvements in self-kindness and self-concept clarity, carrying potential relational ripple effects within family systems. psc is proposed as a flexible, adaptive approach to self-directed psychological change. international journal of evidence based coaching & mentoring

using the purpose anchored team (pat™) framework to diagnose team performance problems: an executive-team coaching case team performance problems may appear as conflict, slow decisions, repeated escalation or weak accountability, yet these symptoms may be generated by conditions at systemic levels. this paper introduces the purpose anchored team (pat™) framework as a theory-informed diagnostic architecture for team performance. pat™ does not propose another list of team-effectiveness factors. instead, it uses stakeholder-derived team purpose as an organising criterion for locating performance problems within the team, within the organisation or in changing ecosystem demands. a 10-month executive-team coaching case illustrates the diagnostic sequence from presenting symptoms to problem formulation informed by multiple case data sources and established theory, intervention locus and operating changes. data included interviews, coaching observations, organisational documents, decision records, pulse measures, stakeholder feedback and practitioner notes. pat™ subsequently informed interventions in purpose clarification, decision architecture, organisational reinforcement and active learning routines. descriptive changes are reported without claiming causal effectiveness or empirical validation of the framework. international journal of evidence based coaching & mentoring

coaching supervision in practice: coaching supervisors’ perspectives on supporting coaches’ professional development coaching supervision is widely advocated as supporting coaches’ professional development, yet the evidence base remains limited. this qualitative study explored how experienced coaching supervisors understand supervision's contribution to coach development. semi-structured interviews with uk-based supervisors, framed by the seven-eyed model, were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. six themes were constructed: contracting the supervisory space; the supervisor's use of self; widening the coach's repertoire; the organisational bind of internal supervision; relational trust as the condition for challenge; and ethical vigilance as shared inquiry. participants positioned contracting, supervisor self-awareness and relational trust as central, and described internal supervision as constraining disclosure. they also moved between repertoire-based and reflexive accounts of development without distinguishing them. the findings represent supervisors’ perceptions and offer directions for supervisory practice, organisational policy and further research. international journal of evidence based coaching & mentoring

negative aspects of self-compassion are negatively associated with adolescents’ mental well-being well-being is essential for everyone, particularly in the sensitive stage of adolescence. to enhance mental well-being in young adults, we must understand its associated factors. this study examines self-compassion, pro-socialness, and nature connectedness as potential factors associated with adolescents’ mental well-being. our sample consisted of 121 participants (60 females, 58 males, and three diverse) in ninth grade, aged 14 to 16 years (m = 14.29, sd = 0.47). they completed questionnaires regarding the hedonic and eudaimonic aspects of mental well-being, self-compassion, pro-socialness, and nature connectedness. mental well-being was positively correlated with the positive scale of self-compassion, r(121) = 0.335, p < 0.001, and negatively with the negative scale, r(121) = −0.457, p < 0.001. results showed that only the negative self-compassion scale was negatively associated with adolescents’ mental well-being, ß = −0.401, p < 0.001. the negative scale includes self-judgment, isolation, and overidentification. this underscores the importance of these factors for the mental well-being of young men and women. adolescents

analysis blinding as a complement to preregistration: a tutorial for network analysis 分析盲法作为预注册的补充：网络分析教程 network analysis has become a popular computational-modeling approach in psychological research and is now increasingly used to address confirmatory research questions. however, preregistration of such analyses remains rare and even when implemented may leave room for researcher degrees of freedom, particularly when data-dependent decisions are difficult to fully anticipate. in this tutorial, we demonstrate how researchers can safeguard against bias by using analysis blinding as a complementary step to preregistration. the method involves temporarily altering the data to remove the key effect of interest while preserving all other aspects. analysis blinding makes it possible to explore important features of the data, for instance, spotting outliers or adjusting the computational model, without introducing bias. in this tutorial, we present three common research questions in network analysis and show how they can be addressed using analysis blinding to safeguard their confirmatory nature. we use data from previously published studies employing network analysis and offer a practical, step-by-step guide along with r code that researchers can adapt to their own data and research questions. advances in methods and practices in psychological science

qualitative development of the daily identity‐related stress and resilience model using daily diaries from lgbtq + youth in the southeastern united states abstract the prevailing reliance on cross‐sectional methods in lgbtq+ mental health research has limited researchers' ability to capture the dynamic, multilevel processes of minority stress and resilience factors as they unfold over time. although socioecological frameworks have been applied longitudinally, they have rarely attended to the interplay of historical, developmental, and short‐term timescales that shape lgbtq+ youth's day‐to‐day experiences. using qualitative daily diary data from a smartphone‐based ecological momentary assessment (ema) study, we pursued two aims: (1) to characterize lgbtq+ youth's daily positive and negative identity‐related experiences using qualitative content analysis; and (2) to develop a conceptual model illustrating how minority stress and resilience factors co‐occur and unfold within daily life. over 28 consecutive days, 50 lgbtq+ youth aged 13–24 ( m age = 18.38, sd = 3.02; 58% transgender or gender‐diverse) living in the u.s. southeast and at elevated risk for suicide completed nightly diary entries describing the most positive and most negative event of their day. qualitative content analysis of 349 identity‐related diaries (108 negative, 241 positive) revealed that minority stress and resilience factors co‐occurred across structural, interpersonal, and intrapersonal socioecological levels within single days, and that identity‐related experiences showed meaningful continuity across days at the within‐person level. drawing on these findings and existing socioecological frameworks of minority stress, we developed the daily identity‐related stress and resilience model , a conceptual framework that positions stress and resilience factors as simultaneous, multilevel processes embedded within individuals' daily lives and shaped by time‐stable social and identity factors across both short‐ and long‐term timescales. implications for future research and intervention development with lgbtq+ youth are discussed. journal of research on adolescence
clinical hypnosis for chronic non-cancer pain: a scoping review international journal of clinical and experimental hypnosis

parental phubbing and problematic mobile phone use among chinese early adolescents: a longitudinal moderated mediation model. adolescence is a high-risk period for problematic mobile phone use (pmpu), which exerts severe adverse impacts on adolescents' physical and mental health. cross-sectional studies have identified parental phubbing as a core predictor of adolescent pmpu, yet longitudinal evidence for this association remains scarce, as do investigations into protective factors that may attenuate this link. grounded in davis' cognitive-behavioral model and bronfenbrenner's ecological systems theory, this one-year three-wave longitudinal study examined the mediating role of core self-evaluation in the relationship between parental phubbing and adolescent pmpu, as well as the moderating role of peer relationships in this mediational process. a sample of 807 early adolescents from southern china (52.4% female; mage = 12.04 years at baseline) completed self-report assessments at six-month intervals. the results of path analysis, adjusting for age, gender, and family socioeconomic status, showed that parental phubbing at time 1 significantly predicted higher pmpu at time 3, and this longitudinal association was significantly mediated by core self-evaluation at time 2, with peer relationships moderating both the direct path from parental phubbing to pmpu and the first stage of the mediation effect (parental phubbing on core self-evaluation). specifically, the associations of parental phubbing with core self-evaluation and subsequent pmpu were significantly stronger among adolescents with poor peer relationships, whereas these associations were attenuated for those with high-quality peer relationships. this study reveals a moderated mediation pattern underlying the longitudinal association of parental phubbing with chinese adolescents' pmpu, and offers culturally informed considerations for the prevention of adolescent pmpu within the chinese cultural context. behavioral sciences

individual alpha frequency ( iaf ) and cognition: potential as a clinical marker and constraint for personalized neuromodulation. a narrative review abstract the individual alpha frequency (iaf) refers to the frequency at which the alpha rhythm shows peak power. this index is of great interest to neuroscience as it represents a marker of cortical timing and temporal resolution of neural processing. renewed interest stems from the opportunity to consider iaf not only as a descriptive marker of intrinsic brain dynamics but also as a neural marker serving as a personalized parameter in neuromodulation interventions. in this narrative review, we synthesize empirical and theoretical evidence that supports current understanding of iaf across methodological, biological, cognitive, clinical, and interventional domains. methodologically, iaf estimation does not follow a uniform approach and would benefit from greater convergence, including explicit separation of the periodic oscillation signal from the aperiodic background. physiologically, evidence indicates substantial heritability and short‐to‐medium‐term test–retest reliability of iaf, while support for clear and stable structural and neurochemical characteristics is weaker. cognitively, iaf modulation is associated with specific abilities, depending on the task and cognitive domain. faster iaf is associated with finer temporal resolution, better attentional and visuospatial performance, and increased processing speed, with more limited and region‐dependent evidence for working memory. clinical and longitudinal evidence suggests that deviations from the expected age‐related trajectory, a non‐linear rise into early adulthood followed by gradual slowing, accompany pathological aging, neurological, and mental disorders. however, these deviations are graded, indicating how far individuals depart from normative values, rather than providing stand‐alone diagnostic cut‐offs. finally, interventional studies on iaf‐tuned neuromodulation are consistent with increased transient neural entrainment and improved performance in the context of substantial iaf index stability. this positions iaf as a constraint rather than a target for personalization: an individual‐specific resonance range within which stimulation is likely to interact optimally with ongoing dynamics, and a candidate parameter for personalized brain stimulation protocols. psychophysiology

learning from neurodivergent students about their mental health and wellbeing during transition to secondary school: a systematic review abstract the impact of transition from primary to secondary education for neurodivergent children is an area where research, though emerging, has not yet produced consistent or conclusive findings. by adopting a neurodiversity‐informed framework, we conducted a systematic review of empirical studies examining the child‐reported impact of this transition on psychosocial and mental health outcomes amongst neurodivergent children such as autistic, children with developmental language disorder, and children with down syndrome (ds). six databases (pubmed, psycinfo, scopus, web of science, assia, and google scholar) were searched from 1995 to july 2026. the review followed the preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta‐analyses (prisma) guidelines for transparent reporting. of the 488 records identified, only 10 studies met the inclusion criteria: longitudinal empirical studies with comparison groups, including minimum two timepoints before and after the transition from primary to secondary school, with child‐reported psychosocial, mental health, or wellbeing data. study quality was assessed using the quality appraisal checklist. given substantial heterogeneity across studies, a narrative synthesis following synthesis without meta‐analysis (swim) guidelines was conducted. key gaps in the existing literature include the near‐total absence of co‐produced or participatory research designs, underrepresentation of specific neurodivergent groups (e.g., children with williams syndrome and ds), and failure to examine intersectional factors such as ethnicity and socioeconomic status as moderators of transition‐related outcomes. findings on the impact of transition on mental health were mixed and inconclusive, while psychosocial outcomes such as school concerns, belonging, and connectedness, emerged as more sensitive and consistent indicators of transition‐related vulnerability. methodological priorities for future research include longitudinal co‐produced designs, intersectional analyses, and inclusive outcome frameworks developed with neurodivergent children themselves. the theoretical and educational implications of this review for the development of evidence‐based, neurodiversity‐affirming intervention studies targeting the transition period are discussed. jcpp advances

psychometric properties of the perseverative thinking questionnaire (ptq) in a mexican sample abstract repetitive negative thinking (rnt) is considered a transdiagnostic process that predicts and sustains emotional disorders. therefore, valid instruments are necessary to measure this construct. this study aimed to assess the psychometric properties of the perseverative thinking questionnaire (ptq) in a sample of 756 mexican adults. due to the lack of consensus on the factor structure of this instrument, both exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses were conducted. evidence supporting the unidimensional structure of the instrument was found, and this structure was shown to be invariant across demographic and clinical variables. the ptq demonstrated excellent internal consistency and showed evidence of convergent validity with emotional symptoms, psychological inflexibility, life satisfaction, and environmental reward. additionally, evidence of discriminant validity was provided concerning emotional symptoms and psychological inflexibility. these findings suggest that the ptq is a valid and reliable measure of rnt in mexican adults, with important implications for both research and clinical practice. journal of psychopathology and behavioral assessment

rescripting suicidal mental imagery in young people: a pilot study of feasibility, acceptability and safety suicidal mental imagery—vivid, intrusive mental images of suicide or death—is common among young people experiencing suicidal ideation and may increase risk of suicidal behaviour, yet interventions directly targeting these images are limited. we conducted a single-arm pilot study evaluating the feasibility, acceptability and safety of a brief, therapist-delivered imagery rescripting intervention targeting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery in help-seeking young people aged 16–25 years with mood disorders and current or recent suicidal ideation. fifteen participants were recruited; 12 were eligible for the intervention and 11 (92%) completed treatment and follow-up. the recruitment target (n = 25) was not met, largely due to service disruptions and clinician capacity constraints. acceptability and safety criteria were met: 73% reported that sessions were not distressing, none felt less safe following treatment, and no participant showed increased suicidal ideation from baseline to follow-up. two serious adverse events occurred but were judged unrelated to the intervention. exploratory analyses showed reductions in suicidal-image frequency, realness, compellingness, intrusiveness and distress, alongside a 62.5% reduction in suicidal ideation severity. our pilot study provides preliminary indications that directly rescripting action-facilitating suicidal mental imagery showed encouraging short-term safety and acceptability signals in young people, supporting evaluation in a larger randomised controlled trial. behavioral sciences

haitian mamas: the development and two-year implementation of an ob/gyn-based preventive behavioral health group in a safety-net hospital setting. perinatal mental health conditions are among the leading causes of maternal mortality in the united states. however, 50% to 70% of perinatal mental health cases go undiagnosed, and of those diagnosed, fewer than 30% receive treatment. at boston medical center, a large safety-net academic medical center in the northeastern united states (us), this treatment gap became apparent when new refugee women's health clinic patient visits increased by 138% following an influx of haitian forced migrants starting in 2021. in response, we developed and implemented haitian mamas, a same-day access preventive behavioral health group within the obstetrics and gynecology department. this quality improvement study evaluates the development of haitian mamas from august 2023 to 2025, using four plan-do-study-act (pdsa) cycles. we evaluated the feasibility of this program across six domains: reach, engagement, integration of measurement-based care, financial viability, adaptability, and provider-perceived acceptability. over two years, 196 women participated in the group, with an average of eight members per group, and there was a progressive improvement in integrating measurement-based care, which rose from 11.5% in cycle 1 to 67.4% in cycle 4. 35% screened positive for moderate to server mental health concerns. a thematic analysis of qualitative data from providers' weekly post-group reflections identified implementation barriers and facilitators for haitian mamas. our findings suggest that the development and implementation of a same-day access, obgyn-based preventive behavioral health group for perinatal patients in a safety-net hospital setting is operationally feasible. behavioral sciences

evolution of university students’ ai dependency and creativity in the technology diffusion process: a four-wave repeated cross-sectional study in china generative artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping higher education, yet potential risks accompany over-reliance on these tools. grounded in rogers’ diffusion-of-innovations theory, the present study employed a mixed-methods design. four waves of independent cross-sectional quantitative data (t1–t4, n = 788) were complemented by semi-structured interviews with 20 undergraduate students. key patterns emerged as follows: (i) across later waves, the direct association between external regulation and intrinsic motivation attenuated, while the indirect association operating via identified regulation strengthened. the path from identified regulation to intrinsic motivation was the only relationship that demonstrated significant cross-pair differences while satisfying invariance requirements for all three wave-pair comparisons. because scalar invariance could not be established, this pattern is interpreted solely as a descriptive group-level temporal trend and should not be read as evidence of intra-individual change. (ii) ai-assisted creativity showed the largest and most consistent downward shift: estimates in later waves were significantly lower relative to the t1 baseline, with effect sizes increasing progressively (δ = −0.391 to −0.549; d = −0.61 to −0.95; all p < 0.001 following holm correction). this pattern remained largely unchanged after adjusting for gender, year of study, and academic major, and held up in four predefined subsamples as well as under propensity-score weighting. (iii) the linkage between ai dependency and creativity was significantly positive only at t3 and became negative but non-significant at t4, pointing to a conditional, wave-specific association rather than a stable linear relationship. (iv) observed wave-level differences for ai dependency and intrinsic motivation did not withstand correction for multiple comparisons. sensitivity tests yielded only two significant coefficients for ai dependency and none for intrinsic motivation; accordingly, these fluctuations are not given substantive theoretical interpretation. retrospective qualitative accounts provided supplementary process-oriented context: participants reported initial exposure to ai driven by prevailing social trends, sustained use based on perceived utility, subsequent disappointment in unreliable or misleading outputs, and eventual shifts toward more strategic, self-regulated engagement. given their retrospective nature, interview narratives were not used to triangulate or validate the quantitative findings. collectively, this work suggests that as ai-supported learning becomes normalized within a diffusion-driven context, group-level indicators of students’ subjective creative experiences tend to decline. higher-education institutions may therefore prioritize protecting learners’ creative agency as an explicit educational goal. behavioral sciences

behavioral phenotypes of omani children with autism spectrum disorder background: autism spectrum disorder (asd) is characterized by substantial phenotypic heterogeneity, which can complicate clinical formulation and intervention planning. despite increasing epidemiological research on asd in the sultanate of oman, systematic behavioral variation among omani children with asd has not been reported in the published literature. this study aimed to explore patterns of behavioral profiles in an omani clinical cohort using multidimensional measures of repetitive behavior and social functioning. methods: we conducted a cross-sectional study of 205 children with dsm-5-confirmed asd (mean age 5.3 ± 2.6 years; 80.5% male) attending specialist services in muscat, oman. parents completed the dimensional assessment of repetitive behavior (darb) and the stanford social dimensions scale (ssds), two multidimensional parent-report instruments. two-step cluster analysis was used to explore clusters representing a continuum of behavioral characteristics. verbal and non-verbal children were also compared across darb and ssds dimensions. results: a two-cluster solution (silhouette coefficient = 0.40, indicating weak-to-fair separation) described a severity gradient: a higher-severity cluster (n = 59, 28.8%) with elevated scores across all eight darb subdomains and lower scores across all five ssds dimensions, and a lower-severity cluster (n = 146, 71.2%). clusters did not differ significantly on the demographic variables examined, including consanguinity (p = 0.489). among verbal children (n = 126), social motivation, affiliation, expressive communication, and social recognition scores were higher than among non-verbal children (n = 79). non-verbal children demonstrated greater sensory–motor stereotypy. conclusions: this exploratory study provides an initial characterization of behavioral variation among children with asd in an omani clinical cohort. the clustering results suggest a continuum of behavioral characteristics, together with differences associated with verbal status, highlights clinically meaningful heterogeneity within the omani asd population. these findings are hypothesis-generating and may help inform future research on individualized assessment and intervention in oman and the wider arab gulf region. behavioral sciences

“eyes on the network” – task complexity and expertise shape visual strategies and mental workload in rail traffic control objective evaluate the sensitivity of eye-tracking metrics to variations in mental workload in rail traffic control, and how they may be modulated by operator experience. background rail traffic control is a safety-critical domain characterized by high cognitive demands. while subjective workload measures are widely used, objective, real-time indicators, particularly eye-tracking metrics, remain underexplored. method eighteen professional rail traffic controllers (9 novice, 9 experienced) performed a simulation-based experiment involving four different scenarios with varying traffic density and task complexity, while wearing a head-mounted eye tracker. measures of gaze behavior and visual strategies (fixations in different areas of interest (aoi)) were computed, and compared to subjective workload measures, to assess the effects of task difficulty and experience. results some measures like pupil dilation showed substantial changes (by ∼100%), while others like stationary gaze entropy showed more modest changes (∼40%), with increased task demand. measures such as fixation rate revealed significant interaction effects with experience, indicating distinct visual strategies of novices vs. experts. compared to experts, novices relied more on global overview displays under higher workload, and reduced planning-related information use, as revealed by aoi analysis. subjective workload measures corroborated with increases in perceived demand. conclusion this study advances mental workload assessment in rail traffic control by demonstrating that eye-tracking metrics are sensitive to workload variations, and also reveal underlying cognitive strategies unique to expertise. application these findings support the development of real-time workload monitoring systems and inform training interventions focused on information integration and cognitive strategies in rail traffic control operations. human factors

searching for the pattern: understanding, assessing, and transforming social settings a historical analysis of systems theory ideas from the biological and physical sciences reveals their infusion into sociology and action-oriented subfields of psychology, including social, organizational, developmental, and community psychology. constructs and processes are identified that are useful for creating a framework to understand, assess, and transform social settings. the central theoretical concept that surfaces is the emergent pattern of dynamic transactions that communicates critical information and meaning, referred to as “social regularity.” this is followed by an examination of the varying definitions and frameworks of proximal social settings (e.g., classrooms, community-based organizations, workplaces) in which individuals derive the bulk of their experiences in forming their character, identity, learning, and well-being. social regularity is at the core of an evolving social-setting model that communicates meaning through several channels—control and power, modes of expressing communication, and the flow of information—that result in corresponding distributional equity outcomes. from these communication channels, an action model for transforming social settings to create more equitable aggregate-level individual outcomes and improved setting outcomes is explicated. corresponding methods of measurement are described. various strategies and tactics are suggested to directly target social regularities. relational-, norm-, and structural-focused examples are provided. perspectives on psychological science

two practices that understate the mental health risks associated with adolescent social-media use why do researchers analyzing the same body of evidence reach different conclusions about whether social-media use poses risks to adolescent mental health? we offer a partial explanation: two common practices can lead researchers to underestimate harm and reach divergent conclusions. first, studies often do not account for risk elevations, relying instead only on correlation coefficients, which are more prone to misinterpretation. second, researchers often rely on highly blended analyses that combine heterogeneous exposures (e.g., multiple digital activities, including “tv watching”), outcomes (e.g., depression with life satisfaction), and populations (e.g., girls with boys), and then treat weak aggregate associations as evidence that specific risks are negligible. this is especially problematic when the central question is whether heavy social-media use is associated with internalizing symptoms among adolescent girls. we illustrate how sequential blending can transform a large and clinically relevant association into a negligible one, which helps explain the persistent disagreement in the literature. we conclude by urging researchers to present their findings in more practically interpretable terms, including elevated risks, and to investigate heterogeneity across platforms, usage levels, populations, and outcomes. perspectives on psychological science

depth or breadth? domain-specific expertise and cross-domain engagement in the development of scholarly excellence scholarly excellence is often equated with deep specialization within a single domain, a premise embedded in doctoral training, peer review, and academic-evaluation systems. however, research from the emerging “science of science,” drawing on large-scale analyses of publications, citations, and career trajectories, suggests a more complex relationship between expertise, cross-domain engagement, and scholarly impact. this conceptual article synthesizes insights from the science of science, cognitive research on expertise, and organizational studies to examine the roles of domain-specific depth and different forms of cross-domain engagement in the development of scholarly excellence. we argue that depth and breadth are complementary capacities whose contributions vary across career stages and institutional contexts. we distinguish between multidisciplinary exposure, interdisciplinary integration, and, in rarer cases, transdisciplinary contributions that extend beyond existing boundaries. domain-specific expertise supports technical mastery, credibility, and efficient knowledge accumulation, whereas integrative forms of cross-domain engagement facilitate recombination, problem reframing, and long-term intellectual influence. we further show how academic-reward structures favor depth while discounting integrative contributions. we conclude by outlining implications for doctoral education, faculty evaluation, and research policy, and by proposing a developmental framework that supports diverse trajectories of scholarly excellence. perspectives on psychological science

an examination of serial mediators linking change characteristics with employee change championing behaviors and positive mental health abstract researchers have identified a range of organizational change characteristics that influence employees' responses to change. however, most research has examined a small subset of characteristics within a single study. we identify six key change characteristics and develop a model where these characteristics are indirectly related to employee change championing behaviors and positive mental health. drawing on theory on the antecedents of change readiness, we identify four serial mediators linking change characteristics with outcomes including employees' change beliefs and positive and negative emotions about change, which in turn influence change readiness. in a three‐wave study of 397 australian employees from multiple organizations, a poor change history and participation in change were indirectly associated with championing behaviors through positive emotions about change and change readiness. transformational change was indirectly associated with championing through negative emotions about change and change readiness. change history was indirectly associated with positive mental health through positive emotions about change, change readiness, and championing behaviors. findings underscore the importance of considering multiple change characteristics and reveal that employees' emotions and change readiness are key mechanisms through which these characteristics shape outcomes. discussion focuses on ways to manage change characteristics to enhance employee responses during change. applied psychology-an international review-psychologie appliquee-revue internationale

perceived neighborhood disadvantage predicts similarity in amygdala representations of negative and neutral images in early adolescents abstract neighborhood disadvantage encompasses multiple co‐occurring adversities, including threat and deprivation, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. applying a dimensional framework to neighborhood contexts may help clarify how distinct features of disadvantage influence brain development. here, we used representational similarity analysis to investigate associations between adolescents’ neural representations of affective valence and neighborhood disadvantage, as measured by caregiver self‐report and the area deprivation index (adi). one hundred and twenty‐one adolescents aged 11 to 14 ( m age = 12.81 years old, 52.07% female, 28.93% white non‐hispanic) completed an emotional reactivity fmri task. caregiver‐reported neighborhood disadvantage was associated with greater representational similarity in right amygdala between negative and neutral images, while no such effect emerged for the adi. follow‐up analyses examined whether specific dimensions of disadvantage drove these effects. although our measure did not map cleanly onto threat and deprivation dimensions, factor analyses revealed distinctions between social (e.g., crime, loitering) and physical (e.g., abandoned buildings, walkability) disadvantage‐related items; our preliminary findings suggest that the effects of reported overall neighborhood disadvantage may be driven by characteristics of the social environment. no associations between caregiver‐reported neighborhood disadvantage or adi were observed for positive/neutral similarity. these findings provide preliminary evidence that neighborhood disadvantage may impact the amygdala's differentiation of negative and neutral stimuli during early adolescence, supporting the view that neighborhoods are a critical ecological context for development. developmental science

the role of mental and physical stress in the occurrence and development of pancreatic cancer abstract pancreatic cancer is a highly aggressive malignancy of the digestive tract, often associated with poor prognosis, short survival, and diminished quality of life upon diagnosis. to improve clinical outcomes and extend patient survival, early intervention at the etiological level is essential to reduce the risk of onset and progression. recent studies have highlighted the significant roles of both psychological and physical stress in the initiation and development of pancreatic cancer. this article systematically examines the link between stress and pancreatic carcinogenesis from the dual dimensions of psychological and physical stress, incorporating mechanisms such as neuroendocrine modulation, immune dysregulation, and behavioural changes. furthermore, it explores individualised stress management strategies for pancreatic cancer patients, aiming to offer new insights for early intervention and comprehensive treatment. stress and health

making space for serendipity and surprise: re‐imagining open science practices in psychological research abstract open science practices, particularly preregistration, have become central to efforts to improve transparency, reproducibility, and rigor in psychological research. at the same time, concerns have emerged that these practices may narrow opportunities for serendipity and surprise, which are critical elements in scientific discovery. in this article, we examine how methodological traditions and research norms shape the conditions under which serendipity and surprise enter the research process. we argue that constraints on discovery arise from the interaction of two reinforcing dynamics: methodological designs that structure what can be observed, and researcher‐centered processes that shape how research questions are generated and interpreted. building on this analysis, we propose a reconceptualization of preregistration as a system that can be refined to better support discovery while preserving transparency. we outline four reforms—foregrounding uncertainty, documenting discovery processes, supporting responsiveness to unexpected findings, and expanding epistemic scope—and identify practices that create clearer pathways for engaging with unanticipated observations. together, these reforms can strengthen psychological science by creating greater opportunity for unexpected observations and perspectives to generate new questions, explanations, and directions for research. social and personality psychology compass
editorial: personality interactions in the workplace: light and dark sides of human behavior. frontiers in psychology

embodied grief in the shadow of violence: an integrative conceptual review of widowhood, trauma, and social constraint violent widowhood remains among the least theorized forms of bereavement. while dominant western psychological models have advanced grief theory, they do not adequately explain grief following intentional spousal loss amid violence, ongoing threat, and gendered social regulation. this integrative conceptual review synthesizes interdisciplinary and cross-cultural scholarship on violent widowhood, traumatic bereavement, embodiment, structural violence, and social constraint to develop a context-sensitive framework for grief after intentional spousal loss. four interrelated dimensions are identified: traumatic bereavement, embodied grief, gendered and culturally situated mourning, and structural violence under enduring threat. these conditions are argued to fundamentally shape grief in violent widowhood. rather than following a linear recovery trajectory, grief is conceptualized as an ongoing process of negotiating identity, embodiment, and social belonging. the proposed framework positions adaptation as relational, context-dependent, and constrained by persistent social and structural conditions, thereby extending contemporary bereavement theory beyond individualistic psychological models. omega-journal of death and dying

bereavement, psychological distress, and inflammation: findings from the midus refresher cohort bereavement can adversely affect psychological and physical health. using midus refresher 1 data, we examined psychological and inflammatory differences between bereaved ( n = 373) and non-bereaved ( n = 490) adults and tested whether depression, anxiety, and stress moderated associations between bereavement and inflammation. participants completed measures of depressive symptoms, anxiety, and perceived stress and provided blood samples for interleukin-6 (il-6), tumor necrosis factor alpha (tnf-α), and c-reactive protein (crp). adjusting for key covariates, bereaved participants reported significantly greater depressive symptoms, anxiety, and perceived stress ( ps < .001) and had higher il-6 ( p = .001) and tnf-α ( p < .001) than non-bereaved participants. psychological symptoms did not moderate associations between bereavement and inflammatory markers. findings suggest that bereavement is associated with concurrent psychological distress and elevated inflammation, but these effects may be partly independent. identifying other psychological and contextual factors may clarify individual differences in inflammatory responses following loss. omega-journal of death and dying
the groningen identity development scale updated: theoretical foundations and preliminary evidence for the validity of the gids-l3 identity-an international journal of theory and research

human-centered ai metacognition: development and validation of a scale for preserving cognitive autonomy in human–ai collaboration the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (ai) is transforming human cognitive activities and creating a growing need to preserve cognitive autonomy in human–ai interactions. although recent research has examined metacognition in ai-mediated environments, existing work has primarily focused on improving ai use and human–ai collaboration, with less attention to how individuals regulate the role and extent of ai involvement in their own cognitive activities. to address this gap, the present study introduced human-centered ai metacognition (hc-aim), defined as the capacity to recognize ai capabilities and limitations, monitor ai-generated information, and regulate the extent to which ai participates in one’s own cognitive activities while maintaining cognitive autonomy. across three studies, we developed the chinese version of the human-centered ai metacognition scale (hc-aims) and conducted an initial psychometric evaluation. study 1 examined the scale structure using exploratory factor analysis and supported a predominantly unidimensional structure with good internal consistency. study 2 examined this structure using confirmatory factor analysis and provided evidence of its convergent validity through its association with general metacognition. study 3 further replicated the scale structure and internal consistency and examined its relationships with ai literacy, collaborative ai metacognition, and autonomous cognitive offloading. hc-aim was positively associated with all three constructs. comparisons of theoretically specified factor models provided preliminary evidence of empirical distinguishability between hc-aim and both ai literacy and collaborative ai metacognition, despite substantial correlations with these constructs. hc-aim was also positively associated with autonomous cognitive offloading, providing complementary self-reported criterion-related evidence for its validity. taken together, the findings suggest that hc-aim represents a contextualized, human-centered form of metacognitive regulation that is closely related to broader metacognitive and ai-related competencies while specifically emphasizing the regulation of ai participation in human cognition. the chinese version of the hc-aims provides a theoretically grounded starting point for investigating human cognition and cognitive autonomy in ai-mediated environments. journal of intelligence

personal and social listening habits in the streaming era – psychosocial model the streaming era has reshaped the ways music is intertwined with personal and social experiences, including engagement, sharing, event participation, discussion, and the creation of meaning. this study introduces the personal and social listening habits (pslhab) model, predicting music consumption habits (mch), by open-mindedness, via the mediation of (a) music mentoring preferences (mmp), and (b) savoring art. a four-stage study, based on two samples ( n1 = 495; n2 = 499) of music listeners, led to the development of the pslhab model. the operational validation confirmed the two new theoretical variables: four factors of mmp (human or algorithmic recommendations; active or passive search) and four factors of mch (personal or social listening; discussing or attending events). moreover, the results show that mmp and savoring art mediate the relationship between open-mindedness and mch, while the preference for active use of algorithmic recommendations is the strongest mediator. the study highlights how personal characteristics and preferences for musical exposure through mentoring influence social and personal behaviors around music, and explores musical exposure’s implications regarding social interactions. psychology of music

developmental and psychological profiles, risk assessment, and recidivism in online versus contact child sexual offending: a systematic review. online child sexual offending, particularly offences involving child sexual abuse material (csam), represents a growing area of concern. however, uncertainty remains regarding whether individuals who engage in online offences differ meaningfully from those who commit contact child sexual abuse (csa) in their developmental histories, psychological characteristics, risk profiles, and treatment needs.a systematic search was conducted in scopus, web of science, and pubmed in accordance with preferred reporting items for systematic reviews and meta-analyses (prisma) guidelines. studies examining developmental, psychological, criminological, risk assessment, recidivism, or treatment-related characteristics of individuals involved in online and/or contact child sexual offending were eligible. twenty-nine studies were included and synthesised narratively by developmental and clinical domain.evidence indicated both overlap and meaningful differentiation between online and contact offending. childhood adversity was reported across offence groups, although sexual victimisation histories tended to be less prevalent among online than contact offenders. broad personality traits showed limited differentiation, whereas clinician-rated psychopathy and antisocial characteristics were generally more pronounced among contact offenders. online and mixed offenders were more consistently characterised by atypical sexual interests and broader paraphilic or hypersexual patterns, although substantial within-group heterogeneity was evident. some studies supported the relevance of csam-specific instruments and dynamic risk measures, but the available evidence did not establish their consistent superiority over static tools developed primarily for contact offenders. recurrence findings from three treatment cohorts were synthesised narratively because differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, denominators, and observation periods prevented meaningful pooling or direct comparison of csam-related and contact offending. limited uncontrolled prospective evidence suggested reductions in offence-supportive cognitions and psychological distress, alongside substantial attrition and continued csam-related offending in some samples.developmental adversity, atypical sexual interests, antisociality, offence history, and self-regulatory difficulties appear to combine differently across online, contact, and mixed offending pathways. risk assessment findings should be interpreted in relation to the population, outcome, and setting in which each instrument was evaluated. further validation is needed to establish whether csam-specific instruments and dynamic measures improve prediction beyond existing approaches. the evidence base remains constrained by heterogeneous definitions, predominantly male and forensic samples, variable follow up periods, and limited prospective treatment research. larger longitudinal studies using harmonised definitions and validated outcome measures are required to clarify developmental pathways, transitions between online and contact offending, and treatment effectiveness. behavioral sciences

substance use treatment and recovery services for emerging adults in the us: integrating developmental considerations for effective intervention and research emerging adulthood is marked by unique characteristics that play a role in the development of substance use (su) problems and access to treatment and recovery services. consistent with the life course health development framework, emerging adults’ (eas’) developmental characteristics, neurological and cognitive states, peer networks, personal definitions of addiction and recovery, and co-occurring mental health conditions all play a role in their su, treatment, and recovery. this narrative review summarizes scientific literature on these key characteristics’ impact on ea services, as well as the current state of the science on treatment and recovery services for eas. based on findings, recommendations are made for researchers, practitioners, and policy makers. for example, more research should focus on eas’ educational and vocational pathways outside of traditional college environments, specific programs for eas that are not solely offshoots of youth or adult services, and the specific needs and desires of eas with su problems. emerging adulthood

emerging adults in wartime: the role of coping activity behaviors, resilience, and fear in mitigating secondary traumatic stress (sts) symptoms the hamas attack on israel and the subsequent iron swords war have profoundly affected emerging adults. the present study examined associations between coping behaviors (active vs. passive) and the intensity of active behaviors, and secondary traumatic stress (sts) symptoms. in addition, it explored indirect associations between coping behaviors and sts symptoms (intrusion, avoidance, and arousal) through resilience and fear. a total of 525 participants aged 18–30 completed an online survey during the first months of the war. active coping was associated with lower fear, higher resilience, and lower sts symptoms compared to passive coping. path analyses further indicated indirect associations between coping behaviors and sts through fear and resilience, with fear consistently associated with all sts symptoms, whereas resilience was primarily associated with avoidance and arousal. the findings contribute to understanding coping processes under prolonged wartime stress and highlight implications for targeted mental health interventions for emerging adults. emerging adulthood

understanding psychological resilience: a longitudinal environment-wide association study in hong kong nature mental health, published online: 20 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00742-1 ke ning, kim, fan et al. use an environment-wide association study to systematically map potential predictors of psychological resilience across a large longitudinal cohort from hong kong. by examining a broad range of individual, social and environmental factors prospectively, the study provides a comprehensive framework for investigating resilience in a non-western population. nature mental health

prevalence and predictors of suicide ideation, depression, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress in iraqi adolescents: a secondary school-based cross-sectional study adolescent mental health difficulties represent a significant public health concern. this study aimed to identify prevalence rates and predictors of suicide ideation, depressive symptoms, and symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder (ptsd) among iraqi adolescents. a cross-sectional quantitative survey design was used. a total of 469 adolescents aged 12–20 years (m = 16.25) participated across eight high schools in baghdad. multiple regression models were used to examine predictors. mean depressive (m = 12.99) and ptsd (m = 30.98) symptom scores were in the ‘moderate’ range, with the majority of participants scoring in the ‘moderate’ or ‘severe’ range (73.1% and 75.5%, depressive and ptsd symptoms, respectively). a total of 12.6% of young people scored in the ‘high risk’ range for suicidal behavior. females reported higher depressive symptoms and higher ptsd symptoms. older age was negatively associated with suicide ideation but positively associated with ptsd symptoms. quality of life emerged as the strongest and most consistent predictor across all models. hopelessness predicted suicide ideation, while ptsd symptoms predicted depression. in summary, adolescents were experiencing clinically elevated rates of depressive and ptsd symptoms on average. a significant minority were also experiencing suicidal thoughts. interventions that enhance functioning, reduce hopelessness, and incorporate trauma-informed approaches may be effective targets for prevention and early intervention. adolescents

a call for greater transparency in piloting 呼吁提高试点工作的透明度 a pilot study is a preliminary investigation conducted before a full-scale research study. although piloting is a common and valuable part of the research process, pilot studies are not systematically reported (or even acknowledged) in the psychology literature. in this article, we argue that establishing norms for regularly acknowledging preliminary research phases can improve many aspects of psychological research. specifically, reporting pilot-study information can help researchers provide a more complete record of the research process, reveal selection biases in research designs that may affect the generalizability of findings, evaluate others’ research more accurately, learn from other researchers’ successes and failures, uphold ethical responsibilities, and improve the methodological practice of piloting. we conclude with three concrete suggestions for near-term changes to help pilot reporting become standard practice: scientific communities and institutions should develop simple pilot-reporting templates, journals should provide clear pilot-reporting guidance for authors, and authors should acknowledge when pilot studies were run and share relevant materials and data. current reporting standards favor conclusive and polished research narratives, but such narratives are the end product of a complex scientific process that should also be shared. a truly transparent science should spotlight processes, such as piloting, that underpin the conclusions scientific articles draw. advances in methods and practices in psychological science

examining the strong black woman schema: pathways to suicide risk in black women through the integrated motivational volitional (imv) model recent studies have shown that the endorsement of the strong black woman (sbw) schema is associated with adverse psychological consequences. despite these findings, there is limited understanding of the pathways or mechanisms through which this schema is associated with harmful mental health outcomes. this study explored the relation between the sbw schema and suicidal ideation through the pathways articulated in the integrated motivational volitional model of suicidal behavior, particularly defeat and entrapment. the current study employed a cross-sectional survey design to examine the relation between the sbw schema and suicidal ideation through defeat and entrapment among 270 black women. a serial multiple mediation analysis revealed an indirect association between the sbw schema and suicidal ideation through defeat and entrapment. this study sheds light on a possible pathway through which suicidal ideation occurs in black women and highlights the need for additional studies that explore black women's experiences with suicide. psychology of women quarterly

bridging infant mental health screening and intervention from nicu to home: a single-center quality improvement project. having an infant admitted to a nicu increases parental anxiety, depression and traumatic stress, heightens infants' developmental and mental health risk, and may disrupt infant-parent relationships. early connections is a dyadic, trauma-informed universal infant mental health program implemented at children's hospital los angeles. child-parent psychotherapy-informed dyadic psychological intervention is offered during admission in the nicu. the parent navigator model utilizes a parent with lived nicu experience to support linkage to early intervention as families transition home. finally, a psychologist provides infant mental health screening and tiered intervention in the interdisciplinary outpatient newborn follow-up program (nfp), a high-risk infant follow-up clinic. this manuscript describes preliminary findings from a single-center quality improvement project to explore implementation of the program from december 2025 through march 2026. of the 63 (55.3%) families who met with the nicu psychologist, 88.9% had at least one infant mental health family session and 65.1% had more than one infant mental health session during their child's admission. of the 66 (57.9%) supported by the parent navigator, 90.9% completed applications for early intervention for their infant; future follow-up will determine the outcome of the application for services. based on outpatient infant mental health screening conducted with 85 patients (50.5% of those who had appointments), 23.6% of infants and 40.0% of toddlers screened in the nfp were at risk for social-emotional concerns, suggesting there may be a continued need for ongoing screening and intervention following discharge from intensive care. as the needs of families and infants change across inpatient and outpatient medical settings, it is important to offer multiple opportunities to screen needs flexibly and provide tiered intervention. behavioral sciences

estimating the effect of physical education reform on college students' mental health with difference-in-differences. facing increasingly fierce competition, mental health issues among college students have become a growing concern in higher education. college physical education (pe) plays a vital role in improving mental health among students. however, its causal effects and potential mechanisms remain insufficiently studied. in this study, we use a difference-in-differences (did) model to investigate the impact of pe reform on college students' mental health. to address individual heterogeneity, common time trends, and potential sample selection bias, the propensity-score matching did (psm-did) method was applied. we analyzed 3066 student-wave observations from 1533 unique students at universities in 26 chinese cities during 2021-2024; each student was observed in two survey waves. the intervention was a one-year compulsory pe reform involving adjustments to course design and expanded opportunities for physical activity. students attending reform-adopting universities in 15 cities constituted the treatment group, while students attending universities without the reform in 11 cities formed the comparison group. a time-varying difference-in-differences model, supplemented by propensity-score matching, examined changes in ces-d-10 depressive-symptom scores using city-level reform adoption dates. results show college pe reform significantly reduced ces-d scores. in the fully adjusted university- and wave-fixed-effects model with city-clustered standard errors (26 cities), pe reform was associated with a 1.22-point reduction in ces-d scores (β = -1.22; se = 0.38; 95% ci: -1.96 to -0.49; wild cluster bootstrap= 0.019). excluding self-rated mental health left the estimate essentially unchanged (β = -1.24). on the matched sample, with sh omitted from the propensity-score model, the corresponding estimate was β = -1.28 (n = 1974). a formal interaction test indicated a larger effect in first-tier cities (= 0.014); academic-year differences were jointly significant (= 0.043). mechanism analysis further indicates that pe reform was also associated with increased exercise habit intensity and exercise frequency, suggesting potential behavioral channels. this study shows benefits of college physical education reform for mental health and offers important policy implications. behavioral sciences

physiological synchrony across modalities within and between individuals: a methodological exploration of crossmodality abstract this methodological study aims at exploring several extensions of physiological synchrony. as yet, synchrony is commonly analyzed within the same physiological modality and between different people, whereas in the present project we were specifically interested in crossmodal synchronies between people (interpersonal), as well as within the same person (intrapersonal). in recent years, interpersonal synchrony has received increased attention as a research field and a methodology in various disciplines where social interaction is pivotal. synchrony is often computed on a time scale of a few seconds, predominantly based on physiological measures or motor behavior. systematic reviews and meta‐analyses have shown that interpersonal synchrony is a phenomenon that characterizes people's social interaction in different contexts. synchrony arises spontaneously in social systems, often outside the awareness of the persons interacting, and is often considered a signature of relationship quality. synchrony was also shown to be induced by salient stimulation contexts, for example by music synchronizing concert audiences. to explore such synchronies, we used a large dataset of 703 participants who listened to classical music in a concert setting. heart rate, heart‐rate variability, electrodermal activity, breathing behavior, and respiration rate were recorded simultaneously in all participants. using the surrogate synchrony algorithm (r package susy), which is based on cross‐correlations, the participants' crossmodal synchronies were determined for all 10 combinations of these 5 modalities. the psychological meaning of physiological synchronies is the goal of empirical aesthetics, and findings were published previously. the present study, however, concerns methodological topics of multimodal synchrony: do crossmodal synchronies arise intra‐ and interpersonally? using surrogate tests as a control condition, we found that about half of such synchronies were significantly present in the dataset at substantial effect sizes. we additionally explored the lag structure of the underlying cross‐correlations to describe the leading‐following dynamics between synchronized physiological modalities. we expected that crossmodal synchronies of modalities representing sympathetic activation would be significantly synchronized positively (in‐phase synchrony). this was, however, not always the case, as co‐activation of sympathetic and parasympathetic signals was also found. in conclusion, the present findings on crossmodal synchronies provide novel information and suggest new measures for synchrony research, which is relevant for both induced synchrony and synchrony of social interaction. psychophysiology

the dyadic universe model: a process theory of centralization, compression, and autonomy in romantic relationships. contemporary relationship science provides rich accounts of attachment, intimacy, and self-expansion, yet remains comparatively underspecified regarding a class of high-intensity romantic relationships in which partners progressively become each other's primary source of identity and meaning. we introduce the dyadic universe model (dum), a process-theoretic framework developed to address this explanatory gap, since existing theories such as attachment, self-expansion, differentiation of self, and the suffocation model explain important aspects of closeness, growth, or strain but do not fully capture the distinctive pattern in which expansion later turns into perceived constraint. this framework is formalized using three core variables: dyadic centralization (c), external-world investment (e), and dispositional pressure (ψ). dyadic centralization captures the extent to which the relationship displaces external domains of identity and engagement; external world investment reflects ongoing participation in those domains; and dispositional pressure represents individual differences in the drive for novelty, growth, and identity diversification. the model proposes a recursive dynamic in which increasing centralization is associated with reduced external engagement, limiting access to novel inputs and contributing to the accumulation of subjective compression. for individuals higher in dispositional pressure, this compression is predicted to intensify over time, eventually activating autonomy-restoration processes that reduce centralization or destabilize the relationship. from this minimal structure, the model derives a characteristic four-phase lifecycle, which are recognition, centralization, saturation, and autonomy restoration, linking the emergence of exceptional relational intensity to its potential transformation into psychological constraint. the dum integrates and extends existing theories of self-expansion, differentiation of self, and relational suffocation by specifying the temporal dynamics through which immersive relationships evolve. it advances a set of falsifiable propositions concerning lifecycle trajectories, individual differences, and dyadic asymmetries, and outlines a coordinated empirical research program across longitudinal, dyadic, and experience-sampling designs. while elements of these dynamics are suggested across existing empirical findings, the model formalizes them into a unified process-level framework and generates explicit predictions requiring systematic empirical testing. by articulating the interplay between centralization, external engagement, and dispositional pressure, the dum provides a parsimonious account of how the same processes that generate profound intimacy may also create conditions for instability. frontiers in psychology
