short-term transitions in first-semester motivation: a three-wave study of undergraduates’ expectancy-value-cost profiles grounded in situated expectancy-value theory and a person-centered approach, the present study employed a three-wave longitudinal design to examine short-term transitions in first-year undergraduates’ expectancy-value-cost profiles across the first semester. participants were 232 chinese first-year undergraduates recruited through course-based convenience sampling from an introductory psychology course. self-efficacy, task values, and perceived costs were assessed at three time points across the semester. latent profile and latent transition analyses identified three recurring profiles: average-all, burdened, and positively motivated. approximately 51% of students remained in the same profile across the semester. meaningful transitions were also observed. specifically, transitions toward less favorable profiles were more apparent from t1 to t2, whereas transitions toward more favorable profiles were more apparent from t2 to t3. gender did not significantly predict profile transitions. these findings suggest that first-year students’ expectancy-value-cost profiles can remain moderately stable while also shifting over short periods within a course. the results highlight the value of repeated assessment for understanding when students experience motivational burden and when their motivational configurations become more favorable. behavioral sciences

the thinking behind the prompt: evidence from collaborative student problem solving with generative artificial intelligence abstract generative artificial intelligence (genai) tools are permeating education but whether cognitive dispositions moderate their benefits remains unclear. in the present work, we examined whether cognitive reflection and intolerance of uncertainty moderate the relationship between prior genai experience and collaborative task effectiveness. specifically, secondary ( n = 114) and tertiary ( n = 57) students, distributed across groups, completed a mystery‐solving task with unrestricted access to a genai tool of their choice. person‐centred analysis identified no cognitive‐attitudinal profiles as the solution collapsed onto three groups defined by the cognitive reflection test (crt) score. in exploratory comparisons, the high‐crt group reported greater post‐task prompting self‐efficacy than the low‐crt group, despite no detectable difference in performance. cognitive reflection did not moderate the experience‐effectiveness link at the group level and uncertainty intolerance did not predict ai reliance behaviours. therefore, cognitive dispositions appear to relate more closely to the subjective experience of working with ai than to objective task outcomes. applied cognitive psychology

is less more? exploring the visual processes of minimalist and complex photography through eye tracking and eeg in a world filled with an overwhelming amount of visual information, the clean and distinctive visual style of minimalist photography stands out. however, empirical research on how minimalist style affects visual cognition and psychological responses remains limited. the present study investigated the effects of photographic style (minimalist versus complex) on viewers’ visual behavior, emotional responses, and brainwave state by conducting quantitative psychological experiments. thirty participants viewed photographs in one of the two styles. eye-tracking, consumer-grade electroencephalography (eeg), and subjective psychological assessment data were collected, enabling comprehensive evaluation of how the participants looked at, responded to, and emotionally engaged with the images. at the level of visual behavior, minimalism elicited significantly reduced number of fixations and saccades, but the duration of a single fixation is significantly longer, and the heatmap hotspots are highly concentrated, presenting a focused processing pattern of fewer but longer gazes. on a psychological level, minimalism evoked significantly less feeling of complexity and greater relaxation, although there was no significant difference in the aesthetics score between the two styles. in terms of brainwave state, viewing minimalist images resulted in significantly higher attention esense levels, while the meditation esense level did not show a significant difference. the results of this study therefore show that minimalist composition may influence the visual search pattern to be more focused, which is compatible with the tendency of simplified organization predicted by the principle of simplification. this study not only deepens the theoretical understanding of the psychological mechanisms of minimalist aesthetics, but also provides practical reference for visual communication and image creation of minimalist composition serving as an effective strategy for guiding the eyes toward the core subject. perceptual and motor skills

museum-based activities and psychological wellbeing: a pre-post study of visual thinking strategies and guided visits across two cultural settings. introduction: museum visits are increasingly recognised as contributors to psychological well-being, but less is known about whether museum activities designed for educational purposes are associated with short-term affective changes. within the asba (anxiety, stress, brain-friendly museum, approach) project, this study examined two educational (non-therapeutic) activities, a visual thinking strategies (vts) session and a standard guided visit, conducted in two culturally distinct settings in milan, italy: the modern art gallery (mag) and the natural history museum (nhm).
methods: in a pre-post design with two between-subjects factors (activity and museum), 135 adults attending 11 group sessions (vts:= 85, 7 sessions; guided visit:= 50, 4 sessions) completed the state anxiety inventory (sai) and six visual analogue scales (vas) before and after the activity and briefly described their experience in an open-ended question. state anxiety was the primary, confirmatory outcome; all other analyses were exploratory. changes were analysed with multilevel models including a random intercept for session, and the open-ended responses with a descriptive content analysis.
results: state anxiety decreased from pre to post ( = -5.55, 95% ci [-6.85, -4.26]; d_av = -0.81) and mood improved ( = +1.07, 95% ci [0.74, 1.40]; d_av = 0.72), with negligible dependence within sessions (icc ≤ 0.04). in a multilevel ancova adjusting for baseline anxiety, no statistically detectable difference emerged between activities (adjusted difference = 0.38 sai points, 95% ci [-2.67, 3.42]). the content analysis suggested that participants reached these changes through different experiential routes: cognitive descriptions prevailed after vts, emotional-aesthetic descriptions after the guided visit, and social-relational descriptions were reported only after vts.
discussion: both educational activities were followed by comparable short-term improvements in state anxiety and mood, although participants described them in different terms. because the study did not include a non-museum control condition and allocation was not randomised, these changes cannot be causally attributed to the museum activities. the findings are preliminary and hypothesis-generating and warrant controlled studies of museum-based activities for wellbeing. frontiers in psychology

second language identity negotiation and willingness to communicate: the roles of belonging and cross-cultural contact. introduction: although both second language acquisition and cross-cultural psychology have increasingly recognised the importance of learners' identity and intercultural experiences, the psychological mechanisms linking second language (l2) identity negotiation to willingness to communicate (wtc) remain insufficiently understood. drawing on identity theory and the multi-level model of wtc, this study examined whether sense of belonging mediates the association between l2 identity negotiation and wtc and whether this indirect association varies according to the quality of intercultural contact.
methods: using cluster sampling, questionnaire data were collected from 468 undergraduate students majoring in spanish at chinese universities. a moderated mediation model was tested to examine the mediating role of sense of belonging and the moderating role of intercultural contact quality.
results: the findings indicated that (1) l2 identity negotiation was positively associated with both sense of belonging and willingness to communicate; (2) sense of belonging partially mediated the association between l2 identity negotiation and willingness to communicate; and (3) intercultural contact quality moderated the first stage of the mediation process, such that the positive association between l2 identity negotiation and sense of belonging was stronger among learners reporting higher-quality intercultural contact.
discussion: these findings suggest that sense of belonging represents an important psychological mechanism linking l2 identity negotiation to willingness to communicate and that the quality of intercultural contact strengthens this association. the study extends existing research by integrating identity theory, the wtc framework, and intergroup contact theory, and provides empirical support for identity-oriented and intercultural approaches to spanish language teaching. frontiers in psychology

a comparative study of grief severity, executive functions, and social support following human vs. companion animal loss losing a loved one profoundly impacts social and cognitive domains, yet the loss of a companion animal (ca) is often an overlooked area of study. this research investigated whether ca loss carries the same weight as human loss by comparing grief severity, executive functions, and perceived social support. the study analyzed 307 participants from turkey (205 human loss; 102 ca loss). results indicated no significant differences between the two groups in terms of grief severity or perceived social support. furthermore, analysis with executive functioning indices revealed no differences between those grieving a human versus a ca. these findings indicate that grief severity, perceived social support, and self-reported executive functioning did not differ significantly between the groups on the measures examined in this study. these findings contribute to the growing recognition of ca bereavement and highlight the importance of addressing the needs of individuals who experience ca loss. omega-journal of death and dying

examining older adults’ preferences for virtual reality applications to support social and cognitive engagement objective to assess older adults’ experience, attitudes, and interests toward virtual reality (vr) applications as part of an early phase in the user-centered focused development of the cognitive activity social technology (cast) vr system. background vr offers opportunities to enhance health and well-being in older adults by promoting cognitive, activity, social, and technology engagement. however, limited research has examined older adults’ user experience and perceptions. method a multi-site study was conducted with 48 community-dwelling older adults aged 65–90. participants interacted with 16 vr applications through hands-on sessions and first-person video demonstrations. they rated user experience, overall attitudes toward vr, and interest in using vr for various activities. results most applications were rated as enjoyable, interesting, and easy to use, with minimal reports of physical discomfort. participants expressed the greatest interest in vr for art, cultural experiences, education, entertainment, and travel, while showing less interest in vr-based social interaction and fitness. overall, participants found vr technology to be enjoyable and easy to use, but were neutral about vr’s usefulness, likely due to the productivity-oriented nature of the usefulness measure. conclusion the findings demonstrated the feasibility, usability, and acceptability of vr applications for cognitive and activity engagement among older adults. application results highlight the importance of designing vr experiences that align with older adults’ preferences and needs. findings inform user-centered design of vr systems to enhance cognitive engagement, social connectivity, and well-being among older adults. human factors

team heart rate dynamics and performance in a simulation-based cooperative task: a multidimensional recurrence quantification analysis (mdrqa) approach objective this study examined whether multidimensional recurrence quantification analysis (mdrqa) metrics derived from team heart rate data predict team performance and team workload under varied team and task demands. background assessing team performance in operational environments is challenging. traditional approaches require task interruptions or ground-truth data that are often unavailable. physiological sensing offers a less-intrusive approach, yet most applications aggregate individual-level data or rely on simple pairwise metrics that do not represent how coupling is organized across the whole team. mdrqa instead embeds multivariate time series into a shared phase space, but evidence linking mdrqa metrics to team outcomes remains limited and mixed. method twenty triads completed a cooperative virtual reality choice reaction time task across four conditions manipulating interdependence and time pressure. mdrqa metrics (percent determinism, average diagonal line length, diagonal line entropy) were extracted from heart rate interbeat interval data. linear mixed-effects models tested whether these metrics predicted self-reported team workload and team performance outcomes including sensitivity and response bias from signal detection theory. results longer sustained coupling predicted increased sensitivity and fewer errors, while greater entropy predicted poorer performance. higher determinism and lower entropy predicted a more liberal response bias. mdrqa metrics did not predict perceived workload beyond condition effects. conclusion mdrqa metrics reflect joint physiological dynamics and predict performance outcomes in triads beyond the effects of task demands alone. application continuously computed physiological coupling metrics may serve as less-intrusive, real-time proxies for team performance in operational environments where traditional assessment is infeasible. human factors

toward a psychology of science: a dynamic cognitive model of the evolution of scientific theories responding to a recent call for the development of a psychology of science, we examine how scientists manage empirical anomalies, a routine yet consequential challenge in scientific practice, and how their responses shape theory development. we argue that defensive anomaly-reduction strategies, which allow researchers to preserve an initial theoretical claim, can generate important secondary benefits. during the emergence phase of a theory, they foster auxiliary revisions that may reduce underfitting and place a fragile theory on a growth trajectory. during the exploitation phase of established theories, they help sustain attention to problems derived from the theory and support cumulative research. however, their accumulation may also increase the risk of overfitting, reduce predictive power, and set the theory on a degenerative trajectory. we illustrate these dynamics primarily through examples drawn from psychological theories, with a focus on responses to replication failures. last, we derive several implications for peer review aimed at fostering scientific innovation. in particular, we propose shifting evaluation away from the consistency of findings, which may penalize emerging research programs and hinder innovation, and toward how inconsistencies are managed, thereby fostering growth trajectories, including for mature programs confronted with anomalies. perspectives on psychological science

fear of being ordinary: development and validation of a questionnaire. social media often presents staged portrayals of individuals' lives, creating the impression that others have exciting and extraordinary experiences. this phenomenon can contribute to unrealistic social comparisons and concerns about living an ordinary life. the present study sought to develop a psychometrically robust measure of individual differences in fear of being ordinary (fobo) using online survey data from a convenience sample of 622 participants (m = 21.88 years; 69% female). furthermore, the study explored associations between fobo, fear of missing out (fomo), the big five personality dimensions, narcissistic traits, and levels of self-reported psychological distress. exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses revealed two correlated factors in the fobo questionnaire: fear of insignificance (6 items) and social media comparisons (3 items). fobo showed the strongest positive correlations with fomo (r = 0.58), depression (r = 0.40), and neuroticism (r = 0.34). daily time spent on social media was also positively associated with fobo (r = 0.26). in conclusion, the brief fobo questionnaire provides a useful tool for further research on the relationship between intense social media use and this specific fear, as well as for evaluating potential strategies to mitigate it. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

psychological profiles of trait mindfulness and school climate in adolescents: examining growth mindset as a precursor to social-emotional competence background: adolescents’ social-emotional competence (sec) is a fundamental aspect of their psychological well-being. although growth mindset is widely recognized as a pivotal developmental asset, its role in predicting how internal resources, such as trait mindfulness, interact with external environments like school climate to shape sec remains poorly understood. the present study addresses this gap by treating growth mindset as a precursor to the distinct psychological profiles defined by mindfulness and school climate, while subsequently evaluating how these patterns predict variations in sec. methods: bolck-croon-hagenaars (bch) a total of 1153 chinese adolescents completed measures of growth mindset, trait mindfulness, school climate, and sec. data were analyzed using latent profile analysis (lpa) within a robust three-step framework. this approach utilized the r3step algorithm to examine growth mindset as a predictor of profile membership and the bolck-croon-hagenaars (bch) method to evaluate profile-specific differences in sec as a distal outcome, thereby ensuring stable estimates by explicitly accounting for classification uncertainty. results: regression analysis confirmed that growth mindset positively predicted sec. lpa identified four distinct patterns based on trait mindfulness and school climate: (1) high mindfulness-high support (high resource integration, hri); (2) high mindfulness-low support (intrinsically advantaged, ia); (3) low mindfulness-high support (environmentally dependent, ed); and (4) low mindfulness-low support (dual-risk, dr). using the r3step procedure, growth mindset was treated as a primary antecedent that significantly predicted profile membership, with higher scores increasing the likelihood of assignment to the hri profile. furthermore, the bch method revealed significant variations in sec across these groups, with the hri subgroup exhibiting the highest level of competence. conclusions: the findings underscore the predictive role of a growth mindset and the existence of heterogeneous adolescent profiles characterized by distinct patterns of trait mindfulness and perceived school climate. the findings suggest that tailored, profile-specific interventions that consider both individual psychological resources and environmental context may be more effective than a one-size-fits-all approach for enhancing adolescents’ sec. behavioral psychology-psicologia conductual

composite multi-stage transfer learning with cross-scene adaptation for personalized in-vehicle gaze estimation transferring gaze estimation models from mobile terminals to in-vehicle driving scenarios faces challenges from differences in device form, viewpoint, and imaging conditions. to address this, this study proposes a cross-scene adaptation framework that integrates composite multi-stage transfer learning with distributed multi-camera fusion for personalized in-vehicle gaze estimation. the framework builds upon a multi-level information element fusion baseline (mief) and explores three transfer paths (cmp1–cmp3) for progressive personalized adaptation from a large-scale mobile source domain to an in-vehicle target scenario. a distributed multi-camera platform is established, producing gaze calibration data (gcd) for cross-session training and driving gaze and road scene data (drd) for visualization validation. a multi-camera fusion model (mcf) is designed with two paradigms, mcf-lite and mcf-plus, to balance accuracy improvement and computational complexity. experimental results demonstrate that the composite multi-stage transfer learning path cmp3 achieves an average error of 0.277 across camera views, with a best single-camera mean error of 0.244. building on this, the distributed mcf-plus model with the full c1 + c2 + c3 configuration further reduces the mean error to 0.160 and the standard deviation to 0.127, with 96.88% of predicted gaze points falling within the target calibration block (error < 0.5). the proposed method provides a feasible technical pathway for personalized adaptation of gaze estimation models from mobile-terminal source domains to in-vehicle multi-camera target scenarios, and offers preliminary experimental evidence for gaze behavior perception and driving gaze heatmap generation in real environments. journal of eye movement research

child emotional reactivity differentiates vulnerability to paternal punitive/minimizing emotion socialization abstract extreme levels of preschool sadness hallmark emotion regulation difficulties and early depression risk. emotion socialization theory proposes that parents’ punitive or minimizing reactions can heighten children's sadness. yet children's constitutionally‐based emotional reactivity may amplify or buffer such forms of parental socialization. we tested whether children's emotional reactivity, indexed at the neural level using the late positive potential (lpp), moderated longitudinal associations between punitive/minimizing reactions and children's sadness. participants were 121 preschoolers (59% girls) and their parents. at child age 3, mothers and fathers reported on their own punitive and minimizing reactions to children's negative emotions, providing separate indices of maternal and paternal behaviors. at age 4, children completed a passive viewing task to assess neural responses to positive, negative, and neutral stimuli. at age 5, children's sadness was indexed via parent report. results revealed that children's neural reactivity to positive stimuli moderated the link between paternal, but not maternal, punitive/minimizing reactions and children's sadness. paternal punitive/minimizing reactions predicted higher sadness at lower levels of child positive reactivity but lower sadness at higher levels of reactivity. this study highlights heterogeneity in children's responses to parental socialization and suggest that neural indices of emotional reactivity may help explain differential vulnerability. findings also underscore a unique paternal role in early emotional adjustment. social development

book review: the feminist killjoy handbook: the radical potential of getting in the way by ahmed, sara ahmedsara. the feminist killjoy handbook: the radical potential of getting in the way. seal press: new york, 2023; 336 pp.: isbn: 978–0241619537. feminism & psychology

exploring perceived relationships between cannabis use and mental health symptoms among emerging adults at high risk for psychosis: a qualitative study cannabis use among emerging adults has reached historically high levels, yet there is growing evidence that cannabis use during this developmental period may exacerbate existing psychopathology and increase risk of developing schizophrenia-spectrum disorders. this qualitative study examines perceptions of how cannabis use impacts psychiatric symptoms among twenty emerging adults (ages 18–24) at high risk for psychosis. participants completed a survey and semi-structured interview. thematic analysis revealed two overarching themes: relief-oriented cannabis use (e.g., coping with social anxiety, depression) and negative sequelae from cannabis use (e.g., social withdrawal, exacerbating symptoms of psychosis). these findings suggest that using a harm-reduction approach as opposed to cannabis abstinence may be more realistic and attainable for this population. also, future interventions are needed that address patients’ perceived inadequacy of psychiatric medications, build social and distress tolerance skills that do not involve cannabis use, and provide psychoeducation regarding dose and potency dependent risks. emerging adulthood

factors associated with substance use behaviour among emerging adults in the african context: a scoping review emerging adulthood is a critical period marked by significant psychosocial transitions that often coincide with increased experimentation with psychoactive substances. a scoping review was conducted to synthesise existing literature to identify the factors associated with substance use behaviour among emerging adults within the african context. this review focuses specifically on african studies to address the critical underrepresentation of african contexts in literature on factors associated with substance use behaviour among emerging adults. this review was guided by the methodological framework proposed by arksey and o'malley and followed the prisma framework. 2410 peer reviewed published articles were identified, after screening 14 were included in the synthesis. the findings identified that substance use is rarely the result of a single factor but rather the convergence of individual vulnerabilities and broader social, environmental, and cultural forces. emerging adulthood

testing anxiety, depression, and cannabis problem severity as predictors of self-initiated cannabis change attempts among young adult women relative to men, women tend to escalate more rapidly to problematic cannabis use, experience more severe withdrawal, and report higher levels of internalizing symptoms, which may impede attempts at change. using two waves of data from a sample of young adult women (wave 1 n = 653, wave 2 n = 584), this study tested whether baseline anxiety, depression, and cannabis problems predicted quit/break attempts six months later. sexual and gender minority status was examined as a moderator. greater baseline depressive symptoms predicted higher odds of any quit attempt and past attempt, but not current attempt. greater cannabis problems predicted lower odds of a current attempt. higher baseline anxiety, depression, and cannabis problems were associated with greater withdrawal, whereas cannabis problems were associated with shorter attempts. anxiety predicted current quit/break attempts among gender minority participants only. addressing internalizing symptoms and withdrawal may help sustain cannabis quit/break attempts among women. emerging adulthood

improving safety frameworks for generative ai and youth well-being policy nature mental health, published online: 19 october 2026; doi:10.1038/s44220-026-00735-0 this perspective evaluates youth well-being policies within ai governance, identifying gaps between ethical frameworks and practical applications. recommendations emphasize culturally responsive design and trauma-informed approaches to enhance user safety and address developmental needs effectively. nature mental health

preserving human judgment in ai-enabled education: the sam model for ai readiness, assessment, and human-in-the-loop decision making. generative artificial intelligence (ai) shifts educational focus from access to information toward judging machine-generated claims and regulating the division of epistemic work. this conceptual article proposes the sam model-self-regulation (s), ambiguity tolerance (a), and methodological competence (m)-as a bounded person-level resource model within broader ai readiness, with educators' ai readiness as a central application. s denotes regulatory capacity, a a disposition-like willingness to tolerate unresolved epistemic ambiguity, and m the capacity to evaluate claims, differentiated into cross-domain m1 and domain-specific m2. sam's distinctive claim is configurational: m should predict independently assessed judgment more strongly at higher s and, under high ambiguity, when a is higher. these relations, the m1/m2 distinction, limited compensability, and incremental prediction beyond shared and neighboring accounts remain hypothetical. the model separates resources from enacted processes, contextual affordances, and outcomes and requires independent performance criteria. for ai-based assessment and learning analytics, educators' interpretations of ai-derived evidence and construct inferences from behavioral traces require validated mappings addressing alternative explanations, comparability, fairness, and use. sam thus offers a research agenda predicting when ai support preserves human judgment rather than merely improving supported performance. behavioral sciences

exposure to negative information about the collective future eliminates the positivity bias for the personal events in the near future abstract personal future projections are mostly more positive than autobiographical memories, despite a negativity bias for the collective future. one underlying reason may be unawareness of the potential interconnectedness of collective and personal futures. in the present study, participants either listened to information about the negative collective future and its relation to the personal future or neutral information about the collective future. then, they generated an important autobiographical memory, a future event that can happen in the next 5 years, and another one that can happen in 10–15 years. results showed that in the condition with negative information only, the future positivity bias disappeared for near future events, but not for distant ones, accompanied by lower intensity of the negative emotions for only distant future events. bias for high intensity positive affect disappeared for both near and distant future events. the study offers a potential explanation for the bias. applied cognitive psychology

midwives’ experiences with prenatal loss: a phenomenological study this study was conducted to examine midwives’ experiences related to prenatal loss. the study employed an interpretive phenomenological design, one of the qualitative research designs. criterion sampling was used. the inclusion criteria were defined as being a midwife who has provided care to pregnant women experiencing prenatal loss and having at least five years of professional clinical experience. a total of 20 midwives were interviewed. seven core themes were identified. the study revealed that as midwives gained more experience with such challenging situations, their coping strategies evolved; they developed broader perspectives and demonstrated more conscious, professional, composed, and empathetic approaches. while the majority of participants were deeply affected by these events, some stated that their emotional state remained unchanged. midwives can be supported with additional education and resources, particularly during the early years of their professional careers, to help them cope with these processes. omega-journal of death and dying

predictors of aggression in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder: a systematic review aggression is a common and impairing co-occurring behavior among children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (asd), negatively affecting developmental outcomes, family functioning, and social participation. although numerous studies have examined factors associated with aggression in asd, findings remain inconsistent, limiting efforts to improve early identification and intervention. this systematic review synthesized current evidence on predictors of aggression in children and adolescents with asd. the review protocol was registered in prospero (crd42023416081). a systematic search of pubmed, web of science, embase, scopus, and the cochrane library was conducted from database inception to 4 april 2024. eligible studies were evaluated using the joanna briggs institute checklist for cross-sectional designs and the newcastle–ottawa scale for cohort studies, and findings were narratively synthesized. thirteen studies met inclusion criteria and were of generally satisfactory methodological quality. across studies, six categories of predictors were identified: demographic, caregiver, core symptom, comorbidity, psychological, and biological factors. social communication deficits and poor sleep quality showed relatively consistent associations with aggression, although these findings were based on only three and two studies, respectively, whereas evidence for other factors—including age, iq, caregiver characteristics, and sensory or biological markers—was mixed. overall, aggression in asd appears to arise from interacting individual, familial, and contextual influences. these findings highlight the importance of assessing communication skills and sleep problems when evaluating aggression risk and suggest that interventions targeting these domains may reduce aggressive behavior. future research should employ longitudinal and cross-cultural designs to clarify developmental pathways and strengthen the evidence base for personalized intervention strategies. psychological reports

flourishing from within: reclaiming the human potential at the heart of positive psychology since its emergence, positive psychology has sought to identify the conditions that support human flourishing. despite substantial empirical advances, the field continues to face conceptual fragmentation and lacks a widely accepted unifying philosophical foundation. this article offers a humanistic re-visioning of flourishing grounded in three organizing metaphors—universal mind, consciousness, and thought—reframed in contemporary psychological language. rather than locating wellbeing primarily in the cultivation of strengths or favorable conditions, the proposed “inside-out” perspective suggests that flourishing reflects an intrinsic human capacity that may become obscured through habitual patterns of thought. from this perspective, growth is understood less as the acquisition of positive traits than as the rediscovery of psychological openness evident in moments of insight, presence, and authentic encounter. intended as a conceptual and phenomenologically informed contribution, the framework employs these metaphors heuristically rather than metaphysically. by integrating philosophical reflection with implications for practice and social change, the article invites positive psychology to move toward a more principle-centered understanding of human potential grounded in meaning, agency, and human development. journal of humanistic psychology

updating deficits in subjective cognitive decline: a differential pattern of executive dysfunction across clinical stages. identifying objective cognitive markers in the preclinical stage of alzheimer's disease (ad), particularly in subjective cognitive decline (scd), is critical for early intervention. while executive function comprises three core components (inhibition, updating/switching), their impairment trajectory during the scd-to-mild cognitive impairment (mci) progression remains unclear. this study aims to systematically compare these components among cognitively normal (nc), scd, and mci individuals to determine the earliest sensitive cognitive indicators of ad pathology. community-dwelling adults aged ≥50 years were classified into nc, scd, and mci groups based on comprehensive screening (moca, scd-q, cdr, adl). all participants completed standardized computerized tasks assessing inhibition (oddball, stop signal task), updating (spatial 1-back, vwm task), and switching (task-cue paradigm). one-way anova with post-hoc tests compared group differences in accuracy and reaction time. scd showed no difference from nc in inhibition but intermediate switch costs; crucially, scd's spatial 1-back performance was significantly worse than nc and comparable to mci, indicating early mci-level updating deficits. visuospatial storage capacity showed gradual impairment. updating ability (visuospatial working memory) is the earliest and stably impaired indicator in scd, serving as a sensitive marker for ultra-early ad screening. these findings suggest that updating ability, particularly visuospatial working memory, is the earliest and most stable impaired executive component, making it a sensitive behavioral marker for identifying high-risk scd and enabling ultra-early ad screening. in contrast, significant impairments in inhibition and switching are delayed or progressive. this provides new scientific evidence for early assessment and targeted cognitive intervention. international journal of clinical and health psychology

temporal-experiential model of progressive illness and unified self (tempus): rethinking psychopathology in chronic disease through narrative identity and self-coherence / modelo temporal-experiencial de la enfermedad progresiva y el yo unificado (tempus): un nuevo enfoque de la psicopatología en las enfermedades crónicas a través de la identidad narrativa y la coherencia del yo progressive chronic diseases such as heart failure, copd, chronic kidney disease, and parkinson’s disease are associated with a substantial psychiatric burden that remains only partly explained by existing psychopathological models. several limitations may contribute to this gap. current models often blur the distinction between objective disease severity and subjective experience, give limited attention to how illness reshapes the temporal structure of the self, and rarely offer a clinically useful distinction between depression and demoralization. we introduce tempus (temporal-experiential model of progressive illness and unified self), a theoretical framework in which psychological vulnerability emerges from disruptions in temporal self-coherence. this construct refers to the capacity to maintain a continuous narrative linking past experience, present functioning, and anticipated future. the model describes interacting components and feedback processes that may help explain why patients with comparable disease severity follow different psychological trajectories. beyond description, tempus is intended to generate testable hypotheses and inform intervention. it also proposes a clearer distinction between depression and demoralization, with potential implications for clinical decision-making. studies in psychology

a critique of the over-politicization of cbt: a voice from the global south cognitive behavioural therapy (cbt) remains a premier evidence-based psychotherapeutic modality globally. however, decolonial and critical literature has increasingly sought to politicize the modality, dismissing it as a western, hyper-rationalist, and reductionist framework that pathologizes structural trauma by locating systemic distress strictly within individual cognitive distortions. this paper presents a critical counter-perspective from the global south, offering an immanent critique that challenges this adversarial academic narrative. rather than treating cbt as a rigid instrument of neoliberal containment, we illustrate how its inherent structural flexibility, goal-focused blueprint, and pragmatic problem-solving stance actively dismantle learned helplessness, shifting vulnerable populations from passive sufferers to active creators of change. we examine how the core cognitive model harmonizes with culturally responsive practice in india, mapping modern individualistic aspirations alongside socio-centric identity networks-such as family hierarchies, religion, and caste-through contextual values clarification. furthermore, we demonstrate that the synthesis of responsive validation and a directive clinical stance, both offered by cbts, functions as an effective "parallel authoritative parenting" approach that mirrors care and discipline (or boundary-setting). in addition, core cbt concepts resonate with traditional buddhist and hindu concepts of the active observer rather than the passive recipient of environmental stimuli, as well as changing perspective to resolve cognitive deadlock. hence, cbt presents robust clinical utility within india's rapidly expanding, educated, and tech-savvy urban populations. finally, we address the paucity of regional research in the mainstream publication world and highlight how regional bodies, such as the asian cognitive behavioural therapies association (acbta) and global bodies like the world confederation of cbt (wccbt), are helping local researchers transition from passive critique toward proactive structural interventions, including standardized cultural adaptation frameworks and showcasing these at global platforms. to summarize, this voice from the global south argues that a dogmatic application of cbt is the real limitation, while its creative, innovative, mindful, scientifically rigorous evolution empowers asian clinicians to deliver world-class, contextually grounded care. current opinion in psychology

is empathy a “double-edged sword”? how empathy with nature shapes tourist well-being in wildlife tourism empathy is regarded as a key affective driver of individual well-being. in the context of a performance-oriented, hyper-mobile society, the target of empathetic concern has shifted “from humans to nature,” and non-human life is increasingly treated as a new anchoring point onto which emotions are projected and well-being restored. extant literature, however, usually reduces empathy to a unidimensional emotional amplifier, overlooking the positive–negative bipolarity inherent in empathic responses and the differentiated effects this polarity exerts on well-being. yet, the gain-and-loss pathways through which empathy with nature influences tourist well-being, together with their boundary conditions, remain unexplored. adopting an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, the study deconstructs the mechanism through which empathy with nature affects tourist well-being by means of in-depth interviews and grounded-theory analysis. three follow-up experiments corroborate the qualitative findings. results reveal that empathy with nature in wildlife tourism bifurcates into positive and negative strands, exerting asymmetric impacts on tourists’ hedonic and eudaimonic well-being. restorative experience operates as a vicarious mechanism linking empathy with nature to well-being outcomes. furthermore, wildlife anthropomorphism asymmetrically moderates these affective pathways—amplifying the harm of negative empathy on hedonic well-being and restoration—while leaving eudaimonic well-being unaffected. based on mainland chinese participants in scenario-based zoo encounters, these findings offer an initial, culturally situated account of how empathy with nature shapes tourist well-being in wildlife tourism. behavioral sciences

effects of acute aerobic exercise on sequentially administered cognitive tasks reflecting working memory subcomponents and heart rate variability. although acute aerobic exercise selectively influences specific subcomponents of working memory, whether such benefits transfer to a subsequent cognitive task engaging a different domain remains unclear. forty-seven participants completed, in randomized order, an exercise condition (10 min of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise) and a control condition, each immediately followed by a visuospatial construction task (the equilibrio game) and a 2-back working memory task, with heart rate variability (hrv) recorded throughout. completion time on the equilibrio task was significantly shorter following exercise than following control,= 292.5,= -2.873,= .004,= -0.481. in contrast, no significant between-condition differences emerged on any behavioral parameter of the 2-back task, including completion time, accuracy, hit rate, discrimination sensitivity ('), and response bias (; alls > 0.05). during the 2-back task, however, sympathetic indices (sns index, stress index, lf/hf ratio) were significantly elevated and parasympathetic/vagal indices (rmssd, sdnn, pns index, hf n.u.) were significantly suppressed following exercise, despite unchanged behavior. these findings indicate that exercise-induced cognitive benefit is task-specific and does not extend to a subsequent task engaging a different working memory subcomponent, even as autonomic activation persists. this dissociation challenges general-arousal accounts of exercise-cognition effects and supports a domain-specific, timing-sensitive framework. journal of intelligence

emotion beyond bias: affective and cultural scaffolding in self-regulation and metacognition intelligent performance depends on how cognitive ability is deployed, and its deployment is regulated by metacognitive and affective processes. this theoretical article concerns regulated deployment, on which the gap between maximal and typical performance depends, and leaves the structure of ability outside its scope. influential decision-science frameworks treat emotion as a bias to be overridden by deliberation and design interventions accordingly; we argue that this view is difficult to reconcile with evidence that emotion and cognition arise from integrated, reciprocally connected networks, and we develop the view that affect functions as an organizing signal for monitoring and control. we derive a hypothesis that, to our knowledge, no study has yet tested directly: for challenges that require regulation to be regenerated over time, or the predictive models from which behavior flows to be reorganized, a culturally mediated route that engages affective, embodied, social, and aesthetic processes should yield change that lasts longer and transfers more widely than a content-matched route without them. we distinguish three classes of behavioral challenge by regulatory structure, locate self-regulated learning and metacognitive calibration within them, separate a testable claim about subjective regulatory effort from a conjecture about the formal control cost of brain-state transitions, and outline a test that could be preregistered. journal of intelligence
efficacy of measurement-based care (mbc) in routine child and youth behavioral therapy: a pragmatic randomized controlled trial psychotherapy research

achievement emotions questionnaire-elementary school: psychometric analysis of a modified version (aeq-es-gn). the achievement emotions questionnaire-elementary school uses pictorial response anchors to assess enjoyment, boredom, and anxiety across academic settings. this study examined the psychometric properties of a modified mathematics version, the aeq-es-gn, in which the original gender-specific faces were replaced by gender-neutral, smiley-based representations. participants were 12,738 students (age at wave 1 = 9.57 years,= 0.83; 50.7% girls among students with available gender information) from 287 schools in estonia, finland, norway, portugal, serbia and sweden. students were in grades 3-4 at wave 1 and grades 4-5 approximately one year later in wave 2. confirmatory factor analyses compared alternative measurement models, followed by tests of longitudinal and multigroup invariance, reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, temporal stability, and associations with mathematics competence. a hierarchical model distinguishing emotions and academic settings was retained, showing a good fit and providing the most appropriate overall solution for subsequent analyses. scalar invariance was supported over time and across gender, grade, and country. scores showed adequate-to-excellent reliability, generally satisfactory convergent validity, and evidence of discriminant validity, although enjoyment and boredom were strongly negatively related. temporal stability was moderate, and associations with mathematics competence were small and theoretically consistent. these findings support the aeq-es-gn as a reliable and valid measure of mathematics-related achievement emotions among students in grades 3-5, while direct comparisons with the original response format remain necessary. behavioral sciences

initial evaluation of the internal structure and internal consistency of the context-adapted perceived peer motivational climate scale (cmi) among nursing students enrolled in a clinical simulation program background/objectives: peer motivational climate may influence how students experience collaboration and learning in group-based educational settings, but its measurement properties have not been examined in nursing students enrolled in clinical simulation programs. the perceived peer motivational climate scale (cmi) was originally developed in sport contexts, and its psychometric properties in this educational context have not been examined. therefore, this study aimed to conduct an initial evaluation of the internal structure and internal consistency of a context-adapted cmi among nursing students enrolled in a clinical simulation program. methods: a cross-sectional psychometric study was conducted with 395 fourth-year undergraduate nursing students at the catholic university of murcia (ucam) who voluntarily agreed to participate, using a convenience sampling approach. the questionnaire was completed before the scheduled clinical simulation activities. participants had previous experience with group work in clinical simulations, and the items referred to the peer group assigned to the upcoming simulation. however, it was not established whether all participants had previously interacted with those specific peers. internal consistency was assessed using cronbach’s alpha and mcdonald’s omega coefficients for the task-involving and ego-involving motivational climate dimensions. the internal structure was examined using exploratory factor analysis (efa) based on a polychoric correlation matrix, minimum residual extraction, and oblimin rotation, followed by confirmatory factor analysis (cfa) using the diagonally weighted least squares (dwls) estimator for ordinal categorical variables. both the efa and cfa were conducted in the same sample. results: the cmi demonstrated high internal consistency for both dimensions, with cronbach’s alpha and mcdonald’s omega coefficients of 0.939 for the task-involving dimension and 0.940 for the ego-involving dimension. exploratory factor analysis was consistent with a two-factor structure, supported by parallel analysis, with items showing clear primary loadings and limited cross-loadings. confirmatory factor analysis showed substantially better fit for the correlated two-factor model than for the one-factor model (estimator-adjusted δχ2(1) = 126, p < 0.001; cfi = 0.991; tli = 0.987; srmr = 0.049), although the rmsea remained elevated at 0.130 (95% ci 0.114 to 0.147). the two factors were positively correlated (r = 0.681). conclusions: the cmi showed high estimated internal consistency and preliminary evidence consistent with a correlated two-factor structure in this sample of fourth-year nursing students enrolled in a clinical simulation program. these findings should be interpreted within the context of a single-institution convenience sample, the use of the same sample for efa and cfa, and the absence of formal content-validity procedures in the target population. the study did not assess other sources of validity evidence, such as temporal stability, criterion-related validity, measurement invariance, or sensitivity to change. the generalizability of these findings beyond fourth-year nursing students at a single spanish university participating in the specified simulation program remains uncertain. further research using independent and more diverse samples, together with formal content-validity procedures and additional sources of validity evidence, is needed to replicate and extend these findings before broader use of the instrument can be considered. behavioral sciences

variations in psychopathy dimensions among incarcerated individuals convicted of violent offenses in romania: the role of offense type, age, and personality traits. psychopathy is a multidimensional construct consistently associated with antisocial and violent behavior; however, its affective-interpersonal and behavioral components may contribute differently to distinct forms of violent offending. the present study investigated variations in psychopathy dimensions according to the type of violent offense and age, as well as the predictive role of agreeableness and conscientiousness in a sample of incarcerated individuals convicted of violent crimes. the sample comprised 500 incarcerated individuals from six romanian prisons (m age = 38.49 years, sd = 10.39), assessed using the self-report psychopathy scale-iii (srp-iii), the levenson self-report psychopathy scale (lsrp), and the agreeableness and conscientiousness dimensions of the big five personality model. data were analyzed using analyses of variance (anova), pearson correlation analyses, and hierarchical linear regression. the results revealed significant differences in psychopathy levels according to the type of violent offense (srp-iii:(2, 484) = 12.13,< 0.001, η= 0.048), with higher psychopathy scores observed among individuals convicted of physical violence offenses. psychopathy decreased significantly with age, particularly in its behavioral dimension. agreeableness and conscientiousness emerged as significant negative predictors of psychopathy (β = -0.179,< 0.001, and β = -0.175,= 0.001, respectively), accounting for an additional 10% of the explained variance. these findings support a dimensional conceptualization of psychopathy and highlight the role of personality traits in the psychological profile of violent offenders. the results have important implications for violence risk assessment and the development of individualized intervention strategies within correctional settings, although the modest proportion of variance explained (13%) and the predominantly small effect sizes observed indicate that these findings should be considered preliminary rather than a basis for standalone clinical decision-making. behavioral sciences
