the relationship between a wildlife conservation project involving scientist-farmer collaboration and farmers' attitudes and behaviors towards conservation science and the environment in switzerland. considering agriculture's significant contribution to the environmental crisis, farmers play a crucial role in conservation. it is thus important to explore the drivers motivating them towards sustainable practices. farmer-scientist collaboration is a promising tool to promote pro-environmental practices, yet empirical evidence on the outcomes of such collaborations remains sparse. in this study, we aim to assess the association between a long-term scientist-farmer collaboration and farmers' attitudes and behaviors towards conservation science and the environment. using three consecutive annual surveys and a longitudinal sample of over 100 farmers, we compared farmers collaborating in a wildlife conservation project with non-collaborators. collaborators exhibited significant improvement in trust towards conservation science between the first and second survey, while non-collaborators showed gradual improvements. both groups enhanced their pro-environmental attitudes and behaviors over time. this study underscores the value of collaboration with ecologists in enhancing farmers' attitudes towards conservation science. it also highlights the intricate relationships between attitudes towards conservation science and pro-environmental attitudes and behaviors. environment and behavior

early mathematics risk in chinese kindergartners: group differences and differential associations of cognitive, motivational, and home factors abstract this study examined mean‐level group differences and differential associations of cognitive, motivational‐behavioral, and home numeracy factors with early mathematics achievement in 173 chinese kindergarten children. covariate‐adjusted group comparisons and moderation analyzes, controlling for age, gender, socioeconomic status, and nonverbal intelligence, compared a sample‐defined mathematics risk (mr) group (bottom quartile) with an average‐achieving (aa) group (middle 50%). digit ran and symbolic comparison showed both significant group differences and predictor × group interactions. working memory and inhibition showed significant interactions without significant group differences. in contrast, task avoidance, social avoidance, formal teaching, and number application differed between groups but showed no significant interactions. thus, mean‐level differences and differential associations identified partially different correlates of early mathematics risk. applied cognitive psychology

with whom you elaborate matters: how learning orientation impacts cross-culture and same-culture information elaboration in culturally diverse teams abstract work teams are increasingly characterized by diverse cultural backgrounds. although research has established that cultural diversity holds the potential to enhance team performance through information elaboration—the exchange, discussion, and integration of task-relevant information—prior work has treated elaboration as an undifferentiated process, leaving unspecified whether it occurs across or within cultural boundaries. we develop a differentiated elaboration perspective that distinguishes cross-culture information elaboration between culturally dissimilar members from same-culture information elaboration between culturally similar members. using a multi-source, multi-wave study of 104 culturally diverse teams comprising 587 members, we found that, as expected, cross-culture elaboration was more strongly related to team performance than same-culture elaboration. moreover, team learning orientation predicted both forms of elaboration, and its indirect association with team performance was stronger through cross-culture elaboration. these findings advance a differentiated elaboration perspective to demonstrate that elaboration that crosses cultural boundaries is more important for diverse teams than same-culture elaboration. this points to opportunities for future research on reaping the benefits of diverse teams. journal of business and psychology

exploring associations between job insecurity and subjective well‐being among dual‐earner couples: the role of spouses' work‐family centrality using an actor‐partner interdependence model abstract job insecurity reflects employees' perceived threat to employment continuity and their powerlessness to retain their job. existing research has largely focused on individual well‐being outcomes, overlooking dyadic stress processes within dual‐earner couples. drawing on conservation of resources theory and the spillover‐crossover model, this study adopts the actor‐partner interdependence model (apim) and apim mediation model (apimem) to analyse data from 300 chinese dual‐earner couples. this study examines actor‐partner associations between job insecurity and multifaceted subjective well‐being, as well as the mediating function of work‐family centrality. constrained apim results indicate robust detrimental actor associations across all well‐being dimensions. partner crossover associations are dimension‐specific, linking job insecurity to elevated spousal negative affect and reduced spousal life satisfaction. further apimem analyses reveal selective, role‐specific mediating effects of work‐family centrality, encompassing both theoretically grounded intrapersonal spillover pathways and atypical inconsistent mediation pathways. these findings refine understandings of dyadic job insecurity transmission. theoretical and practical implications are discussed. stress and health

graduate students trapped between pressures and screens: a multi‐wave longitudinal network and cross‐lagged panel study abstract chinese graduate students face multiple pressures from academic, familial, social, and personal sources, like academic learning inefficiency (difficulty completing research tasks), campus unfamiliarity (poor environmental adaptation), and certification pressure (obligation to obtain professional credentials). that may drive many to overuse short‐form videos as a coping strategy. however, how these pressures dynamically relate to video overuse over time remains unclear. we conducted a three‐wave longitudinal study ( n = 2471) using network analysis, cross‐lagged panel network analysis (clpn), and random intercept cross‐lagged model (ri‐clpm). results revealed three findings. first, across all three waves, strong associations existed between learning inefficiency and campus unfamiliarity, as well as between the ideal‐reality gap (discrepancy between expected and actual graduate life) and social adjustment. central nodes were mainly certification pressure and parental expectations. second, clpn indicated that short‐form video overuse showed the strongest autoregressive edge; the strongest cross‐lagged edge was from social pressure to personal stress. school pressure appears to have had a stronger impact on other variables at the subsequent time point, while both school pressure and family pressure appear to have exerted a greater contemporaneous influence on other variables. school pressure and family pressure may have subsequently increased short‐form video overuse. last, ri‐clpm indicated that higher overall pressure levels significantly predicted increased video overuse at the next wave, but the reverse effect was non‐significant. implications include prioritising certification pressure and parental expectations, proactive school pressure management, and addressing video overuse by targeting its pressure drivers rather than the behaviour itself. stress and health

safety in disclosure: an integrated model of dyadic disclosure of marginalized group members across identities to dominant group members abstract self‐disclosure is a well‐documented facilitator of positive intergroup contact. the present work adopts a dyadic perspective to integrate models of disclosure and responsiveness from two previously distinct literature: experience‐based disclosure in interracial interactions and identity disclosure among individuals with stigmatized identities. this integrated explanatory framework broadens the scope of prior models to encompass disclosure experiences across a wider range of contexts and marginalized groups—including members of racially minoritized groups, people with disabilities, and sexual minorities—during interactions with dominant group members. we first outline individual and contextual factors that shape marginalized group members' decision to disclose. following their disclosure of an identity or identity‐related experience, we delineate intended and enacted responsiveness from dominant group members. we then highlight how the responsiveness of dominant group members informs marginalized group members' perceptions of responsiveness, and subsequent intrapersonal and relational outcomes. likewise, we provide evidence of distinct outcomes for dominant group members following their response. finally, we highlight how this framework can encourage novel insights and research, such as consideration for disclosure processes of people with intersectional identities. this approach illustrates how perceptions of both marginalized and dominant group members jointly shape disclosure, responsiveness, and outcomes across intergroup contexts. social and personality psychology compass

effects of serotonin transporter genotype and (un)predictable maternal separation on affective, cognitive, and social behaviors in female rats abstract serotonin transporter (sert) variation is linked to depression risk after stress, conferring an increased risk to sert‐linked polymorphic region (5‐httlpr) short‐allele carriers, who show heightened sensitivity to cumulative stress and childhood maltreatment. to elucidate the neurobiological mechanisms underlying sert × early‐life adversity interactions, animal models capturing this genetic vulnerability are of translational relevance. we evaluated four maternal separation (ms) paradigms to determine how different forms of early‐life stress influence adult behavior in female sert‐deficient rats, given the higher prevalence of depression in women and the limited translational value of male‐only preclinical findings. we applied several behavioral tests to wildtype (sert +/+ ), heterozygous (sert +/− ), and homozygous (sert −/− ) knockout females exposed to ms: predictable 3 h/day (ms180) or 6 h/day (ms360), unpredictable 3 h/day (msu180), or unpredictable 3 h/day plus unpredictable maternal stress (msus180). controls were 15‐min handled. sert −/− females exhibited higher anxiety‐like responses, passive stress coping, and increased social exploration. ms180 and ms360 induced some anxiety‐like behaviors, while ms360 increased hedonic responding. females responded differently to ms depending on their sert genotype. first, some anxious behaviors of sert −/− females were attenuated when exposed to unpredictable ms (msu180 and msus180). second, msu180 reduced object recognition in sert −/− females, while enhancing it in sert +/− females. third, sert +/− females exhibited less passive stress coping when exposed to ms360 than all other groups. neither predictable nor unpredictable ms exposure increased vulnerability to depressive‐related behaviors in sert‐deficient females. variations in sert expression may confer some beneficial effects in response to ms, depending on the specific genotype and behavioral domain evaluated. genes brain and behavior

prevalence of mental disorders associated with intimate partner violence victimisation by gender, sexuality, and child maltreatment history abstract purpose intimate partner violence (ipv) is prevalent and associated with adverse mental health outcomes. this analysis reports national prevalence estimates of mental disorders among australian adults who have experienced lifetime ipv victimization, by gender, sexuality, and child maltreatment history. methods using data from the nationally representative australian child maltreatment study ( n = 7022, aged 16 years and older), prevalence was calculated for five mental disorder categories (i.e., major depressive disorder, generalized anxiety disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder, alcohol use disorder, any mental disorder) by type of ipv victimization (i.e., no ipv, any ipv, psychological, physical, sexual, multitype). results any ipv victimization was associated with significantly higher prevalence of any mental disorder (55.3%), generalized anxiety disorder (18.5%), alcohol use disorder (28.5%), major depressive disorder (28.1%) and post-traumatic stress disorder (10%) compared to those without a history of ipv. prevalence was generally consistent across different types of ipv victimization. bisexual individuals ( n = 375) exhibited higher prevalence of mental disorders compared to heterosexual individuals, across all forms of ipv, while participants with diverse gender identities ( n = 88) showed elevated rates of generalized anxiety disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder, compared to women and men. child maltreatment history further amplified prevalence, with multi-type child maltreatment associated with elevated prevalence across the different forms of ipv victimization. logistic regression analyses indicated ipv victimization was associated with increased odds of mental disorders, with the strongest associations observed for post-traumatic stress disorder across ipv types (ors = 3.2–6.0). conclusions findings suggest that early adversity (child maltreatment) and later-life adversities (ipv victimization) contribute cumulatively to the risk of mental disorders, with heightened risk evident for diverse genders and sexualities. these findings highlight the substantial public health burden associated with mental health disorders among ipv victims and the need for increased attention to prevention and early intervention efforts, including improved screening for ipv within healthcare settings and accessible, trauma-informed mental health support for ipv victims, including sexuality and diverse gender populations at elevated risk. journal of family violence

development and psychometric validation of the pandemic risk perception scale in healthcare professionals. introduction: perceived pandemic-related risk may influence emotional responses, preventive behaviors, and psychological adjustment among healthcare professionals working in high-risk clinical settings. this study aimed to develop and evaluate the psychometric properties of the pandemic risk perception scale (prps) in healthcare professionals.
methods: a cross-sectional psychometric study was conducted with 405 healthcare professionals aged 22-65 years working in emergency and critical care settings in southern spain. the prps was developed from an initial pool of 23 items and reduced to 12 items based on item analysis and exploratory examination of its dimensional structure. its factor structure was subsequently examined using confirmatory factor analysis. internal consistency was assessed using mcdonald's omega. evidence of validity based on relationships with other variables was examined through correlations with depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and psychological wellbeing.
results: confirmatory factor analysis supported a unidimensional structure, with satisfactory overall model fit (χ = 168.31, df = 54, cfi = 0.99, tli = 0.99, rmsea = 0.07, 90% ci [0.06, 0.08]). standardized factor loadings ranged from 0.56 to 0.92, and mcdonald's omega was 0.95. prps scores were positively associated with depressive symptoms ( = 0.44, < 0.001) and negatively associated with psychological wellbeing ( = -0.22, < 0.001). the association with generalized anxiety symptoms was small and not statistically significant ( = 0.069, = 0.164).
conclusion: the findings provide preliminary evidence supporting the prps as a brief and reliable measure of perceived pandemic-related risk among healthcare professionals. its associations with depressive symptoms and psychological wellbeing provide additional evidence of validity based on relationships with other variables. further validation in independent and diverse samples is needed before extending its use to other populations, healthcare systems, or future public health emergencies. frontiers in psychology

quechua translation and validity of the revised mental health inventory in peruvian adolescents. introduction: adolescent mental health is a growing public health concern, particularly among indigenous populations, where linguistic and cultural barriers may limit access to appropriate psychological assessment. therefore, having brief and culturally adapted instruments in indigenous languages is essential to improve mental health assessment and research among quechua-speaking adolescents.
objective: to translate and culturally adapt the revised mental health inventory-5 (r-mhi-5) from spanish into southern quechua and examine its psychometric properties in peruvian adolescents.
methods: a total of 2,978 adolescents from angaraes, huancavelica, participated in this instrumental, quantitative, cross-sectional study. participants completed the southern quechua version of the r-mhi-5 and a sociodemographic questionnaire. structural equation modeling and item response theory were applied.
results: the southern quechua r-mhi-5 showed adequate content validity (aiken's > 0.70) and a two-dimensional structure comprising psychological well-being and psychological distress, with satisfactory fit indices (cfi = 0.99, rmsea = 0.03, srmr = 0.01). reliability was adequate for both dimensions ( = 0.72; = 0.78), and measurement invariance by sex was supported. item response theory analyses showed satisfactory item functioning. item 4 showed the highest discrimination and information for psychological well-being, whereas item 3 showed the highest discrimination and information for psychological distress. the scale provided greater information at intermediate levels of well-being and at intermediate-to-high levels of psychological distress.
conclusion: the southern quechua version of the r-mhi-5 showed adequate psychometric properties supporting its use to assess mental health among quechua-speaking adolescents. its brief format, two-dimensional structure, reliability, measurement invariance, and item-level performance support its application in research and mental health assessment in community settings. frontiers in psychology

development and psychometric validation of the faithful insight scale among muslim university students. despite growing recognition of spirituality's role in psychological functioning, the literature remains critically devoid of psychometrically sound instruments capable of measuring faith-based cognitive insight within muslim populations, as existing tools are predominantly anchored in western secular frameworks inadequate for capturing islamic epistemological dimensions. the present study aimed to develop and psychometrically validate the faithful insight scale (fis) among al-azhar university students. a sequential multi-phase design was employed across two independent samples: an exploratory sample ( = 679) and a confirmatory sample ( = 843), alongside a retest subsample ( = 140). content validity was established through expert panel review, exploratory factor analysis examined the underlying structure, and confirmatory factor analysis evaluated competing models. construct validity and reliability were comprehensively assessed. results revealed a robust four-factor hierarchical structure encompassing constructive interpretation, surface-depth integration, meaning-value perception, and moral conscious awareness, demonstrating excellent model fit, strong convergent and discriminant validity, excellent internal consistency, and adequate temporal stability. the fis constitutes a culturally grounded and empirically rigorous instrument that authentically integrates islamic epistemological principles within contemporary psychometric methodology, offering researchers and practitioners a validated tool for advancing theory and evidence-based practice in islamic psychology and muslim mental health contexts. frontiers in psychology

“now you know, don't be indifferent”: the emotional correlates of learning about historical violence and their relationship with current prosocial motivation abstract how does learning about historical violence inspire prosocial action today? prior work has focused on whether such experiences are (emotionally) impactful but seldom tested the mechanisms of impact. we propose a framework of actor‐specific emotional pathways connecting knowledge of historical violence to contemporary upstanding intentions: empathy for victims, moral emotions toward exemplars (e.g., feeling inspired), and toward perpetrators (e.g., guilt). we tested this in a pre‐registered quasi‐experimental study among dutch youths ( n = 1,371) participating in a holocaust museum program, using structural equation modeling to compare post‐visit responses to a pre‐visit control group. participants surveyed after the program reported higher empathy for victims, positive emotions toward exemplars, and negative emotions toward perpetrators than participants surveyed before the program. however, only empathic concern toward victims mediated the relationship between participating in the museum program and upstanding intentions against antisemitic bullying. these findings highlight the central role of victim‐centered narratives and inform educational efforts to foster present‐day moral engagement. journal of applied social psychology

inclusive musical environments in educational contexts: a conceptual framework for equity, participation, and student wellbeing. this review develops a framework for examining the conditions under which musical environments may support equity, participation, and situated student wellbeing in educational contexts. to this end, it brings together literature from music education, educational psychology, inclusive education, music therapy, and critical studies of gender, disability, and intersectionality. recent research has linked music education with self-esteem, belonging, social-emotional learning, emergent literacy, movement, and inclusion; however, there is extensive heterogeneity in designs, populations, measures, and contexts. accordingly, the article does not begin from the premise that music is inclusive, but from the need to identify the pedagogical and relational conditions that make equitable musical participation possible. peer-reviewed studies published between 2018 and 2026 were analyzed by distinguishing three evidence domains: studies and reviews with direct implications for school contexts; broader educational scholarship from higher education, ensembles, and music clubs; and complementary therapeutic evidence. in light of this body of research, musical inclusion can be organized around three mechanisms of preventive equity: multimodal pedagogical access and situated representation; recognized participation and voice; and expressive safety, belonging, and situated wellbeing. the article argues that music may support equity when its pedagogical design broadens the legitimate ways of learning, participating, and contributing within a shared practice. by doing so, the article shifts the discussion from the general benefits of music toward the conditions that make a musical experience inclusive, at a time when recent research is increasingly examining musical participation in relation to wellbeing, belonging, identity, agency, assessment, and institutional conditions. frontiers in psychology

sustained effects of peer prosocial modeling on children's sharing behavior abstract this research examined whether children are sensitive to the level of generosity demonstrated by peer prosocial models and whether such modeling has a lasting effect on promoting children's sharing. four‐ and 6‐year‐old chinese children ( n = 120) were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. in the high generosity condition, children watched a video in which four peers each sequentially shared 8 out of 10 tokens with anonymous recipients. in the moderate generosity condition, four peers each shared 4 out of 10 tokens. children then themselves participated in a sharing task. the results showed that 6‐year‐olds, but not 4‐year‐olds, shared significantly more in the high generosity condition than in the moderate generosity condition. about two weeks later, children engaged in a second sharing session without exposure to modeling. strikingly, the differential effect of the conditions for 6‐year‐olds persisted during the second sharing session. taken together, the findings highlight the developmental emergence of young children's remarkable capacity for fine‐tuned and sustained social learning. social development

using a contemplative practice intervention to improve educators’ attitudes toward students with emotional and behavioral disabilities educators working with students who exhibit challenging behaviors often experience high levels of stress and burnout. they may also struggle to maintain positive attitudes about this population, especially if they have had challenging experiences in the past. in this study, we examined the feasibility and preliminary impact of a contemplative practice intervention on educators’ flourishing and their attitudes toward students with emotional and behavioral disorders (ebds). quantitative and qualitative data were collected from a convenience sample of 61 graduate students enrolled in four education courses at a small u.s. mid-atlantic university. we used a mixed-methods approach to examine the feasibility and preliminary impact of the intervention on educators’ attitudes toward ebd students and explored whether changes in the flourishing subdomains explained the effects of the intervention on educators’ attitudes. we also analyzed educators’ perceptions of the intervention. implications for research and practice are discussed. behavioral disorders

motivational and discriminative aspects of context in renewal and reinstatement of operant behavior in mice abstract renewal, reinstatement, and other forms of recovery of learned behavior after extinction have been interpreted in terms of the concept of context . context is defined here as the field of stimuli that is interrelated with the behavior of an individual in the present. two important classes of stimuli that comprise context are discriminative stimuli and motivating operations. two experiments examined interactions between discriminative and motivational aspects of context in the renewal and reinstatement of operant behavior following extinction in mice. in experiment 1, mice received all operant acquisition and extinction sessions under 24 hr of food deprivation. in experiment 2, mice received half of acquisition and extinction sessions under 24 hr of deprivation and the other half under nondeprived conditions. in both experiments, mice were tested for renewal and reinstatement after extinction, one group under 24 hr of deprivation and the other nondeprived. results showed that the extent to which recovery occurred depended on relations between motivating operations (a) during acquisition/extinction learning and (b) during tests for renewal and reinstatement. translational implications for the study of recovery of behavior after extinction in nonlaboratory circumstances are discussed. journal of the experimental analysis of behavior

impact of cognitive training on professional drivers’ cognitive profiles and performance abstract this study explores the cognitive profiles of professional drivers and presents a pilot evaluation of a computerized cognitive training (cct) intervention, aiming to assess its feasibility and potential effects on cognitive performance and driving outcomes. to investigate how specific cognitive domains relate to real-world driving behavior, the research was structured in two experiments. experiment 1 involved 160 professional drivers who completed cognitive assessments to examine correlations between cognitive abilities and driving safety metrics. the results revealed significant relationships, particularly noting that coordination abilities were inversely correlated with crash rates. experiment 2 included a subset of 47 drivers from the initial group, who participated in an 8-week cct program. pre- and post-intervention assessments measured cognitive performance, safety metrics, and driving styles. the intervention led to significant improvements in cognitive domains, while driving styles, as expected, remained stable. however, no improvements were observed in driving metrics. in conclusion, while cct effectively enhances cognitive performance among professional drivers, its transfer effects to driving safety metrics remain unsubstantiated. as a pilot study, these findings offer a preliminary foundation for further research to explore the relationship between cognitive enhancements and driving outcomes, and to evaluate cct’s potential in improving road safety. discover psychology
special educators’ and occupational therapists’ professional learning through transdisciplinary practice journal of occupational therapy schools and early intervention

computational approaches to cyber-syndrome: a scoping review with considerations for adolescent mental health cyber-syndrome denotes the physical, social, and thinking disorders arising from problematic cyberspace interactions, with its thinking dimension encompassing cognitive deficits (e.g., attentional impairment, executive dysfunction) and affective disturbances (e.g., mood disorders, emotional dysregulation). conventional assessment approaches, relying primarily on self-report questionnaires and laboratory-based tasks, are unable to capture the rapid, context-dependent fluctuations of mental states in real-world digital environments. leveraging advances in computational psychiatry, affective computing, and machine learning, this paper presents a scoping review that maps, rather than validates, the computational approaches available for inferring the cognitive and affective states of cyber-syndrome from digital behavior. because the construct still lacks established diagnostic instruments, the review is positioned as an assembly of the evidence base that its future operationalization will require rather than as a validation of it. it situates cyber-syndrome within the cyber–physical–social–thinking (cpst) space framework, reviews the principal data sources, and covers the computational methods used to analyze them. it then synthesizes evidence from adolescent studies and examines the research institutions and open-source platforms that have driven methodological progress in the field. finally, it discusses key challenges and outlines future directions essential for clinical translation and real-world deployment, particularly in adolescent mental health. adolescents

measuring self-control in adolescents: psychometric investigation of different forms of the brief self-control scale in italian adolescents background: self-control is crucial for promoting long-term goal-directed behaviors and avoiding involvement in risky behaviors. the brief self-control scale (bscs) is one of the most used tools. as poor attention has been paid to its psychometric properties among adolescents, we aimed to investigate them in youth. methods: in study 1 (n = 504, 61% male; mage = 15.67) we tested different bscs versions. in study 2 (n = 795, 53% male; mage = 16.39), we tested the best-fitting solutions resulting from study 1. we analyzed invariance across sex and age groups (middle and late adolescents), reliability and validity. results: the 7-item two-dimensional (impulse control and self-discipline) solution proved to be the only one confirmed with an independent sample of adolescents and was invariant across sex and age groups. internal consistency was questionable for the impulse control subscale and adequate for the self-discipline subscale. the subscale scores were negatively related to risk factors for addictive behaviors and problematic use of video games. self-discipline was related to problematic video gaming over and beyond the effects of other risk factors. conclusions: the 7-item bidimensional bscs is useful to measure self-control in italian adolescents. adolescents

not heard or remembered: a daily assessment of experienced intersectional invisibility abstract intersectional invisibility is the experience of not being remembered, attended to, differentiated, or given credit for contributions, and is most likely to be experienced by people with multiple stigmatized identities. in the present study, we used a smartphone‐based longitudinal daily diary design to examine the frequency and downstream consequences of experienced invisibility as they unfold in daily life. over the course of 10 days, 301 participants reported their daily experiences of invisibility, sleep quality and positive affect, and pre‐ and post‐diary measures of well‐being and academic outcomes. as predicted, number of stigmatized identities positively predicted daily experiences of invisibility. for each additional stigmatized identity, the odds of reporting any instance of invisibility on any given day increased by 18%. daily experienced invisibility was associated with poor outcomes, especially for those with multiple stigmatized identities, including reductions in daily positive affect and sleep quality, and pre‐ to post‐diary decreases in well‐being and academic outcomes. there was also evidence of cumulative effects on a short timescale: experienced invisibility from the previous 3 days predicted lower positive affect and worse sleep on the present day. this research suggests invisibility is a chronic experience with negative consequences, experienced by people with multiple stigmatized identities. british journal of social psychology
