risk and protective factors associated with misinformation susceptibility in young adulthood abstract the spread of misinformation poses a societal challenge, giving rise to concerns regarding younger generations who grow up immersed in digital environments. in this study, we combined scientific insights with participatory research (focus groups with youth and interviews with parents and police officers) to identify risk and protective factors in misinformation susceptibility. a total of n = 1980 participants aged 18 to 34 completed the misinformation susceptibility test alongside validated measures of cognitive, social, and ideological scales. results showed that more social media use, more conservative political preference, and higher receptivity to pseudoscientific profoundness related to poorer veracity discernment, while higher education, greater need to belong, more open-minded thinking, and identifying as male related to better discernment. importantly, different forms of social media use were differentially related to veracity discernment. active engagement (e.g., posting and reacting) was associated with worse veracity discernment, while passive engagement (e.g., browsing) showed the opposite pattern. a network analysis further revealed that digital maturity may have indirect beneficial relations with veracity discernment. these findings suggest that misinformation susceptibility is associated with a constellation of cognitive, social, educational, and ideological factors. beyond fostering education and analytic reasoning skills, interventions may need to target digital behaviors, peer norms, and social motivational needs to build resilience against misinformation in young adults. computers in human behavior reports

analogical social perspective taking to shift parents' views on adolescents’ social media privacy: a proof-of-concept intervention study parental monitoring of adolescents' social media use creates tension between safety, autonomy, and trust. teenagers often experience monitoring as an invasion of privacy, while parents may view it as responsible protection. such misaligned perspectives could fuel parent-child conflict. we propose that parents may egocentrically underweight adolescents' privacy concerns, partly because their protective role makes safety-focused judgments feel appropriate. in a preregistered experiment ( n = 293 us parents), we tested whether a brief social perspective taking (spt) exercise could shift parents' views. to mirror their teenagers' experience of parental monitoring, treatment parents imagined instances of their privacy being violated by someone with power over them. control parents imagined comparably uncomfortable situations that lacked a privacy violation. treatment parents reported greater perceived discomfort over teenagers' privacy violations and placed more value on teenagers' privacy than control parents. we found no differences in parents’ valuing of trust or their hypothetical monitoring behavior. assuming these findings are not the result of some experimental artifact, they offer preliminary support for the effectiveness of analogical spt, in which the perceiver is placed in an analogous situation with their usual power position reversed. computers in human behavior reports

social competence among gaming girls; a scoping review gender differences in gaming behavior have long been in the research spotlight. girls appear to have more positive outcomes of gaming than boys, but a few years ago, findings indicated that the influence of gaming on social competence is gendered, working in disfavor of girls. findings seem to be mixed, which initiated this scoping review of research on the links between gaming and social competence among female gamers. the review investigates if there are empirical evidence of gendered differences in gaming’s influence on social competence. based on a selection of 52 contributions published after 2000, the analysis uncovered a lack of set standards for measuring social competence and gaming habits. yet, we found no support of claims that gaming impairs the social development of girls. computers in human behavior reports

from microstates to network connectivity: age-related differences in resting-state electroencephalography and their implications for cognitive abilities in adulthood. the relationship between resting electroencephalography brain characteristics and cognitive abilities, particularly in the context of aging, remains unclear. in this study, we analyzed dynamic microstates, power spectrum, and functional connectivity in electroencephalography resting-state data collected from 123 younger individuals (17-32 years) and 99 older adults (60-81 years) experiencing normal aging, under both eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. we also examined correlations between these brain features and cognitive abilities, including working memory, processing speed, and inhibition. our results revealed age-related differences in the balance between microstates c' and d, as well as in power across the delta, theta, and alpha bands, and in intra- and interhemispheric connectivity patterns. older adults also exhibited an anterior shift and decreased asymmetry in power. notably, significant associations emerged between these brain features and cognitive abilities, particularly in forward and backward working memory, with the effects being more pronounced in the older group. our findings indicate a decline in overall resting-state electroencephalography brain activity with age, along with a shift in the balance between attentional and default mode networks, emphasizing the strong connection between these neural changes and cognitive abilities. family communication and child outcome during the pandemic. the covid-19 pandemic led to a worldwide crisis in which most families sheltered in place for long periods of time. we know that children, preschool through adolescence, generally suffered negative consequences of the shutdown, but we know less about the ways in which families communicated with each other during the pandemic or how this might be related to child outcome. the studies presented in this special issue examine this question from multiple theoretical perspectives and employing multiple methodologies. both what was talked about and how it was talked about were studied. individual difference factors, including family structure and resources, parental stress and depression, and child age, were considered. across studies, findings converge on the role that open and elaborative parent-child communication plays in positive child and adolescent mental health outcome. implications and lessons learned are discussed. global predictors of child and parent well-being: a scoping review to inform culturally adaptive frameworks global frameworks for measuring child well-being enable international comparisons but show conceptual and methodological gaps. indicators prioritizing cross-country comparability often focus on measurable, negative outcomes, with limited attention to positive or context-specific aspects. we aimed to identify empirically supported components of child, parent, and child–parent well-being worldwide and to compare them with the united nations children’s fund (unicef) child well-being components. we conducted a scoping review of studies published between january 2013 and december 2024 in medline, embase, cochrane, cinahl, psycinfo, eric, and the social sciences citation index. eligible studies assessed factors related to child, parent, or child–parent well-being or reported the development and validation of relevant scales. studies on emergencies, special exposures, or populations, non-empirical work, and papers in languages other than english or japanese were excluded. using descriptive content analysis, we generated a list of empirically reported well-being components and compared these with the unicef child well-being components. of 6,139 records identified, 331 studies met the inclusion criteria. data extraction yielded 670 well-being component entries, which were grouped into 59 categories. forty-five denoted novel or expanded constructs, including partner support, parenting style, family cohesion, and parental health, whereas 14 matched with unicef indicators. most evidence focused on the individual and relational levels, with limited attention to the contextual and policy dimensions. the pooled components provide a flexible evidence base adaptable to national, cultural, social, and policy contexts. integrating parent and household modules in child surveys may enhance understanding of family processes and support context-sensitive monitoring of well-being. journal of happiness studies

online stepped care for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder: a randomized controlled noninferiority trial stepped care approaches can improve access to posttraumatic stress disorder (ptsd) treatments by matching clients to an intervention level that suits their needs. this randomized controlled non-inferiority trial evaluated the efficacy of an online stepped care approach for ptsd. the approach had two treatment steps: (1) this way up (twu; an online self-guided therapy); and (2) cognitive processing therapy (cpt; standard format therapy), adopting pre-specified criteria for stepping up between treatment steps. stepped care was evaluated compared to cpt delivered via telehealth among 84 adults with ptsd and subthreshold ptsd (86% female, 87% white, aged 18-79). stepped care cost less than cpt in terms of clinician time (by 8-10%), but cpt had less dropout (26% versus 43%). both groups demonstrated significant improvements in ptsd (caps-5: g = 1.19 to 2.09; pcl-5: g = 1.23 to 2.59), depression (dass-21: g = 0.63 to 1.13), and quality of life (aqol-8d: g = -0.46 to -1.02) over time (baseline, post-treatment, 3-month follow-up, 6-month follow-up), with no differential rates of change over time. stepped care was non-inferior to cpt on the clinician-rated ptsd measure (at post-treatment) and for depression at all time points. non-inferiority could not be established for the pcl-5 and quality of life measures, with outcomes favoring cpt. the stepped care approach was feasible, even among participants with high symptom severity and complexities. however, future research is needed to address attrition and improve outcomes compared to cpt, and to identify which clients would benefit from initially receiving low-intensity therapies. behaviour research and therapy

motivation matters in homophobic language reclamation: effects on collective action intentions and self-esteem among gay individuals language reclamation is often treated as a monolith, yet gay people reclaim homophobic labels for distinct reasons. we investigated the relationships of three motivations to reclaim language—regaining control, consolidating ingroup relationships, and humor—with collective action intentions to support the gay community and self-esteem among gay people, as well as whether ingroup identification mediates these links. in a three-wave longitudinal study with one-month intervals (nt1 = 950; nt2 = 637; nt3 = 485), we found that regaining control and consolidating relationships as motivations to reclaim homophobic language predicted stronger identification with gay people, which, in turn, was associated with greater intentions to engage in collective action and higher positive self-esteem. instead, reclaiming language for humorous purposes predicted weaker identification, which was associated with lower collective action intentions and lower positive self-esteem. our findings indicate that the correlates of reclamation depend on why language is reclaimed. reclaiming language to regain control and, primarily, reclaiming language to consolidate relationships are associated with benefits that humor-based motivation is not. therefore, our research provides information on which forms of language reclamation may be more effective for the emancipation of the gay community and its members. journal of homosexuality

metacognition in ai-supported second language learning: a systematic review of constructs, measures, and evidence (2016–2026) metacognition has informed research on second and foreign language (l2) learning for three decades, while ai tools have supported such learning for nearly as long. yet, no review has examined how the field conceptualises and measures metacognition under ai mediation. this systematic review identified 60 eligible studies published between 2016 and may 2026. each study was coded on fourteen dimensions anchored in established taxonomies and appraised with the mixed methods appraisal tool. only four eligible studies fall within the pre-chatgpt portion of the review window, from january 2016 to november 2022; 56 were published during the subsequent three and a half years. three findings emerge. first, measurement is narrowly concentrated: 98% of the 56 post-chatgpt studies measured self-reported metacognitive regulation, and 66% relied on self-report alone. only one study in the full corpus measured metacognitive accuracy. five post-chatgpt studies combined an ai-absent comparison with process-level data, and only one of these also measured judgement accuracy. second, 41% of post-chatgpt studies used tools that combined two or more functional orientations within a single interface, a configuration not represented by the field’s inherited four-category taxonomy of ai applications. third, none of the 18 contrast-based studies assigned the regulatory operation to the system in place of the learner. in every design that specified the division of labour, the learner retained that operation; three designs did not specify it. the condition most in need of testing therefore remains untested. reported findings skew positive, but correlational and qualitative designs account for a disproportionate share of that evidence. the review concludes with a research agenda centred on calibration and process data. journal of intelligence

beyond structure and change: ergodicity and the dynamic organization of intellectual development. in developmental research, it is assumed that development is ergodic, i.e., differences between children reveal how individuals change over time. across four longitudinal studies, we examined ergodicity across cognitive systems-including attention, working memory, reasoning, and cognizance-timescales and developmental phases. we found that development was not globally ergodic. in study 1, spanning ages 4-17, cross-sectional relations partially resembled patterns of change. individual development involved overlapping, process-specific periods of acceleration, consolidation, and differentiation rather than one common developmental timetable. study 2, spanning ages 4-12, showed short-term convergence and partial profile correspondence, with relational integration as the main carrier of change. study 3, spanning ages 6-13, revealed that psychometric organization was highly stable across three waves, but children changing broadly in the first annual interval were not the same as children changing in the second. in study 4, 5-7-year-old children were intensively trained on attention control and examined three times on other processes. the trained processes formed a recognizable common organization, but within-person coupling was substantially weaker than between-person coupling, rank correspondence declined with temporal distance between waves, and group dynamics represented individual children only approximately. across phases, the carriers of change shifted from attention-related control, through relational integration, toward complex reasoning. psychometric, although strong across time, was very weakly related to developmental g (i.e., phase-sensitive mechanisms transforming states of psychometric g over time), indicating that population-level cognitive organization does not determine individual development. implications for psychometric and developmental theories are discussed here. journal of intelligence

a pedagogical-interindividual model of situated critical thinking in higher education. critical thinking is an essential competency in higher education, particularly in contexts characterized by complexity, uncertainty, information overload, and technological transformation. however, various models explain critical thinking primarily from cognitive perspectives, thereby limiting understanding of the conditions that foster its activation, regulation, and advancement in authentic educational settings. this article proposes a pedagogical-interindividual model of situated critical thinking in higher education, developed through a conceptual review of theoretical and empirical literature regarding critical thinking, metacognition, motivation, social interaction, language, and instructional mediation. the model is organized as a relational and functional architecture rather than as a linear sequence and distinguishes interconnected components according to their respective functions: teacher instructional mediation as an instructional-contextual condition; argumentative socio-linguistic interaction as an interindividual mechanism; motivation and metacognition as individual factors of activation and regulation; critical cognitive processes as the operational core; situated critical thinking as performance; and evidence-based decision-making as an educational outcome. the model hypothesizes that situated critical thinking may emerge from direct and indirect relationships among students' internal resources, discursive practices, and intentionally designed pedagogical conditions. journal of intelligence

opening the window of the mind: do large language models possess human-like visual attention? when people read a spatial description, their eyes move through empty space as if the described scene were present, a signature of imagery-driven attention documented by spivey and geng. language models have no eyes, but they are routinely credited with spatial understanding on the basis of verbal answers, and such answers are ambiguous: a model can name the right direction by echoing a directional word the passage happens to contain. we ask whether responses to spatial descriptions are governed by the configuration described or by the vocabulary used to describe it. adapting the spivey and geng materials, we hold each scene’s layout fixed and vary its linguistic support across four versions: one naming the direction, one conveying only the configuration, one reordering the same sentences, and one inserting a directional word that contradicts the layout. five models from the qwen and glm families were probed with a forced-choice direction report, an unconstrained narration, a two-dimensional reconstruction, and a plain relational question, together with control conditions that vary the position and register of the inserted word, shuffle the object list in the prompt, remove the imagery framing, and offer an explicit indeterminate option. analysis treats model-by-scene cells as units, with cluster-bootstrap intervals and mixed-effects models, across 14,900 responses. passages that convey a layout without naming a direction are answered near ceiling, reconstructed and narrated in the correct object order, and unaffected by reordering, by shuffling the prompt’s object list, or by removing the imagery framing: directional vocabulary is not what these responses track. three apparent limits on that competence proved to be artifacts of measurement. a misleading word is resisted on three quarters of trials when it precedes the layout and on none when it follows it, so the manipulation indexes recency rather than representational strength; a downward bias on axis-free scenes disappears once declining is permitted; and narrations judged unfaithful by direction coding are faithful when scored by object order. layout recovery is robust, and spatial evaluations that vary a single response format risk measuring their instrument. journal of intelligence

examining computer-science students’ metacognitive beliefs and reported practices in verifying ai-generated code: a concurrent mixed-methods study generative artificial intelligence (genai) accelerates programming, but its educational value depends on whether students check generated code before accepting it. this concurrent mixed-methods study examined which beliefs accompany such checking among computer-science students at one chinese university. survey responses from 294 students were analyzed with an exploratory structural equation model treating three practices as separate outcomes: checking code line by line before use, practicing without ai, and declining in advance to delegate. robustness checks included ordinal estimation, acquiescence modeling, split-half replication, and multiverse analysis; eleven students were interviewed. verification-dispensability belief, endorsing reasons for treating further checking as unnecessary, was the only construct negatively associated with all three practices in every robustness check. other beliefs were narrower or inert: perceived ai literacy accompanied line-by-line checking alone, generic metacognitive self-regulation none. delegation breadth, the number of activities handed to genai, was unrelated to all three: volume of delegation said little about checking. interviews exposed a mismatch between self-reported categories and actual workflows: students allocated checking by task purpose, accepted process-level understanding, and delegated verification to other ai models, a practice unmeasured by the survey. the data are cross-sectional and self-reported, so these are associations requiring behavioral and longitudinal confirmation. journal of intelligence

influence of driving experience on visual search, attentional cue utilization, and inhibitory control: implications for driving performance. background: driving requires the integration of visual search, attentional processing, cue, and response inhibition. driving experience and regular driving exposure may influence these cognitive processes, but their relative effects across specific cognitive performance remain unclear.
methods: this cross-sectional inter-group comparative study included 47 subjects-23 experienced and 24 non-experienced drivers. participants completed visual search, posner cueing, and stop-signal paradigms using psytoolkit. group differences were analyzed using parametric and non-parametric tests, with correlations assessing associations between driving experience and cognitive performance.
results: experienced drivers showed a lower mean ssrt than non-experienced drivers (226.9 ± 20.1 ms vs. 237.3 ± 10.9 ms; unadjusted= 0.028), with the difference reduced after holm correction (adjusted= 0.056). mean go reaction times were similar between groups. in the cueing task, experienced drivers showed reduced reaction times for both valid (~410 ms) and invalid (~470 ms) trials (u = 125.5,= 0.001), indicating more efficient attentional reorienting. visual search time was also lower in experienced than non-experienced drivers (median 950 ms vs. 1050 ms;= 0.238).
conclusion: driving experience was associated with faster inhibitory responses and better attentional efficiency, with smaller differences in visual search performance. these findings suggest experience-related cognitive adaptation and support the inclusion of attention and response-inhibition training in non-experienced driver education. journal of eye movement research

temporal dynamics of visual awareness as a function of the level of processing of the stimulus and report requirements: an erp study abstract recent evidence suggests that the stimulus level of processing (lop) modulates the two event‐related potential (erp) correlates of visual awareness—the visual awareness negativity (van) and late positivity (lp)—yet it remains unclear whether lop also affects their temporal dynamics. in addition, recent studies using no‐report paradigms have raised doubts about whether the lp constitutes a genuine correlate of awareness. in this study, we examined the erp correlates of visual awareness and its temporal dynamics as a function of stimulus level of processing (lop) and report condition (report vs. no‐report). in the report condition, participants performed either a low‐level (color: blue vs. red) or high‐level (category: animal vs. object) discrimination task and indicated whether they had seen the target. in the no‐report condition, they counted occurrences of a task‐irrelevant but lop‐congruent stimulus. we computed the van and lp by pooling aware and unaware trials within each condition. the van component was absent in both tasks and report condition, likely influenced by early sensory activity and variations in stimulus–mask soa. the lp was clearly visible across conditions, yet its amplitude was not modulated by the lop. critically, significant lp components were observed in both report and no‐report conditions; although attenuated and slightly delayed in no‐report trials, the lp remained present. this pattern replicates previous findings showing that the lp/p3 is sensitive to post‐perceptual task demands yet also shows that it may persist even when response‐related processes are removed. these findings suggest that late post‐van activity may not correspond to a single unified erp component but rather reflect a combination of post‐perceptual processes and aspects of conscious stimulus evaluation. psychophysiology

blunted neural error monitoring amplifies the adverse effect of childhood maltreatment on depressive symptoms: time‐domain and time‐frequency analysis abstract performance monitoring (pm) has been suggested as a promising cognitive factor to explain individual differences in the association between early maltreatment and depression, yet evidence remains limited. from a monitoring vs. executive perspective, this study thus comprehensively examined whether and how the neurophysiological (ern and its time‐frequency decomposition components) and behavioral (posterror accuracy) indicators of pm interacted with childhood maltreatment on young adult depressive symptoms. a total of 192 chinese university students ( m age = 21.08 ± 1.91 years; 59.4% girls) completed self‐report questionnaires and an eriksen flanker task while eeg activity was recorded. the results showed that blunted vs. heightened ern and error‐related delta were more likely to amplify the adverse effect of childhood maltreatment, especially emotional neglect, on young adult depressive symptoms. however, error‐related theta and posterror accuracy did not show such interaction effects. the findings showed strong robustness across a series of sensitivity analyses. the results provide preliminary evidence that blunted error monitoring but not executive ability, reflected by ern and error‐related delta, may be a neurobiological moderator that underlies maltreatment‐related depression, which deepens the cognitive control underpinnings of depression. however, given the high‐functioning sample, caution is warranted when generalizing these findings in high‐risk clinical samples. psychophysiology

psychosocial adjustment to stigma among young adults with chronic visible skin disease. objectives: living with a stigmatizing skin disease may hinder normative development during emerging adulthood. the present study aimed to examine indirect effects of internalized stigma in the relationship between social stigma and psychosocial adjustment among young adults with visible chronic skin diseases. indicators of psychosocial adjustment spanned several domains: mental health (depression, anxiety, quality of life), physical health (somatic symptoms), intimacy and health behaviour (physical activity).
design: this cross-sectional study recruited young adult patients with chronic skin disease from an outpatient dermatology clinic. data were obtained through self-report, electronic medical records and a physical exam.
methods: young adults (n = 195, m = 28.06 years; 49% female) with psoriasis (55%), atopic dermatitis (23%) or hidradenitis suppurativa (22%) self-reported sociodemographic information and measures for social stigma (psq), internalized stigma (wbis-adapted) and psychosocial adjustment (phq-9, gad-7, dlqi, sss-8, dis, days of physical activity per week). bootstrapped mediation analyses tested indirect effects of internalized stigma on the relationship of social stigma and each psychosocial adjustment outcome, controlling for covariates.
results: indirect effects of internalized stigma on the relationship of social stigma with each outcome were significant (p's < .01, r = .10 to .64).
conclusions: findings indicated that stigma has implications for many areas of functioning and well-being, highlighting how emerging adulthood contextualizes the experience of living with the stigma of visible skin disease. internalized stigma was a major driving force, serving as a potential target for clinical and psychoeducational interventions to improve the well-being of young adults with chronic visible skin disease. british journal of health psychology

risk and protective factors of food insecurity among children in low-income families in the united states: application of the multiple disadvantage model. this study investigated relationships between low-income children's food insecurity and five factors: social disorganization, social structural factors, social relationships, health/mental health, and access to services. a sample of 12,215 low-income children and parents was extracted from the 2021 national survey of children's health. logistic regression results showed the likelihood of such children's food insecurity to be associated positively with several factors: racial discrimination, child aged 6-10 years, child aged 11-13 years, child aged 14-17 years, black child, child's chronic health condition, family member mental health problem, supplemental nutrition assistance program participation, receipt of special supplemental nutrition program for women, infants, and children, and lunch program participation. as well, children's food insecurity likelihood was associated negatively with parents' age and education, neighbor support, parents' general health and mental health, and receipt of temporary assistance for needy families. research implications include interventions at the individual level (e.g., screening for food insecurity, treatment of sick or mentally ill family members), community level (e.g., food pantries, neighbor support network), and macro level (e.g., advocating for racial/ethnic minorities, expanding cash and food benefits). european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

validation of the brief pathological narcissism inventory and its association with cyber intimate partner violence in portuguese emerging adults. background: cyber intimate partner violence (c-ipv) refers to abusive and controlling behaviors enacted through digital technologies toward a current or former intimate partner. previous research suggests that pathological narcissism may be associated with c-ipv.
methods: this study examined the psychometric properties of the brief pathological narcissism inventory (b-pni), the frequency of self-reported c-ipv perpetration and related behaviors, and the association between c-ipv perpetration and pathological narcissism among emerging adults. the sample comprised 371 participants aged 18-25 years (m = 21.52, sd = 1.97), of whom 78.7% were female.
results: confirmatory factor analysis provided support for the a priori two-factor model of the b-pni (cfi = 0.982, tli = 0.965, rmsea = 0.076), comprising grandiose and vulnerable narcissism. the b-pni showed satisfactory internal consistency and theoretically expected associations with psychopathological symptoms and broader personality dimensions. overall, 79.5% of participants reported at least one c-ipv behavior, with 61.5% reporting online control, 62.0% online jealousy, and 31.5% online intrusive behaviors. c-ipv perpetration was positively and significantly associated with both grandiose and vulnerable narcissism, although the associations were small in magnitude.
conclusions: the findings provide preliminary support for the use of the b-pni among portuguese emerging adults and indicate that pathological narcissism is associated with c-ipv perpetration. given the modest magnitude of these associations, narcissistic traits should be considered as one of multiple individual and relational factors potentially involved in c-ipv. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

measurement heterogeneity and pooled prevalence of academic procrastination among health sciences students: a systematic review and meta-analysis. background/objectives: in health sciences students, academic procrastination can affect performance, mental health, and professional development. this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate the pooled prevalence of study-defined elevated academic procrastination among health sciences students and to describe the methodological and measurement characteristics of the instruments used to assess it.
methods: a systematic review with meta-analysis was conducted. we included observational studies reporting the prevalence of academic procrastination among undergraduate students enrolled in health sciences programs, including medicine, nursing, dentistry, psychology, and related health professions. the reported measurement characteristics of the instruments used to assess academic procrastination, including validity, reliability, and cut-off criteria, were reviewed and systematized. the meta-analysis was performed employing a random-effects model and the double arcsine transformation (freeman-tukey) to stabilize variance. subgroup analyses and meta-regressions were calculated to explore possible sources of variation.
results: twenty-six studies were included with a total of 8211 students. the pooled prevalence of study-defined elevated academic procrastination was 55.35% (95% ci: 46.55-63.98%, i= 98%). the prevalence was higher in nursing students (62.60%), followed by psychology (61.67%), medicine (52.62%), and dentistry (45.76%). the most commonly used instruments were the procrastination assessment scale for students (38.5%), academic procrastination scale (23.1%), tuckman's procrastination scale or its adaptations (15.4%), academic procrastination scale by mccloskey and scielzo or related aps versions (11.5%), lay's procrastination scale (7.7%), and mhca (3.8%). most studies used non-probabilistic sampling, and only 8% validated instruments specifically for their target populations. reliability coefficients were generally adequate (α = 0.75-0.95). the meta-regression revealed a slight upward trend in prevalence as a function of publication year, although this was not statistically significant.
conclusions: academic procrastination appears to be frequent among health sciences students; however, the pooled estimate should be interpreted as a descriptive summary of study-defined prevalence rather than as a universal prevalence estimate, given the very high between-study heterogeneity and the variability in instruments, cut-off criteria, and population-specific validation. educational institutions should implement prevention and support strategies, while research should prioritize instrument validation, measurement standardization, and transparent case definition criteria. european journal of investigation in health psychology and education

the meta-analytic relationship between exposure to domestic violence and dissociative symptoms abstract purpose domestic violence and the impact it has on victim-survivor’s mental health remains an international public health concern. dissociation has often been linked to traumatic experiences and may present as a protective defense mechanism for victim-survivors of domestic violence. this meta-analysis sought to examine the meta-analytic relationship between domestic violence exposure and dissociative symptoms. method the results of a systematic literature search of psycinfo, medline, web of science and ptsdpubs yielded 1331 studies, 12 of which were eligible for review. two random effects meta-analyses were conducted to investigate the strength of the association between (1) physical domestic violence exposure and dissociation symptoms and (2) multi-type domestic violence exposure and dissociative symptoms. results the meta-analyses showed significant positive associations between dissociation symptoms and both physical domestic violence ( r = .37; 95% ci = 0.19 − 0.55) and multi-type domestic violence ( r =.28; 95% ci = 0.22 − 0.34) exposure. most of the studies are cross-sectional therefore causality cannot be inferred. the studies within the physical domestic violence analysis demonstrated considerable heterogeneity, i² = 84%, potentially due to variation in population samples and measures of domestic violence and dissociation symptoms used. conclusion this review indicated that physical domestic violence and multi-type domestic violence are moderately associated with dissociative symptoms. future research within this field would benefit from increased use of psychological and coercive control assessment tools to measure the impact of all forms of domestic violence to increase construct validity of the pattern of domestic violence being measured. journal of family violence

comparing childhood, chronic, and recent adversity on internalizing symptoms and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis functioning. objective: examine how childhood, chronic, and recent adversity associate with internalizing symptoms and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activity among women in a low-resourced context.method: data come from the bachpan study (2014-2022), a longitudinal cohort of mothers in rural pakistan.childhood adversity was assessed using retrospective reports of adverse childhood experiences.chronic adult adversity was defined as adversities experienced across two or more prior study waves (baseline, 1 year, 2 years, and 3 years), and recent adversity was assessed at the 6-year wave.outcomes, measured at the 6-year wave, included depressive symptoms (patient health questionnaire-9), anxiety symptoms (generalized anxiety disorder-7), and hair cortisol.generalized linear models examined associations for each adversity separately and simultaneously.results: in our sample of 900 mothers, we find that childhood, chronic, and recent adversity were each associated with higher depressive and anxiety symptoms, particularly at the highest levels of exposure.chronic adult adversity and recent adversity showed dose-response relationships with internalizing symptoms.when examined together, recent adversity was the most robust predictor of depressive and anxiety symptoms.meanwhile, associations between adversity and cortisol were more modest but suggest evidence of blunted cortisol levels at the highest levels of childhood and recent adversity exposure.conclusions: findings highlight the importance of considering the differential effects of childhood, chronic, and recent adversity for health.although early intervention remains critical, addressing ongoing stressors may yield meaningful health benefits.even if adversities are not eliminated, reducing them can have a significant impact on health. public significance statementthis study clarifies how childhood, chronic, and recent adversity relate to psychological and physiological outcomes.findings suggest that childhood, chronic, and recent adversity are associated with poorer mental health, with recent adversity showing particularly strong associations with current mental health.these results highlight the importance of addressing ongoing stressors, alongside early prevention efforts, to improve health outcomes. health psychology

the ties that bind: how interpersonal connections shape latinx immigrant health. emerging scholarship has identified posttraumatic distress as a critical health disparity affecting recently immigrated latinx youth and families. indeed, trauma exposure is highly prevalent in families and children that flee violence and seek asylum in the united states and relates to a number of physical and mental health conditions. an interpersonal lens is useful for conceptualizing risk and resilience in this group, wherein interpersonal traumas, like family separation, appear critically associated with health disruption, and interpersonal sources of belonging, such as attachment, peer networks, and cultural values, explain variance in resilience and positive health outcomes. the effects of training type and affective stimuli on promoting physical activity: based on the approach-avoidance training paradigm this study examined whether approach-avoidance training (aat) could promote physical activity among insufficiently active individuals. two experiments tested typical and consequence-based aat using neutral physical activity and sedentary stimuli in experiment 1 and physical activity images with positive and negative affective valence in experiment 2. across the two experiments, single-session aat was associated with increased approach (vs. avoidance) tendencies and immediate postintervention physical activity. the overall pattern of findings suggested that consequence-based aat may hold greater behavioral promise under affective stimulus conditions. these findings provide preliminary support for the role of automatic processes in physical activity promotion. journal of sport & exercise psychology

the forgotten continent? a scoping review of psychosocial research in african youth sport youth sport is increasingly recognized as a platform for fostering physical health and psychosocial development. yet, the vast majority of existing knowledge stems from research in western contexts. on the african continent, home to nearly 25% of the world’s youth, studies remain scarce, though emerging literature highlights sport’s transformative potential amid diverse cultural, socioeconomic, and geopolitical realities. this scoping review synthesizes english-language, peer-reviewed research on youth sport across africa’s five geopolitical regions. seven shared psychosocial themes emerged: socioeconomic barriers to participation, gender-based inequities, positive youth development and sport-for-development peace outcomes, coaching efficacy and leadership, mental and physical health benefits, globalization and talent migration, and sport tourism and community impacts. findings demonstrate the sport’s capacity to address local challenges. by mapping shared and region-specific themes, the review offers a comprehensive overview of youth sport knowledge in africa while identifying key gaps to guide future psychosocial research on the continent. journal of sport & exercise psychology

youth sport players’ enjoyment in team practice sessions: the daily impact of coaches and basic psychological need satisfaction sport enjoyment can be a quality marker of players’ sport experience, signaling a basic need-supportive, psychologically healthy sport context linked to better well-being and health. yet, little is known about its day-to-day variability in team practice. fifty norwegian adolescent female handball players ( m = 14.57, sd = 1.03) completed brief questionnaires before, during, and after 11–12 practice sessions across 4 weeks. a two-level bayesian model estimated within-person, same-occasion associations between perceived need-supportive and need-thwarting coach behaviors, basic psychological need satisfaction (autonomy, competence, and relatedness), and sport enjoyment. in practice sessions, when players perceived more need-supportive (β = 0.116) and less need-thwarting (β = −0.064) coach behaviors, they reported higher enjoyment. of the basic needs, only competence need satisfaction was associated with sport enjoyment (β = 0.069). in practice, reducing need-thwarting coach behaviors, increasing need-supportive coach behaviors, and creating competence-satisfying team practice sessions can help improve how enjoyable team practice feels for adolescent team-sport players. journal of sport & exercise psychology

parent–child emotion regulation within competitive youth sport families: a qualitative multiple case study youth sport participation can lead to stressful experiences for athletes and parents, and the manner in which negative emotions are regulated impacts their experiences and continued involvement. as primary socialization agents, parents and family members uniquely influence young athletes’ emotional regulation within youth sport contexts. the purpose of this study was to examine emotion regulation dynamics within competitive youth sport families. employing a multiple case study methodology, semistructured interviews were conducted with five distinct family units, comprising competitive youth athletes aged 11–12 years, their parents, siblings, and grandparents to understand the developmental implications of familial emotion regulation practices in youth sport. findings indicated that transitions into competitive sport altered family identities and roles in emotional support, while a focus on effort sometimes overshadowed athletes’ emotional needs. these results align with existing models of emotion regulation and highlight the importance of equipping parents with adaptive coregulation strategies. journal of sport & exercise psychology

altered temporal features of visual processing in subjective cognitive decline. objective: subjective cognitive decline (scd) is possibly the earliest known stage of alzheimer's disease. individuals with scd report perceiving a decline in their cognitive functioning and express concern about it. however, when assessed with standard neuropsychological tests, they perform within normal limits.
method: the present study focuses on the temporal features of visual processing in scd using the random temporal sampling technique. this method reveals the perceptual oscillations which occur during a visual task by presenting stimuli with randomly varying signal-to-noise ratio through time. fourteen individuals with scd and 15 others without (i.e., controls), aged between 60 and 85 years old, took part in the study.
results: participants with scd performed within normal limits on neuropsychological tasks, as did the control group. in the experimental task, participants had to recognize briefly presented five-letter french words. the results take the form of classification images, which depict how visual processing efficiency fluctuates over time and across different frequency bands of signal-to-noise ratio oscillations. the classification images reveal significant differences between groups on the temporal patterns of visual processing. a machine learning classifier was used to categorize the data of individual participants according to group membership. the classifier achieved 79.3% classification accuracy using 18.0% of the available features.
conclusions: even though scd individuals show no detectable cognitive impairment in neuropsychological testing, random temporal sampling can reveal anomalies in their perceptual function. (psycinfo database record (c) 2026 apa, all rights reserved). neuropsychology

getting off-tract: correlational tractography of white matter integrity and cognitive intraindividual variability in a large sample of community-dwelling older adults. objective: cognitive intraindividual variability (iiv), or the dispersion across neuropsychological task performance, is a sensitive marker of neurocognitive aging, but its tract-specific white matter correlates are not well characterized. this study used correlational tractography to identify pathways whose microstructural integrity relates to iiv in older adults.
method: participants were a diverse sample of 510 community-dwelling older adults (= 66.6 years,= 8.4) from the health and aging brain study-health disparities cohort. iiv was computed as the intraindividual standard deviation of demographically normed performancescores across a multidomain battery. diffusion mri connectometry in dsi studio tested partial spearman associations between iiv and quantitative anisotropy, adjusting for sex and intracranial volume, with permutation testing and false discovery rate adjustment (0.01).
results: higher iiv was associated with lower quantitative anisotropy primarily in commissural corpus callosum, fronto-subcortical, and interhemispheric long-range connection fibers. tracts of the forceps minor were the most robust to sensitivity analyses. effects were small in magnitude, with the primary connectometry threshold corresponding to an effect size of 0.09, but spatially specific, accounting for 7.57% of total whole-brain tract volume.
conclusions: overall, we found that iiv maps onto distributed, tract-specific differences in white matter microstructure. findings support iiv as a marker linked to structural network-level white matter integrity and should motivate longitudinal work to further clarify its neuroanatomical substrates. argentinean validation of the early trauma inventory-self-report (eti-sr) in an adult sample. objective: adverse childhood experiences affect long-term mental and physical health. in argentina, the lack of validated tools limits accurate assessment of early trauma and hinders prevention strategies. this study adapted and validated the early trauma inventory-self-report short form for argentine adults and provided an initial standardized estimate of early trauma prevalence.
method: a total of 418 argentine adults (= 30.6,= 10.1; 74.4% female) completed the early trauma inventory-self-report short form through web-based data collection. confirmatory factor analyses were conducted using the weighted least squares estimator to evaluate competing models. internal consistency was assessed using cronbach's α and mcdonald's ω coefficients. external validity was examined through correlations with age and educational level.
results: the bifactor model demonstrated the best fit to the data, supporting the presence of both a general trauma factor and specific trauma domains. internal consistency indices were acceptable for most subscales, although lower values were observed for the general trauma dimension. positive associations were found among trauma dimensions, and physical trauma showed significant relationships with age and educational level. high prevalence rates of early trauma were observed, with most participants reporting at least one adverse experience.
conclusions: the early trauma inventory-self-report shows adequate psychometric properties for use in argentina, providing preliminary support for its validity in this context. these findings contribute to addressing an important limitation in health measurement and support the development of standardized assessments for early trauma in argentina. further research using more representative samples is needed to confirm these results. integrating art-based activities in racial stress and trauma treatment: therapists’ perspectives on benefits, challenges, and techniques. objective: racial stress and trauma profoundly affect the mental health of racialized individuals, yet culturally responsive therapeutic approaches remain underdeveloped. art-based activities may provide alternative pathways for emotional processing and engagement. this study explored therapists' perspectives on integrating art-based activities into racial trauma treatment, focusing on clinicians trained in the healing racial trauma protocol, a manualized cognitive-behavioral intervention.
method: semistructured interviews were conducted with 10 therapists (six black, indigenous, and people of color, four white;= 36.6 years; 70% female) who had delivered the healing racial trauma protocol. framework analysis was used to identify themes related to prior use of art-based activities in psychotherapy, perceived benefits and barriers, client suitability, therapists' experiences of discomfort discussing race, and conditions necessary for effective integration.
results: therapists reported multiple benefits of art-based activities, including increased engagement, emotional expression, and insight. creative activities were considered particularly helpful for clients with limited verbal expression or tendencies toward overintellectualization. barriers included client hesitancy, cultural considerations, and practical constraints. white therapists described discomfort navigating racial dynamics, highlighting the importance of cultural humility and supervision. effective integration depended on flexible timing, individualized adaptation, and adequate training and support.
conclusions: findings support a preliminary process model identifying key components for the ethical and effective integration of art-based activities into racial trauma treatment. results inform therapist training and culturally responsive clinical practice. (psycinfo database record (c) 2026 apa, all rights reserved). psychological trauma-theory research practice and policy

distinguishing moral injury from burnout, secondary traumatic stress, and depression in animal care workers: a condition differentiation analysis. objective: animal care workers operate in conditions involving substantial occupational stressors that can significantly impact their mental health and well-being. despite a growing awareness of these stressors, moral injury, a values-based condition arising from violations of deeply held moral beliefs, has not been empirically established in this population as a relevant condition distinct from burnout and compassion fatigue, the constructs that dominate the literature. the present study examined whether moral injury is empirically distinguishable from burnout, secondary traumatic stress, and depression and whether current frameworks adequately identify morally distressed workers.
method: a sample of 291 u.s.-based animal care workers completed the moral injury outcome scale, professional quality of life scale-5, and patient health questionnaire-9. condition differentiation was evaluated through correlation, regression, classification, and profile analyses.
results: moral injury shared 17%-39% of variance with adjacent constructs, leaving 61%-83% unique variance. after controlling for depression, the moral injury-secondary traumatic stress association became nonsignificant while the moral injury-burnout association persisted. moral injury demonstrated incremental validity for both depression and functional impairment beyond all professional quality of life scale subscales (δ² = .073 and .012, respectively). the shame subvariant drove depression prediction (β = .39) while trust violations did not. professional quality of life scale and depression scores alone correctly classified only 66.2% of moral injury caseness, whereas adding moral injury outcome scale subscales improved classification to 84.7%.
conclusions: moral injury is empirically distinguishable from burnout, secondary traumatic stress, and depression, while existing assessment frameworks may fail to detect nearly half of morally distressed animal care workers, with implications for clinical assessment and intervention.
