reducing the shirom–melamed burnout measure: development and validation of nine-item and three-item short forms. job-related burnout is a central concern in occupational health psychology, yet practical constraints often limit the use of comprehensive measures. the 14-item shirom-melamed burnout measure (smbm-14) is widely used and grounded in a three-facet symptom framework consisting of physical fatigue, cognitive weariness, and emotional exhaustion, but its length can be prohibitive in multiconstruct surveys and repeated-measures research. across nine samples organized into four phases, we developed a nine-item short form (smbm-9; three items per facet) and a three-item ultra-brief form (smbm-3; one item per facet). item reduction and structural results supported the intended three-facet structure of the smbm-9 and the selection of a one-item-per-facet smbm-3 composite. internal consistency estimates were high for the smbm-9 and lower, as expected, for the smbm-3; both forms nevertheless showed high convergence with the smbm-14 and established burnout measures. across cross-sectional, panel, and daily diary designs, the brief forms reproduced the expected pattern of associations with work stressors, affective and distress-related constructs, and work and health outcomes, with the smbm-9 tracking the smbm-14 closely and the smbm-3 showing modest differences consistent with its brevity. additional longitudinal and within-person findings supported the usefulness of the brief forms in repeated-measures contexts, including high convergence with the smbm-14 and similar relations with day-level work demands. these findings support the smbm-9 as the preferred brief substitute when researchers want balanced coverage of the smbm-14 facets, whereas the smbm-3 is likely to be the more useful option when brevity itself is the primary objective and assessment space is severely constrained. (psycinfo database record (c) 2026 apa, all rights reserved). journal of occupational health psychology

from sampling to stopping: the p300 erp component and beta power contribute to reward-related decision commitments. optimal stopping problems provide a framework for studying decision-making under uncertainty, balancing the trade-off between information sampling and decision commitment. we investigated deviations from normative strategies in human decision-making and examined the neural mechanisms underlying decision commitment versus sampling using electroencephalography (eeg). forty participants viewed sequences of beads drawn from fictitious urns and attempted to infer the majority bead colour in each urn, while their eeg activity was recorded. after viewing each bead, participants could choose to sample more by drawing another bead (draw choice) or to stop sampling and infer the contents of the urn (urn choice). a bayesian ideal observer model and parametrised models were used to predict participant behaviour. participants undersampled relative to the ideal observer, particularly in the more uncertain condition where the proportion of bead colours was close to chance (60/40 or 0.6), with the model better capturing behaviour in the easier 80/20 (0.8) condition. stimulus-locked p300 amplitudes showed larger responses for urn choices and a gradient of increasing amplitude as draws approached commitment. larger frontal erp responses were also observed under higher uncertainty (0.6 condition). beta oscillatory activity was stronger for urn choices in the high uncertainty condition, with fast beta (20-30 hz) activity driving final commitment to a decision. beta power was further predicted by model-derived action values. by integrating behavioural, computational, and neurophysiological data, this study advances our understanding of active information sampling versus decision commitment in reward-related probabilistic environments. neuropsychologia

disentangling oscillatory and aperiodic neural activity in autism: a spectral parameterization analysis of neurofeedback intervention. background: autism spectrum disorder (asd) is characterized by atypical neural oscillations and heterogeneous alterations in excitation/inhibition (e/i) balance, the directionality of which varies across individuals, neural circuits, and developmental stages. while alpha-band neurofeedback (nfb) is a promising intervention, its underlying neurophysiological mechanisms remain unclear, partly due to the conflation of periodic and aperiodic signals in traditional eeg analysis.
methods: this randomized controlled trial recruited 40 children with asd, assigned to either an experimental group (alpha-training nfb) or a no-feedback group. resting-state eeg and behavioral assessments (srs, abc) were collected pre- and post-intervention. we employed spectral parameterization to decompose neural activity into aperiodic (1/f slope, offset) and periodic (periodic alpha power, center frequency) components.
results: nfb training yielded significant behavioral improvements in social cognition and relating skills. physiologically, the experimental group exhibited a significant steepening of the aperiodic slope (increased exponent), reflecting a reduction in neural noise and potential optimization of inhibitory modulation. furthermore, we observed enhanced periodic alpha power and an acceleration of the alpha center frequency (acf), indicative of improved neural efficiency and maturation. these physiological shifts in frontal and occipital regions were significantly correlated with improvements in behavioral scores.
conclusion: alpha-training nfb was associated with improvements in caregiver-rated behavioral scores and modulated spectral features of resting-state eeg in children with asd. these findings validate the utility of spectral parameterization markers in evaluating neuromodulatory interventions. behavioural brain research

would the provision of pet-related services improve the health of pet-owning people with hiv? abstract background : approximately half of people with hiv (pwh) in the united states own pets. while pets may support physical and mental health, they also require socioeconomic resources that may exacerbate existing barriers to healthcare among pwh, as these resources can compete with those needed for healthcare. this study examined whether a cohort of pwh in florida felt that receiving various free pet-related services would better enable them to access their own healthcare and whether endorsement was associated with hiv care engagement and clinical outcomes. methods : data were drawn from wave 3 of the florida cohort (2021–2023) and included 206 pet-owning pwh. participants reported whether access to free pet food, veterinary care, or pet boarding services would improve their ability to access their own healthcare. survey data were linked to florida department of health hiv surveillance records, including viral load measures from the prior year. hiv care outcomes included missed hiv care visits in the past year, missed antiretroviral therapy (art) doses in the past month, and viral non-suppression (>200 copies/ml). open-ended responses were analyzed thematically to identify additional pet-related services. results : most participants (79%) reported that access to free pet-related services would help them better engage with their own healthcare. participants with poorer hiv care outcomes were more likely to report that pet-related supports would be helpful for their healthcare access. missed art doses were significantly associated with the endorsement of free pet food and pet boarding services, and viral non-suppression was significantly associated with endorsement of free pet food. open-ended responses identified additional pet-related services, including pet insurance, grooming services, behavioral support, pet medications, emergency veterinary care, and pet-friendly housing. conclusions : the helpfulness of pet-related services for participants’ access to healthcare was commonly reported among pet-owning pwh and was more frequently endorsed by individuals with poorer hiv care outcomes. these findings suggest that the economic cost of pet caregiving may interfere with healthcare engagement among pwh. integrating pet-related support into programs serving pwh may help reduce barriers to care and support both human and animal wellness. human-animal interactions

long-term developmental trajectories of callous-unemotional traits inform daily emotional reactivity to stress during the transition from late adolescence to young adulthood abstract callous-unemotional (cu) traits are linked with various psychosocial maladjustments. scant research has investigated its developmental pattern during the transition from late adolescence to young adulthood, and whether the pattern may function as a mechanism against daily stressors in stressful contexts. this study adopted a multi-timescale approach to elucidate how long-term developmental trajectories of cu traits relate to both socioemotional maladjustment and daily emotion dynamics during the transition period. a three-wave longitudinal study ( n = 313; m age = 18 years, 72% female, 30% white) with two 30-day daily diary bursts embedded over three years was conducted. latent growth curve modeling revealed a modest group-level increase in cu traits. higher initial levels and faster increase in cu traits were associated with higher depressive symptoms and peer problems and lower empathy and peer attachment in wave 3. multilevel modeling showed that individuals with faster growth in cu traits displayed lower daily emotional problems, blunted reactivity to stress, and reduced stress-unrelated emotional fluctuations; these associations persisted over two-and-a-half years. these findings suggest that the developmental growth of cu traits may buffer daily stress reactivity in the short-term but could be maladaptive in the long-term. development and psychopathology

double disadvantage? wellbeing among vietnamese migrant parents of autistic children. background: culturally and linguistically diverse (cald) parents of autistic children typically report poorer mental health, yet their subjective wellbeing (swb) remains poorly understood. this study examined swb among vietnamese migrants (vm), one of australia's more socioeconomically disadvantaged cald groups, focusing on those raising autistic children, and compared them with general population (gp) parents.
procedure: participants were 487 australian-residing parents (m = 40.0, sd = 7.12, 71.9% female, 136 having an autistic child), including 197 vm parents. swb was measured first, followed by mental health and demographic information, using an anonymous online survey available in english or vietnamese. hierarchical regression tested whether being vm, having an autistic child, or their interaction predicted swb, controlling for income.
results: having an autistic child was associated with lower swb (b = -4.59, se = 1.97, t = -2.23, p = .020) while being vm alone predicted higher swb (b = 3.71, se = 1.62, t = 2.29, p = .022). however, their interaction was significant and negative (b = -7.68, se = 3.00, t = -2.56, p=.011), indicating that vm parents of autistic children had the lowest swb among all comparison groups. this result remained significant even after controlling for stress and depression.
conclusion: vm parents of autistic children experience markedly lower swb than their gp counterparts, despite reporting lower psychological distress. these findings highlight culturally specific unmet needs and underscore the urgency of culturally responsive support for cald families. research using culturally-appropriate methodologies is essential to advance understanding of swb in cald communities. journal of autism and developmental disorders

the digital trap in the quest for perfect parenting: the relationship between parenting perfectionism and cyberchondria abstract background cyberchondria, characterized by excessive online health-related information seeking accompanied by increased health anxiety, has been associated with various psychological factors. however, research examining its relationship with parenting-specific characteristics remains limited. this study aimed to examine the association between cyberchondria severity and parental perfectionism and to evaluate the role of socio-demographic variables in this relationship. methods this quantitative study was conducted using a cross-sectional correlational survey design. data were collected from 475 mothers with children in early childhood using the cyberchondria severity scale (css), the multidimensional parental perfectionism scale (mpps), and a sociodemographic questionnaire. correlation, regression, and moderation analyses were performed. moderation effects were tested using the hayes process macro (model 1). results the findings revealed a significant positive correlation between cyberchondria severity and parental perfectionism. regression analyses indicated that parental perfectionism was a significant predictor of cyberchondria severity, accounting for a substantial proportion of the variance in the model (r 2 = 0.573). higher levels of education, employment, income, and the absence of chronic illness were significantly associated with parental perfectionism, whereas age was not significantly associated. moderation analyses showed that education and income levels significantly strengthened the association between cyberchondria severity and parental perfectionism, indicating that this relationship was more pronounced among individuals with higher socioeconomic status. employment status and chronic illness did not demonstrate significant moderating effects. conclusions the findings suggest that greater cyberchondria severity is associated with higher levels of parental perfectionism and that this association varies according to socioeconomic characteristics. in particular, education and income appear to strengthen the relationship between cyberchondria severity and parental perfectionism. these results highlight the importance of considering socioeconomic factors when examining the interplay between online health-information seeking behaviors and parenting-related psychological characteristics. bmc psychology

quality of work life and professional ethics among occupational health professionals: a social exchange theory perspective abstract background despite the increasing complexity of ethical challenges in occupational health settings, limited attention has been paid to the ethical conduct of occupational health professionals themselves. this study examined how quality of work life is associated with professional ethics among occupational health professionals, guided by social exchange theory. methods a cross-sectional survey was conducted among 200 occupational health practitioners in east azerbaijan. data were analysed using spss and smartpls, involving pearson correlation, t-tests, anova, and structural equation modelling. measurement models were validated for reliability, convergent and discriminant validity, and common method bias. results the findings showed a statistically significant but modest positive association between the total quality of work life score and the total professional ethics score ( r = 0.281, p < 0.01). the strongest domain-level correlation was observed between human capabilities development and professional autonomy ( r = 0.330, p < 0.01). human capabilities development, safe work environment, and social integration were positively associated with professional responsibility, professional autonomy, and trustworthiness. however, the model explained only 21.4% of the variance in professional responsibility, 18.6% in professional autonomy, and 8.2% in trustworthiness, indicating modest explanatory capacity and particularly limited explanatory power for trustworthiness. conclusion the findings suggest that quality of work life may be a relevant organizational factor associated with professional ethics in occupational health practice. the study highlights the potential importance of developmental and relational aspects of work in supporting moral responsibility, while acknowledging that causal conclusions cannot be drawn from the cross-sectional design. these findings are especially relevant for policymaking in developing countries where ethical conduct is central to workplace safety and public health credibility. bmc a systematic review of gender differences in the relationship between problematic smartphone use and depression abstract background problematic smartphone use (psu) has been increasingly linked to depression, but evidence on whether this association differs by gender remains inconsistent. this review synthesizes the existing evidence on gender differences in the psu–depression association. methods four academic databases (pubmed, web of science, scopus, proquest) and one academic search engine (google scholar) were searched, with the original search conducted through september 2024 and an updated search completed in may 2026. the review was prospectively registered on the open science framework and followed the prisma guidelines. eligible studies examined gender differences in the association between psu and depression. quality was assessed using the mixed methods appraisal tool (mmat). results of the 16 included studies, 13 were cross-sectional and three longitudinal. fifteen studies statistically tested and found a positive psu–depression association. gender patterns were divided: five studies found the association stronger in females, five found it stronger in males, and six found no significant gender difference in the qualitative synthesis. one longitudinal study provided direct evidence of bidirectionality. conclusion findings on gender differences in the psu–depression association are far from uniform, with comparable numbers of studies supporting female vulnerability, male vulnerability, and no difference. observed gender patterns likely reflect moderating factors including usage type, age group, cultural context, and measurement heterogeneity rather than a fundamental difference in vulnerability between men and women. the predominance of cross-sectional designs and reliance on self-report instruments limit causal inference, and longitudinal and mechanistic research is needed to clarify the underlying associations. osf registration https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/e5sgn bmc psychology

can blind box buying be addictive?: measurement and associations with gambling disorder among chinese adults. background: blind boxes are gambling-like products with increasing popularity worldwide. accumulating evidence has shown that blind box over-purchasing is a rising problem, yet no validated tool exists for its addictive components. besides, the link between problematic blind box buying and gambling disorder (gd) has never been tested. to fill these knowledge gaps, the current study tested the psychometric performance of the problematic blind box buying scale (pbbs) and further examined the associations between problematic blind box buying and gd at both construct and symptom levels using bivariate correlation and network analysis, respectively.
methods: the sample consists of 1324 chinese adults (52.3% female, m = 33.13, sd = 6.73) who have experience with blind box buying.
results: results from exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis consistently suggested the unidimensionality of pbbs. this scale also showed good internal consistency, convergent validity, and concurrent validity. the positive correlations between problematic blind box buying and gd were found at both construct and symptom levels. chasing loss was the central node, while the conflict symptom of gd and the relapse symptom of problematic blind box buying were the bridge symptoms in the network of problematic blind box buying and gd.
conclusions: the current study is the first exploratory investigation of problematic blind box buying and its relationship with gd. it provides evidence for the validity and reliability of pbbs for measuring problematic blind box buying. moreover, its findings also support the addictive potential of blind box buying and the associated risk with gambling disorder. these findings provide practical insights for the regulation and policy of blind box commerce and gd intervention. bmc psychology

how technostress creators are associated with cognitive overload: the mediating role of emotional exhaustion in academia abstract background based on the transactional model of stress and coping and cognitive overload theory, this study explores the association of technostress creators with cognitive overload in academia. specifically, the authors examined the mediating role of emotional exhaustion on this relationship. method the authors surveyed higher education students from universities in china. we employed a time-lag survey method to test the relationships between the variables used in the research model, utilizing partial least squares structural equation modeling (pls-sem) through smartpls. results the findings indicate that technostress creators, modeled as a higher-order construct reflected by five lower-order dimensions (techno-complexity, techno-overload, techno-invasion, techno-insecurity, and techno-uncertainty), significantly and positively correlate with cognitive overload and emotional exhaustion. emotional exhaustion is also significantly and positively associated with cognitive overload. furthermore, emotional exhaustion was identified as a significant mediator, though this mediating role should be interpreted as data-inferred and requires confirmation through longitudinal or experimental designs. these findings advance the application of the transactional model of stress and coping and cognitive load theory in digital learning environments. this study offers two key theoretical contributions. first, it extends technostress research by identifying cognitive overload as positively associated with technostress creators among higher education students. second, it reveals emotional exhaustion as a novel mediating mechanism explaining how technostress creators correlate with cognitive overload. policymakers should design targeted interventions such as counseling services and stress management workshops to mitigate technostress, while academic institutions and teachers can implement strategies to help students manage technology-related academic stress. conclusions these findings advance the application of the transactional model of stress and coping and cognitive load theory in digital learning environments. this study offers two key theoretical contributions. first, it extends technostress research by identifying cognitive overload as positively associated with technostress creators among higher education students. second, it reveals emotional exhaustion as a novel mediating mechanism explaining how technostress creators correlate with cognitive overload. policymakers should design targeted interventions such as counseling services and stress management workshops to mitigate technostress, while academic institutions and teachers can implement strategies to help students manage technology-related academic stress. bmc psychology

personal innovativeness and digital entrepreneurial intention: a social cognitive perspective and the moderating role of ai adoption abstract background despite the rapid growth of digital entrepreneurship and increasing adoption of artificial intelligence (ai), existing explanations of digital entrepreneurial intention (dei) remain fragmented and inconsistent. prior studies have primarily focused on either individual cognitive factors or technology adoption, while limited attention has been given to how ai-supported environments interact with psychological mechanisms underlying entrepreneurial intention formation. this limitation is particularly relevant in emerging economies, where digital entrepreneurship increasingly develops within technology-intensive environments. methods drawing on social cognitive career theory (scct), this study examines the roles of personal innovativeness and digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy in shaping dei, while also investigating the moderating role of ai adoption. cross-sectional survey data were collected from 472 university students in vietnam and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. results the findings indicate that personal innovativeness positively influences both digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy and digital entrepreneurial intention. digital entrepreneurial self-efficacy also significantly predicts dei and serves as an important cognitive mechanism linking innovativeness to entrepreneurial intention. furthermore, ai adoption strengthens the relationships between innovativeness and intention, as well as between self-efficacy and intention, suggesting that ai-supported environments may enhance the translation of cognitive resources into entrepreneurial motivation. conclusion this study contributes to the literature by extending scct into digitally intensive entrepreneurial contexts and clarifying how technology-assisted learning and information environments interact with individual cognition in shaping entrepreneurial intention. the findings also provide practical implications for entrepreneurship education and ai-supported entrepreneurial learning among university students in emerging economies. bmc psychology

examining the roles of retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback in learning among autistic adults retrieval practice enhances learning and is most effective when feedback is provided. despite robust evidence that retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback benefit numerous clinical populations, these techniques have not been studied in autism. in two experiments, we measured retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback effects on associative memory in autistic and non-autistic adults residing in the united states. participants attempted to memorize semantically unrelated word pairs, which were then reviewed during a practice phase consisting of retrieval practice with and without feedback. in experiment 1, word pairs were presented to participants (40 autistic; 40 non-autistic) auditorily. in experiment 2, stimuli were presented visually and restudy trials were added to the practice phase. additionally, feedback for retrieval practice trials was manipulated between-subjects (80 participants per group) and a four-alternative recognition test was used in the practice phase. in both experiments, the testing phase consisted of cued recall. both experiments yielded benefits of feedback following initial retrieval practice across groups. in addition, experiment 2 demonstrated that both groups benefited from retrieval practice compared to restudy, even without feedback. our results suggest that the well-documented effects of retrieval practice, particularly in concert with post-retrieval feedback, extend to support learning among autistic as well as non-autistic individuals. lay abstract every autistic person has their own unique sensory, perceptual, and social experiences that impact learning in different ways. although many autistic learners have average or above-average iq, individuals with a diagnosis of autism have an increased likelihood of co-occurring learning disabilities and episodic memory difficulties. these memory-related challenges make it especially important to identify strategies that can support learning in autistic populations. retrieval practice may be one such strategy, which involves testing oneself on previously learned information. notably, retrieval practice supports learning among many clinical populations who experience memory and learning difficulties, yet it has not been investigated among autistic learners. this study measured the effects of retrieval practice and post-retrieval feedback among autistic and non-autistic adults (40 per group in experiment 1; 80 per group in experiment 2) residing in the united states. the task was divided into three sections. first, participants completed a “learning” block where they attempted to memorize unrelated word pairings (e.g., typing flower ). second was a “practice” block, in which they reviewed the recently learned word pairs. practice trials consisted of retrieval practice with feedback, retrieval practice without feedback, and restudy. in restudy trials, participants reviewed the full word pair (e.g., typing flower ) and selected the second word (e.g., flower ) among a list of three similar words (e.g., blossom, bud, bloom ). in retrieval practice trials, participants were given the first word (e.g., typing ) and attempted to remember its corresponding word (e.g., flower ). in feedback trials, after participants made their response, they were presented with the full word pair (e.g., typing flower ) regardless of their accuracy. in the third and final “testing” block, participants’ memory for word pairs was tested once more. this allowed us to compare the effect of retrieval practice with feedback, retrieval practice without feedback, and restudying on final test performance. in addition, we measured the generalizability of the testing effect in different learning contexts (listening to word pairs in experiment 1; reading word pairs in experiment 2) and retrieval practice formats (cued recall in experiment 1; multiple choice in experiment 2). in both experiments, the benefits of feedback following retrieval practice were evident, and retrieval practice was a more effective learning strategy than restudying word pairs. these outcomes were present in autistic and non-autistic learners alike. this study is the first to demonstrate that retrieval practice with feedback promotes learning in autistic adults. it is well-documented that autistic individuals face suboptimal educational and vocational outcomes compared to their non-autistic peers; thus, strategies that support learning are important to study. these findings contribute to a large body of existing research affirming retrieval practice as a flexible learning strategy that is most effective when accompanied by feedback and may have the potential to improve outcomes for autistic learners. autism

preliminary reliability and validity of the m-chat-s, a new autism screening tool for school-aged children. identifying autism early is critical for ensuring timely access to appropriate educational and clinical supports. current autism screening practices primarily focus on toddlers; universal practices for identifying the substantial portion of autistic children who arrive at school age without a diagnosis are lacking. this study evaluates the preliminary reliability and validity of the modified checklist for autism in toddlers-school age version (m-chat-s), a novel screener designed for early school-age children, with separate versions for verbally fluent and minimally verbal children. a total of 165 caregivers and 107 educators completed the m-chat-s, along with the social responsiveness scale, second edition (srs-2), to test convergent validity, and the child behavior checklist (cbcl), to test discriminant validity. findings demonstrate strong internal consistency across versions (cronbach's α = .79-.92) and robust construct validity. children with preexisting autism diagnoses scored higher on the m-chat-s than nonautistic children. both test-retest reliability and interrater reliability were in the moderate range. despite these limitations, the m-chat-s demonstrates promise as a screening tool that could facilitate earlier identification of autistic children in school settings. future research will involve a partnership with school districts to support school-based validation and implementation.lay abstractchildren with disabilities have a right to a free and appropriate public education in the united states. children who are not identified by the time of school entry are likely to miss out on appropriate services and supports to which they would otherwise be legally entitled. many studies show that a large portion of individuals who are ultimately diagnosed with autism are not identified until by the time they start school.screening tools can help identify children who may be on the autism spectrum. universal autism screening is currently recommended for toddlers, but not school-age children. to address this gap, we developed the modified checklist for autism in toddlers-school age version (m-chat-s) for children in early elementary school. this study tested the consistency and accuracy of the m-chat-s for both verbally fluent and minimally verbal children.we asked 165 caregivers and 107 educators to complete the m-chat-s and compared their responses to other well-established measures of autism traits and behavior. overall, we found that the m-chat-s had good reliability, meaning that the items in the measure were consistent with each other. children with a known autism diagnosis scored higher on the m-chat-s than non-autistic children. m-chat-s scores were more strongly related to another autism screening tool (the srs-2) than to a survey of general behavior (the cbcl). however, test-retest reliability (whether the same rater's score stayed consistent over time) and interrater reliability (whether two different raters agreed on scores) were lower than expected.these results suggest that the m-chat-s may be a useful tool for identifying autistic children in early school years. future research will involve partnering with school districts to be able to reach as many children as possible, including autistic children who have not yet been identified. if validated further, this tool could help schools and families recognize children who need autistic support, leading to earlier access to services. autism

from visual attention to literacy: symbol search deficit predicts future reading difficulties from age 3 abstract poor reading has been associated with impaired simultaneous visual processing of multiple graphic symbols composed of separable features, a behavioral marker of reduced visual attention based on parietal dysfunction. we designed a visual search screening test, consisting of finding the (unique) black circle among circles combined with a bar of various length and location (black symbols) versus among circles of various colors. the temporal gap between these symbol and color search conditions was previously validated as a significant visuo‐attentional contributor of reading between ages 8 and 11, predicting its performance with moderate sensitivity, as reading difficulty is multifactorial, but high specificity. here, we established its good positive predictive value in a longitudinal study with the same children being screened in kindergarten (at 3, 4, or 5 years old) and later assessed for reading performance at the second semester of third grade (at 8 years old). we also assessed 4 and/or 5 years old children with the knowledge of letter names, the early reading of classmates’ first names and of small frequent words. the visual search screening test predicted future reading performance with lower correlation strength but as early as 3 years old, providing more lead time for specific preventive educational or clinical intervention during kindergarten in a subgroup whose pathological visual search performance at age 3 was associated with a 5.7 times greater likelihood of later reading difficulties. developmental science

rethinking food at work: an examination of structural and social constraints and resource loss across the work-home interface abstract although food-related behavior has become a topic of growing interest in organizational research, it is typically studied as a matter of individual choice about food content. in this study, we expand this conceptualization by examining the temporal, structural, and social contexts in which food-related decisions unfold. based on an inductive analysis of interviews with workers managing type 2 diabetes, we examine how structural and social constraints at work influenced workers’ capacity to make and enact food-related decisions, including what, when, where, and how to eat. applying tenets of conservation of resources (cor) theory in the final stages of our analysis, we show how workplace conditions can function as a resource caravan passageway, shaping workers’ access to several interrelated personal resources (e.g., time, energy, and willpower) critical to making and enacting these decisions. drawing from participants’ accounts, structural and social constraints at work contributed to recurring cycles of resource loss across the work-home interface, leaving workers increasingly vulnerable to future threats. beyond broadening the conceptualization of food-related behavior in organizational research, our findings extend work design theory by highlighting the need to account for how workplace conditions affect workers’ capacity to manage personal needs within and around work systems. we also offer an empirical elaboration of cor theory by illustrating how resource loss cycles unfold in everyday experiences across the work and home domains. we conclude by highlighting practical strategies organizations can adopt to support workers’ capacity to make and enact food-related decisions and promote well-being and performance at work. journal of business and psychology

from lived experience to digital advocacy: eating disorder recovery content creation on social media abstract objective despite the importance of incorporating individuals with lived experience in the collaborative development and delivery of eating disorder (ed) services, a paucity of research has addressed the role of content creators with lived experience within the context of social media in contributing to help‐seeking and recovery spaces. this qualitative study documents content creators' experiences of recovery‐oriented content creation and informal digital support through social media platforms. it also explores how content creators contribute to recovery‐oriented communication, prevention, and co‐design of digital interventions. method a total of 10 italian female content creators in stable recovery from eating disorders (i.e., no relapse in the past 5 years) were recruited via the instagram community #diccicomeaiutarti and they were interviewed. results through a reflexive inductive thematic analysis five overarching themes were identified: (1) using lived experience to build recovery‐oriented narratives and communities, which highlighted lived experience as a relational resource for fostering recovery and shared meaning online; (2) social media as a double‐edged sword, describing social media as both a supportive and potentially harmful space for ed recovery; (3) communication strategies for effective engagement, focusing on how participants adapted communication practices to the affordances and limits of different platforms; (4) social networking, prevention, and health promotion, which framed online activity as part of a broader prevention and health advocacy effort; and (5) providing hope in digital peer support, illustrating how structured peer‐support contexts reshaped the sharing of lived experience and hope in recovery. discussion finally, the findings of the present study suggest that content creators can meaningfully contribute to the prevention and treatment of ed when integrated into supervised, ethically framed digital networks. the co‐production of interventions with individuals who have recovered can engender a more humanised form of digital health communication, strengthening therapeutic engagement and supporting recovery‐oriented public health strategies. european eating disorders review

bidirectional longitudinal associations between problematic social media use and emotional symptoms in adolescents: results from a random intercept cross‐lagged panel model abstract introduction problematic social media use (psmu) and emotional symptoms are consistently associated during adolescence; however, the directionality of this relationship remains debated. methods the present study examined the bidirectional longitudinal associations between psmu and emotional symptoms in a large sample of italian adolescents using a random intercept cross‐lagged panel model (ri‐clpm), which disentangles stable between‐person differences from within‐person changes over time. a total of 1562 adolescents (baseline m age = 16.36 years, 56.7% female) participated in a three‐wave longitudinal study across 1 year and completed self‐report measures of emotional symptoms and psmu at each wave. results at the between‐person level, adolescents who consistently reported higher levels of psmu also reported persistently higher levels of emotional symptoms, indicating a stable dispositional association between the two constructs. at the within‐person level, higher‐than‐usual levels of psmu were concurrently associated with higher‐than‐usual levels of emotional symptoms. most notably, significant bidirectional spill‐over effects emerged: within‐person increases in psmu predicted subsequent increases in emotional symptoms, and increases in emotional symptoms predicted subsequent increases in psmu. emotional symptoms also demonstrated significant carry‐over effects across waves. conclusions these findings highlight the importance of disaggregating within‐person and between‐person effects and support the conceptualization of the association between psmu and emotional symptoms as a dynamic feedback loop during adolescence. journal of adolescence

effectiveness of digital psychological interventions for adolescents with chronic pain and comorbid anxiety and/or depression: a systematic review and meta‐analysis of randomized controlled trials abstract background adolescence is a high‐risk period for co‐occurring conditions like chronic pain, anxiety, and depression. although digital psychological interventions offer a scalable and accessible alternative to traditional care, their comprehensive efficacy in addressing these interconnected symptoms remains underexplored. this meta‐analysis evaluates the effects of digital interventions on pain in adolescents with comorbid emotional problems, with secondary outcomes including anxiety and depressive symptoms. methods we systematically searched five databases for randomized controlled trials through october 5, 2025, ultimately including 12 studies. statistical analyses were performed in review manager 5.4 and stata 17.0 using a random‐effects model and specifically focused on adolescents with comorbid conditions. the review protocol was registered with prospero. subgroup analyses were conducted based on intervention type (internet‐based cognitive behavioral therapy [icbt], self‐management, and internet‐based acceptance and commitment therapy [iact]). results a total of 12 studies involving 1403 adolescents were included. meta‐analysis indicated that digital interventions significantly improved pain (smd = −0.21, 95% ci: [−0.35, −0.06]) and anxiety (smd = −0.15, 95% ci: [−0.21, −0.10]). the effects of digital psychosocial interventions on depression were not statistically significant. conclusion digital interventions show potential in managing pain and anxiety among adolescents with comorbidities. future efforts should prioritize integrated intervention programs that combine pain management with emotion regulation, establishing them as foundational components within the broader care system to complement routine clinical practice. trial registration this systematic review was prospectively registered with prospero (crd420251270961) on 12 december 2025. registration details: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/view/crd420251270961 . journal of adolescence

parental responses to youth disclosure: how guilt induction shapes future communication and actions abstract introduction youth disclosure is the primary way parents gain knowledge about their adolescent children; it is linked with better youth adjustment and encouraged by supportive parenting. when youth disclose a transgression, parents may feel torn between stressing wrongdoing to reduce misbehavior and responding neutrally to maintain future disclosure. this study employed vignettes to investigate how social domain and parental responses influence adolescents' expected future disclosure and behavior while exploring evaluations of parental responses as explanatory variables. methods u.s. undergraduate students ( n = 358, m age = 19.76, sd = 1.48; 77% female) evaluated vignettes about disclosing a behavior to a parent as a teen. behaviors varied by domain (moral, prudential, multifaceted, personal); parental guilt‐inductive statements varied by criticism focus (person or behavior) and highlighted harm (parent or direct). participants rated how parental responses would have affected their future disclosure, (mis)behavior, feelings of rejection, guilt, and shame, and evaluated responses' acceptability. results neutral responses reduced expected future disclosure the least, followed by behavior‐critical responses (especially those highlighting direct harm), which suppressed future disclosure less than person‐critical responses for all but personal issues. behavior‐critical responses were most effective at reducing expected future (mis)behavior, with the strongest reductions across responses for moral and prudential issues. effects on acceptability, felt rejection, and felt guilt/shame help explain the primary findings. conclusions parents may balance reducing problem behavior while maintaining open communication by responding to adolescents' disclosure with inductive statements focusing on the direct, negative effects of the misbehavior rather than criticizing the adolescent as a person. journal of adolescence

dispositional and cultivated mindfulness: therapists’ views and experiences and the role and order of the ffmq facets in the process of mindfulness cultivation abstract objectives this study aimed to investigate therapists’ experiences regarding dispositional and cultivated mindfulness. it explores the role and order of the five facet mindfulness questionnaire (ffmq) skills in the process of mindfulness cultivation, definitions of dispositional and cultivated mindfulness, the specific skills and techniques taught by professionals, and the theoretical order of the mindfulness cultivation process. method structured interviews were conducted with ten clinical practitioners and therapists from diverse mindfulness backgrounds, including mindfulness-based stress reduction (mbsr), mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (mbct), acceptance and commitment therapy (act), dialectic behavior therapy (dbt), and mindfulness self-compassion (msc). using a preregistered interview guide that focused on definitions, skills, techniques, and the cultivation process of mindfulness, we conducted a rule‑governed content analysis to categorize relevant text passages. results nine therapists defined dispositional mindfulness according to common literature, while all therapists agreed on the proposed definition of cultivated mindfulness. the therapists highlighted various skills and techniques used in their interventions, with acting with awareness and nonjudgment being prominent. the proposed model of mindfulness cultivation was generally accepted, with minor adjustments suggested. differences in mindfulness traditions were noted, particularly in the emphasis on self-compassion and acceptance. conclusions therapists are knowledgeable about dispositional and cultivated mindfulness and integrate these concepts into their interventions. the proposed model of mindfulness cultivation aligns well with practical experiences but requires enrichment with additional components. the study suggests that mindfulness cultivation involves diverse skills and techniques, emphasizing the need for individualized approaches in therapeutic settings. preregistration this project was preregistered on osf: https://osf.io/xm84u/overview . registration https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/u2fz4 mindfulness

toward a more ethical scientific practice: meditation-based lifestyle modification (mblm) as a potential starting point abstract can meditation support ethical scientific practice? and how might this work? considering the contradictory evidence for the impact of commonly practiced mindfulness meditation on moral change currently available, berryman et al. (2025) suggested that meditation programs should include additional ethical components. we fully agree with this recommendation and add further arguments in favor of it, informed by traditional meditative approaches. moreover, we argue that ethics-enriched meditation approaches might in general yield stronger effects than meditation without ethics. preliminary evidence for this view comes from studies that examined meditation-based lifestyle modification (mblm), a program that includes an ethics component. mblm may be used as a potential starting point for exploring the impact of ethical components on scientific practice. however, such ethics-enriched meditation programs could prove beneficial far beyond the scientific community. mindfulness

conspiracy beliefs as a metacognitive dimension of intergroup attitudes: a novel framework for interventions abstract apart from their well‐established associations with individual characteristics, experiences of existential threats and either objective or perceived structural circumstances in which people live, conspiracy beliefs are now being increasingly recognised as a reflection of group‐related motivations, identity‐protective motives, prejudice and stereotypes. as conspiracy beliefs and intergroup attitudes share definitional characteristics as well as extensive networks of social, psychological and contextual correlates, their content and function allow us to see them as an intergroup phenomenon. to provide a more nuanced understanding of conspiracy beliefs, we situate them within the tripartite model of intergroup attitudes as an additional, metacognitive dimension. drawing from their metacognitive character as often biased insights into outgroups’ intentions and actions, and expanding the socio‐functional model of prejudice, we propose an operational research roadmap that specifies when and for which conspiracy beliefs the intergroup‐based approach is likely to be effective. european journal of social psychology

stabilising repair in psychological science abstract psychological science has responded to the weird critique through a broad agenda of inclusion, expanding the diversity of research participants, international collaborations and systems of scholarly recognition. while these reforms have generated important gains, concerns about epistemic inequality persist. this article argues that many contemporary reforms function as forms of stabilising repair : institutional responses that absorb critique by broadening participation and visibility while leaving underlying distributions of epistemic authority largely unchanged. drawing on debates in decolonial scholarship, i show how inclusion can become a substitute for transformation when critique is translated into administratively manageable questions of representation. the result is a discipline that becomes superficially inclusive without necessarily becoming more diverse. i then review emerging proposals for institutional capacity building and epistemic reconstitution, arguing that a genuinely global psychology requires infrastructural pluralisation : the development of multiple centres, networks and knowledge infrastructures through which psychological theory, methods and research agendas can be produced, sustained and recognised. european journal of social psychology

‘working through’ interpersonal transgressions: the role of narration (and re‐narration) in the self‐forgiveness processes of wrongdoers abstract this research examines how wrongdoers may use narration to ‘work through’ a transgression committed, towards self‐forgiveness and reconciliation. in study 1 ( n = 30), reflexive thematic analysis was used to identify narrative types observable in wrongdoers’ storying of a recent interpersonal transgression, informing our conceptual framework. we developed a quantitative tool for assessing wrongdoers’ narration—the interpersonal offense narration scale (ions) and, in study 2 ( n = 349), used linear mixed modelling to examine how wrongdoers’ narrative processes develop over 72 h post‐transgression. results indicate that past‐contextualization (contextual explanations) was related to genuine self‐forgiveness and willingness to reconcile; self‐contextualization (exploring identity (in)congruence) was related to self‐punishment and self‐exoneration; self‐distancing (big‐picture abstraction) was related to down‐regulating self‐punishment and self‐exoneration; and redemption (moral learning) was related to genuine self‐forgiveness and willingness to reconcile, and reduced self‐exoneration. the findings thus highlight the differential functions of distinct narrative processes for interpersonal wrongdoers working‐through their wrongdoing toward self‐forgiveness. european journal of social psychology
